It's a good thing I’m a production controller - I'm used to dealing with confusing systems! Online, eh? Fancy that. I still prefer a good pen and paper, myself. You can  see  what you’re doing. This digital world… it’s all so fleeting. And what about your job? How’s that new project going? The one with the, what was it, the eco-friendly packaging? It’s…challenging. The suppliers are being incredibly slow with the samples. We need to switch to biodegradable materials for the new line, but finding something that's both sustainable  and  doesn't fall apart when you look at it is proving difficult. Mr. Henderson is breathing down my neck about deadlines, naturally. Men. Always breathing down necks. Henderson, was it? Sounds like a right one. You work too hard, you know. All that studying, all those qualifications… you need to have some fun. You're not getting any younger, you know. Thanks, Gran. I'm trying. I'm going to that art exhibition with Leo next weekend. The one at the Fitzwilliam. Leo, is it? A nice young man, seems polite enough.

…and honestly, the waiter looked at me like I’d asked him to solve quantum physics when I tried to ask for extra gravy. "Sauce supplémentaire, s'il vous plaît" – I thought I'd remembered it right from school French! Apparently not. Oh, you and French. It’s always a disaster, isn't it? You’d think after all those GCSE lessons,  something  would have stuck. Mine’s pretty rusty too, but at least I can usually manage “un café, s'il vous plaît” without causing an international incident. It’s more than rusty, it’s fossilised! I nearly ordered a horse instead of a ham sandwich. Seriously. I think I said “cheval” instead of “jambon”. The look on his face… Oh, bless you! Well, at least you’re providing entertainment. How's the trip going otherwise? Apart from risking equine consumption? It’s good, reet good actually. Seeing Paris is…well, it’s Paris, innit? Though I'm missing proper Yorkshire puddings somethin’ fierce. Fancy a trip to Betty's when we get back? I’m craving a Fat Rascal. Betty’s sounds divine. Though honestly, I'm already dreading going back to uni. Assignments are piling up, and Professor Davies is  still  banging on about the scientific method and falsifiability. It's exhausting. Tell me about it. My biology coursework is killin’ me. It’s all dissecting worms and calculating cell division rates. I'd rather be watching the footie. Did you see that Arsenal game last night? Absolute belter! I did! Saka was on fire. Honestly, they're looking really strong this season. Though, my brother keeps trying to convert me into a Spurs fan. The audacity! Spurs? Now  that  is a lost cause. They’re…well, they try. But they’re not Arsenal. Speaking of lost causes, have you heard back about that summer internship at the lab yet? The one you were really hoping for? No, nothing. I’m starting to assume it's a firm no. It’s really frustrating. I thought my application was pretty strong, especially with the research I did for my Extended Project Qualification. They’re probably swamped with applications. Don’t give up hope yet. You're brilliant, you'll find somethin' else. Maybe that placement with the environmental group you mentioned? Maybe. It's not quite the same - less lab work, more fieldwork. But it would be  something  to do over summer, rather than just stacking shelves again.

… honestly, I just about jumped out of my skin. It was  huge . Not one of those little house spiders, oh no. This thing was… substantial. Like a tarantula, but, you know, British. Oh, you and your spiders, Brenda! You get so worked up. Probably just a daddy long legs, blown in with the wind. They're harmless. Harmless?! Doreen, it was hairy! And it was  looking  at me. Judging me, I tell you. I swear it was calculating the best route to crawl onto my face. I had to get Malcolm to deal with it. He's much braver. Malcolm, bless him. Always the hero. Though I bet he just put a glass over it and let you release it in the garden. That’s what my George does. Says it’s cruel to… well, you know. Something like that. He did a lot of muttering about ecosystems and natural predators. Honestly, sometimes I think he prefers the company of creepy crawlies to me. Anyway, it reminded me of that time we had a mouse in the attic last year.  That  was a nightmare. Oh, don’t even start on the mice. Now  they  are proper pests. Spiders, I can tolerate, as long as they stay up high. But mice… they chew through everything! We had one at the school, years ago. Little blighter got into the biscuit tin in the staff room. Chaos. Exactly! And the noises! Little scratching and scurrying at 3am. It drives you mad. Malcolm set traps, of course. I refused to go near them. Too squeamish. I understand that. George used to be a dab hand with traps, back when he was working on the farm. Though he always said live traps were better. More humane, he said. Though I suspect he just didn’t fancy cleaning up the… aftermath. A sensible man. Speaking of creatures, have you noticed how many birds are about lately? The garden is absolutely teeming with them. Robins, blackbirds, even a little wren building a nest in the ivy. Oh, yes! It’s lovely, isn’t it? Especially now the weather’s getting nicer. Though those starlings are a menace. They’ll steal anything that isn't nailed down! I was putting out bread for the ducks last week and a whole flock descended and cleared the lot in seconds. Cheeky birds. I’ve got a feeder, and it’s constantly being raided.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork after Mum died was just… relentless. It felt like every single organisation needed a death certificate, a copy of the will, a signed confession - you name it! Did you have that with your father? Oh, my dear, don't even  mention  it. Father was a bit of a hoarder, bless him, so finding anything was a trial even  before  he passed. But yes, the paperwork. It was biblical. And the sympathy cards… well, you get a lot of those. It's the well-meaning but utterly useless offers of help that get you, isn’t it? "Let me know if there's anything I can do," they say, then vanish. Exactly! Everyone wants to  say  something, but few actually  do  anything. It’s been… just over a year now, hasn't it? Still feels so raw sometimes. The Lewy Body Dementia was so cruel. She wasn't  herself  for so long before… before the end. A truly horrible disease. My sister, Bronwyn, she lost her husband to something similar. Vascular dementia, but with overlapping symptoms. So confusing for everyone involved. It steals them bit by bit, doesn't it? Makes you grieve the person while they’re still… present. It does. It absolutely does. And the guilt. Feeling guilty about… everything. Whether you said the right thing, did the right thing, if you should have pushed for a different care home. It’s exhausting. What about you? You mentioned retirement… was teaching always your plan? Always, really. Though I didn't start straight away, mind. After school, I did a bit of travelling. Spent a year in Canada, working on a fruit farm, of all things! Then, a bit of secretarial work to save up for college. Always gravitated back towards children, though. Loved the energy, the honesty – even the chaos! Ended up teaching primary school for thirty-five years. Mostly Year 3. Year 3! Goodness. That’s a pivotal age. So much change happening. I’m secondary, history. Bit older, slightly more…sophisticated anxieties, I suppose. Although, sometimes I think twelve-year-olds are no less chaotic than seven-year-olds. Just with more hormones. Oh, believe me, I saw my fair share of hormonal outbursts! It's just a different flavour. You said Dorchester, didn’t you? You were born there? That's lovely. My grandmother, on my mother's side, she came from near Dorchester.

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it all just took my breath away. Did you see how  low  that balloon came? It felt like you could almost reach out and touch the basket. I did! A bit too low for comfort, if you ask me. Though, beautiful, undeniably. Makes you wonder about the skill involved, doesn’t it? And the nerve. Imagine trusting yourself to a giant bag of hot air. Exactly! It’s a bit mad, really. Makes grading essays seem incredibly sensible. Speaking of sensible, look at Winston. He’s completely fixated on that rabbit. Honestly, he thinks he’s some sort of hunting dog. He's all bark and no bite, our Winston. More likely to trip over his own paws than catch anything. Still, it's good to see him enjoying the freedom. He's a city dog at heart, isn't he? Doesn't quite know what to  do  with all this space. He does love a good sniff though. All those new smells. It’s a hundred times better for him than pavements and exhaust fumes. This is why we need to do this more often, isn’t it? Get away from everything. Though… look at those power lines stretching across the field. Quite ruins the aesthetic, doesn’t it? They do. Always a reminder we’re not  completely  escaping civilization. Still, I’d rather have electricity than not, even if it does look a bit… intrusive. Reminds me of Dad’s insistence on bringing the portable telly camping. Oh god, yes! Remember that? The arguments with Mum about the batteries? It was supposed to be a ‘digital detox’ and he was watching snooker in a field. Classic Dad. Absolutely. And the time he tried to cook a full English breakfast on a camping stove? The smoke alarm went off for a good hour. We were the talk of the campsite. Oh, don’t remind me! Speaking of camping and costs… I was just looking at some prices for a proper glamping trip. Yurt, proper bed, the whole shebang. It’s… ambitious. Ambitious as in… expensive? Let me guess, upwards of £200 a night? More like £250 if you want anything remotely decent. It just feels a bit… excessive. We’re capable of pitching a tent, aren’t we? Remembering how, that is. We are. Though, after the last attempt, I swear the tent had a vendetta against us.

…and honestly, the humidity today is just  suffocating . Not like a nice, warm summer humidity, but a thick, cloying sort. Did you feel it on the court, David? It was sticking to me like…well, like damp tennis balls. Aye, felt it alright, Sarah. Proper muggy. Not a day for sprinting, that's for sure. Makes you long for a good Yorkshire frost, doesn’t it? Though, mind you, those get a bit brutal on the joints as you get older. This weather’s been proper weird this year, hasn’t it? Seems like spring just sort of…melted into summer without a proper showing. Exactly! No build-up. It feels like we skipped a season. Which, actually, makes me think about lesson planning. I'm trying to get my students interested in seasonal language - describing weather, harvest festivals, that sort of thing – and it’s hard when the weather isn’t  doing  seasons! They’re all international students, so the British obsession with talking about the weather is already a bit lost on them. International students, you say? What are you teaching then? English as a Foreign Language. Mostly adults. It’s rewarding, but you get all sorts. I had a chap from Brazil last week who was convinced “chuffed” meant angry. Apparently, it has a very different connotation where he’s from. Oh, bless him. Language is a funny thing, isn't it? I deal with people all day – gym members, mostly – and trying to explain things clearly is a skill in itself. Gotta watch the jargon. "Core stability" means nothing to half of 'em, even though it’s crucial for decent form. It’s a bit like coaching, really. Figuring out  how  someone learns is half the battle. That’s a brilliant point. It’s the same with language learning. I’ve been reading this book, actually, on neuro-linguistic programming. Quite dense, but it talks about mirroring and pacing – adapting your communication style to the learner's. Seems to be having some effect, I think. One student who was completely blocked when speaking is now at least attempting full sentences. NLP, eh? Sounds a bit… posh. Not something they were covering at school back in Leeds, I can tell you. Just straight rote learning if you were lucky. I left school at sixteen, went straight into retail, then worked my way up with the gyms. Always been more practical, I suppose.

…and honestly, lad, I don’t know  why  they keep changing the mark schemes. It’s a nightmare! Last year it was all about ‘showing working’, this year it’s ‘elegant solutions’. What  is  an elegant solution to a simultaneous equation for a fifteen-year-old, eh? It’s just maths, not a blooming art competition! Sounds stressful, Grandma. Mr. Harrison keeps going on about showing our workings too. Says it’s 50% of the mark. Aye, well, Mr. Harrison’s a good ‘un. Taught our Graham, didn’t he? A right clever lad, Graham always was. Though never could understand why I worried so much about dust. Said I’d polish the furniture ‘til the wood wore thin! She always did. Still does, doesn’t she, love? Can’t abide a speck of dust. Reminds her of her mother, I reckon. Your Grandma’s mother was… meticulous. Your Grandpa's right, Arthur. Mother was… particular. But a clean house is a sign of a clear head, I always say! Now, has anyone seen the biscuits? I swore I left a tin of shortbread on the coffee table. I think I had the last one, Grandma. Sorry! They were really good. Oh, you cheeky monkey! You always were a biscuit bandit. Never mind. I’ll put the kettle on, then. Are you two wanting a cuppa? Oh, go on then, lass. A nice brew always hits the spot. Especially with a bit of milk and two sugars for me, please. Doc says I shouldn't, but what does  he  know? He’s a southerner. Just one sugar for me, thanks, love. Trying to be good, see. Though a biscuit wouldn't go amiss, even without the shortbread. Trying to be good at eighty-something? That’s a new one, Arthur! I’ll see what I can rustle up. Although, honestly, this kitchen… it needs a good sorting out. That drawer with all the plastic containers? It’s a disaster zone. I offered to help with that, Grandma. Remember? Last weekend? Did you? Oh, bless you, you did. I keep forgetting. This marking takes it out of me, honestly. Trying to decipher what these youngsters are writing… it’s like hieroglyphics sometimes. They don't write properly anymore, do they? All text speak and abbreviations. Can’t read a proper letter to save their lives. It’s just quicker, Gran. And everyone does it.

… honestly, this roundabout is the devil’s own work. Three times now we’ve gone round it! And it’s not like I’m not familiar with roundabouts, mind you. Darlington’s  full  of them. But this one… it's specifically designed to confuse. Alright, alright, keep your hair on, love. It’s just a roundabout. Though I agree, it’s a bit…enthusiastically designed. Are you  sure  the satnav’s taking us the quickest route? It feels like we’ve been heading north for the last hour when the gig’s definitely south-west. That’s the thing, isn’t it? I don't trust these things implicitly. Remember when we tried to go to Hawes and it took us through that farmyard? Nearly ended up in a cow shed, we did! I’d rather have a proper map, truthfully. Old school. You and your maps. It  was  a memorable farmyard, though. The look on the farmer’s face! Still, the satnav  usually  gets it right. Let me have a look… hmm. It  is  being a bit… optimistic about this back road. Oh, brilliant. It says there’s roadworks ahead. Roadworks? Oh, fantastic. Just what we needed. And knowing our luck, it’ll be those temporary traffic lights with the sensors that don’t work, so you have to practically ram the car to get it to change. Don’t even go there. I have a very vivid memory of last year’s detour through Ambleside because of similar lights. Nearly missed seeing The Levellers as a result. Speaking of which, are you excited for tonight? I’ve been listening to their old stuff all week - ‘Beautiful Day’ is still a belter. Absolutely! I haven't seen them live in years. Though I'm more looking forward to a proper pint afterwards. That pub near the venue does a lovely local ale. Remember the ceilidh we went to there last autumn? That was a right laugh. My ankles still haven't fully recovered! Your ankles  always  complain after a ceilidh, Brenda. You throw yourself into it with such enthusiasm! You nearly took old Mr. Henderson out with a rogue eightsome reel. Well, he shouldn’t have been standing in the line of fire! He kept stepping on my toes, the grumpy sod. Anyway, back to the navigation. I think we need to ignore the satnav for a bit and head for the A65.

…and honestly, the exposed brick was  trying  to be industrial chic, but it just looked…sad. Like it was giving up on being a wall. Harsh, Liv, harsh. Though I get you. That whole ‘distressed’ look needs to be done properly. It felt…forced, didn't it? Like they’d just hit it with a hammer for five minutes. Five minutes and a prayer, more like. And the lighting! Fluorescent strips. In a  restaurant ? It was soul-destroying. Right, what are we actually getting? I’m starving. I need something substantial after that architectural crime scene. I was eyeing up the full English. Properly needed after all that walking around Shoreditch. You? Ooh, tempting. Maybe just eggs Benedict. Feeling slightly…refined after critiquing questionable design choices. Speaking of questionable choices, how's Chloe doing? She seemed properly down last week. Yeah, she's having a rough time with that Miller account. Apparently, he’s micro-managing everything. Changing details at the last minute, demanding revisions for the sake of revisions. She’s completely gutted. Keeps second-guessing herself. Ugh, Miller. He sounds dreadful. He was like that in uni, wasn’t he? Always had to have the ‘perfect’ line weight. It's exhausting. Tell her to stand her ground. She’s a brilliant designer, he’s just…difficult. I have been. She’s trying, but it's wearing her down. She was talking about maybe looking for something else, which is a shame because she really liked the firm. Anyway, back to things more pleasant: have you started thinking properly about the brief for the university project? The communal living one? A little. It's bugging me, actually. “Innovative, sustainable, communal living for young professionals.” It’s so…vague. What does that even  mean ? Do we build a co-living space with mandatory yoga and kombucha on tap? Don't give them ideas! I was thinking more along the lines of modular design, something adaptable. Maybe focusing on shared amenities that foster a sense of community without being overly prescriptive. Like a workshop space, a communal kitchen garden… That’s good, actually. The garden idea is nice. We could incorporate vertical farming. And what about the actual structure? I was toying with the idea of using cross-laminated timber. It's sustainable, relatively quick to erect, and it looks good if done properly. CLT is solid. We'd have to be mindful of cost, though.

…and honestly, the roundabout at the A1 junction is just  asking  for an accident. People just don’t seem to understand yielding anymore. It’s terrifying pulling out sometimes. Oh, tell me about it! I cycle that bit sometimes, to get to Millie’s, and it's…an experience. You get these lorries just  bearing down  on you. You’d think people would give a bit more space. Exactly! Space, awareness… basic manners! It’s like everyone’s in a rush to nowhere. Honestly, it’s worse than London driving, and that’s saying something. How was Millie’s yesterday, by the way? Did you have a good time? Yeah, it was good. Really good actually. She’s got a new boyfriend, you know. Oh? A new one? That’s… frequent. What’s he like? Don’t tell me he’s another musician. No, thankfully! He's called Liam. He works at the council, funnily enough. So, quite sensible, apparently. He’s doing a degree part-time in… environmental something. Environmental? That sounds…solid. Sensible is good. She needs sensible sometimes. Is he from around here? He's from Nottingham, actually. Met him through a friend of a friend. They went to a gig, but it wasn’t a  musician  gig, so that’s a win. She seems really happy, though. Really. I haven't seen her this…relaxed in ages. Well, that’s lovely to hear. It’s awful when they’re constantly flitting from one disaster to another. Remember Ben? The one with the ferret? Oh God,  Ben . Don’t remind me. The ferret was the least of our worries, honestly. The unpaid bills and the constant borrowing… Precisely. This Liam sounds like a breath of fresh air. You should invite him over for dinner, all of us. Get to know him. We haven’t had a proper family dinner in ages. That’s a good idea. Though Millie might kill me if I try to orchestrate anything too soon. She likes to take things at her own pace. Fair enough. But maybe casually mention it? “Mum and Dad were saying it would be nice to have you and Liam over for a roast sometime”? Just throw it out there. Okay, I can do that. So, how was your meeting with Harrison Chemicals? Still trying to wrestle that contract from them? It’s like pulling teeth. Old Man Harrison is a shrewd negotiator.

…and honestly, the ‘dynamic team player’ bit just feels so  empty . Like, everyone writes that, don’t they? It doesn’t actually  say  anything about what I can  do . Exactly! It's jargon city. Scrap it. They want to know what you bring to the table, not that you can regurgitate buzzwords. Let’s focus on specifics. This job description – it’s for the Digital Content Producer at BBC Birmingham, right? Yep. The one I sent you. Feels almost… intimidating, reading it again. So much about analytics and social media strategy. I’m comfortable with social media, obviously, but the analytics side… that’s where I wobble. Wobble is okay. Everyone wobbles somewhere. But you've produced some amazing audio features for that local podcast, haven't you? That demonstrates a solid understanding of storytelling, which is massively transferable. We need to hook that in. Think: 'Successfully conceptualised and delivered [number] audio features, resulting in a [percentage] increase in listener engagement.’ Numbers always help. Ooh, I  did  track the download numbers for those. Okay, okay, that's good. But what about the bit where it says “experience with Adobe Premiere Pro”? I’ve dabbled, you know, cut a few things for the podcast, but I’m hardly an expert. Right. Don't lie, obviously. But “dabbled” sounds… weak. “Familiar with Adobe Premiere Pro, with experience in basic editing and audio mixing for podcast production” is much better. Frame it as a learning curve, a willingness to upskill. They’re often looking for potential as much as experience, especially in the BBC. That’s true. They do have training budgets, don’t they? It’s just… it feels like I’m constantly selling myself short. Always focusing on what I  can’t  do rather than what I  can . My teaching background helps with communication, organisation, all that… but how does that translate to radio? Are you kidding? Teaching is  perfect ! You’re explaining complex things to people all the time. That's exactly what you’d be doing with audio content – making it accessible and engaging for a wider audience. Put that in! “Proven ability to communicate complex information clearly and concisely, honed through experience in education.” It's gold! You’re ruthless! But you’re right. I always downplay that. Okay, so less ‘dynamic team player’, more ‘proven communication skills’. More focus on the podcast, and framing the Premiere Pro thing as “willingness to learn”.

…and honestly, the whole thing just feels…stuck. Like I’m orbiting the same idea for the tenth year running. Another pitch meeting, another polite ‘we’ll be in touch,’ another nothing. It’s exhausting, Sarah. I can see that. You’ve been putting so much energy into the tech start-up, and it’s admirable, really. But if it’s truly draining you, even with the potential upside… well, maybe it  is  time to seriously consider something different. You said you were thinking about the pottery thing again? Yeah. Ridiculous, isn't it? Me, a bloke who used to build software, suddenly wanting to spend his days covered in clay. But remember that weekend workshop we did in the Cotswolds? I haven’t felt that…centered…since. Properly  lost  in something, you know? I do remember. You were like a different person. And your pieces were genuinely good, Ben. Not just ‘good for a beginner’ good, genuinely good. Better than anything  I  could produce, certainly. But a full career change…it’s daunting. Exactly. Daunting is an understatement. But this house-sitting is giving me headspace. No work emails pinging, no board meetings… just the smell of eucalyptus and the sound of kookaburras. It’s made me question everything. I've been doing some research. There’s actually a surprisingly strong market for handmade ceramics, even here in Australia. Especially if you focus on a niche. A niche? Like what? Well, I was thinking functional art. Not just vases and bowls, but things that are  used  and loved daily. Unique mugs, beautifully crafted serving dishes, maybe even tiles for kitchens. Things with a bit of personality. I’ve been sketching designs, and… honestly, I’m getting excited. That  does  sound different. And a lot less stressful than chasing venture capital. How feasible would setting up a small studio be? Would we need to come back to the UK? That’s the big question. I think we could actually do it here. Rental costs are comparable to parts of the UK, and the lifestyle… well, no offense to Dorset, but this is pretty amazing. I found a couple of industrial units on the outskirts of Perth. Nothing fancy, but enough space for a kiln, a potter’s wheel, and a small workshop. Perth… hmm. That's a long way from family. But it's also a new adventure. And I could definitely get some teaching supply work there if needed.

…and honestly, the delivery driver just  left  it on the doorstep, didn’t even knock! It’s a miracle Finn didn't decide it was a new plaything and dismantle the whole thing before I got to it. Honestly, the things you worry about when you have a two-year-old… ‘Stroy! ‘Stroy! Ach, you’re telling me! Though my worries back then were more about scraped knees and head lice than rogue grocery deliveries. Remember young Master Alistair, Bernard? Once tried to trade his packed lunch for a particularly interesting earthworm. Alistair! That boy was a character. Always negotiating. Tried to convince me he deserved  two  puddings because he’d "thought very hard" all morning. Though, thinking hard is precisely what he wasn't doing, usually. Right? They’re little negotiators from the moment they can babble. Finn’s already working on me to let him have biscuits before dinner. Pure manipulation. It's exhausting. So, about this engagement…you two haven’t been avoiding us, have you? Bernard’s been muttering about needing to start looking at venues. He’s already got a spreadsheet, you know. He always does. A spreadsheet for everything. It's his method of controlling the chaos. Though frankly, the chaos usually wins. And a wedding… It wouldn't be a proper engagement without a bit of chaos. No, we haven't been avoiding you! It’s just…well, things have been a bit overwhelming. Juggling Finn, trying to sort out some sort of routine, and then…the whole house situation. It’s just a lot. The housing is impossible, isn't it? Even for people with good jobs. Young couples can’t get a foot on the ladder, and the schools are bursting at the seams. I remember when the local primary had two classes per year. Now they're turning the gym into classrooms! It’s the influx, isn't it? Not just generally more people, but the change in demographics. All those Polish builders, skilled workers, good people, but it's put an enormous strain on the infrastructure. We need more houses, more schools, more doctors… That’s part of what’s stressing us out. If we were to, you know,  think  about expanding the family, even the idea of finding a bigger place… It feels impossible. And the school catchment areas are ridiculous. You need to own a mansion just to get your kid a place.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the car park passes at the doctors is just ridiculous, isn’t it? They’re saying you need a pass now, even just to drop someone off. It’s like they  want  people to be late for appointments. Oh, don't even get me started on that! I drove Mum down last week, and nearly got a ticket. Honestly, the attendant was so officious. Said it was ‘clearly stated’ on the website. Clearly stated in tiny font, buried on page three, more like. It’s all about squeezing money out of people, isn’t it? Exactly! It’s the principle. It’s not about the money, it’s the sheer inconvenience. Anyway, enough ranting about Fradley’s parking woes. How are you feeling? You sounded a bit off on the phone. Just a bit under the weather, love. That bug that's going around, I think. Headachy, achy, the whole shebang. Nothing a good lie-down and a cuppa won’t fix… eventually. It's just… tiring. Reminds me of when I had that awful flu back in '98. Missed nearly a week of work then. Old Mr. Henderson had to cover my sales route. He practically had a breakdown! Oh dear! He always did seem a bit…flustered. Remember him trying to explain the new filing system to everyone? It was like watching a toddler attempt astrophysics. Oh, bless him. He meant well. Speaking of work, things are alright, steady. Although, trying to motivate the sixth formers to cover lunch duties feels like herding cats these days. They’ve all got their heads buried in their phones. No sense of responsibility. It's a different generation, isn’t it? Though to be fair, sixth form was a  long  time ago for both of us. Do you ever think about… about Sarah Jenkins? From our year? Sarah… Wow. Haven't thought about Sarah in years. Wasn't she brilliant at the piano? Absolutely phenomenal. She was going to go to the Royal College of Music, wasn’t she? She was. I remember her playing at the school concert. Brought tears to your eyes. Pity what happened, really. Moving to London, getting involved with… well, you know. A bad crowd. Yes. It’s sad. Shows you, doesn't it? Talent isn't always enough. It's the choices you make. Still, wishing her well. It feels a bit ancient history now.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of replies to that announcement was mental. I thought we'd get a bit of a ripple, maybe a few retweets, but it just  exploded . Three times the engagement we anticipated. Aye, social media's a beast, isn't it? Especially Twitter. It's a good thing you’ve got a handle on it, Hamish. Remember when you thought Facebook was just for sharing holiday snaps? Don’t remind me! My Auntie Moira was constantly tagging me in pictures of her cat. Still is, actually. But this is different. For work, Twitter’s become invaluable. We’re using it now to gauge public opinion  before  campaigns launch, not just react to things afterwards. It’s a proper early warning system. That's smart. We're dipping our toes in that water too, at the university. Primarily for promoting events, showcasing student work, that sort of thing. But I’m finding it hard to move beyond just broadcasting. Getting proper  conversation  going is the tricky bit. It is. It's not enough to just shout into the void. You need to actually  listen . And reply. And be…human. We started doing these little ‘Ask Me Anything’ sessions with senior staff on Twitter. Huge success. People were asking surprisingly intelligent questions, and it humanised the whole organisation. An AMA, eh? Interesting. I’d be surprised if our professors would be keen. Some of them still think email is cutting edge. Professor MacIntyre practically refuses to believe anything that happened after 1985. You always get a few dinosaurs. But they’ll come around. Show them the numbers. Demonstrating impact is the key. What about you personally? Still a lurker, or do you actively… Twitter? Mostly lurk, to be honest. I follow a few academics, some political commentators, and… well, I confess to following a few accounts dedicated to obscure Scottish history. You know how it is. Aye, I do. I've got a soft spot for accounts that dig up old photos of Edinburgh. It's strange, seeing the city your grandparents knew. I'm more action-oriented on Instagram, though. That’s where I share my photography. Keeps me sane, away from all the work stuff. Instagram? You and your fancy cameras! I respect it, I really do, but I can barely work the settings on my phone. Though, I did use it once to document the sheep shearing at my brother’s farm.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of glitter at that festival was a biohazard. I’m still finding it in places I didn't know  had  places. Did you even manage to escape Glasto unscathed? Unscathed is a strong word. More… glitter-adjacent. It’s mostly confined to my wellies which are currently residing in the garden, posing a threat to unsuspecting wildlife. How was your weekend with Leo, though? You seemed really excited about it. It  was  good. Really good. Until… well, until his mate Dave turned up. Oh no. Dave? The one who thinks mansplaining is a legitimate flirting technique? The very same. He spent a solid hour telling me about the intricacies of craft beer, as if I’ve never had a pint in my life. I literally just nodded and smiled and pretended to be fascinated, because Leo looked so mortified. Ugh, that’s the worst. Having to become a human bobblehead for the sake of peace. Leo's usually good at shutting that down, isn’t he? He tried! He really did. But Dave is one of those guys who just… doesn’t get boundaries. It felt like I was on display. It kind of dampened the evening, honestly. I started wondering if Leo even noticed how annoying he was, or if I was the only one. He absolutely noticed, you know. Leo’s a good guy. He probably just didn’t want to make a scene. Trust me, dealing with difficult people is my  job . You’d be surprised how much passive-aggressive behaviour I witness. Honestly, sometimes I think I should write a book – “The Subtle Art of Avoiding Escalation”. You totally should. You’d be rich! Speaking of jobs… how was your shift yesterday? You looked completely drained when you came in. Don’t even get me started. We had a Code 99 – attempted suicide. It was… a lot. A young woman, early twenties. Just completely overwhelmed. We got her stabilized, thankfully, but it stays with you, you know? It's draining even when things  go  well. Oh, Lizzie, I’m so sorry. That sounds absolutely awful. It's just… unfair. You do such important work, and it must be so emotionally taxing. It is. But it's also… rewarding, when it is. It’s why I do it. Anyway, enough doom and gloom. This is supposed to be a relaxed evening catch-up.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Derek is just exhausting. He calls every other day complaining about something. Now it’s the heating bill. The  heating bill , honestly! As if we don’t all have bills. Dad, you know he worries. It’s just how he deals with things. He’s never been… practical, has he? Remember when he tried to build that shed and it collapsed within a week? Oh, don’t remind me! I had to help him clear up the mess. He was convinced it was the wood’s fault, not his shoddy construction. But yes, he does fret. And it  is  a hefty bill this year, isn’t it? Everything’s gone up. Hefty? It’s extortionate! But it’s not the money, it's the constant needing to soothe him. Anyway, back to the point - he's confirmed he  is  coming down for Christmas. Said he’s booked the train. Good. That’s something, at least. Will he need picking up from the station? Holsworthy isn’t exactly on a major line. I said I would. Though honestly, that’s another hour and a half each way. And with the new car… Oh, the car! Tell us about it. You haven't stopped talking about it since you got it. Is it really as marvellous as you say? Marvellous doesn’t even begin to cover it! It’s a Ford Focus, a nice, sensible thing, but with all the bells and whistles. Sat nav, reversing camera, even heated seats! Makes a world of difference on these chilly mornings. Much better than that old banger I was driving. You deserve it, Dad. You’ve been putting it off for years. And it’ll make trips like collecting Derek from the station much easier. That’s what I thought. But it means I’ll be leaving earlier, getting back late… it just adds to the chaos. Speaking of chaos, what about Christmas dinner? Are we still doing the usual? I was thinking so. I can do the turkey, I’ve got a good recipe. And Sarah offered to do the stuffing. That sounds perfect. I can handle the dessert. Chocolate Yule Log, maybe? It’s a bit traditional, but everyone loves it. Lovely. Though, your mother always made the best Yule Log. No one's ever quite managed to replicate it. I know. I try. It's just…never quite the same.

…and honestly, Arthur, I’m telling ya, this subjunctive mood is going to be the death of me. Honestly! I’ve been at this Duolingo lark for six months now and it’s still just…gibberish. “Si yo fuera…” What  is  “si yo fuera”? It’s like they’re deliberately trying to confuse us. Now, now, Dot. Don’t get yourself into a state. Six months isn’t long, you know. I tried picking up Italian once, after that holiday to Tuscany. Lasted about a fortnight. Found the rolling ‘r’s…unmanageable, frankly. Italian sounds lovely though, doesn’t it? More melodic than Spanish. Spanish feels…staccato. And the grammar! It’s not like English where you can just kinda…wing it. Everything has a gender! A  table  has a gender! Well, everything has a  grammatical  gender, Dot. Don't get too existential about the furniture. It’s just a linguistic quirk. I suppose it’s something to do with the roots of the language, the Latin influence and all that. You were a teacher, you’d know. I  was  an EFL teacher, Arthur. Teaching  English  to foreigners, not grappling with the nuances of a language that seems determined to remain foreign! And the ‘ser’ and ‘estar’… oh, don't even get me started. “To be” in two different flavours! It's madness. It wouldn't happen in Scouse, I can tell ya that much. No, I imagine ‘being’ is fairly straightforward in Liverpool. Straightforward and colourful. But look, you’re using Duolingo, aren’t you? That’s a bit…basic, isn't it? I remember reading something about immersion being the best method. Immersion? I’d need to move to Barcelona, wouldn’t I? Which, lovely as it sounds, isn’t exactly feasible on a teacher’s pension. Besides, I've tried those language exchange apps. Ended up talking to a seventeen-year-old boy from Madrid who mostly wanted to discuss football. My Spanish isn’t up to debating offside rules. Hmm. Fair point. You know, I was reading about Catalonia the other day. Apparently, they’re all bilingual, Catalan and Castilian. It must be easier learning a second language when the first one is so similar. Aye, well, that's true. It's easier if you’ve got a foothold. Like if I’d learned French at school, then maybe Spanish would be a doddle. But we all had to do German, didn’t we?

…Right, so that's all the utility bills for the last year, Dad. And this slightly terrifying pile is… everything else. Honestly, it's like a historical archive in here. Have you  seen  a bank statement from 1998? It’s printed on what feels like papyrus. Don't I know it. Your mother kept  everything . Said you never knew when it might be useful. Though, honestly, I haven’t needed a gas bill from 1987 in… well, ever. What’s this folder labelled “Important – Do Not Discard”? Sounds ominous. That’s the one I was hoping you could shed some light on. It’s seemingly random documents – old insurance forms, a receipt for a very expensive camera, a clipping from…  The Sun  featuring Kelly Brook. Oh, good lord. Kelly Brook. Right. That'll be from, oh, twenty-odd years ago. I remember that. Your mother had a bit of a… fondness for her. Probably saving it for… reasons. Don’t ask me. Women are mysterious creatures. So, completely irrelevant to any important paperwork? Fantastic. Okay, let's focus. These are mostly banking things, it looks like. Deposits, withdrawals… a lot of cheques. Do you remember if Mum did any online banking back then? Online banking? In the nineties? Blimey, no. Everything was posted, wasn’t it? Remember that little plastic thing they used to give you to verify transactions? Very high tech. You’re lucky you weren’t around for it. I spent hours balancing the chequebook. Absolute nightmare. Sounds… relaxing. I'm trying to get a handle on her overall finances, just for probate, you know. It’s surprisingly difficult to reconstruct everything without a digital trail. It's almost a corpus linguistics problem, really – trying to extract meaning from this mess of textual data. Corpus what now? You always were a clever lad with your fancy book learning. Just focus on the numbers, son. See what came in, what went out. It's not rocket science. Speaking of which, I need to book flights for Aunt Carol's wedding in Malaga. Have you got any tips? I'm completely lost with all these websites. Malaga? Nice! Skyscanner is usually pretty good, or Google Flights. Set up price alerts. And be flexible with your dates, even a day either side can make a huge difference. I've been trying to scan these documents into digital form, but the scanner’s ancient.

… honestly, I still can’t believe you nearly ran us into that forecourt. A  forecourt , Leo! It wasn’t exactly subtle. Alright, alright, lay off. I told you, it was a weird angle. The lights were reflecting off the pumps, and I misjudged the distance. It wasn't ideal, I admit, but 'nearly ran us into' feels a bit dramatic, doesn’t it? Dramatic? You were aiming for the unleaded! I distinctly saw you correct  hard . And honestly, those petrol stations are just designed to catch you out, aren’t they? All angles and shiny surfaces. It’s a conspiracy, I tell ya. Probably run by Big Oil, making it harder to fill up and forcing us to spend more. Right. Big Oil's grand plan revolves around confusing drivers at Sainsbury’s petrol stations. Makes perfect sense. Look, I'm used to driving around city centres, tighter spaces. Coming out onto the A19 and then immediately needing to navigate a petrol station… it threw me. The A19 was fine! You were grand on the dual carriageway. It was the  petrol station . And it wasn’t just any petrol station! It was that one near Washington. They always have queues, and it’s always a faff. Proper nightmare fuel. They need to re-think the layout. Okay, I’ll grant you, Washington services are…suboptimal. But honestly, you drive so defensively it's exhausting sometimes. You practically braked for a pigeon back in Durham. It  was  a rather large pigeon! And they dart about, you know? It’s common sense. Besides, you were hogging the middle lane for a good five miles before that, so don't come at  me  about driving habits. Hogging? I was maintaining a steady speed! And it's less 'hogging' and more 'being aware of potential hazards'. Unlike some people who are preoccupied with conspiracy theories about petrol stations. Speaking of hazards…did you see that biker back there? Absolutely  flying  it. Oh, aye. One of those ones who thinks the roads are their personal racetrack. Honestly, they give me the fear. Zipping in and out of traffic. It's only a matter of time before something serious happens. They’re surprisingly good riders, though. You’ve got to have a lot of skill to pull off some of those manoeuvres. They’re just…enthusiastic. Enthusiastic and utterly reckless, more like. My Uncle Geoff used to be a biker, back in the day.

…and honestly, the way Murray used to grind out those points, just relentless. It wasn't flashy, but it  worked . It's something a lot of these young players seem to be missing these days. All power, no patience. Yeah, Mum. You always say that. But Alcaraz is pretty amazing, isn’t he? The way he moves... He  is  incredible. The athleticism is just… phenomenal. And he’s got the shots to back it up. Different era, you know? It’s become so physically demanding. Murray was strong, obviously, but Alcaraz is on another level. Remember when tennis was more about finesse, about clever placement? I do. And don't get me wrong, I appreciate Alcaraz. He's a fantastic player, genuinely. But there’s something about the British style of play, the grit, that I always connect with. That’s why I was so thrilled when you decided to take up proper coaching, Leo. It's alright. Mr. Davies is…intense. He makes me do  loads  of drills. Like, seriously, hundreds of forehands. My arm felt like it was going to fall off yesterday. He’s building your foundations. That’s good! Repetition is key. I had a coach like that when I was younger, learning taekwondo. Brutal, but effective. You need to develop that muscle memory. He's a good coach, supposedly. Old school. Mrs. Peterson down the road, whose son he coaches as well, says he's very knowledgeable. Though she also says he doesn't suffer fools gladly. That’s an understatement. He told me my footwork was “resembling a newborn giraffe” this morning. A  giraffe , Mum! Oh dear. Well, he’s trying to get you to improve! It’s all constructive criticism. Think about Federer, even  he  had to work relentlessly on his technique. Though he made it look effortless, of course. Remember that backhand? Poetry in motion. Federer was…elegant. A true artist. Alcaraz is more like a hurricane. Powerful, unpredictable. I saw him play Djokovic at Wimbledon last year, what a match! Just breathtaking. It was amazing! I watched it with Ben. We were both shouting at the TV. Ben reckons his serve is untouchable. It’s pretty good, yes. But Djokovic can return anything. Anything! That’s what makes  him  so remarkable. The mental strength. Have you seen him play a bad game, Leo? Rarely. He’s a machine. And mentally very, very tough.

Right, seriously though, these napkins… they genuinely look like someone’s nicked a pair of knickers and cut ‘em into squares. Gran, did you  choose  these? Now, Leo, don’t be rude! They’re perfectly nice napkins. And your Grandma’s got good taste, even if you don’t appreciate it. They were on offer, alright? Three packs for a fiver at Home Bargains. You can’t argue with that. Honestly, Leo’s not wrong though, Mum. They  are  questionable. It's a bit… unnerving. They remind me of that time at uni, when Ben started calling me ‘Panties’… long story. Oh, here we go. Uni nicknames. Remember “Captain Chaos” for Liam? And Sarah was always “The Duchess”. Good times. Were those stories ever truly explained? Oh god, not the uni stories again. I’m trying to enjoy my dinner, thanks. Is the turkey alright, Dad? It looks a bit… pale. It’s fine, lad. A little pale, maybe, but it's cooked through. Your Auntie Carol always overdoes it, practically cremating the bird. I’ve learned from her mistakes, see? Speaking of Carol, did she get to Florida alright? I was worried about her flying over on her own. She's not as sprightly as she used to be. She landed safe and sound, Gran. She sent me a picture of her by the pool. Said the weather was amazing, naturally. She’s already moaning about the portion sizes though - apparently, everything’s ‘massive’ over there. Good. She needs a bit of sunshine. It’ll do her good. Still think America's a bit far, mind. Such a long flight. Remember when we flew to Barcelona, and Leo spent the whole time complaining about his ears? I was seven! And they  hurt ! Besides, Barcelona’s nothing like America. It’s practically next door. Actually, thinking about travelling… last time we were all together like this, we were talking about visiting New York. Remember that? Never quite got around to it. We always talk about it, don’t we? It’s always ‘next year’. Although, I'm quite happy here, thank you very much. Airports are a nightmare. All that rushing about. And the security! True. But imagine Christmas in New York! All the lights, the ice skating… the shopping! Oh, don’t mention shopping! I still haven’t finished mine. Got to get something for young Thomas, and I’m completely stuck.

…and honestly, the spreadsheets are just multiplying. It’s like they breed when I’m not looking. Old Mr. Henderson keeps adding ‘essential’ columns, and honestly, half of them are just colour-coded lists of his favourite biscuits. Oh, bless him. Sounds like you’ve got a bit of a character on your hands, love. Still, project coordinating  is  supposed to be organised, isn’t it? It's a world away from marking GCSE papers, I tell you. The drama! This year's English Literature cohort… honestly. Drama's everywhere, Elsie. Just different flavours. My barley crop's looking a bit peaky, to be honest. Rain's been patchy, and the nitrogen levels are all over the place. It's a constant battle against nature and fluctuating fertiliser prices. Speaking of which, anyone fancy a bit of homemade bread later? I picked up some decent flour down at the market. Ooh, yes please, Dad! That sounds amazing. I’m definitely running on fumes after work. This whole saving-for-a-deposit thing is exhausting. Flats in Brighton are… well, let’s just say they require a small loan from a friendly dragon. Brighton is expensive! You’d be better off looking a little further afield, wouldn’t you? Perhaps somewhere commutable from Norwich? Plenty of nice villages. And I could help with decorating, of course. Always happy to wield a paintbrush. Mum, I appreciate the offer, but I really want to be independent. Plus, all my friends are down in Brighton. It's a bit scary thinking about being the only one not living  in  the city. I went out with Chloe last weekend – she’s just bought a tiny little flat-share – and she was saying how brilliant it is to finally have her own space, even if it's just a corner of a living room. Space is overrated. Ask any farmer. It just means more to maintain! Though, I suppose for a young woman building a life, it’s different. Still, don’t get yourself into too much debt, eh? Remember young Michael from the village? Borrowed a fortune for a fancy tractor, then the farm went under. Oh, don’t start on Michael, Arthur. That was a complex situation! He wasn't very good with money, let's just say. And his wife… well, she had expensive tastes. This is different. Lily’s sensible. Aren’t you, love?

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of new stuff in Marks and Spencer is overwhelming. It’s like they’re deliberately trying to make you spend money. Did you see those little smoked salmon and cream cheese bites? Utterly unnecessary, but I almost bought them. Almost? You usually succumb to unnecessary M&S temptations. I’m impressed. Though, to be fair, their food hall  is  a danger zone. They’ve really upped their game since… well, since forever, really. I know! I’m trying to be sensible. I’ve got enough things in the fridge as it is. We need to eat this chicken. Although, I am tempted by those ready-made pizzas… the stone-baked ones. Quick supper, you know? No pizzas. We’re having chicken and vegetables. You promised. Besides, we had pizza last week. And the week before. We're spiralling. Alright, alright. Chicken it is. How was your appraisal today, then? Don’t tell me it was all sunshine and roses. Knowing the office… Pretty much as expected. Lots of "you're a valuable asset," which is code for "we expect you to do the work of three people for the salary of one." And then a vague suggestion of “leadership potential” that requires another course. Another  expensive  course. Oh, those appraisals. Always the same. They dangle the carrot of promotion but then make the jump ridiculously difficult. Did you push back at all? About the workload? I tried. Politely. Mentioned that perhaps distributing tasks more evenly might improve overall team morale and productivity. Got a sympathetic nod and a promise to “look into it.” Which translates to nothing. Standard. Right. Vegetables need chopping. Speaking of things that require more effort than they should, have you seen that new documentary about equine welfare? It’s heartbreaking. The conditions some of those horses are kept in… No, I haven't. I avoid stuff like that, usually. Too depressing. Although, I did catch a bit of  Trapped  again last night. Utterly gripping. That Icelandic scenery is stunning, even when it's raining sideways.  Trapped  is fantastic. So claustrophobic. Have you finished the crossword yet? The one in the Sunday Times? I’m stuck on 17 across. “Obsolete form of communication .” Let me guess – you’ve been wrestling with that for two days? It’s “telegram.” Of  course ! Telegram. I knew it was something like that. My brain just wasn’t cooperating.

…and honestly, the queue at Urban Outfitters was mental. Absolutely  mental . I swear, everyone in Sheffield decided they needed a new oversized hoodie all at the same time. Tell me about it! I popped in earlier for a little browse, ended up wrestling a woman for the last floral dress. Floral, mind you, in November. People are wild. Are you wearing that new jumpsuit you got then, Liv? Aye, this one. It's surprisingly comfy, actually. Thought I'd be constantly hitching it up, but it’s alright. What about you, Maisie? Looking rather…glammed up for a pre-night-out chat. Just fancied a change, like. Normally I’m all about comfort, but I thought, why not? It's velvet, feels amazing. And I’m attempting heels. Emphasis on  attempting . Oh, Lord. Heels and you, Maisie, is a legendary combination of bravery and eventual disaster. Remember that time at Popworld? Don't you  dare  bring up Popworld! I maintain that floor was unreasonably slippery. It wasn’t my fault. It always isn't, love. Speaking of outfits, I’m just in jeans and a nice top. Playing it safe. Don't want to be worried about wardrobe malfunctions all night. Plus, I'm planning on  proper  dancing, and sensible shoes are key. Sensible is good, Hayley. Sensible is smart. I'm similar to you, just a comfy dress and boots. No point looking good if you can't move. Although Liv looks alright in that jumpsuit. Does it have pockets? Pockets are essential for a night out. It does! Massive pockets. Perfect for a lipstick, phone, maybe even a sneaky packet of biscuits later on. You never know. Biscuits? Liv, you're a woman after my own heart. But seriously, anyone else worried about getting ID'd? I feel like I look about twelve again lately. I always get ID'd. Always. Even though I’m practically ancient. I swear the bouncers just enjoy the power trip. I’ve started carrying my passport. It’s a bit much, but less hassle than arguing. My passport's definitely seen better days. Gets a bit crumpled in my bag. I usually just hope for the best. Sarah, what about you? You always look effortlessly cool, do you ever get trouble? Nah, I've not had an issue for a while. Though I did once get asked for ID when I was buying paracetamol. Paracetamol!

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Brenda from accounts! She actually suggested I wasn’t prioritising Mr. Harrison’s travel arrangements properly because I was ‘too busy with the charity bake sale’. Too busy! As if raising money for the hospice is some kind of frivolous hobby. Brenda sounds… Brenda. You know, she probably thinks arranging stationery is a vital national security operation. Don’t let her get to you, love. You’re brilliant at your job, and everyone knows it. Mr. Harrison would be lost without you. Easy for you to say, you’re not the one facing down a spreadsheet-wielding dragon every Monday morning. It’s just… exhausting sometimes, dealing with people who fundamentally misunderstand what’s important. It makes me wonder if some people are just… wired differently. You know? Like, utterly lacking in empathy. Well, that’s the beauty of it, isn’t it? The vast spectrum of human personalities. Makes life interesting, even when it's frustrating. Though, I agree, a bit more empathy wouldn’t go amiss. It reminds me of that book we were reading about past lives… remember? The one about soul connections? Oh, yes! The one where you were convinced you were a Roman gladiator and I was Cleopatra's handmaiden? Don’t mock the gladiator! It felt… right. Anyway, it got me thinking. Do you believe in soul mates? Not necessarily romantically, but people you’re just destined to know, to have a connection with, across lifetimes? Hmm. I'm…open to the idea. It’s comforting, isn’t it? The thought that these relationships aren’t purely random. But I struggle with the whole predetermined destiny thing. Feels a bit limiting. Maybe we  choose  our soul connections. That’s a good point. Maybe it’s not about fate, but about recognizing something familiar. A spark. Like when we first met, at that awful 1920s themed party. You looked amazing in that flapper dress. And you looked like you’d wandered out of a detective novel. Honestly, it was all terribly cliché. But it  worked . Though, if I could visit any period in history, it wouldn't be the roaring twenties. I’d go to the Italian Renaissance. Imagine being a fly on the wall, witnessing Michelangelo paint the Sistine Chapel. Ooh, good choice. I’d go for Victorian London. All that fog and mystery… imagine the conversations in the coffee houses.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is ridiculous. They’re implementing this new CRM system, supposedly to make things  easier , but it’s just adding another layer of admin. Honestly, sometimes I think they just invent work to justify people's jobs. Sounds about right. Government work is the same, just… slower. Everything moves at a glacial pace. Did you manage to finish that jumper you were knitting? The teal one? Almost! Just the sleeves to weave in. It’s for little Leo, you know, Millie’s boy. She's absolutely smitten with him. It’s funny, isn’t it? How quickly grandparents get wrapped around their fingers. Oh, absolutely! My Mum’s already threatening to buy him a full football kit, despite him being six months old and barely able to hold his head up! It's the grandparental instinct, I think. So, how was your weekend, Sarah? Anything exciting? Not exactly  exciting . Went to the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge. Trying to be a bit more… cultured, you know? I felt a bit out of my depth, though. Everyone seemed to be having very serious conversations about brushstrokes and whatnot. Cambridge! Lovely. I always feel a bit intimidated in art museums too. I can appreciate things are beautiful, but deciphering the  meaning … that’s where I get lost. It's probably the Lincolnshire in me; we’re more practical folk. Oh, don’t start with the regional stereotypes! Just because you’re from Boston doesn’t mean you can’t appreciate art, Helen. Though I  will  admit, there's a certain bluntness to Lincolnshire folks that I admire. It’s all good-natured ribbing! But seriously, sometimes I think our language is a minefield. I was on a call with someone from Texas last week, and I couldn't understand a word they were saying. It wasn’t just the accent, it was the phrasing… everything. Blimey. Texas, huh? I saw a documentary about gun ownership over there. Terrifying. It makes you think about how different things are. We moan about knife crime here, but… It’s a different culture entirely. I saw something on the news about a school shooting. It’s just… unimaginable. The violence in society is getting worse, isn’t it? It’s depressing. It truly is. And it’s creeping into everything. Even seemingly safe spaces. Speaking of depressing… I walked past the old graveyard on Park Road yesterday.

…and honestly, the state of the kitchen is a  disgrace . Liam left a mountain of dirty dishes  again . It’s like living with a toddler, honestly. You wouldn't believe the state of it. Sounds about right for Liam. He’s a good lad, but domestic duties? Not his forte. Still better than my flatmate, though. He tried to cook pasta in the kettle last week. The  kettle ! No way! Seriously? That’s… impressive levels of cluelessness. Mine’s alright. A bit messy, leaves his socks everywhere, but at least he doesn’t attempt to boil pasta in electrical appliances. We did have an incident with burnt toast setting off the alarm, though. See, this is why I’m starting to think Uni accommodation isn't all it's cracked up to be. Back home, me mam would have had a right go at anyone doing that. Proper ‘right telling off’ you know? None of this passive aggressive notes. Yeah, it’s a bit of a lottery, isn't it? I miss having my Nan nearby, honestly. She’d sort everything out. Plus, she always has cash. Speaking of which, are we still doing the shop for the party tomorrow? My student loan’s looking a bit…sparse. I can chip in a bit. I picked up a shift at the pub, so I have a little extra. But honestly, everyone needs to remember to bring  something . We can't rely on just the three of us. Especially after Sarah promised to bring snacks and then ‘forgot.’ Sarah's a nightmare. She’s all talk. Remember when she said she was a whizz at baking? Her cake tasted like cardboard! Still, she’s good for a laugh. Did you hear she's trying to convince everyone that ‘aluminium’ is pronounced ‘a-loo-min-ium’? What?! That's… spectacular. Where is she getting this information? Is she trying to start a linguistic revolution? I swear, some people. I get enough grief already with my accent. People always think I'm trying to do a fake London accent, but it's just how I actually speak! Oh, I get that. People always assume I’m posh because I’m from Norfolk. It's ridiculous. It's just fields and tractors, not Downton Abbey! Anyway, back to Sarah… cardboard cake, ‘a-loo-min-ium’… she's a character. She is. Right, shopping list. Crisps, dips, drinks… we need nibbles.

…and honestly, the library at Lancaster is  nothing  like the one at Uni of Bolton. It's just…massive. Like, you get lost. And everyone's so quiet, it's creepy. You could drop a pin and hear it echo. Sounds a bit intimidating, love. Bolton's library was cozy, wasn't it? Always someone having a natter. Still, good to be stretching your wings, eh? Istria’s a world away from Bolton, and Lancaster too, come to think of it. This seafood risotto is  gorgeous  though. Honestly, the best I’ve had. Can I have some of yours, Gran? Mine’s…fishy. Not in a bad way, just…more fishy. Of course, you can, Liam. Just a little bit. You always were a fussy eater, weren’t you? Though, you ate a whole plate of mussels last week, so maybe you're changing your ways. He's got your stubborn streak, Margaret. Though, I think it’s balanced out by his mother’s charm. This wine is very drinkable as well, a good local variety I imagine? Dad, you’re always trying to analyse the wine! Just enjoy it. And yes, I definitely get the stubborn streak from Gran. But the charm is  all  mum. Oh, go on! You’re a charmer yourself, Amy. Speaking of stubborn, remember old Mrs. Higgins? Nearly refused to let me check her blood pressure last week. Said it ‘messed with her aura’. Honestly, the things you hear as a midwife… Did she have a tattoo? Old Mrs. Higgins? I saw some amazing tattoos in town today. This guy had a whole sleeve, dragons and stuff! I’m thinking about getting one, maybe. Liam! You're only fifteen! You can't get a tattoo yet. And dragons? Really? I know, I know. But I was just saying! Maybe when I'm eighteen. Something small. Like… a dog paw print. We  are  getting a puppy when we get back, aren’t we? That's the plan, son. A Labrador, I believe your mother's decided? Though getting a puppy and starting secondary school at the same time… that's a busy year for you, isn’t it? How’s the bus journey to school looking? Still packed to the rafters? Awful. Absolutely awful. Everyone’s crammed in like sardines. Ben nearly lost his phone this morning. Someone was trying to shove past. Miss Davies said she’s writing to the council  again , but nothing ever happens.

…and honestly, Doreen, the cream tea at Land’s End wasn’t  quite  what I’d built it up to be. Bit dry, the scones were. Though, the clotted cream… well, you can’t fault the clotted cream, can you? Never, Arthur, never fault the clotted cream. Sounds lovely though, all the same. Cornwall. Always wanted to properly  see  it. Just quick day trips when the children were little, dashing to the beach and back. You and David must’ve had a good time. We really did. It was… restorative. David was brilliant, actually. He took on a lot of the navigation, which was a godsend considering my directional skills are, shall we say, lacking. We stayed in that YHA near Porthleven, the one overlooking the coast. Absolutely stunning. YHA, eh? Fancy that. David volunteering, mind you. Always a good egg, that boy. You two looked right as rain in those photos, by the way. That one by the lighthouse… magnificent. Is that Lizard Point? It is. The Lizard. We spent a good hour just watching the waves crash against the rocks. David was trying to identify all the different seabirds. He’s gotten quite into ornithology, surprisingly. He used to be all about football and… well, you know. Men and their hobbies, eh? Football one minute, puffins the next! Still, good for him. Keeps him occupied. Speaking of occupied, how was the cycling? You said something about a rather ambitious route? "Ambitious" is putting it mildly. “Yorkshire in a Day.” Don’t. Just don't. It was… challenging. Beautiful, breathtakingly beautiful scenery, but my legs are  still  protesting. We underestimated the hills. Seriously underestimated. Yorkshire in a day! Good grief, lad. That’s a proper slog. Sounds like you deserve a lie down and a nice cuppa. More than one nice cuppa, come to think of it. You’re speaking my language, Arthur. Though, it wasn't  all  agony. We stopped at this little village pub, did a cracking ploughman's. And the people were so friendly. That's the best part of travelling, isn’t it? Meeting the locals. Did you see many crabs, Arthur? You always did have a soft spot for crabs. Always ‘ave. Little scuttling chaps. Didn't get much chance, mind you. David was determined to see every stone circle and ancient ruin within a fifty-mile radius. Crabs took a backseat, I’m afraid.

…and honestly, the catering at that conference last week was  criminal . Seriously, beige buffet, beige everything. You’d think for a ‘Future of Tech’ summit they could at least manage something colourful, eh? It tasted like it had all been pre-made in…well, Doncaster, probably. No offence. None taken, lass. Doncaster’s alright. Beats Cambridge for proper pubs, anyway. This lasagne’s much better than beige, though. ANON’s a cracking cook, she is. It’s just a Jamie Oliver recipe, really. Nothing special. But thanks, Ben. Yorkshire folk are hard to please when it comes to food, aren’t they, Maya? You always seem to have a strong opinion. It’s not about being hard to please, it's about standards! You grow up with proper gravy and Yorkshire puddings, and then suddenly you're presented with a watery sauce and a sad, flat pancake. It’s a cultural trauma, I tell ya. Speaking of trauma… how’s things with Liam going, ANON? You’ve been awfully quiet about him lately. Oh, um… it’s complicated. Complicated is code for “it’s a right mess,” isn’t it? Spill the beans. Last time I saw you two you were practically joined at the hip. It’s not a  mess , exactly. It’s just…we’re taking a break. A break? What does that even  mean  anymore? Is that like, a socially acceptable way of saying “I’m seeing other people”? No! It’s not that. We’ve just been… arguing. A lot. About stupid things, mostly. Like how to load the dishwasher. Seriously. Loading the dishwasher? That’s proper mental. My nan used to have wars over that with my grandad. Always insisted the plates had to face  north . See? It's a fundamental disagreement! But also… a bit pathetic. What are you  really  arguing about, ANON? I think…I think we want different things. He’s happy staying here in Cambridge, working as a mechanic. Which is great, perfectly valid. But I’m…I’m starting to feel stifled. I want to travel, maybe do a PhD, move somewhere…bigger. He doesn’t get it. He thinks I'm being unrealistic. Right. He's not ambitious enough for you. I’ve been there. Remember Dave? The one who thought a night down the pub was a cultural experience? Oh,  Dave . Bless him. He was a decent lad, but…yeah. Didn't have the travelling bug, did he?

…and honestly, the churros were  life changing . I’m already craving them. Did you have a good weekend? You look…rested. Which is a miracle considering what you do for a living. “Rested” is a strong word. More like… momentarily not actively dealing with crises. It was busy, a couple of particularly rough admissions. But yeah, needed this quiet kitchen time. Barcelona sounds incredible though. You were only gone three days, it feels like a lifetime since we last properly spoke. Fill me in on  everything . Beyond the churros, obviously. Everything? Where do I even begin? It was… chaotic in the best way. Remember how I was worried about getting lost on the metro? Utterly pointless worry. It’s so easy to navigate! And the architecture! Gaudí is just… mad. Beautifully, wonderfully mad. Park Güell was insane. Tourist trap, sure, but worth it. Oh, I’ve seen pictures of Park Güell. It looks like something out of a fairy tale. You always did have a good eye for finding the slightly eccentric. Did you manage to avoid all the stag dos? That’s what I was worried about, knowing how popular Barcelona is for that. Surprisingly, yes! We stumbled into a couple of bars that were… lively, let’s say, but mostly avoided the full-on chaos. We did end up at this amazing tapas place, though, recommended by a local. Tiny, packed, everyone shouting… it was perfect. I’m officially obsessed with Patatas Bravas. I think I ate my weight in them. Sounds perfect. I’m glad you had such a good time. It’s good to see you actually switch off. You’ve been working so hard on that project at work, it’s been stressing you out. Speaking of work, I’m thinking of applying for that advanced course in trauma-informed care. It’s a big commitment, but I really feel like it would help… you know? That’s brilliant, honestly. You’d be amazing at it. And totally worth the commitment, I reckon. You're already so good with people, it would just build on that. What does it involve, evening classes? Yeah, two nights a week, plus some placements. It's a bit daunting thinking about fitting it all in. Still, need to keep progressing, right? What about  you ? Any grand plans for the future, beyond consuming vast quantities of Spanish cuisine? Have you thought any more about… Paris?

…and honestly, the paperwork is the worst part. You spend more time justifying  why  you’re doing something beneficial for a child than actually  doing  it. It’s utterly draining. Though, having said that, seeing a student finally ‘get’ something… that makes it all worthwhile, doesn’t it? Absolutely. You need those little victories, or you’d drown in red tape. My life’s less paperwork, more… persuasive arguing with investors. Similar principle, actually. Just different stakeholders. Persuasive arguing. That sounds far more glamorous than filling in learning support plans. What exactly  do  you do then? You mentioned something about starting your own business when we were waiting for the coffees. I run a tech start-up. It’s called ‘Local Lens’. Essentially, we create immersive virtual tours for small businesses. Restaurants, hotels, even estate agents. Makes their online presence much more engaging, you know? Trying to compete with the big boys, that’s the challenge. That’s fascinating! Very forward thinking. So, you’re based in London still? Everything feels very London-centric these days. Born and bred, me. Can’t imagine living anywhere else, though I’m increasingly needing to escape it. Hence, North Cyprus. This is my second time here this year. Needed a bit of sun and peace. You’re not from around here, are you? Your accent… it’s lovely, very West Country. Dorchester, originally. Moved around a bit, but Dorset will always be home. I'm a teacher, primary school. That's why I needed a break too, to be honest. The end of term always takes it out of you. Plus, this is a far cry from grey skies and playground duty. Right, primary school. That’s… a lot of energy. My little niece used to drive my sister mental. Constant questions, boundless enthusiasm. Respect. I tried a bit of teaching myself, actually. A summer scheme for coding, aimed at teenagers. Disaster. Oh dear! What went wrong? They were just… not interested! Honestly, I’d spent weeks crafting this brilliant curriculum, thinking I was going to inspire the next generation of programmers. They wanted to film TikTok videos. It was humbling, to say the least. Realised pretty quickly coding bootcamps weren't for me. Well, you can't win them all! They live on their phones, it's the reality. It’s hard to compete with that. I try and integrate technology into my lessons, but it’s a constant battle to keep their attention.

…and honestly, Liam, I just don’t  get  Brenda. She leaves her dishes in the sink for days. Days! It's not like we're living in a student hall anymore, it's a proper flat! Aye, Brenda’s a character alright. Though, to be fair, she  is  swamped with that new project at work. Remember she was saying she’s having to pull ridiculous hours? That doesn’t excuse a biohazard growing in the kitchen, does it? And it’s not just the dishes. It’s the hair! Everywhere. On the sofa, in the bathroom… I found one in my tea this morning, I swear. Right, okay, the hair is a bit much. She really needs to invest in a hoover, or at least a lint roller. But look, we knew what we were getting into, didn't we? Brenda's, well,  Brenda . She’s always been a bit… chaotic. Chaotic is an understatement. It’s like living with a whirlwind of half-finished craft projects and empty biscuit packets. And then there’s Mark. He’s just… quiet. Mark’s alright. A bit of a wallflower, yeah, but he’s always polite. He cleans up after himself, doesn’t make a fuss. Honestly, he's the balancing force in that flat. Brenda would probably have wallpapered the kitchen if it wasn’t for Mark calmly pointing out it wouldn’t be practical. True. It's just... sometimes I miss having a flat with people who were, you know, on the same wavelength. Like when it was just me and Chloe. Remember how we’d have movie nights every week and actually, like,  talk  about things? Now it's either Brenda rambling about her alpaca farm dream or Mark staring intently at a houseplant. Aye, I remember. Those were good times. But you were always moaning about Chloe stealing your biscuits. Everyone’s got their quirks. And look, this is good practice for the real world, innit? You can’t choose your colleagues, and you certainly can’t choose all your housemates. Easy for you to say, you don’t  live  there! You’ve got your posh student accommodation, all minimalist and clean. I’m practically developing allergies to dust bunnies and glitter glue. Posh? It's a tiny room above a pub, love. And it's not exactly sparkling. It smells faintly of stale beer and regret. But it's  my  stale beer and regret, and I don’t have to share it with someone who thinks decorating with feathers is a good idea.

…and honestly, Doreen, I’m telling you, they’ve shrunk the biscuits! Used to be a proper handful, a good dunker. Now? They barely touch the tea. It’s daylight robbery, that’s what it is. Oh, Arthur, not the biscuit shrinkage again. You say that every time. It’s inflation, dear. Everything’s getting smaller and more expensive. It's not a personal vendetta against your digestive biscuits. Inflation, my foot. It's just greedy companies. Think they can get away with anything, they do. Still, at least we got the sprouts. Not the best looking, mind you, a bit… floppy. But they’ll do for Christmas dinner. Floppy sprouts are better than no sprouts, Arthur. And I got a good price on them. Five for a pound! Though young Timmy next door was giving me a right earful about wanting Brussels sprouts just for  him  this year. Says he’s developed a ‘sophisticated palate’. Sophisticated palate at seven! Fancy that. Timmy. A little posh now, is he? Remember when he used to eat mud pies? Oh, I remember. I had to fish a pebble out of his mouth once. Goodness me. Anyway, the butcher was very busy, had to queue for ages. But I managed to get a nice bit of turkey breast, and that Cumberland sausage you like. Good, good. Sausage is essential. Got enough bread rolls? Don't want a repeat of last year, having to eat sausage with crackers. That was a low point. Plenty of rolls, Arthur, don’t you worry. And I got some of that chutney you like, the one with the figs. Though it was a bit more than I usually pay, that inflation thing again kicking in, see? Figs, eh? Not a bad choice. Still think raspberry and ginger is superior. But figs will do. Did you manage to get that Christmas pudding I asked for? The one with the brandy butter… it’s the only kind worth having. I did. It was the last one! Nearly lost it to Mrs. Higgins, she was hovering like a vulture. She always wants the good ones. I had to be quick. It’s in this bag here. Heavy, that one is. They pack ‘em solid now. Good woman, Doreen. You're a marvel. A real marvel. So, everything’s in then? Presents are hidden? No chance of little Timmy finding them? Everything’s safely tucked away in the attic.

…and honestly, lad, I don’t know  why  they keep changing the mark schemes. It’s a nightmare! Last year it was all about ‘showing working’, this year it’s ‘elegant solutions’. What  is  an elegant solution to a simultaneous equation for a fifteen-year-old, eh? It’s just maths, not a blooming art competition! Sounds stressful, Mum. I’m just glad I’m nearly done with GCSEs. Though Physics is… well, Physics is still Physics. Aye, Physics. Always a tricky one. Your Grandad here barely scraped through it, didn't you, Arthur? More interested in tinkering with engines than triangles, he was. She’s not wrong. Triangles never fixed a Ford Anglia, let me tell you. Though I reckon I could build you a mark scheme for that, Doreen. Plenty of steps involved! Oh, you would, wouldn’t you? You always were a practical man. Now, are you two comfortable enough? Can I get you another cuppa? I made Brenda’s shortbread, you know, your favourite, Arthur. Don't mind if I do, lass! Brenda always made a cracking shortbread. Better than anything you get in the shops. And comfortable as can be, thank you. This armchair is a godsend for these old bones. Me too, dear. Lovely and warm in here. Not like that draughty old house we had in Hull, eh Arthur? Remember the winter of ‘63? Frozen pipes for weeks! Don’t remind me. Had to melt the ice with a camping stove! Nearly burned the kitchen down. That was a bit of a panic, that was. Wow, really? Sounds…intense. Intense is one word for it! Your Gran was a force of nature then, she was. Always had a plan, even if it involved a camping stove and a potential house fire. Speaking of plans, I was thinking, Michael – that’s you, love – maybe you could give your Grandad a hand with the garden next weekend? He’s been moaning about the weeds. Ugh, weeds? Mum! Now, now, be polite. It’d be lovely for both of them. And a bit of fresh air would do you good, glued to that computer screen all the time. He’s a good lad, Michael. Always willing to help. Unlike some! Now, now, Doreen. I  helped  with the garden. I pointed out where the weeds were. That's a crucial contribution, you know. Strategic weed identification. Strategic weed identification?

… honestly, I reckon it’s all a bit poncey, this collagen stuff. Gran's been going on about it for weeks. Says it's the secret to her ‘youthful glow’. Honestly, she looks… exactly the same.
