Gran's are good at that, aren't they? Mines swears by goose fat. Goose fat! Says it cures everything from arthritis to a bad mood. You’d think she was a medieval apothecary. Goose fat? Right. My Nan just spends all day watching daytime TV and complaining about the price of biscuits. More effective, frankly. Did anyone see that new documentary on Netflix about sleep? Properly messed me up. Now I’m obsessively tracking my REM cycles. Oh,  that  one! The one about how we're all chronically sleep-deprived and basically ruining our brains? Yeah, that was… uplifting. I downloaded one of those sleep apps. It just tells me I'm awake when I'm trying to fall asleep. Very helpful. They’re all just another way to sell you something, aren't they? Another gadget. Remember when everyone lost their minds over Fitbits? Now they're gathering dust in drawers. I'm more worried about my mum trying to sell me essential oils now. She’s joined a pyramid scheme, I’m convinced. Essential oils, collagen… the list goes on. It's like everyone's suddenly a health guru. Makes you wonder if anyone just…  is  okay, or if we’re all constantly trying to fix something. Speaking of fixing things, anyone heard from Jamie? He was supposed to be sorting out the broadband this morning. No, not a peep. Typical Jamie. Last time he “fixed” something, he managed to disable the entire kitchen. Remember the great toaster incident of ‘21? Oh god, yes! The smoke alarm was going off for hours. The flat smelled like burnt bread for a week. He’s a menace with electrical appliances. Seriously. He once tried to build a computer from scratch and nearly electrocuted himself. He's got enthusiasm, I’ll give him that. Just… lacks… technical competence. It’s a dangerous combination. Still, better him than one of us trying to wrestle with BT Openreach. Their customer service is designed to induce existential despair. It really is. I spent three hours on the phone with them last week trying to get my bill sorted. Three hours! And the guy on the other end sounded like he was actively fighting sleep.

…and then I was proper stressing about the dissertation deadline, honestly. Felt like I was gonna fail everything. Anyway, enough about me being a drama queen. What are we getting from the shops tomorrow? I’m practically living on toast at this point. Right, let’s see. Milk, definitely. Bread, you’re right about the toast. Your Dad’s been moaning about needing more coffee, the strong stuff, not that fancy instant rubbish. And we’re completely out of biscuits. Remember young Ethan here practically inhaled the last Jammie Dodgers? Hey! They were good! And I was studying! Needed the sugar rush for geography. Studying and biscuit consumption are not mutually exclusive, Ethan. Though a balanced diet is always recommended. We also need more loo roll, don’t we? I was the one who pointed that out last time, wasn’t I? You always point out the loo roll, Dad. It's your thing. Okay, milk, bread, coffee, biscuits, loo roll… anything else, Mum? I was thinking maybe some fruit? Apples or something. Good shout, love. Apples, and some bananas. Your Dad needs to eat  something  other than ready meals when he’s working away. He’ll be back in London on Sunday, and I don’t want him collapsing with exhaustion. Oh, and speaking of collapsing...did you manage to get rid of that fly that was buzzing round earlier? It was driving me mad! I tried! It wouldn't go away! I swatted at it loads, but it just kept doing circles. It landed on your arm for a second, Mum! Ugh, don’t remind me! Nearly had a heart attack. Your father eventually got it with the rolled-up newspaper. Brutal, but effective. Serves it right. Little blighters. I got bitten by something last night, though. On my ankle. It's proper itchy. Let me see. Looks like a mosquito bite, or possibly a midge. Have you put anything on it? Just a bit of antihistamine cream. It’s not helping much. Feels like it's swelling up. Try some tea tree oil, pet. It's a natural antiseptic and good for bites. I’ve got some in the bathroom cupboard. Or a paste made of baking soda and water can draw the itch out. Ew, baking soda paste sounds gross. It does sound… not pleasant. I’ll try the tea tree oil first. Thanks, Mum. So, shopping list - confirmed: milk, bread, coffee, biscuits, loo roll, apples, bananas, tea tree oil acquisition.

…and then Mr. Harrison  actually  made us do star jumps for being late. Star jumps! Like we’re five years old! Honestly, the cheek of it. No way! Mr. Harrison? He's usually so chill. What was the excuse this time? Was it Leo winding him up again? He’s the master of subtly annoying teachers, you know. Not Leo, surprisingly. It was Mia and Chloe, chatting away about some TikTok trend right as the bell went. He just…lost it. Said it was disrespecting the learning environment. Star jumps! It was mortifying. My sports bra was  not  prepared. Oh, that's brutal. I can’t believe he'd do that. He knows most of us have, like, growth spurts happening constantly. Sports bras are a battlefield. Speaking of P.E., did you see the new equipment they got? I think Mrs. Davies is trying to bribe us into actually  liking  rounders. The bright orange bats? Yeah, they’re…something. Still won’t make me suddenly brilliant at it, though. Honestly, I'm just praying for the athletics season. I'm actually alright at long jump. What about Science? Did you finish the homework on the periodic table? I’m completely stuck on isotopes. Ugh, the periodic table. Don’t even get me started. Honestly, I just copied Finley's. He’s a genius when it comes to that stuff. And yes, isotopes are evil. It's all just a blur of protons and neutrons and…argh. It makes my head hurt. Did you see that video EmzExplains did on atomic structure? It actually made a bit more sense. EmzExplains! Omg, she’s brilliant, isn’t she? She explains everything so simply. I love how she uses analogies. Way better than Mr. Peterson's droning on about electron shells. Have you seen her latest one on climate change? It’s really scary. Yeah! I watched it last night. It  is  scary. Makes you feel a bit helpless, doesn’t it? Mum was going on about reducing our carbon footprint afterward. It’s good, but…it feels like one drop in the ocean, you know? Totally! It does. Anyway, back to school drama. Have you heard anything about what happened with Zara and Oliver? Apparently, it’s a full-blown social media war. Oh,  no . They were together like, five minutes ago. What's happened? I saw something on Instagram, a really cryptic story from Zara with sad music, but I didn’t know what it was about.

… honestly, I feel like I’m wading through treacle. My head’s proper pounding. Think it’s just a cold, though, yeah? Not…the thing. Definitely just a cold. You’ve been complaining about a tickle in your throat since Tuesday. The thing would’ve knocked you sideways by now. You've had both boosters, haven’t you? And the flu jab? You're basically Fort Knox when it comes to respiratory illnesses. Aye, I had ‘em all. Honestly. It’s just… draining. I even tried one of those vitamin C fizz things. Tasted like someone dissolved a highlighter pen in water. Sounds about right. Remember that time you insisted lemon and ginger cured everything? You practically forced me to drink that concoction when  I  had man-flu. It does help! Honestly! Though, thinking about feeling rough… it reminds me of that food poisoning I got in Brighton last year. Now  that  was awful. Oh god, don’t even  mention  Brighton. I had to spend the entire journey home with you making noises that shouldn't be possible from a human being. And the state of the hotel room… A dark time. It felt like I’d personally offended every bacteria in a five-mile radius. Although, watching Lloyd Grossman on  MasterChef  while being simultaneously ill wasn’t…terrible. He's so comforting, isn’t he? Lloyd Grossman? Really? That’s your sick-day comfort viewing? I would've thought something a bit more dramatic. Like, hospital dramas. You’re always fascinated by hospitals. It’s just… the routines, the procedures. And the people watching. It’s fascinating! Like, I was reading this article about how they’re using AI now to analyse body language – in A&E, specifically – to predict who’s likely to leave without being seen. No way! That’s…kind of creepy. And slightly dystopian. So, a camera just…watches people and decides if they’re going to be a bother? Well, apparently, it's more nuanced than that. It’s looking at things like micro-expressions, posture, how people interact with staff. The idea is to flag patients who might need extra support, or reassurance, before they decide to just walk out. Avoids wasting resources, apparently. Still feels a bit…Big Brother-ish. Plus, doctors are supposed to be  good  at reading people. That’s part of their job, isn't it? Not replacing it with an algorithm. It’s not meant to replace them!

Right. ‘Quixotic’. Twenty-two points. Honestly, this board is a disaster area. You’ve all deliberately blocked every decent space. Deliberately? I simply played the best tiles I had, dear. It’s called strategy. Besides, you had a perfectly good spot for ‘jazz’ last turn, and you wasted it on… ‘elm’! Oh, don’t start you two. It’s all good-natured ribbing. Though I must say, Margaret, 'elm'  was  a strange choice. It felt…defensive. It was a holding pattern! I was waiting for a vowel! This game is cruel. Reminds me of trying to get a parking space at the Trafford Centre on a Saturday. Utter gridlock. The Trafford Centre…a monument to consumerism. Though, I confess, I did get a rather fine pair of socks there last year. But the traffic…yes, appalling. Worse than trying to get a decent cut of lamb from Wilkinson's butcher on a Friday. The queue snakes around the block. Speaking of Wilkinson’s, I need to pop in tomorrow. They’re getting a new delivery of Cumberland sausages. Apparently, Mrs. Higgins was practically elbowing people out of the way last week to secure hers. Honestly, people! It's a sausage. Though, you do make a good shepherd’s pie with those, I’ll grant you that. Did you see that article in  The Wire  magazine about the resurgence of vinyl?  The Wire ? Still going, is it? I used to read it religiously. My students would roll their eyes when I’d rabbit on about post-punk. You always had impeccable taste in music, Agnes. Remember that jazz festival we went to in Edinburgh? The one with…what was his name? The saxophonist with the unruly hair? Oh, Hamish MacIntyre! A wild man. He nearly set fire to the stage with his solos. Those were the days. Though, I suspect if I tried to go to a concert now, I’d need a Sherpa. Speaking of Edinburgh, I've been meaning to ask, Agnes, did you ever get around to putting those photos from your trip on Facebook? The ones of the castle? Not yet, David. I'm still wrestling with Facebook. It's all so…performative. Everyone showing off their perfectly curated lives. I prefer a good, old-fashioned postcard. Oh, come on, Agnes, it's just a bit of fun! I put up photos of the garden this morning. Got sixteen likes already.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of people at those exhibitions was just  staggering . Not like a little village fête, you know? We’re talking halls stretching on for what felt like miles, all crammed with machinery. You wouldn't believe the noise! Oh, I can imagine. Germany does scale well when it comes to engineering shows, doesn't it? Hanover, particularly. I spent a fair bit of time there myself, though not selling printing systems, I confess. I was with a firm developing industrial coatings. Dull as ditchwater compared to what  you  were doing, I suspect. Dull? Not necessarily! Coatings are crucial. Everything needs protecting from the elements, doesn’t it? But yes, printing… that was a different beast altogether. The whole thing started, really, with a frustration. Existing systems were so… clunky. Slow. Wasteful. My husband, bless him, was a brilliant engineer. He’d been tinkering for years, and I, well, I had a bit of an eye for marketing, for what people  wanted , even if they didn't know it themselves. A good combination, I’d say. Engineer and…the persuader. That’s often how it works. What specifically did you improve? Was it the speed? The quality of the print? It was a bit of everything, actually. He designed a completely new ink delivery system, which dramatically reduced wastage, and then we coupled that with a digital control panel - unheard of back then, late seventies, early eighties. Most things were still mechanically controlled. We weren’t the first with digital, of course, but we were clever about  how  we used it. And it was smaller. Massively smaller than the competition. We called it the ‘MicroPrint’. Catchy, eh? Very. It sounds like you tapped into something. Did you patent it, the ink system? Oh, absolutely! Several patents, in fact. He was a meticulous man. And then, the real challenge began: getting it  to  market. Germany was key. The Drupa exhibition in Düsseldorf… that was where everything changed. We’d booked a tiny stand, thinking we’d be lucky to get noticed. But the reaction… it was phenomenal. Printers from all over the world came to look. Drupa! A leviathan. I remember seeing some of the machines on show there, even the coating ones were enormous. What was it about the German market that made it so receptive? They're incredibly technically minded, the Germans. They appreciate precision engineering. And they aren’t afraid to adopt new technology if it delivers demonstrable benefits.

…and honestly, Mr. Davies makes English Lit feel like decoding ancient hieroglyphs. He  loves  dissecting every single comma. It’s exhausting! Like, can't we just enjoy the story? Aye, sounds a bit like Old Man Hemmings, my English teacher. Used to bang on about the Oxford comma for a full lesson. Drove us all mad. But he did have a point, mind you. Language is…precise. It  needs  that precision, even if it doesn’t feel like it when you’re sixteen and just want to read about vampires. Vampires are important literary devices, Dad! And it's not just commas, it's the etymology of  everything . He was going on about the origins of 'quinoa' yesterday. Quinoa! Who needs to know that on the way to applying for university?! Well, a good university will want to know you've got a curious mind. And quinoa  is  an interesting word, now you mention it. From the Quechua language, derives from ‘kinwa’. Been around for thousands of years. Better source of protein than a lot of things, too. You should try it when we get to Cornwall, maybe find a farmer’s market? Ugh, farmer’s markets. Sounds…rustic. I’m more of a city girl, you know? Honestly, I'm still trying to decide what to apply for. I was thinking maybe Philosophy? Philosophy, eh? That’s a good one! Bit different. What sparked that? I don't know. I just… like thinking about why things are. Like, what  is  real, and stuff. Mr. Peterson in RE actually makes that interesting, unlike Mr. Davies makes Shakespeare. Although, thinking about it, philosophy feels a bit…useless. Will I even get a job? Useless? Now that’s daft. Thinking’s never useless. It’s the foundation of everything. And Philosophy graduates end up in all sorts – law, journalism, even business. Though, if you’re worried about a job, maybe consider something with a bit more…practical application alongside it? Psychology, perhaps? Maybe. Look, is this the right way? I haven’t seen a sign for the A30 for ages. Aye, it is. Just coming up now. We took that little detour through Worcestershire to avoid the traffic near Birmingham. Much more scenic, though. Worcestershire… try spelling  that  in an exam. Don't even! The counties are a nightmare. And the pronunciation! Is it Wooster-shire, or Wor-chester-shire? Depends who you ask!

…and honestly, the catering at that conference last week was  criminal . Seriously, beige buffet, beige everything. You’d think for the price they were charging, they could at least manage some colour, eh? It was in Birmingham, mind you. Never trust Birmingham catering. Beige, eh? Sounds grim. I’m used to a packed lunch, so anything’s an improvement, really. Though me dad’s packed lunches weren’t exactly gourmet. Always a cheese and pickle, without fail. Every. Single. Day. Your father was a man of habit, that’s for sure. Mine was the same with his Sunday roast. Yorkshire pudding, obviously. Couldn't have a Sunday without a Yorkshire. Said his mother made the best, naturally. All mothers do, don’t they? Ooh, a proper Yorkshire pudding! Now  that  is something. My grandma used to make ‘em like, enormous. They’d practically fill the tin. Doncaster puddings are the best, obviously. Though I reckon she put a secret ingredient in, something she wouldn’t tell anyone. Sounds good. I haven’t had a proper roast in ages. Just end up grabbing a kebab after work most nights. Easier, you know? Not much cooking involved. Kebabs are good for a quick fix, yeah. Though this is the benefit of being forced to cook for other people, isn't it? Gets you out of your routine. So, are we definitely doing a curry then? I picked up a decent Madras paste. Curry sounds lovely, dear. Not too hot, though. My stomach isn't what it used to be. Remember that vindaloo I tried at that Indian place in Brighton, years ago? Thought I was going to be sick all night. Haha, yeah! You were clutching your stomach the whole way home. Should’ve known better, ordering a vindaloo, old man! You and spice don't mix. Right, Madras it is, then. Mild-ish Madras. I can always add some chilli flakes for you, Leo, if you’re feeling brave. Although, judging by your kebab intake, I suspect you’re used to a bit of kick. I can handle a bit, yeah. Though I'd rather get my heat from a sneaky Nandos peri-peri sauce than a proper chilli, to be honest. Speaking of heat, how's your mum doing, Amelia? Haven’t seen her since… Christmas, was it? She’s alright. Still moaning about my brother not calling enough. You know how she is.

…and honestly, the shift last night was  mental . Stag do. Absolute chaos. They thought it was hilarious to order increasingly ridiculous cocktails and then try and name them after their mates. Ended up with something called ‘The Kevinator’ which was basically anything brightly coloured I could find. Oh, dear. Sounds… engaging. You don't look like you've had much sleep. Still, at least it's a story, right? Bit better than marking essays on the subjunctive, I suppose. Definitely better. Though my feet are killing me. You look remarkably cheerful for a Saturday morning spent presumably knee-deep in grammatical rules. How’s the teaching going? Still wrangling teenagers with a tenuous grasp of the past perfect? Don’t even  start  me on the past perfect. It’s a constant battle. Actually, I’m running a little workshop this afternoon on using tenses in creative writing. Trying to get them to see it’s not just about rules, it’s about  effect . It's… a challenge. What about you? Still thinking of sticking with the bar long-term? I remember you mentioning something about a history degree. Yeah, the history degree is… gathering dust, sadly. It’s a good fallback, I guess. Paying off the student loan’s a priority, and the bar pays the bills. Plus, it’s not the worst. Good money, meets people, good craic, as they say. Though I do sometimes wonder if I should be doing something… more. I know that feeling. I love teaching, genuinely, but sometimes I wonder if I should have gone down the academic route properly, stuck with the research. It’s the freedom, isn’t it? The ability to really delve into something. Exactly! Although freedom doesn't pay the rent. Speaking of things that don't pay the rent…Have you finally bitten the bullet and started driving lessons? I remember you saying how much you hated the thought of it. I have. And I deeply regret it. My instructor is… let's say,  enthusiastic . He keeps shouting instructions like I'm a fighter pilot. And parallel parking? Don’t even go there. I nearly mounted the curb this morning. Oh, that's classic. I passed first time, thankfully. My dad drilled me relentlessly in an empty car park for weeks. It’s surprisingly useful though, now I think about it. Being able to just… go. Have you thought about where you’ll drive once you’ve passed?

…and honestly, Doreen, you wouldn’t  believe  the traffic getting ‘ere. Round the A11, a right kerfuffle. Had to go all the way round Attleborough just to get back on track. Thought we were going to miss break proper! Oh, Arthur, you always say that about the A11! It can't  always  be a kerfuffle. Though, I suppose it  is  getting busier. Did you have your coffee yet? I put the kettle on as soon as I saw your car pull up – you looked flustered. Right, apologies for the delay. Found this old box in the attic. Think it’ll do nicely for the donations at the bell ringing fundraiser. It’s a bit scuffed, but sturdy enough. Good on you, David. That’s a proper good idea, that. Folks are always more willing when they can  see  where their money’s going, even if it’s just into a nice box. Though, mind you, I still reckon a banner would be best. Something bright, saying "Help us ring for joy!" A banner? Arthur, you’re always thinking big! We’re just raising a bit of money for new ropes, not building a cathedral. The box is perfectly adequate. Besides, where would we even  put  a banner? David’s garden's the only space big enough. Doreen’s right, Arthur. We're keeping it simple. I’ve already spoken to Mrs. Higgins about donating some of her geraniums to decorate the table where the box will sit. Nice splash of colour. Though I must say, that reminds me, your begonias are looking rather splendid, Doreen. Oh, thank you, David. I’ve been giving them a good feed. They enjoyed the rain we had last week. They remind me of the Gambia, actually. Such vibrant colours everywhere. We went there a few years back, you remember? Gambia? Lovely place. Bit hot for my liking though. Give me good old Norfolk any day. Though I did hear a story about someone pretending to be ill over there… now what was his name? Seemed to be in the papers a bit… You’re thinking of that case with the man and Munchausen Syndrome, Arthur. Horrible business. Faking illnesses for attention. Extraordinary behaviour. They said he travelled around specifically seeking out medical treatment, creating a whole elaborate story. That's the one! Extraordinary is right. Makes you wonder what goes on in some people’s heads.

…and honestly, the interface is just  awful . It’s like they actively tried to make it less intuitive. I keep accidentally favouriting things I don’t even like! It’s supposed to be a music discovery app, not a frustrating puzzle. Which one are you on about now, Lila? You’ve downloaded, like, five new music apps this month. “VibeCheck”. Honestly, the name alone should have been a warning. It promised personalised playlists, but it just keeps giving me… yacht rock.  Yacht rock , Leo! Do I  look  like I listen to yacht rock? Yacht rock? That's a niche. You’ve got good taste, though, rejecting it. Is it better than that 'SoundSurge' thing you were obsessed with last week? The one that only played songs from 1983? Oh god, don't even remind me. That was a dark time. SoundSurge was an…experience. But at least it was consistently bad. VibeCheck is just  inconsistent . Sounds stressful. I'm sticking with Spotify, thanks. Simplicity is key. Speaking of key… did anyone see that new horror film, 'The Hollow'? Oh yeah! Chloe and I went last night. Proper jump scares, innit? I nearly spilled my popcorn all over that bloke in front of us. Oh, tell me everything! I'm a wimp, but I love a good scary movie. Especially if I can hide behind a cushion for most of it. Leo was clutching my arm the entire time. Like a limpet. Hey! It was legitimately terrifying! That scene with the… you know… the thing in the well? Oh, yes. That was… unsettling. I heard it’s based on a local legend around here, something about old man Hemlock and his farm. Old man Hemlock? I think I remember my nan telling me stories about him. Something about disappearing livestock? That’s the one. Apparently, his well was cursed. Honestly, I’m going to have trouble sleeping now. Right? Anyway, Chloe and I grabbed pizza afterwards. Best cure for post-horror trauma. She was asking about your holiday plans, Amy. Have you and Mark actually booked anything yet? We’re thinking Greece, maybe Crete. Mark’s been really stressed with work, so we both need a beach and some sunshine. It's proving difficult to find something within budget, though. Everything is so expensive these days. Oh, Greece is amazing. I went to Santorini a few years ago, it was beautiful. Have you looked at Airbnb?

…and honestly, the sat nav took me the scenic route, didn’t it? Right through Blofield, then down those tiny lanes near the Yare. Nearly lost a wing mirror, I did. Thought I was going to end up in the river! Blofield, eh? Always a bit of a nightmare round there. Though, you'd think a modern sat nav would know better. Mine rarely leads me astray, though admittedly I don't go much further than the shops these days. Keeps things simple. You still driving that Volvo, Arthur? Still the Volvo, yes. Good old reliable. Bit of a beast to park, mind, but she’s solid as a rock. Though, I'm starting to think, at my age, maybe I  should  be thinking about something a bit…smaller. Something easier on the old legs. Especially with the parking in Norwich getting worse by the day. You say that every time you drive, Arthur! You’ve been saying you’ll get a smaller car for ten years! And honestly, that Volvo is a lovely car. You look very distinguished in it. Distinguished? I look like a lorry driver trying to navigate a bicycle lane! Seriously though, the cost of everything is going up. Petrol, insurance… it’s crippling. Remember when you could fill up for twenty quid? Twenty quid? Gosh, Arthur, you’re talking ancient history now! More like sixty now, isn’t it? Though, I mostly rely on the bus these days. Safer that way, and a lot cheaper. Though having said that, the bus service isn’t what it used to be. Used to run like clockwork, now you're lucky if it turns up. That’s true. Old Mrs. Higgins missed her doctor’s appointment last week because the bus just…didn't show. She was fuming. She had to get a taxi, and you know how expensive those are. Exactly! It's all a mess. Trying to get anywhere these days feels like an ordeal. And speaking of getting anywhere, how did  you  two get here today? Eileen, did Cyril drive? Cyril dropped me off, yes. He said the A47 was absolutely jammed. Apparently, there was an accident near Dereham. Took him nearly an hour and a half from Costessey. Aye, heard about that on the radio. They’re widening that stretch, aren’t they? Been going on for months. Makes things even more chaotic. Honestly, you’d think they’d plan these things better.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork! I thought teaching endless equations was bad, but  this  is another level. Honestly, I'm starting to think we should’ve just stayed put. Remember how lovely the garden was getting? Mum, you said the garden was too much work after your hip. And you weren't keen on being so far from Dad. This is closer to him, which is the main thing, isn’t it? Plus, the bungalow is all on one level. No more stairs! Though, this traffic on the M6 is dreadful. Are we nearly there yet? Feels like we've been driving for hours. “Are we nearly there yet?” Sounds like you two when  you  were little. We’re still a good hour, maybe more, from Manchester, love. This is the M6 – notoriously slow. At least we have the tea and biscuits to keep us going. Margaret, another biscuit? They’re ginger, your favourite. Thank you, David. Ginger snaps  are  a weakness. It’s just… the thought of unpacking everything  again . I swear, every time we move, my back feels ten years older. And speaking of backs, how’s yours been holding up? You didn’t mention needing another physio appointment. It’s alright, mostly. A bit creaky in the morning, but nothing a strong cup of tea can't fix. Though, the consultant did say I need to be more active. Easier said than done, particularly when the weather’s like this. This move might actually  force  me to get out more, exploring the area around Dad. That's good. It'll be nice for you to have something to focus on. And Dad will be thrilled, he's been saying how much he misses having you nearby for ages. He’s been muttering about needing help with his internet again. He’s hopeless with technology, your father. Absolutely hopeless. Reminds me of poor old Mr. Henderson from down the street. Tried to book a flight to Malaga online… ended up accidentally signing up for a timeshare in Florida! The stories he told… Oh, that’s brilliant! Airports are a nightmare anyway. I had a dreadful experience last month trying to fly back from a job – a transcription gig in Amsterdam. Delayed for six hours because of fog. Absolute chaos. Everyone was crammed into that tiny departure lounge, and the food options were… questionable, to say the least.

…and then Mr. Henderson just  looked  at me, all stern, and said, "Honestly, Bethany, you’re spending far too much time on that TikTok. It'll rot your brain!" Honestly, Mum, it’s just dance challenges, it's not like I’m learning how to build a bomb. Right, well, Mr. Henderson’s a bit…old school. He taught history for thirty years, remember? He probably thinks anything invented after the printing press is the downfall of civilization. Though, a little less screen time wouldn't hurt, darling. By the way, I have  amazing  news. Oh? Is it about Gran? Is she feeling better? She sounded a bit wheezy on the phone yesterday. Gran’s fine, she’s actually knitting a whole new set of ridiculously colourful socks. No, this is about… well, remember your bike? The blue one, the Raleigh you loved? Luna? You mean… you found it? Seriously? After all this time? I thought it was gone forever! It was stolen like, three months ago! I did! Well, PC Davies did, really. Apparently, a couple of lads were trying to sell it at the car boot sale down by the pier this morning. They’d painted over some of the blue, tried to make it look black, but Davies recognised the distinctive scratch on the frame. The one you got when you… what was it? Tried to jump the kerb outside old Mrs. Gable’s? Oh,  please . Don't remind me! I was convinced she saw the whole thing and was silently judging me. And seriously, he recognised it  after  they tried to repaint it? He's a hero! Where is it? Is it okay? It’s in the shed, I’ve given it a bit of a clean. The brakes need adjusting, and they did a terrible job with the paint, bits of blue are still showing through. But it’s structurally sound. It just needs a bit of TLC. Oh my gosh, I need to see it! Can I go look now? Please? I haven’t been out cycling properly in ages. I've been borrowing Liam’s old mountain bike, but it's so heavy and clunky. Luna was perfect. Hold your horses, speed demon. We’ve got shepherd’s pie in the oven, it'll be ready in half an hour. You can go inspect Luna  after  you’ve eaten. And maybe, just maybe, we can go for a cycle along the seafront tomorrow, weather permitting?

Right, I officially surrender. Rhys is a  monster  at Ticket to Ride. Honestly, it's like he’s predicting my every move. Monster is a bit strong, isn't it, Sarah? I just… appreciate efficient route planning. It’s a skill, you know? Like understanding train dynamics. Actually, speaking of which… Did you know the steepest gradient on a mainline railway in the UK is on the Lickey Incline? Oh, here we go. Another Rhys train fact. Prepare for a full lecture. It  is  interesting, Gareth! It’s 1 in 37! They used to attach a banker engine – a helper engine – to the back of the train to get it up the hill. Bankers, you say? Reminds me of my time working with railway charities. We did a lot of work supporting retired signalmen and engine drivers. Good, solid folk. So, Sarah, are you admitting defeat, then? Fancy a cuppa? I made a batch of Welsh cakes this morning. Defeat is putting it mildly, Alun. I may have to concede all my railway shares to Rhys at this rate. And Welsh cakes sound  divine . Honestly, I’m fueled solely by caffeine and the distant hope of blocking Rhys's route to Edinburgh. Don't worry, love. It's just a game. And Welsh cakes do rather improve everything, don’t they? I brought some bara brith as well, if anyone’s interested. Bara brith  and  Welsh cakes? This holiday is turning into a national carbohydrate festival. I’m in. Though, I’m still plotting my continental domination on this board. I'm aiming for Berlin. Berlin’s ambitious! You'll need a lot of blue cards for that. And avoid letting Sarah recover – she's deceptively strategic when she’s angry. Deceptively strategic? I’d like to think I’m consistently strategic. It’s just Rhys is… unnervingly good. It’s probably something to do with growing up in Cardiff – he was born on a railway line, I swear. Don't be ridiculous, Sarah. Though Cardiff  is  a railway hub. My grandfather worked at Cardiff General station for forty years. He used to tell me stories about the steam trains… a completely different world, of course. Speaking of different worlds, Alun, how’s the charity work going? Still dealing with fundraising and the usual paperwork? Keeps me busy. We’re focused on providing support for homeless veterans at the moment. It's heartbreaking, but rewarding work.

Right. That's… underwhelming. Seven points for 'elm'. Seriously? I thought I was being clever with the 'm'. Clever placement, maybe. Not a clever word, though. You need to think bigger, love. Think… Q, Z, J. Those are the money letters. Easy for you to say, Mr. ‘Jazz’ for 32 points last turn. You’re just a natural. It’s unfair. Pure skill, darling. Pure skill. Though, admittedly, landing on that double word score definitely helped. Still, you're better at strategy games, aren’t you? Settlers of Catan, you  destroy  me. That’s different. Catan requires ruthlessness. Scrabble just requires a ridiculously good vocabulary, and apparently, luck. It’s like life, isn’t it? Is it? Going deep there, El. Over a game of Scrabble? Well, isn't it? Some people are born with all the vowels and consonants aligned in their favour. And some of us are stuck with a rack full of vowels and a lingering sense of inadequacy. You’re ridiculous. You’re a brilliant lecturer, you’re published… don't tell me a board game is making you question your existential purpose. It’s the Norfolk air. It makes you philosophical. Plus, being back at Mum and Dad’s… it sparks something. They’re  so  board game obsessed. It’s practically a national sport in this house. Every holiday, it’s Monopoly, Cluedo, Scrabble. It’s a ritual. More intense than London, for sure. I mean, we play things, but it's more likely to be a quick co-op video game after work. Less… commitment. London life is… fleeting. Everyone's too busy. Exactly! And it extends to the drinking culture too, I think. Here, it’s a leisurely pint in the pub, chatting to everyone. Back home, it’s… shots and speed. Get in, get plastered, get out. No nuance. That’s a fair point. The pub culture around here is genuinely different. It's… social, rather than transactional. In London, it feels like people are often trying to  achieve  something with their drinking, not just… enjoy it. Networking, showing off, proving something. You’ve hit the nail on the head. It's exhausting just thinking about it. Here, Dad's already planning our next pub visit. He’s got a whole route mapped out, apparently. 'The Full Norfolk' he calls it. Three pubs, different ales at each. Sounds… ambitious. And probably involving a very early night.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of cardboard from unpacking is ridiculous. I thought I’d be feeling settled by now, but it’s still everywhere. It’s like living in a Amazon warehouse. Tell me about it. Remember when we helped Mark move, and he just  left  all the boxes in the spare room for three months? Said he was “strategically storing things.” Strategic chaos, more like. Men and their…systems. Honestly, a tidy house is a tidy mind, and I can't  function  with clutter. You alright with the lasagne, Anya? Made a bit extra knowing your appetite. It’s amazing, Kerrie, honestly. Thank you. It’s the first proper meal I’ve had in days. Just microwave meals and takeaway since the move. It's exhausting, even with Leo helping. Leo’s a good lad. Always willing to lend a hand, isn't he? Although, he did nearly put the fridge on the landing last time he helped someone move. Don't remind me! I swear, he thinks gravity is more of a suggestion than a rule. It’s just… the whole process is making me question everything. Like, did I  need  that bookcase? Was it a sensible purchase? You always need a bookcase, dear. What’s life without books? And don’t worry about sensible. I spent a good ten years thinking a hot pink armchair was a good idea. It clashed horribly with everything. Oh, I remember that armchair! It was… bold. You were going through a phase, weren’t you? A phase of questionable taste, as it turned out. But you learn. Speaking of learning, how’s that Master's going, Anya? Still enjoying the research? It’s…okay. It feels a bit pointless sometimes, to be honest. All this theory, and then I’m just an administrator. It's not like I'm using it day-to-day. Liam keeps telling me I'm being self-deprecating. He's right, you are. It’s still a massive achievement, having a postgraduate qualification. My sixth form results feel like a lifetime ago. Though, they were good enough to get me where I am, so can't complain. This project co-ordinator role is keeping me busy, at least. Don’t underestimate practical experience, Rhys. These days, it’s often valued more than a piece of paper. And Anya, you’re brilliant at what you do. Organised, efficient…you probably keep that whole office running single-handedly.

… honestly, Mum, this clutch is  killing  me. I swear it’s getting worse. Maybe I should just bite the bullet and get a new car? Something a bit… less vintage. Oh, Leo, not this again. Your grandfather would be turning in his grave. That Morris Minor is practically family. Besides, you said you were saving for that trip to France. A new car will swallow your funds whole. France can wait. My left leg can’t. Seriously, this hill start we just did nearly rolled us back into that Deliveroo bike. And remember Uncle Barry driving it? He stalled going up Primrose Hill and practically caused a pile-up! Barry has always been a dreadful driver. That’s beside the point. It's a charming car, Leo. And it gets you from A to B. Mostly. We’re nearly there, anyway. Just past Camden. Gosh, look at the traffic. “Charming” isn’t the word I’d use when I’m fighting the steering wheel and praying the brakes hold. Speaking of which, is this errand absolutely essential? It feels like half of London is heading to Primrose Hill for a Sunday stroll. It is essential! It’s Mrs. Henderson’s 80th. And I promised I’d deliver the little porcelain shepherdess. She collects them, you know. Honestly, the lengths some people go to… Still better than being stuck in the office, though. Right, Mrs. Henderson and her sheep. Sounds thrilling. How’s work anyway? Still battling publishers over comma splices and marketing budgets? You make it sound dreadful. It’s… stimulating. We’ve got a particularly fiery debate going on at the  TLS  at the moment – digital versus print. Young Tim down in Sub-Ed is convinced everything should be online, interactive, podcasts, the whole shebang. And you're holding the line for paper and ink? Someone has to. There’s something… tactile about a book, Leo. The smell, the feel of the pages. An ebook just isn’t the same. It’s the  experience . Although, admittedly, the subscription numbers are… shifting. Tim’s got a point about accessibility. I get it. I do. But I still prefer a physical book. It feels… permanent. Plus, you can’t really scribble notes in the margins of a Kindle. Though, digital’s good for travelling. Lightens the load. Precisely. It’s not one or the other, is it? It’s about finding a balance.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of that seagull! It swooped down, nicked the chip right outta me hand, and then just… glared at me. Glared! Like  I  was the one in the wrong. You and seagulls, Liv. It’s a lifelong battle, isn’t it? Same happened to me in Blackpool last year. Bold as brass, they are. Took a whole sausage roll, the greedy buggers. Oh, Blackpool. God, remember when we all went to Blackpool after our A-Levels? That was chaos. Chaos is an understatement, Chloe. Absolute, unadulterated chaos. I think I lost a shoe on the Pleasure Beach. Still haven’t found it. Lost a shoe? You always had dodgy footwear, Elsie. Probably just fell apart from the sheer excitement. Hey! They were perfectly good sandals at the time! They just weren’t designed for intense rollercoaster speeds, apparently. They were those glittery ones, weren’t they? The ones that shed glitter  everywhere ? I think I was still finding glitter in me hair for weeks. Aye, and Lewis nearly got us all arrested for trying to sneak into that arcade after closing time. Remember, Lewis? Thinking we were proper spies. I was feeling resourceful! It was a perfectly logical plan at the time. Plus, I really needed to win a giant Pikachu. Priorities, eh? Logical? You climbed over a fence and tripped the alarm! It was less  Mission: Impossible  and more  Keystone Cops . The security guard was  fuming . He looked like he’d rather be anywhere else, honestly. All we got was a right telling off and ushered outta there. Worth it though, wasn’t it? The memories. Speaking of holidays, did anyone actually have a relaxing one this year? I spent mine mostly stressed about my dissertation. Relaxing? Nah. I went camping with me dad. “Get back to nature,” he said. “Bonding experience,” he said. It rained non-stop for three days. We spent the entire time crammed in the tent playing cards and arguing over whether the beans were cooked enough. Sounds idyllic. Camping’s not for me. Too many bugs. And the toilets…don’t even get me started. I went to Benidorm with me mates. Actually, it was pretty chill. Loads of sun, cheap cocktails…the usual. Though, I did end up accidentally entering a talent show. No way! Chloe, you? A  talent show ? What did you do?! It was a karaoke night, alright? And after a few sangrias, I just… volunteered.

… honestly, the condensation inside the tent was worse than being  in  the rain. And believe me, it  rained . Biblical, it was. Proper deluge. Still, wouldn't trade it for a week in Barbados. Oh, Arthur, you and your winter camping. It sounds utterly miserable! Though, I s’pose there’s a certain grit to it, isn’t there? I mean, deliberately seeking out discomfort. As a therapist, I find that… interesting. Aye, Dad’s a glutton for punishment. But he’s got a point, Mum. It’s not about the comfort, it’s the… well, stripping things back. No phone signal, no distractions. Just you, the elements, and figuring out how to stay warm. It’s remarkably grounding. Exactly! Grounding! That’s a good way to put it, Calum. Folks nowadays, they're too plugged in. Always needing stimulation. This forces you to  be  present. You notice things you’d never normally see. The way the frost forms on the heather, the tracks of a pine marten in the snow… even the smell of the damp earth is different in the winter. The smell of damp earth? Arthur, you romanticize dampness. I spent enough years as a nurse dealing with trench foot to have no fondness for it whatsoever. But I  do  understand the appeal of disconnecting. I’ve sent patients out on mindful walks for less. It's that exposure therapy idea, but naturally occurring. Facing a minor challenge – cold, damp – builds resilience. It’s a different kind of resilience than, say, dealing with a hospital ward, Mum. It’s… primal. And it changes your perspective. You appreciate hot tea and a warm bed an awful lot more, that's for sure. Last February, when the wind was howling and the snow was up to your knees, I was genuinely grateful for a waterproof sock. A waterproof  sock . You get used to appreciating the small things! I remember one trip to the Peak District, years ago. Temperature plummeted overnight. Woke up with my water bottle frozen solid. Had to melt the ice with my body heat just to get a sip. Oh, Arthur! You're awful. You'd get hypothermia just telling the story. Seriously though, is it safe? All alone out there in the winter? Don’t you worry about getting into trouble? We’re careful, Mum. Proper preparation is key. Layers, emergency shelter, knowing the terrain. Dad’s meticulous about it.

…and honestly, the whole thing just felt  pointless . All that build-up, all that hype, for… that? It was like they’d run out of ideas five minutes before the ending and just slapped something on. Woah, hold on. ‘The Crimson Horizon’? Pointless? I thought it was brilliant! Visually stunning, the score was incredible, and the ambiguity… that’s what made it! You’re telling me you didn’t understand the symbolism of the collapsing lighthouse? Symbolism? Ben, pet, it was a lighthouse falling over. It’s a lighthouse falling over! They could’ve at least  tried  to make it more nuanced. It felt like they were trying too hard to be clever, you know? Like, "Ooh, look at us, we’re doing art!" When really it was just…pretentious. Honestly, give me a good, solid thriller any day. Something where things actually  happen . Pretentious? That’s harsh. I think you’re missing the subtext. It was about the decay of tradition, the loss of guidance… It was about a bloke who lost his keys and had to climb a really tall lighthouse! Look, I appreciate a bit of depth as much as the next lass, but sometimes a story just needs to…work. It needs a beginning, a middle and an end that actually  connects . Have you read anything good lately, by the way? Something a bit…grounded? I just finished ‘Project Hail Mary’ by Andy Weir. Proper sci-fi, really good. You might like it. It’s clever without being…art house, I guess. Andy Weir... the ‘Martian’ fella? Aye, I’ve heard good things. I’m currently wading through ‘Middlemarch’. George Eliot. It’s a commitment, to say the least. ‘Middlemarch’? Seriously? That’s… intense. You’re braver than I am. I tried it at uni and just got lost in all the social commentary and the sheer length of it. It’s slow burn, yeah. But it's fascinating. All these little lives intersecting, all these hidden motivations... It's a bit like real life, to be fair. Speaking of real life, are we stopping for those pasties I was telling you about? I'm proper starving. The ones in that little bakery just off the A1? Absolutely. I’m up for a good pasty. Anything in particular? Traditional Cornish? Steak and kidney? Ooh, tough one. Maybe a pork and apple? Something a bit sweet with the savoury, you know.

…and then the dragon, honestly, it just  hated  spreadsheets. Absolutely loathed them. Wouldn’t even look at one. Which, considering it was supposed to be protecting the King’s treasury – which was organised entirely in Excel – was a bit of a problem, wasn't it? A dragon who doesn't like Excel? That's silly! Dragons like gold! My dragon likes Lego. He’s building a spaceship. A really big one. That  is  a much more sensible dragon pastime, Arthur. Much more sensible. Though, a spreadsheet dragon… it just came to me! He kept accidentally deleting formulas and causing chaos. What's a formula? Is it like a potion? Kind of, Lily. It's a little instruction for the computer to do a calculation. Like adding things up. Or… well, it's complicated. You'll learn about them when you’re a bit older. It's what I use to keep track of… everything at school. Attendance, marks… sometimes even biscuit consumption. Biscuits?! You keep track of biscuits? Only to make sure everyone gets a fair share! It’s important work, honestly. Though arguably less important than building a spaceship, Arthur. Is it a realistic spaceship? It’s got lasers! And a robot dog! And a slide! Ooh! Can the robot dog do Brownie things? Like promise things? That’s a good question, Lily. What  did  you do at Brownies tonight? Was it fun? It was okay. We learned the Brownie Promise again. “I promise to do my best…” and then all the things. Miss Davies said we have to really  mean  it when we say it. And do you mean it? Sometimes. It’s hard to remember all the bits. Especially about helping other people. What if they’re mean? That's a very good point. It’s still important to be kind, even if someone isn't kind to you. It doesn’t mean you let them walk all over you, but you try to be the bigger person. It’s… a bit like when you're building with Lego and someone knocks your tower down. Do you knock  their  tower down in return? No! You rebuild yours bigger and better! And maybe you help them rebuild theirs. Exactly! You’re a very wise dragon-spaceship builder, Arthur. So, the Brownie Promise… tricky stuff. Do you want to talk about something else? Maybe PlayStation? Did you get to play tonight?

… honestly, Arthur, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not a criticism, mind, just an observation. You’ve got a bit of, well, everything on that jumper. Jam, I reckon? Probably is, Doreen. Didn’t notice. Early start. Bit of a struggle getting going this morning. And this jumper  is  comfortable, you have to admit. Practical. Doesn’t need ironing. Practicality’s one thing, looking like you’ve been wrestling a particularly sticky fruit farm is another. Speaking of which, I was reading an article about those southern fruit farms. Apparently, they’re struggling to get pickers now. Brexit, mostly. Aye, seen that. Pity. Used to go apple picking as a lad, down near Maidstone. Glorious stuff. Reminded me of stories my grandfather told, about his own grandfather working the land. All gone now, of course. Like those deserted medieval villages. Did I ever tell you about the one near Ilkley Moor? You have, several times. You’re obsessed with deserted medieval villages! Something about the grit and resilience of those folk, wasn't it? While I’m more interested in why anyone would willingly choose to live on a bog in the first place. It’s the  history , Doreen! The stories embedded in the stones. Anyway, talking about struggles… these roadworks near my place are a nightmare. Been going on for months. They started something, then stopped, then started something else. Absolute chaos. Oh, don’t even start me on the roadworks. Bradford's perpetually under construction. It’s a full-time occupation just navigating around them. Have you had your fill of breakfast? I made far too much toast. Lovely toast, thank you. Just about. And this jam… is this homemade? It’s delicious. It is. Rhubarb and ginger. Grown it myself, mostly. Thinking of expanding the herb garden this year. Basil did fantastically well last summer and I’m hoping to get some decent rosemary going. Good for you. Keeps you busy. Keeps the mind active. Important when you’re… well, at our age. People start treating you like you’ve lost your marbles the minute you hit sixty. Don't be daft. We’re not  old , Arthur. Just… experienced. Though I did get a very patronising look from the checkout assistant at Sainsbury’s yesterday. Asked if I needed help reaching something on the top shelf! Happens to the best of us. You know, I had a mountain of junk mail this morning.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of Quality Street toffees this year was  shocking . Dad, you really went to town, didn't you? I thought we’d be eating them until Easter. Well, they were on offer, love. Three for two. Couldn’t resist. Besides, your sister practically lives on them, doesn’t she? Speaking of living on things, I’m currently sustaining myself entirely on leftover brie and crackers. New Year’s resolutions clearly started and finished on January 1st. Anyone else feel that way? Oh, absolutely. I tried the ‘dry January’ thing for all of three days. Then Brenda at work brought in mince pies…it was a lost cause. How’s the writing going, darling? Any interesting briefs come your way? It’s… alright. Mostly social media stuff. A lot of “engaging content” about bathroom tiles. Thrilling, I know. Though, I did get a request for copy about dog grooming yesterday. Which, frankly, is more up my street than porcelain. Speaking of dogs, has Winston been his usual self? He seemed a bit off his colour yesterday when I was taking the bins out. Didn’t even bother chasing the postman. That’s usually a highlight of his day. He’s been a bit quiet, you’re right. I gave him his worming tablet this morning – he  hated  that, naturally. Tried to hide it in a bit of sausage, but he’s too clever for that now. Just spat the sausage out and gave me the stink-eye. Winston’s a pro. My friend’s labradoodle eats anything and everything, even socks. She has to be seriously vigilant. Though, she’s become obsessed with Facebook groups dedicated to the dog. Apparently, there’s a thriving community for owners of fluffy, apricot-coloured doodles. Facebook… Honestly. I still don't get it. Brenda keeps showing me pictures of her holidays. Always somewhere exotic. Last week it was the Maldives. Makes my weekend trip to Brighton seem rather… underwhelming. Don't feel bad, dear. Brighton is lovely! I remember when we went, you got completely lost trying to find that little antique shop. Remember? You ended up asking a seagull for directions! I did  not  ask a seagull for directions! I asked a man with a rather impressive beard. He pointed me vaguely towards the seafront. Ended up two streets in the wrong direction. You two are brilliant. So, Dad, any plans for a proper holiday this year?

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of him! Saying he ‘forgot’ my birthday? Like it’s a minor detail! It’s not forgetting to buy milk, Ben, it’s forgetting  my birthday ! Oof, that’s rough, Chloe. Really rough. Ben does have a…selective memory, doesn’t he? It’s always been his thing. Remember when he "forgot" Aunt Carol’s 60th? Don't  remind  me. Mum was fuming. Honestly, I’m starting to think he does it on purpose just to see how much chaos he can create. It’s exhausting. And now he's saying he's 'too busy' to actually  make  plans for Christmas. Too busy? He spends most of his time scrolling TikTok! Maybe he’s stressed with work? Is the project going okay? He did seem a bit frazzled last time we spoke. He claims it’s fine. But you know Ben. ‘Fine’ usually means ‘currently holding everything together with sticky tape and a prayer.’ Anyway, enough about my brother’s failings. How’s the PhD going? Still wrestling with the data? Oh God, don’t even get me started. It’s… a process. Trying to make sense of the survey data is like trying to herd cats. Seriously. I’ve spent the last three days just cleaning it, and I still think there are rogue entries somehow. Plus, my supervisor is breathing down my neck about publishing something,  anything , even a preliminary finding. That sounds…intense. I’m glad all I have to worry about is writing catchy slogans for laundry detergent. Slightly less existential angst involved. Though, the brief for the new campaign is  terrible . Apparently, we need to make washing powder “aspirational.” Who finds washing powder aspirational?! Honestly?! That’s…a new level of marketing madness. You’re a copywriter, you should be able to spin anything though. You always were good at making things sound amazing. Remember that time you convinced Mrs. Davies in sixth form that your essay on  Wuthering Heights  was actually about the socio-economic impact of sheep farming? Hey, desperate times! And she gave me an A! Speaking of desperation, I’m seriously considering taking on another freelance project just to have a bit of a buffer. Rent in London is…well, you know. It's criminal. Tell me about it. I swear, half my student loan vanishes before I even see it. That’s why I’m still living with my parents, to be honest.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of beige in that kitchen is depressing. Beige units, beige walls, even the bloody splashback was beige! You’d think they’d try for  something  with a new build, wouldn’t you? Beige is the safe option, love. People don't want to put off potential buyers with strong colours. Though, you're right, it  is  a bit… bland. Speaking of buyers, have you been following the market at all? Still mental, isn’t it? Mental doesn’t even  begin  to cover it. I was looking at properties near Richmond Park the other day - just casually browsing, mind you - and a semi-detached, needing a full refurb, is going for over a million. A  million ! When I bought my place, all those years ago, I got a lovely little cottage for a fraction of that. Tell me about it. Remember when we were kids, Mum and Dad moaning about paying £40,000 for this house? We thought  that  was extravagant. Now look at it. It's probably worth… what, half a million even? Easily. Location, location, location. And schools. Kingston’s always been desirable. Though, even out in Surrey, it’s gone crazy. I was talking to Brenda at work – her daughter’s trying to get on the ladder, and it’s a nightmare. She’s working two jobs just to save for a deposit. It's awful. It feels like a generation is just locked out of home ownership. Anyway, enough gloom. I need to distract myself. I did that Pilates class this morning, and my core is screaming. Pilates? That sounds… civilised. I attempted a brisk walk around the park this morning, and nearly got taken out by a rogue Labrador. My cardio is definitely lacking. I need to be more disciplined. Maybe I should join you at this Pilates thing. You absolutely should! It's not strenuous, honestly. Mostly just controlled movements. And the instructor, Chloe, is lovely. We could go on Tuesday evenings? They've got a beginner's class. It’s better than collapsing on the sofa with a packet of biscuits, which is my usual Tuesday evening routine. Biscuits are a perfectly acceptable Tuesday activity. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise. Though, I suppose a bit of exercise is good. Keeps the arteries clear. I've been trying to do more walking during my lunch break. It's a struggle, though.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of data is mental. Like, we’re talking terabytes of transcribed speech just this month. It’s all for this new project on regional dialect shifts, fascinating stuff, but  so  much to check for annotation errors. Honestly, sometimes I feel like all I do is say "no, that's not standard Geordie, that's just someone having a bad day!" Terabytes? Crikey. Sounds…intense. My biggest data headache is usually just making sure my simulations are running without crashing the university’s servers. Though, trying to explain the nuances of soil mechanics to someone who thinks concrete just…happens, that’s a different kind of data wrangling. How’s the funding for all that, by the way? Heard rumblings about the Budget yesterday. Oh, the Budget? Nightmare fuel. Apparently, research funding is getting…reshuffled. Which is university speak for ‘probably cut’. My boss was practically radiating anxiety this morning. She kept muttering about ‘impact assessment’ and ‘value for money’. Like a linguistic study on how accents change isn’t valuable! It's cultural heritage, innit? Totally. It’s short-sighted. They always target the stuff that doesn’t have an immediate, obvious monetary return. Infrastructure projects get all the love, naturally. Which, I’m benefitting from, don’t get me wrong, but… balancing the books on the backs of humanities research feels wrong. Did it affect arts funding too? Massively. Apparently, a lot of smaller theatres are facing real difficulties. It’s just… depressing. I was hoping to see  Wicked  again soon. I know it’s a bit… mainstream but I absolutely  love  it. The costumes are incredible.  Wicked  is brilliant! My sister’s completely obsessed. She’s seen it, like, five times. I’m more of a Sondheim man myself –  Into the Woods  is my go-to. But a good spectacle is a good spectacle. Did you see that revival of  Guys and Dolls  in London last year? No, I missed that one. Was it good? I saw a touring production of  Matilda  a couple of years back, and honestly, the kid playing Matilda stole the show. Had more stage presence than some seasoned professionals I've worked with! She was amazing. The  Guys and Dolls  revival was fantastic. The choreography was spot on, and the lead had a fantastic voice. It reminded me why stage musicals are still relevant, despite everything. They're just...escapism, aren’t they?

…and honestly, the whole thing feels like a betrayal of what used to be good about this city. Another glass tower, another soulless apartment block. They call it ‘regeneration’, I call it wiping the slate clean of any character. Aye, you’re tellin’ me. Used to be you could walk down Bold Street and know everyone, every shop, every story. Now it’s just… chains. Identikit high street, anywhere in the country. Though, I gotta say, that new Italian place isn’t bad. Proper pizza. Small mercies, eh? Though even that’s probably a pop-up, destined to be replaced by another vape shop in six months. It’s all so transient. Makes you wonder what the point is, you know? All this striving… Striving for what, exactly? New gutters? ‘Cause these are a right state. They’re leaking like a sieve, apparently. That’s what your wife said, anyway. Said you were tackling it finally. Yes, well, tackling is a generous word. I’ve watched three YouTube videos and now I feel… marginally less clueless. She’s right about the gutters though. It’s always something around here. It’s funny, isn't it? Spending your days dissecting Shakespeare and then ending up arguing with a corroded piece of metal. Life’s a funny thing, isn’t it? I always fancied bein’ an actor, you know. Proper thespian. Did am-dram for years, played everything from Macduff to the Artful Dodger. Nearly went to RADA, actually. Seriously? RADA? You never mentioned that! Aye, well, life got in the way. Family commitments and all that. Plus, needed to earn a living. Taxi driving pays the bills, doesn't rewrite Shakespeare. Though you get all sorts in the back of a cab. Once had a fella who claimed to have been an extra in  Star Wars . Said he was one of the stormtroopers. Oh, brilliant! That’s the sort of thing you only hear in Liverpool. You know, I was thinking about that painting I bought at the car boot sale last week. The one of the docks. The one with all the grey? Yeah, saw it leaning against your hallway wall. Bit gloomy, innit? Gloomy, yes, but there’s something… evocative about it. The artist clearly knew this city. It feels genuine, unlike a lot of the ‘art’ you see in the galleries these days. I reckon it was a steal at twenty quid.

… honestly, I still can’t believe how cheap the pierogi were in Białka. Like, ridiculously cheap. Did you manage to snag any for the road? I was too busy trying to wrestle the awning down in that gale. Just a small bag, yeah. They didn’t look  quite  as lovingly made as Babcia used to do, but for a fiver? I wasn’t complaining. And don’t worry about the awning, it’s fine. A bit wonky, maybe, but fine. This road is… well, it’s certainly giving the campervan a workout. Look at those hills! Workout is an understatement! I’m starting to feel every pothole in my spine. And the scenery is lovely, don’t get me wrong, but it's all just… trees. Mile after mile of trees. It’s a bit monotonous, isn't it? Reminds me of the New Forest, but… bigger. And Polish. It  is  a lot of forest. But look, there's a little village up ahead. Stone buildings, thatched roofs… that's more like it. It's different from anything I’ve seen in Lancashire, that’s for sure. Speaking of different, how are you feeling about this whole trip? Really? You’ve been awfully quiet since we left Zakopane. Oh, I’m enjoying it. Truly. It's just…being away, you know? It makes you think. About everything. About…stuff. I've been having a proper clearout mentally, if that makes sense. Trying to decide what's worth keeping, what's just clutter. Clutter in your life, or actual physical clutter? Because I know you’ve been meaning to sort through everything at the house for ages. That spare room is legendary. Both, actually. Mostly mental, but the physical stuff is a symptom, isn’t it? Years of accumulating… things. Memories attached to things. It’s exhausting. I keep thinking about selling the house. Just… releasing myself from it. Selling the family home? Wow. That’s… big. Are you sure? It feels… Cambridge. It  is  Cambridge. I know, I know. But what use is Cambridge if I’m not  in  Cambridge? And frankly, the upkeep is a nightmare. And the memories...they’re just…heavy sometimes. This little campervan, ironically, feels lighter. Easier. That's fair. Though you’ll regret it if you get rid of your book collection! Seriously, that’s a national treasure. Look, we don’t have to make any life-altering decisions today.

…and then Miss Davies  actually  said, “Honestly, Chloe, you’ve written a novella, not answered question three!” It was ridiculous. Like, I gave context, I gave examples… she just wanted a bullet point list! Sounds about right. Sixth form teachers and their insistence on brevity, even when the topic demands… well, a novella. Are you stressing too much about these exams, love? You’ve been working so hard. Aye, she has. Keeps herself locked away in her room, she does. Though, to be fair, she’s always been a bookworm. Remember when she used to build forts out of the sofa cushions and ‘run’ a library? Charged us all a penny to borrow a book! Dad! That was  years  ago! And it wasn't a penny, it was a sweet wrapper! A valuable currency at the time. It’s lovely to hear you reminiscing. It makes this trip… easier. Preston isn't exactly a glamourous destination, is it? Just the supermarket run. Still, beats being stuck at home worrying about the train strikes. Honestly, they’re at it again? Aye. Keeps coming up. Brenda at work was fuming, she had a doctor’s appointment in Manchester. Ended up having to get a taxi, cost her a fortune. And the price of petrol these days… It’s insane. Honestly, everything’s just going up. Even books! I wanted that new fantasy one, the one everyone's talking about, but it’s like twenty quid! Maybe we can look for it in Waterstones in Preston? They sometimes have deals. Or we could check online. Although, nothing beats the smell of a new book, does it? It reminds me of the Hay Festival… We haven't been in ages. Maybe next year? Hay? That's a long drive, isn’t it? And expensive. We were talking about maybe finally sorting out the garden instead. Getting that patio laid and all. The garden  does  look a bit of a state. But Hay… I've always wanted to go. It sounds amazing. All those authors and talks. We can dream. Listen, are you feeling alright, darling? You’ve been a bit quiet since we left St Anne’s, apart from the Miss Davies rant, understandably. I’m okay. Just… tired, I think. These exams are draining. Plus… well, I haven't really told anyone yet... What is it, love? You can tell us anything. I… I think I might be poorly.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of things your father has accumulated! It’s like an archaeological dig in here. Another box of old comics? Really, Arthur? He never throws anything away, does he? It's a…habit. A rather frustrating habit when we’re trying to make space. I thought we’d tackled the comics last year, Nana. Tackled? Dear girl, we  moved  them. Into the attic. Which is now overflowing. Honestly, it's a wonder the roof hasn’t collapsed. Speaking of which, where  is  Arthur? Shouldn’t he be helping? He’s…um…he’s upstairs. With his headphones on. He said he was “researching”. Researching usually means watching some obscure documentary on YouTube about vintage biscuit tins. Biscuit tins? Good Lord. He’s been doing that since he was a lad. Remember that time he tried to build a robot out of them? Oh, Nana, don't remind me! The ‘Tin Can Terror’, as he called it. It mostly sparked and smelled of burning wires. Honestly, the boy and his inventions. Though, he did get a commendation for that weather station he built in school. He was showing me his new drone earlier. It’s got a camera and everything. He wants to film the market square. Says it’ll be “art”. A drone? Good heavens. What’ll they think of next? All this technology. I barely manage the television remote. It feels like everyone's living in the future except me. I still prefer a good book. And a proper conversation, not staring at little flickering screens. It has its uses, Nana. I use it for school - research, communication with students… though I admit, sometimes I think it's all a bit much. It’s isolating, isn’t it? Especially for someone like Arthur. Isolating? Now, what do you mean by that, love? Well… he’s been a bit… distant lately. More than usual. I think the anniversary of his mother’s passing is hitting him harder this year. He’s not saying much, and he’s retreated into his hobbies even more than usual. He hasn’t been himself. He gets really quiet sometimes, and he won't eat. He just sits and…stares. Oh, the poor lamb. Losing his mother was a terrible blow. He was always so close to her. So like her, actually - with that quiet, thoughtful nature. But he  must  talk. Bottling things up just makes it worse.

…and honestly, the wireless card in this thing is  dodgy . Keeps dropping the connection. It's brand new, you’d think they’d test these things, wouldn't ya? Right, Ben, you’re the tech wizard, have a go. See if you can spot what’s happening. Let me have a look, Al. New laptop, eh? Fancy. What spec did you go for? Don't tell me you fell for the marketing hype and got a load of RGB lighting you don't need. Nah, sensible stuff. I needed something that could actually  run  Photoshop without sounding like a jet engine taking off. Ryzen 7, 16 gig of RAM, decent graphics card. It's just…the internet. It’s driving me mental. I was trying to watch some MMA highlights on YouTube earlier, and it kept buffering. MMA, yeah? Still at that, then? Thought you were trying to get into golf with your uncle. He was going on about needing a playing partner. Golf? Don't remind me. Two hours of walking slowly after a tiny white ball…nah. MMA is more my speed. Keeps you sharp, y’know? Besides, I'm getting proper into it - different techniques and all that. Alright, looking at the network settings… hmm. Seems like the driver is up to date. It’s not a Bedford issue, is it? Our internet is normally rock solid. No, it's fine with everything else. My phone’s fine, your laptop was fine when you brought it round last week… just this new machine. It’s frustrating, innit? I’ve got a deadline for that poster design for the music festival, and I can't even reliably download reference images. Music festival? Which one? The one down near Woburn? I helped old Mr. Henderson with his garden, he's doing security there. Said it’s a nightmare every year, loads of youngsters… Yeah, Woburn. Small world. And yeah, it'll be a handful. Listen, while you're here, do you remember those weird little computer games we used to play on Dad's old Commodore 64? The pixelated ones with the loading screens that took forever? Oh god,  Manic Miner ? Or  Jet Set Willy ? Absolute torture, but addictive as hell. The loading times were insane. You’d make a cup of tea in the time it took to get to the first level. I was more of an  International Karate+  man myself.

… honestly, I was expecting pierogi to be everywhere. This place is lovely though, isn't it? Very…Scandi-chic for Tarnow. Did you see the little succulents on each table? It  is  nice, yeah. A bit surprised myself, I thought it'd be all red-and-white tablecloths and babushka dolls. But it's good, a little bit of something different. And the coffee is actually decent, which is a minor miracle around here. You alright? You’ve barely touched your apple cake. Oh, it's lovely, really. Just…thinking. It’s strange being here. Poland. Never imagined I’d end up in Poland. Feels a million miles from Cambridge. Well, you always said you wanted to  escape  Cambridge. Remember all those dramatic pronouncements about needing a fresh start? And look at you, semi-retired TEFL queen, globe-trotting… well, technically, just Poland-trotting at the moment. ‘Globe-trotting’ is a bit strong. More like… flitting. And it’s not exactly glamorous when it’s funded by Mum, is it? It feels… pathetic, sometimes. Like I haven’t actually  achieved  anything. Don't be ridiculous. You're a brilliant teacher, even if you are mostly teaching dodgy businessmen online now. And you’re doing something. You’re  living . Remember Aunt Carol? Stuck in that house with Uncle Bernard, doing crosswords and slowly disappearing? You’re having an adventure. Carol had… issues. It's different. She was completely controlled. It's more that... I feel adrift. Like I'm not really  anyone  anymore. I used to have this… identity, you know? Cambridge graduate, aspiring historian. Now I’m… what am I? A slightly eccentric expat with a fondness for strong coffee? You’re my slightly eccentric friend who’s trying to figure things out. And that’s okay. You always were a bit of an existentialist, though, weren’t you? Remember that phase in uni where you only wore black and read Sartre? Don’t remind me! Horrific. Worse than my brief, ill-advised attempt at a juice cleanse. Speaking of which, have you been keeping up with your running? You seemed so motivated. Honestly? Not so much. Life got in the way. Work's been hectic, prepping for the new curriculum. And… I fell off the wagon a bit. The wagon? Oh. Right. Yeah. The biscuits, mostly. Then the wine. Then… well, you know. It’s stupid, I know. I was doing so well.

…and honestly, the queue for the loos was ridiculous! Like, genuinely a twenty-minute wait. You’d think for a steam fair of  that  size, they’d have more facilities. Gran, did you manage okay? I know your knees were playing up a bit. Oh, I managed. Bit of a struggle, mind you. Had to lean on young Millie here most of the time. Though honestly, all that noise! Gave me a proper headache. Beautiful engines though, absolutely beautiful. Reminded me of my uncle Bertie. He was obsessed with those things. He really was, wasn’t he? Always talking about pistons and whatnot. I remember him trying to explain it to me once. Went right over my head. But yes, the queues were awful. I was worried about Mum needing the loo constantly with her bladder, and there just wasn't anywhere accessible quickly enough. Did you see if they had any disabled facilities marked clearly, Millie? I did look! There was a ‘disabled toilet’ sign, but it was blocked by a stall selling those… miniature steam engines. Seriously. You had to practically climb over a table of plastic trains to get to it. And it wasn’t particularly  accessible  accessible, you know? Tight space, didn’t look like a proper radar key lock. Typical. Always the way, isn't it? They slap a sign up and think that’s job done. Doesn't account for actually getting  to  it. Makes you wonder if anyone actually  uses  these facilities to test them. Exactly! It's all well and good saying it's accessible, but it needs to be practical. Still, the fair itself was good. Worth the money, even with the hassle. Speaking of money... have you two been looking at properties around here at all? Briefly. Just online, mostly. Don’t even  start  me on the prices in Bournemouth. It's insane! I saw a tiny flat overlooking the gardens, and it was nearly £300,000. For a one-bed! Back in Gillingham, you can get a  house  for that. Bournemouth is posh now, Millie. Always was a bit, but it’s gone right through the roof. Remember when we used to come here as kids? You could get fish and chips for a pound! Now it's... well, you know. It’s the London effect, isn’t it? Everyone moving out during lockdown and driving up the prices. I've been looking in Poole, a little further out.

…and honestly, the draught coming under that door in the spare room is  criminal . You'd think after all this time, your father would have sorted it. Honestly, a polar bear would feel a chill. Now, Mum, don’t start on Dad. He's been busy with the garden. And it’s Thirsk in October, a draught is practically expected! It’s bracing. Though, I do agree, it’s a bit much. Leo, have you felt the chill in there? Nah, not really. I was building a fortress out of cushions, so I didn’t notice. It’s pretty epic, by the way. Sounds like it. Good use of the spare room, son. She’s right about the weather, though. Properly turning now, isn't it? We had a bit of a downpour on the drive over from Kendal. Dreadful. Dreadful is an understatement. Reminds me of a November in ‘63, we had floods right up to the church hall. Old Reverend Ainsworth nearly lost his prize-winning chrysanthemums. Oh, Mum, you and your stories! That was nearly sixty years ago. Leo, don't encourage her. Anyway, we were talking about plans for tonight. I was thinking fish and chips, then a film? Yes! Can we watch that Marvel one? The new one with the… uh… space battles? Sounds good to me. Though I might be nodding off halfway through a space battle. My brain prefers a good biography. Honestly, these superhero films… Speaking of brains, have you seen what’s happening on that Twitter thing? Your cousin Margaret sent me a link. Apparently, there’s a right kerfuffle about someone misspelling ‘definitely’. Oh, dear. The internet. A breeding ground for outrage. I try to avoid it, honestly. Far too much negativity. I use it for school stuff mostly – communicating with parents. Some of them only check Twitter. It’s a modern world, I suppose. Twitter's cool! I follow all the gaming channels. They post funny memes. Memes. Right. I’m still trying to figure out how to properly work the smart TV. It's all streaming services and apps. Gets a bit overwhelming. It’s a far cry from adjusting the aerial on the old valve radio, I can tell you that. Oh, those were the days. Simple pleasures. I much preferred listening to the wireless. And people had manners! No one writes letters anymore, everything is a text.

…and honestly, the dentist said Leo’s getting a bit sloppy with his brushing again. Honestly, it’s like talking to a brick wall. I tell him, ‘Leo, two minutes! Two minutes is  barely  anything!’ But two minutes is a  long  time, Mummy. Like, forever! It doesn’t feel like forever when you’re thinking about superheroes, does it? Or building Lego castles? It’s about making a habit. Speaking of habits, have you both remembered to tell me about your hearing tests tomorrow? I don’t  want  to do a hearing test! It’s boring. They just make you wear headphones and listen to beeps. It's not  that  boring, Harry. And Mrs. Davies said it's important to make sure we can hear everything at school. Exactly. Mrs. Davies is very wise. And it’s quick. Think of it as… a super hearing power check! Are you both alright to go with Grandma? She’s offered to take you. Okay, if Grandma's taking us. But can we get a treat after? We’ll see. Depends on how well you both sit still for the beeps! Right. Back to more pressing matters... Ashaad’s mum called. Ashaad's got chickenpox. Oh no! Poor Ashaad. Can we still have a party with him later? Sadly, no sweetheart. He’ll be stuck inside for at least a week. It throws a bit of a spanner in the works for your combined birthday plans, doesn't it? It’s not fair! We wanted to play laser quest  with  Ashaad. I know, darling. It is a shame.
