Though, to be fair, he  was  a history student taking the optional Modernism module. Perhaps he’s just clinging to the idea of objective truth in the face of all that literary…wiggliness. Probably. How was the staff meeting? Still arguing over the curriculum changes? Oh, don’t even get me started. Professor Chen is absolutely insistent that we need to incorporate more explicitly patriotic elements into the syllabus. As if Virginia Woolf needs  more  context to be appreciated! It feels…wrong, somehow. Like we’re being asked to sanitize everything. It does. It’s a fine line, isn’t it? We're supposed to be fostering critical thinking, not nationalistic fervor. Did you manage to push back at all? A little. I pointed out the potential for misinterpretation, and that focusing too heavily on 'national spirit' might actually  detract  from a nuanced understanding of the texts. But he just smiled that infuriatingly polite smile and said, “We must consider the larger context, Dr. Davies.” The larger context. Always the larger context. Speaking of which… …have you noticed the air’s been particularly bad these last few days? My throat feels constantly scratchy. Dreadful, isn’t it? This haze is relentless. I saw a report saying the pollution levels are off the charts again. It’s bizarre, walking home discussing Woolf and national curricula while basically breathing in particulate matter. Sometimes it feels a bit surreal living here. It does. I miss clear skies. Remember walking along the Norfolk coast? You could see for miles. Oh, Norwich…the vast emptiness of the Broads. And breathing air that didn’t taste vaguely metallic. I do miss that. Though, I don't miss your mum's constant attempts to set me up with single farmers. Fair point. She’s a force of nature, my mother. Still, it’s a trade-off, isn't it? The life we have here, the work, the students… it's fulfilling, even with the bureaucratic nonsense and the smog. It is. And the food! I’d genuinely struggle to live without proper dumplings again.

…and honestly, the rosemary’s gone a bit funny. I should’ve used it last week. Still, it’ll be alright with a little extra thyme, won’t it? Just boosts the flavour, really. Sounds good, love. You always were a magician with herbs. Though, speaking of things going a bit funny, have you seen the state of the photo albums? I was trying to find that picture of Millie graduating, and it’s just… chaos. Oh,  please . Don’t start on the photo albums. Last time you tackled those, you ended up spending a whole afternoon trying to identify Great Aunt Mabel in every single black and white snapshot. She  was  a prolific attendee of family gatherings! It’s important to document these things. And Millie wants that photo for her uni application. Says it shows “personal growth and achievement”. Honestly, these kids… Personal growth and achievement through a slightly blurry graduation photo. Right. Well, I'm sure Millie's got plenty of  actual  personal growth and achievement to showcase. What about lunch? Are we still on for that pub quiz at The Dog & Duck? Definitely. I’ve been strategising all morning. I’m confident we can beat old Mr. Henderson this time. He thinks he knows everything about 1980s music, but I’ve been doing my research. Good. He gets far too smug. Though, his knowledge of obscure bird species  is  rather impressive. I was attempting to look up a common garden bird yesterday and he rattled off its Latin name. Show off. You two and your competitive streak! It's exhausting just watching you. How was your day, dear? Anything exciting happen at the office? Exciting? Not exactly. Old Mr. Peterson tried to send an email to the entire department addressed “To Whom It May Concern”. I had to subtly correct him. It's like teaching a goldfish to tap dance, honestly. Oh, poor Mr. Peterson! He's a sweetheart, though. A little… technologically challenged. I had a pretty good day. Landed a new client - a small bakery, actually. They need help updating their social media. It’s good, creative work. That’s fantastic, darling! A bakery! You’ll be surrounded by cake. Perfect inspiration. Though, don't bring any in here – I'm trying to be good. This roast needs to be edible, not sabotaged by a sugar rush. Speaking of watching what we eat…did you catch that new documentary on Netflix about ultra-processed foods?

… honestly, it’s just taking  ages  to get anywhere now. They’ve rerouted the 10 again, haven’t they? It used to go right past the shops on Mill Road, now you have to walk like, ten minutes from the nearest stop. It's a proper pain. Oh, that’s annoying. I hadn't noticed, to be fair, I cycle most of the time. But Mill Road without easy bus access feels…wrong. It’s the lifeblood of Cambridge, isn't it? Packed with everything. What were they thinking? Beats me. Something about ‘optimising routes’ and ‘reducing congestion’ they said on the council website. Optimising for who? Certainly not people trying to get to the shops! We were trying to get to the Cambridge University Press bookshop yesterday, and it was a mission. Ah, that’s a good one. I haven't been in ages. They always have a surprisingly good selection of…well, everything, really. Not just academic stuff. Did you find what you were looking for? Eventually. After the bus saga. I was after a specific poetry collection, and they had it. But on the way back, we walked past this student protesting outside the Senate House. Oh yeah? What about? Cambridge always seems to have a protest brewing somewhere. Something about tuition fees, fairly standard. But he had this amazing sign. It said, "My future’s worth more than your endowment!" It was brilliantly worded. He was getting a fair bit of attention, loads of people were stopping to take photos. That  is  good. Very pithy. It’s a lot different from protests back when I was at uni, wasn’t it? More…organised, less about individual flair. Definitely. Though to be fair, Durham wasn’t exactly a hotbed of radical activity. Sunderland, where I did my undergrad, was a bit more lively, bits of activism. But Cambridge…it feels different. More performative, maybe? That's a good way to put it. It's certainly…polished. Everything here is. I think it’s part of the Cambridge bubble. It felt a world away from Nottingham when I was there. Completely different vibe. More practical, less…historical weight, I suppose. That’s what I mean. Durham felt…heavy, in a different way. All that collegiate history, the castle, the cathedral. You felt like you were constantly walking in the footsteps of people who’d been there for centuries. Exactly!

…and honestly, the portion sizes were ridiculous! I mean, I haven’t seen chips like that since… well, since we were kids raiding Nan’s pantry. Did you two manage to finish yours? Nearly! I slowed down towards the end, though. Proper pub grub, wasn't it? Absolutely rammed, too. Luckily, you booked, Mary. It was lovely. Though, I’m still thinking about that chocolate brownie. Should have left room. So, how are you finding retirement, Mary? Really properly finding it, now you’ve had a few weeks. Is it everything you hoped? Oh, it’s…different. A lot of adapting. I miss the structure, I think. And the kids, of course. Though honestly, teenagers haven't changed a bit since  my  days as one. Still full of angst and drama. Kevin keeps asking if I’m bored. I tell him I’m ‘strategically resting’. He rolls his eyes. Strategically resting! I love that. You always did have a way with words, Mary. Reminds me of trying to explain quadratic equations to my brother. Pure poetry, coming from you, but absolute gibberish to him. Oh, bless him. He was never a maths head, was he? Speaking of heads, how's Liam? Still keeping you on your toes? He is, yes! He's coming up next weekend, actually. To Hunsonby. He’s never really been  properly  north before. Just quick airport runs and things. Trying to prepare him for the…well, the quiet. Birkenhead is  bustling  compared to Cumbria. He’ll love it. It’s beautiful up there. Fresh air, stunning scenery… a complete contrast. Though, maybe warn him about the local dialect? It’s…distinct. Distinct is putting it mildly, Sarah. You’ll have to translate for him, love. They speak a language all their own up there. It’s English, of course, technically. But… evolved. I’ve been trying to decipher some of it myself since moving closer to your mother. Oh, God, you’re right. It’s like a different universe. My Nan always says things that just…hang in the air. And the speed of it! They talk so fast! It’s a challenge. Liam's pretty good with accents, though, he's had his fair share dealing with all our family. He’ll manage. He’s resourceful. It’s just… different to anything he’s used to. Are the kids excited he's coming? They are. Amelia keeps asking if he's bringing her a 'proper' Lego set.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of people trying to get onto the Jubilee line at North Greenwich was unbelievable. You’d think they were giving away gold, not access to a concert. The O2. A monument to…well, to commercialism, really. Still, good you got to see Lizzo. You were buzzing about it for weeks. Buzzing is an understatement! But the travel…it almost negated the enjoyment. It really makes you appreciate not having a car, though, doesn’t it? All that parking hassle. Though sometimes, when we’re thinking about a proper holiday… Don’t even  start  with the holiday planning. I’m bracing myself. Where are we aiming this year? Somewhere requiring a car, I suspect. Well, the kids are hinting at Cornwall. Properly hinting. Promises of building sandcastles and eating pasties. But getting all the paraphernalia  to  Cornwall, without a car? It’s a logistical nightmare. We’d be better off hiring a van. A van sounds…sensible. Less stressful than squeezing everything onto trains and then hoping for a reasonable taxi at the other end. Look, there’s the Cutty Sark! Still looks magnificent. Always did. It does. It’s amazing to think of the journeys that ship made. Tea, spices, all sorts. Everything was measured in…what  was  it, gallons and pounds back then? It's so bizarre trying to translate old recipes that use those measurements. It's not a direct conversion to cups and ounces, is it? It's always a bit off. You and your baking. It's a serious business. No, definitely not direct. It’s all imperial versus metric, isn’t it? A nightmare for anyone trying to replicate a Victorian sponge. Speaking of things from the past, do you ever think about how fundamentally different life was for people even a hundred years ago? Walking along here, past all this…modernity. Constantly. It’s the river itself, I think. It feels…ancient. Like it’s seen everything. All the empires, the struggles, the constant change. We’re just a tiny blip in its timeline. A slightly stressed blip, trying to get to Cornwall without a car. Exactly! But seriously, it’s overwhelming sometimes, isn’t it? The speed of everything. Everyone is so…connected, yet somehow more isolated. Is it progress? Or just…different? That’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? I don’t know. I think maybe it’s just…complex.

…and honestly, the signal in this house is  awful . I swear, I have to stand by the window to get two bars. It’s ridiculous, considering how much we pay for broadband these days. Did you manage to get through to the school about the sports day details, Mum? Oh, love, don’t even start on the broadband. It’s always been dodgy, hasn’t it? Especially when it’s raining proper cats and dogs like it is now. Honestly, feels like the whole of Kent's underwater. And yes, I spoke to Mrs. Peterson. Sports day is still on, rain or shine, apparently. They’ve got a ‘wet weather plan’ which involves everyone squeezing into the hall. Sounds chaotic! Chaotic is an understatement! Little Leo will be beside himself if he can’t run the sack race. He’s been practicing in the garden all week, tripping over everything. I’ve got a video, it’s hilarious. I’ll show you later. He’s so determined, that one. Oh, bless him. I’m just hoping it doesn’t turn into a mud wrestling event. Honestly, primary schools and outdoor events… a risky combination! Speaking of determined, Elsie's been obsessed with Barnaby Bear all week. She  has  to sleep with him, take him everywhere. Barnaby Bear? Oh, the one you ‘built’ at that Build-a-Bear workshop? That was a lovely day out, wasn't it? She was so excited picking out his stuffing and little heart. It was. Although, the price of a slightly-squishier bear is rather extortionate! It’s just…she’s gotten so attached. And it’s constantly being dragged around, covered in who-knows-what. That’s Elsie, through and through. Everything’s a full-on attachment with her. Reminds me of when I was little, I had this rabbit called Reginald. Absolutely  lived  for Reginald. You used to tease me mercilessly about it, didn’t you, Sarah? Oh, I did! Reginald went  everywhere  with you. Even to the swimming pool! Mum nearly had a fit when she saw you trying to take him into the shallow end. Oh dear, I’d quite forgotten that! She was a sensitive little thing, your sister always was. Cried for hours if Reginald got a bit wet. It’s lovely to see that bond carried on with Elsie and Barnaby. Though, it does make washing a bit…complicated.

…and honestly, the sheer  space  here is doing my head in a bit. Back in Wellington, everything’s… compact. This feels almost… wasteful, even though it's lovely. Wasteful? You, the man who once built a three-story treehouse for the kids on a postage stamp of a section? Don't talk to me about wasteful. It’s just different, isn’t it? A different kind of freedom. And we’ve got the whole of November here. Time to think. Which, frankly, is what I wanted. Remember all that talk before we left about needing to actually  plan  things, instead of just… reacting? Right, the ‘intentional living’ phase. Bit cringe, if I’m honest. But you’re right. I’ve been procrastinating on the business stuff, pretending a decent tan and some Aussie sunshine will magically solve the issues with ‘Global Gadgets’. It won't. No, it won’t. You need to decide about the Seattle expansion. Are you going to go for it, or not? Because dithering is just losing momentum. And frankly, seeing you stressed about it is… stressful for  me . Harsh, but fair. Seattle… it’s a big leap. And committing to that means less time here, less time… well, less time for everything. Remember Sarah and Ben talking about potentially moving to Perth? They were on about us all trying to coordinate a longer stay next year, maybe even a proper Christmas together. Oh, yes! That would be amazing. Imagine Christmas on the beach, instead of battling Dorset drizzle. Though, honestly, if ‘Global Gadgets’ is taking over your life again, that’s not going to happen. Precisely. And that brings me to another thing… I’ve been thinking about getting a proper Operations Manager. Someone to actually  run  the day-to-day, leaving me to focus on the big picture stuff – new product development, that sort of thing. It feels… daunting. Letting go of control. That's good, though! It shows growth. You’re realizing you can’t do everything yourself. It’s a sign of a successful entrepreneur, actually. And it would free you up. You’ve talked about taking that woodworking course for ages. Remember? Don’t remind me. You’ll have me crafting tiny wooden koalas before I know it. But seriously, you're right. It's scary but necessary. Ok, Seattle: I'll make a decision by the end of the week. Operations Manager: actively start advertising next week.

…and honestly, the way she said ‘bath’ sounded like ‘barth’. Like, actively trying to pronounce it wrong. It just…grates, doesn’t it? Especially when you know they’re doing it  on purpose . You and accents, eh, Liv? You’re proper sensitive about ‘em. Remember when we were at university and that lad from Cornwall tried to convince us 'cream tea' was pronounced differently? Oh god, yes! The utter  audacity . He genuinely thought he was right. And you were fuming, Liam. Absolutely fuming. I was! It’s just…basic! It’s the way things are  said . It's not a matter of opinion! Anyway, this is nothing compared to Sarah trying to do a Yorkshire accent after visiting Becca last weekend. It was offensive. Offensive, I tell you. Oh, I bet! Becca’s accent is proper strong. I sometimes struggle to understand her dad, even  I’m  Northern! Though, to be fair, he likes to mumble. Speaking of Becca, anyone seen her Fitbit stats lately? She's been smashing it at the gym, apparently. She sent me a screenshot, looked like she’d practically run a marathon. Good for her. I need to get back into that. I've been living on takeaways and Pokémon Go since I finished uni. Honestly, I spent three hours yesterday trying to catch a shiny Magikarp. It's ruining my life. Pokémon Go? Really, Liam? You're a graduate! I thought you’d have moved past that. I’m trying to advise people on tax returns all day, and you’re chasing digital monsters! Lay off her, Liv. It's just a bit of fun. Besides, you were proper addicted to Candy Crush for a while there. That was different! That was…stress relief. It required tactical thinking. Whereas Pokémon…it’s just walking around staring at your phone. It's a good excuse to get out though, isn't it? Better than being cooped up. Remember that camping trip last summer? That was a disaster. It poured down, and someone – no names mentioned – forgot the tent pegs. Don't remind me. I spent half the night trying to fashion tent pegs out of sticks. It was a truly humbling experience. And then there was that badger… Oh, the badger! Proper aggressive little thing. Scared the life out of us all. Fight or flight kicked in, and I instinctively grabbed a tin of beans. Looking back, it was a terrible idea.

…and honestly, the referee were blind as a bat! Didn’t see young Timmy get flattened by that lad from Diss clear as day. Diss, mind you, always play a rough game. Always ‘ave. Oh, Arthur, you and your football. Honestly, you get more worked up over a village match than the Prime Minister does over… well, anything, really. Did you have a nice roast, dear? I thought the potatoes were a bit gluey, if I’m honest. They were a little…firm, Gran. But the gravy saved them. And Dad, you  always  say the referees are blind. It’s become part of the match-day experience! It is, isn’t it? She’s right, Arthur. It’s tradition. Although, I have to admit, watching village football is… a unique experience. A bit more… enthusiastic than the Premier League. Enthusiastic? They were trying to take ‘is legs off! And it weren't even a proper tackle! Proper tackles you see on the telly, you know. These lads… they just barge. Barge and hope for the best. Reminds me of politics, actually. All barge and no substance. Oh, don’t start on politics, Arthur. It’ll ruin a perfectly good apple crumble. Speaking of crumble, did everyone enjoy it? I used Bramleys from old Mr. Henderson’s orchard. Lovely apples, they are. It was delicious, Mum. Seriously. And Dad, you’re right about the politics. It’s utterly exhausting watching it all unfold. The constant…performative outrage. It's designed to distract, isn’t it? Keeps people from looking at the actual issues. Speaking of distracting, how’s the research going, love? Still buried under student essays? You have no idea. Deadline week from hell. They all leave it to the last minute, naturally. It’s either brilliant insights or… well, let’s just say plagiarism is surprisingly common. It’s disheartening, really. You pour your heart into trying to inspire them, and… Plagiarism, eh? Cheeky blighters. Back in my day, you wouldn’t dream of it. You’d get a right telling-off from old Mr. Grimes, the headmaster. He ruled that school with an iron fist. A teaspoon, more like. A small, shiny iron fist. Oh, Arthur. You and your stories. Mr. Grimes sounded terrifying. Still, you survived him. And you always said he had a soft spot for you, even if he didn't show it. It’s amazing how school sticks with you, isn’t it?

…and honestly, the thought of another essay on post-structuralism just makes me want to curl up and  disappear . I’m seriously considering just…leaving. Dropping out. Woah, hold on a minute. Leaving? Like…completely? You were so buzzing about uni when we first got here, El. What’s happened? I know, I know. But it's not  buzzing  anymore, is it? It’s just… relentless. And pointless, almost. I feel like I’m learning to write essays  about  thinking, rather than actually  doing  any. It's suffocating. And everyone else seems to be thriving, networking, knowing what they want to do with their lives. Don’t compare yourself to everyone else, El. That's the worst thing you can do. Especially here. Everyone puts on a show. Besides, you’re brilliant. You just approach things differently. Remember when we were kids and you’d build these incredible dens in your garden? Like, architectural masterpieces? You were always thinking outside the box. Oh god, the dens. Mum hated them. Always complaining about the washing line being draped with blankets and branches. She said I was ‘creating a fire hazard.’ She was so dramatic. Your mum  was  a bit dramatic, wasn’t she? Mine just told me to wear sensible shoes. Speaking of which…are those the same boots you wore when we went hiking in the Lake District last weekend? Maybe? Why? El, they are  covered . Like, archaeological dig level covered. There's definitely peat in there. And something…green? You’ve tracked half of Lancashire through this room. Honestly! Oh, shush you. It’s character building. Besides, it’s a long walk to the library. What? Character building for the carpet, maybe. Seriously, get a brush. But anyway, back to the dropping-out thing. Have you talked to anyone at the university? Student services? Your personal tutor? I haven’t. I feel…stupid, admitting I'm struggling. Like I should just be  coping . It's all everyone talks about, isn’t it? ‘Resilience’ and ‘growth mindset’... it's exhausting. El, there's no shame in asking for help. That’s what they're there for! And honestly, you're not stupid. You're just… you. You always were fiercely independent. Remember that time you refused to ride your bike without stabilisers for  years ? You insisted on running alongside it, holding on, until you nearly collapsed from exhaustion? Oh my god, don't remind me!

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails I had waiting for me after just  three  days off was criminal. Three days, Zara! I felt more stressed  returning  to work than I did before I left. Three days? Oh, no. That is rough, Liv. Pearson is…intense. I’m used to a lot, obviously, marketing deadlines are brutal, but three days feels minimal for that kind of backlog. Did you actually switch off, though? Be honest. You’re terrible at switching off. Guilty as charged. I checked my emails at least twice a day. Old habits, you know? It’s the project coordinator in me – always worrying something will fall apart if I’m not looking. It’s such a pointless anxiety, really. How  was  your holiday? You didn't mention it properly earlier. Properly  escaped  did you? Oh, it was bliss. Cornwall. Proper Cornish cream teas, bracing walks along the cliffs, the whole shebang. No signal for half of it, which was… liberating. I actually forgot what my phone looked like for a couple of hours each day. It was glorious. We went with Ben, obviously, and his sister and her boyfriend. Ben! How is he? Still relentlessly cheerful? And you and Ben… things still going well? It feels like ages since I’ve properly grilled him about his five-year plan. Relentlessly cheerful is a good description. Yes, things are really good. Actually… …he proposed. Zara! No way! Seriously?! Oh my god, that’s amazing! Let me see the ring! When? Where? Tell me everything! I’m so, so happy for you both. It was last week, in St Ives. He took me for a walk at sunset, the classic move, I know, and then… well, he got down on one knee. It was lovely. The ring’s at the jewellers getting sized. We’re thinking of a small wedding next summer, maybe somewhere in the Cotswolds. Oh, that sounds  perfect . You’ll be the most beautiful bride! I’m officially a bridesmaid, right? Don’t even try to get out of it. Absolutely! I wouldn’t dream of it. You’re essential bridesmaid material. We need your organisational skills for sure. Planning a wedding is going to be…an experience. Which reminds me, how's your flat hunt going? You were saying last time we spoke that you wanted to move closer to work. It’s a disaster. Absolutely.

…and honestly, lad, I don’t know  why  I bother sometimes. Three days delivery they said. Three days! It’s been a week, and still no sign of them garden gnomes. Honestly, gnomes. You’d think they’d be prioritised. Mmm-hmm. Right. Gnomes. Did you check the tracking number, Gran? Of course, I checked the tracking number! It says “in transit” since Tuesday. "In transit" could mean anything! It could be in Timbuktu for all I know. That’s the trouble with this internet shopping, isn’t it? You’ve no control. Give me a proper shop any day, wandering around a garden centre, picking ‘em up yourself. Yeah, but then you've got to  go  to a garden centre. This is easier. I'm just trying to find a decent graphics card, and it's a nightmare. Everything’s either sold out or costs like, a fortune. A graphics card? What for? More of them computer games, I suspect? Not just games, Gran! For my coding projects! I told you, I’m building a simulation for my A-Levels. Need something that can actually  handle  it. I've been looking on eBay mostly. They sometimes have better deals than Amazon. eBay, eh? That’s a bit of a gamble, that. You get all sorts on eBay. Used, broken… I’ve had a few dodgy dealings on there myself. Remember that antique teapot I bought? Said it was Royal Doulton, turned out to be… well, definitely  not  Royal Doulton. Yeah, but you can check the seller’s feedback, can’t you? And read the descriptions properly. I'm looking for ones with loads of positive reviews. And I'm specifically looking for ‘tested and working’. Tested and working… That’s what they all say! You’ve got to be careful, love. Amazon’s got that A-to-Z guarantee, at least. If something goes wrong, you can get your money back. It’s a bit more hassle, but at least you’re protected. That’s true. But even on Amazon, the prices are mental. This one card I want is £500! On eBay, I saw one going for £350, but it ended five minutes ago. I missed it. Five hundred pounds for a… a bit of plastic and wires? Good grief! What did we do before all this technology? We managed perfectly well with a good pencil and a bit of paper.

…and honestly, the price of biscuits these days! You wouldn’t believe it. A packet of digestives - a  packet  - is nearly three quid! Used to be you could get two for a pound, easy. Grandad, you say that about  everything . Remember when you were complaining about the cost of a pint last week? It was £4.80! You were acting like the world was ending. Well, it  is  practically ending with these prices, isn’t it? It's daylight robbery. I remember a time when a pint was… oh, I don't know, a shilling? A bob? Something sensible. It’s just… everything feels so expensive now. Even the telly license. Things do go up, Grandad. Inflation, supply chain issues, you know the drill. It’s complicated. I was reading a report at work about it, actually. It's impacting production costs massively. We’re struggling to keep prices down for clients. Production costs? Clients? You and your fancy job. What  exactly  do you do again? You always talk about production controllers and I still haven’t a clue. Is it anything like what your mum used to do at the council? Sort of, but more… proactive. I manage the flow of materials and schedules for a manufacturing company. Basically, I make sure they have everything they need, when they need it, to make their products. It’s a lot of spreadsheets and problem-solving. Mum was more reactive, dealing with things  after  they went wrong, mostly. Spreadsheets… sounds dreadful. I used to be quite good with numbers, you know. Before… well, before things changed. Used to help old Mr. Henderson at the bookies, keeping his accounts straight. Though he always suspected I was skimming a bit off the top, the old rogue. Grandad! You weren’t! A bit of harmless exaggeration. He just wasn't a trusting man. Anyway, enough about dodgy bookmakers. What about you? Still seeing… what’s his name? Liam? Alex. And no. We broke up a couple of weeks ago. Oh. Oh dear. That's not good, is it? What happened? He seemed like a nice enough lad. A bit scruffy, perhaps, but polite. It just… wasn’t working. We wanted different things. He’s got his music, and touring, and I’m trying to build a career here. Long distance is hard, and constantly fitting around his schedule was exhausting. That’s a shame, love.

… honestly, the thought of actually  being  at the airport on Christmas Day fills me with dread. Like, picture it – everyone stressed, delayed flights… It’s a logistical nightmare. You’re telling me! I saw a TikTok of someone trying to get through security on Christmas morning, dressed as an elf. It was chaos. Though, thinking about it, if we  did  fly, I could bring back proper Tim Tams. You can't get the real deal over here. Tim Tams are good, I’ll give you that. But I’m still voting for driving. It’s more… festive. We can stop for a cheeky full English along the way. And besides, I've already told Mum we're coming on Boxing Day. Backing out now would be… problematic. Boxing Day’s good, yeah. Gives everyone a bit of breathing room after the big day. Although, driving that far... you reckon the roads'll be bad? I drove home from my auntie's last New Year’s Eve, and it took  eight hours  to do a three-hour trip. Potentially. But flying feels… wrong. It just doesn’t  feel  like Christmas. Remember last year, Dad tried to make a Christmas dinner for twelve in that tiny campervan? That was more Christmas spirit than any airport security check could offer. Oh god, the burnt sprouts! And the turkey was barely cooked! Still, points for effort. Speaking of Christmas dinner… I'm thinking of doing a proper goose this year. I've been watching a lot of Mary Berry. A goose? That's ambitious, even for you. Remember that disastrous attempt at a soufflé? Hey! That was a one-time thing! This will be different. Goose is apparently incredibly flavorful. I’ve even found a butcher who sources them locally. Sounds fancy. We usually just go with a turkey, roast potatoes, all the usual suspects. Although, my mate back home – out in the bush – reckons he accidentally hit a deer on the way to get a Christmas tree last year. Said it was a bit… confronting. Oh, brilliant. Roadkill and Christmas cheer don’t really mix. Poor deer! Eugh, don't even. We had a fox rummaging through the bins last week. Bold as brass it was. Staring right at me through the window while it ate all the leftover pizza. Little thief. Foxes are getting braver every year. They probably know we're soft touches.

… honestly, I still can’t believe Old Man Hemmings tried to tell me my Sat Nav was broken because it had a 'funny voice'. Said it sounded like I was being directed by someone from… well, somewhere  not  Cambridge. Oh, Hemmings. He’s a treasure. What voice  were  you using, then? Did you go for something exotic? Exotic? No! I just… I liked the Welsh one. It sounded cheerful. Apparently cheerful isn't acceptable in his book. He insisted a proper Cambridge accent should be guiding me. Like the car itself has regional prejudice! He's probably just stuck in his ways. Remember when he complained about the colour of Sarah's car? Said anything that wasn’t British Racing Green was 'un-British'. Oh god, yes! The poor girl. It was a lovely shade of burgundy. He just couldn't get past it. So, are we still good for the drive to Stansted tomorrow, then? I’ve got a ridiculously early flight. Yeah, absolutely. I’ve checked the car over, oil’s fine, tyres are good. Bit of a beast, this old thing, but she gets us where we need to go. She’s seen better days, though, admittedly. “Beast” is a polite word for it, Liam. It sounds like it's constantly pleading for retirement. But yeah, it’ll do the job. Especially with  you  driving, you’re the most sensible of the three of us. Oi! Speak for yourself, Ethan. And don't encourage me to go faster than legally permitted. I’m not trying to end up with Hemmings tutting at  me  for dangerous driving. Speaking of driving, do you think we should leave, like,  really  early? Stansted security is always a nightmare, especially on a Tuesday. Good shout, Chloe. I’d rather be bored in the departure lounge than frantically rushing, missing my flight. Midday is the plan, right? Maybe bump it to 10:30? 10:30 sounds sensible. Gives us plenty of buffer. And it avoids the worst of the Cambridge traffic. Though, honestly, with everyone cycling everywhere, I sometimes think it's  more  chaotic than London. You just don’t appreciate the beauty of Cambridge cycling, Liam. It's an art form. A near-death experience, but an art form nonetheless. It’s a free-for-all, that’s what it is. I swear they have no concept of road markings. I nearly got taken out by someone wearing a full mortarboard and gown last week.

…and honestly, the guitar solo just  came  out of nowhere. Like, one minute it’s all mellow vibes, and the next it’s shredding. It’s insane. Have you guys heard of Stellar Bloom? Stellar Bloom? Nah, sounds a bit… spacey, innit? I’m more into the grime stuff, you know, Central Cee, Dave… proper London sounds. Keeps it real. That guitar stuff is alright, but it lacks a bit of… punch. I think it depends on the song, yeah? Stellar Bloom’s got some stuff that’s pretty chilled, but that track Leo was talking about, 'Nebula Drift', is properly energetic. It’s got that progressive rock feel, a bit like Pink Floyd, but… updated. Exactly! It's not all just wailing guitars. The drummer is incredible too. It’s the layers, man. It's properly complex. Though, my dad keeps going on about how “it doesn’t have a proper melody”. Old people, honestly. Your dad listens to music? Thought he was all about the news and complaining about the traffic. My old man only knows Elvis and anything on Radio 2. Seriously. He tried to tell me Central Cee sounded like “noise”. Noise! Haha, mine’s obsessed with classical. Says it’s “intellectually stimulating”. He tried to get me into Bach, but honestly, after about five minutes it just sounds like… scales. I prefer something with a beat, you know? Speaking of beats, did you guys see the new Dune? Oh, the film? Brilliant! Visually stunning. The sound design was mental. I’m doing a project on sound waves in physics at the moment, and honestly, thinking about how they created  those  sounds… it's incredible. The vibrating bass in the Harkonnen scenes… you could  feel  it. Dune? Yeah, yeah, saw it with my cousin. Bit long, though, wasn’t it? I almost fell asleep during one of the desert scenes. I mean, it looked good, don't get me wrong, but I needed snacks every twenty minutes to stay awake. It  is  long, but in a good way. It builds the world properly. And the science is pretty accurate, considering it’s sci-fi. Like, the whole concept of sound not travelling as well in the desert atmosphere… Leo, you’d probably appreciate that bit for your physics project. Actually, yeah! I was reading about that. The lower atmospheric pressure reduces the speed of sound and dampens the vibrations.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Balanceability was a bit of a faff. All that wobbling! I was expecting a bit more…well, balance, from all of you! Leo, you were practically horizontal at one point. I  wasn’t  horizontal! I was…streamlined! Like a rocket! No you weren’t. You fell over. A lot. Did not! Only three times. More like eight, darling. But you both did brilliantly to keep trying. It’s really about getting over that fear of falling, isn't it? That’s half the battle with anything new. Remember when you were learning to ride your bikes without stabilisers? Same sort of thing. That was scary. I kept thinking I was going to crash into Mrs. Higgins' bushes. You did nearly! But you didn’t. You persevered. And look at you now, whizzing around the park like professionals. It’s the same with school, too. Sometimes things feel really hard, but you keep at them, and then suddenly, you get it. Like maths? Maths is really hard. Maths  can  be tricky. But you’re getting there. I heard you aced your times tables test this week. I did! Miss Davies gave me a star sticker. A  gold  star sticker! I got a silver one. For writing a really good story about a magical unicorn. That’s wonderful, sweetheart! I'm so proud of both of you. Speaking of school, have you been chatting with Freya? Her family’s house is a complete mess right now with the renovations. Yes! She said they're making a massive kitchen. And…a swimming pool! A swimming pool?! Wow! Does it have a diving board? Apparently, it's going to be quite the setup. They're even building a little manmade waterfall! Sounds rather extravagant, doesn’t it? But Freya said her dad really wants it. Can you dive into waterfalls? You  can , but it's really dangerous. You need to know the water is deep enough and there are no rocks hidden underneath. Diving into unknown water is a big no-no, okay? We'll stick to the swimming pool at Comberton, alright? Okay. But waterfalls sound cool. They do, visually. What were you two talking about at school today? Anything interesting? We talked about cats! It’s National Cat Day in Japan today, apparently! Lily told me! She said they give cats special treats and everything. That’s lovely.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of beige in this flat is a bit startling, ANON. It’s lovely, don’t get me wrong, very Cambridge-y, but where’s the personality? Back home, everything’s a bit brighter, a bit more… chaotic, like. Chaotic is a good word for your family, Lila. Though, to be fair, beige is just… calming. I’ve been needing calming lately. It's a deliberate aesthetic choice. So, Doncaster’s all colour then? Oh, aye. Mums always got somethin’ clashing. Lilac with orange, that sort of thing. It’s… comforting, in a way. Though I did try to convince her to repaint the living room before I left. She said it was ‘perfectly good paint.’ You know how mums are. Anyway, enough about my floral-assaulting childhood. How’s the running going? You were saying you were training for that half marathon? It  was  going. Key word:  was . I managed three runs last week and then… well, Mark happened. And my motivation just evaporated. Mark? Again? What’s he done this time? Is it the ‘forgetting to text back for twelve hours’ thing again? Because honestly, if he’s still pullin’ that… Worse, actually. He said… he said he needs space. Like, ‘I need to focus on my pottery’ space. Pottery, Lila! He’s been taking a pottery class for  two weeks . It's a blatant excuse. Pottery? Right. Well that’s a new one. Focus on his pottery. Honestly, men. Seriously, what does he think you are, a kiln? You're brilliant - a production controller, a postgrad – and he needs space to… mould clay? Exactly! And it’s not even good pottery, apparently. His instructor said it's… 'developing potential.' Developing potential! He's 27! That's a polite way of saying it looks like something a six-year-old made. Oh, love, that’s awful. You deserve better. You deserve someone who’s excited about  you , not a lump of clay. Have you told him exactly that? Proper Yorkshire bluntness is needed here. I tried. I said, “So, you're choosing clay over me?” and he launched into this whole thing about needing artistic expression and being ‘found’ again. It was… infuriating. Ugh, ‘found’ again. The classic. They all need ‘finding’. Honestly, I think they just like the drama. Look, you need a distraction. Forget the running for a bit, it’s clearly tied up with him in your head.

…and honestly, Arthur, I don’t know  how  you manage to consistently beat me at Dominoes. Every week! It’s scandalous. You’re a sneaky one, you are. It's skill, Auntie Brenda, pure skill. And a bit of luck, obviously. Though Grandad does try to give me hints when you’re not looking. Nowt wrong with a little tactical assistance, lad. Keeps things interesting. Besides, your Auntie Brenda gets  far  too competitive. You'd think the fate of the nation rested on those little dominoes! Oh, don't you start, George! It's good for the brain, keeps me sharp for the little terrors at school. Honestly, trying to explain fractions to eleven-year-olds is more challenging than any domino game. Did I tell you about young Finley trying to use a chocolate bar to demonstrate halves? No way! Did it work? Not really. Ended up mostly  eaten  before he got anywhere near explaining anything. Honestly… they’re a handful. Speaking of handfuls, whose idea was this double pepperoni? I’ll be needing an early night after this. Now, now, Brenda. A bit of indulgence isn’t going to hurt. You deserve it after wrangling those young’uns all week. Remember Old Man Hemmings? Used to say a good pizza and a bit of company was all a man needed. Did you know Liam’s dad took him to that new Italian place in town, ‘Bella Notte’? Apparently, the pizzas there are bigger than my head. Bella Notte, is it? Expensive, I hear. We’re better off with a takeaway, aren’t we, George? Less fuss. Though, I suppose for a special occasion... Easter’s just around the corner, isn’t it? Have you thought about what you’re getting the bairns? I got young Emily a little pony grooming kit. She’s mad about horses, that one. And for Michael... well, he wanted a new football, so a new football it is. Simple as that. What about you, Brenda? I’m stuck. Finley wants one of those… what are they called? Those scooters with the big wheels? The ones all the kids are scooting around on. They’re an absolute fortune! Plus, I think he’d end up launching himself down the bank. Those Razor scooters? They're wicked! I saw Josh on one the other day doing a trick. Nearly fell off, though. He’s a growing lad, your Finley.

…and honestly, the pub quizzes in Cambridge are  nothing  like back home. They’re all so…intellectual. Like, ‘Name the obscure 17th-century botanist who discovered the Lesser Spotted Newt.’ Back in Sunderland, it was ‘What was Ant & Dec’s first show?’ You know, proper questions. Ha! That  is  a difference. I suppose it reflects the student population here. Everyone’s got a PhD halfway through their twenties, or aiming for one. Birmingham pubs were…mixed. A bit of both, I’d say. Did a fair bit of general knowledge, but also a fair bit of pop culture. Exactly! And the atmosphere! No one gets properly  rowdy . It’s all polite nodding and considered answers. I miss the shouting. I miss Sharon from the Red Lion yelling ‘It’s bloody Deal or No Deal!’ at the top of her lungs when the music started. Sharon sounds like a legend. Speaking of yelling… you won't believe what I tried to make for dinner last night. Oh god, lay it on me. Was it another one of your ‘experimental’ culinary adventures? Remember the beetroot risotto? Don’t remind me. That was… a learning experience. No, this was… kale and butternut squash curry. Kale and butternut squash… curry? That sounds… virtuous. Very Cambridge. It  was  trying to be virtuous. It failed. Utterly. It tasted like sadness and vaguely orange regret. I even followed a recipe! From a reputable food blog! Reputable doesn’t necessarily mean tasty. You should stick to things you know. Like pasta. You make a mean carbonara. You’re right. I'm a simple man. Pasta is my comfort zone. Though, I saw Jamie Oliver on the telly the other day advocating for grated courgette in Bolognese… Oh, don’t even  start . Jamie Oliver is a menace. A well-meaning menace, maybe, but a menace nonetheless. Trying to sneak vegetables into everything. It's an outrage! Give me a proper, meaty Bolognese any day. None of this ‘hidden goodness’ nonsense. I know, I know. It feels… subversive, somehow. Like he’s attacking our cultural heritage with a grater. Although, on the subject of celebrities… have you been following that whole drama with that actor, you know, the one from that sci-fi show? Oh, Liam Hemsworth? The one who apparently hates vegetables? I saw a headline about it. Apparently, his ex-wife, Miley Cyrus, was trying to get him to eat more greens and he was staging silent protests involving steak.

Right, okay, okay. No acting! That’s the rule, Rhys! You  cannot  act it out. It’s supposed to be descriptive clues, not a full-blown mime show! But it’s more fun, isn’t it, Cerys? You’ve got to admit, my impression of a… a badger digging for worms was pretty spot on! It was mostly just you scrabbling on the floor, to be fair. Details, Gareth, details! Artistic license! Besides, Dad was nearly in stitches. Weren't you, Dad? Oh, absolutely. Reminded me of a particularly enthusiastic otter I once saw trying to get a crab. Though I’m not sure badgers are quite as graceful. You’d find a connection to an otter in a cement mixer, I swear, Gwyn. It’s a lovely cottage, though, isn't it? So peaceful. Much needed break from everything. Yes, it is lovely, Mum. But back to the game! Rhys, seriously, you’re going to break something. And it’s my turn. Ugh. “Eucalyptus Tree.” Right. Okay. It’s… a tree. A very tall… Australian… thing. Koala food! Yes! It’s koala food! Good! See? Describing, not pretending to be a tree swaying in the breeze. It’s a bit of a giveaway when you say ‘Australian thing’, isn’t it? Fine. I’m not very good at this. Your turn, Gareth. Don't even  think  about doing your impression of a eucalyptus tree. Very well. “Hip Replacement.” Right. This is going to be…challenging. Okay. It's…medical. It involves a joint. An older person… might need one. Oh, this is difficult. Is it something to do with your hip? Mum! No clues! That’s cheating! Is it something they do after a fall? Sometimes people have bad breaks, you see. A new… ball joint! They replace the old one with a new ball joint! Yes! Exactly! A new ball joint! See? Rhys understands. He understands a good descriptive clue. Okay, okay, you win this round. It was a good one. Though slightly morbid. My turn again. "Bubble Wrap." Oh, this is fun. It’s… plastic. It’s got air inside. You… pop it? Packaging! It's for protecting things in packaging. Yes! Good one, Mum! You’re a natural at this. I'm rubbish. I just want to act everything out. It's in my blood, you know. A performer, that’s me. You’re a wonderful storyteller, Rhys.

Honestly, Rhys, you’re ruthless! Another point to the Welsh contingent. It’s hardly a fair fight, is it? You two ganged up on me and David again. Now, now, Bronwyn. It’s called strategy, love. And frankly, your ‘strategy’ of playing every Queen you draw isn’t exactly subtle. Besides, Gareth’s the one who actually  won  that round. I just provided moral support. And a well-timed distraction. Distraction? You were loudly complaining about the lack of bara brith in this cottage the entire time! It was less a distraction and more a national grievance broadcast. Oh, leave the poor man to his cravings. Honestly, a holiday in England and no proper Welsh cake? It  is  a tragedy. Though, to be fair, this cottage is lovely. Mum, you did well finding this place. So peaceful. It  is  nice, isn't it? A little bit of countryside quiet is exactly what we all needed. Though I did nearly trip over a sheep this morning. They just wander about as if they own the place. They practically do, Mam. Hereford's sheep central. They probably think  we're  the ones trespassing. Right, reshuffle. I’m feeling lucky. I'm going to attempt a grand slam, you have been warned. A grand slam in cribbage? Ambitious, even for you, Rhys. You remember what happened last time you tried that? The audible groan from Bronwyn was heard in the next village. Don’t remind me! He ended up with zero points. Zero! It was glorious. I haven’t stopped teasing him about it since. Speaking of teasing, David, you’ve been awfully quiet. Nursing your losses, are you? Just observing. Trying to decipher the Welsh mastermind plan. It's…complex. Years of strategic sheep herding experience probably play a part. Actually, reminds me of old man Evans back in Cardiff. He could win at dominoes blindfolded. Legend has it he once… Oh, here we go. Another Gareth anecdote. Prepare for a lengthy tale involving livestock and unparalleled gamesmanship. It's a good story! He used his sheepdog, Bryn, to subtly block his opponents' view of the dominoes. Bryn was impeccably trained. Only in Wales. Really. It's something else. You two are wonderfully eccentric. It's one of the things I love most about coming home with you. Even though it means facing relentless card game defeats. You know, it's lovely to see you all like this.

…and honestly, the lecturer just kept going on about post-structuralism! Like, who  needs  to know this stuff to be a journalist? It feels so pointless. Oh, uni, eh? Still complaining about it, then, Liv? I thought you were settling in. Settling in to being completely bewildered, maybe. It’s just… different to A-Levels. Miles different. At least at sixth form, you knew  why  you were learning things. This feels like intellectual gymnastics for the sake of it. It’s a shock to the system, isn't it? I remember feeling exactly the same when I started my apprenticeship. Suddenly you're expected to apply things in a real-world setting, and all the theory feels… distant. Although, thankfully, numbers are pretty universal. Less room for interpretation than, say, the meaning of life according to Derrida. You’re telling me. My degree was… intense. But the payoff is worth it. Being on the ship, applying all that engineering knowledge, finally  seeing  it work… that’s when it clicks. Easier said than done, though, isn’t it, Tom? Some of us are still trying to figure out  what  we want to do. I'm still balancing college with shifts at the shop. It's exhausting. And Mum's been really poorly lately with her chest, so I'm trying to help out around the house too. Oh no, how is your Mum, Chloe? Is she seeing a doctor regularly? Yeah, she is, but it's just… dragging on. It's not serious, thankfully, just constant coughs and wheezing. She keeps saying she's fine, but I can tell she’s struggling. It’s making Christmas a bit stressful, trying to figure out what to get her when all she wants is to feel better. That sounds awful. Definitely make sure she rests up. Christmas is supposed to be relaxing, not extra worry. Speaking of Christmas, has anyone actually started their shopping yet? I'm officially panicking. I have family scattered everywhere. Aunt Susan  specifically  requested a scented candle, but I have no idea what scent she likes! You're better organised than me. I haven't even thought about it. I was hoping to just… contribute to a group present. Keeps it simple. Plus, I've been working crazy hours prepping for deployment. They're really pushing us hard right now. Aw, that sounds tough, Tom. You look after yourself. So, Chloe, what are you thinking of getting your Mum?

…and honestly, the traffic was  brutal . Absolutely brutal. Worse than the M25 at rush hour, and that’s saying something, innit? Took me nearly two hours just to get from Bishop’s Stortford to here. Two hours! Two hours?! Blimey, Gran. That’s awful. Did you take the A10? It’s usually fairly decent. Decent? Decent?! Honey, there was an accident near Puckeridge. Total standstill. Had to detour through all these tiny villages… lanes really, barely wide enough for a Mini. And everyone was just… crawling. See, this is why I say cycling is the way to go. Fresh air, exercise, and you just  breeze  past all that. Breeze past? You try cycling up the hills around here, Liam. You’d be walking it before you got to Great Shelford. And, frankly, I'm not dressed for Lycra and a helmet just to pop to the shops. He’s got a point, Gran. Cycling  is  good for getting around Cambridge, though. It’s so flat! Remember when I cycled to your house last summer? Took me about forty minutes. Forty minutes? Yes, well, you’ve got young legs, love. I used to cycle everywhere when I was your age, mind you. But getting older… it's different. Plus, I like my comfort. A nice warm car, that's what I like. Even if it does get stuck in traffic. But even  driving  in Cambridge is a nightmare now. All those cycle lanes, one-way systems… It’s designed to confuse people. Remember when Dad used to just… know every shortcut? Your father? He knew every back alley in London, let alone Cambridge. Used to drive a black cab, remember? He could navigate blindfolded. Though, even  he  complained about the congestion charge. “Robbery!” he used to call it. He did. He was  very  vocal about the congestion charge. It’s still a bit pricey, isn’t it? Especially if you’re just popping in for a quick visit. It is. Makes you think twice, doesn’t it? Honestly, I’m starting to wonder if I should just get the train more often. It’s probably less stressful, even if it's a bit of a faff to get to the station. The train's alright, but it's not exactly door-to-door, is it? You still have to get a bus or a taxi from the station here. True. Although, there's that new bus route now, the one that goes right past the shops on Mill Road.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of dialects even  within  a relatively small area like East Anglia is astonishing. People from, say, Wisbech sound completely different to someone from Chelmsford, and they’re not  that  far apart geographically. It's a goldmine for research, though, isn't it? Absolutely. It's why I applied for this role, really. Though I did spend a year teaching English in Spain, and that opened my eyes to linguistic diversity too. Not just Castilian, obviously. Spain, you say? Fascinating place. Spent a little time poking around the Basque country once, years ago. Extraordinary language. Completely unlike anything else in Europe. Utterly isolated, linguistically speaking. A real puzzle. Oh, the Basque country! I've read so much about it. It’s pre-Indo-European, isn’t it? A complete outlier. Makes you wonder about the layers of history and migration. Makes your research a lot tougher, I imagine. It does! Having zero cognates is… challenging. But rewarding. It definitely makes you appreciate the shared roots of a lot of European languages. So, Professor Davies, did your research ever take you abroad much? Occasionally. Primarily focused on historical linguistics, so a lot of dusty archives. I did a stint in China, though, many years ago. Attempting to trace the origins of certain loanwords in English – surprisingly, a few turned up via the Silk Road. A long shot, admittedly, but… one has to follow the leads, eh? China! Wow. That's a leap from the Welsh Marches. Oswestry, wasn’t it? I’ve never actually been to Wales. My mum's side is Welsh, but we always holidayed in Cornwall. Oswestry, correct. Border town. Bit of both worlds, really – England and Wales bumping up against each other. You should visit. Stunning countryside. And they take their rugby  very  seriously, you know. Rugby? Are you a fan, Professor? My brother practically lives and breathes the stuff. He's convinced England will win the next World Cup. Optimistic, your brother. I’ve been following rugby for… well, let’s just say a  long  time. It’s a grand game, of course, but the Welsh have a certain… passion for it. It's ingrained in their culture. Arguably more so than football. Though don't say that to many people in London! You're right about London. Football's a religion there. I lived there for a couple of years after graduating.

…and honestly, the amount of people who just  dumped  water on their heads and didn’t donate anything was ridiculous. It was all performative, you know? Like, “Look at me, I’m charitable!” But no actual money went to the Motor Neurone Disease Association. Oh, don’t get me started on that! I remember Mum was absolutely furious because Uncle Barry just filmed himself with a tiny jug and barely got wet. Said it was enough. Enough! It’s a charity, Barry, not a photoshoot. Classic Barry. He's always been a bit… economical with his generosity. Though, to be fair, he probably thought the ice would give him hypothermia. He's convinced any temperature below room temperature is a health hazard now. How  are  your parents, by the way? It's been ages. They’re good, good. Mum's still determined to run a marathon, even at her age. Honestly, she’s fitter than I am. Dad’s complaining about his knees, naturally. Still refuses to acknowledge he needs to cut down on the biscuits. Oh, Dad and his biscuits. A love story for the ages. Seriously though, they look well in the photos you post. It’s just… weird being back here, isn't it? Feels like no time has passed and a lifetime simultaneously. Remember building dens in the garden with cushions and blankets? Vaguely! I was always more into raiding the biscuit tin with you, Sarah. You were a strategic biscuit hoarder, I remember that. It’s so strange being back at Mum’s. Suddenly I'm remembering all the form-filling she used to do for us. School trips, medical stuff… she was a champion form-filler! I’m battling with a recruitment application form for a candidate at the moment - it’s asking for their grandmother’s maiden name! Honestly! It’s bonkers, isn’t it? The level of detail some companies require. I'm grading essays all day, and sometimes I think the students put more thought into their TikToks. Speaking of…did anyone see Amelia’s engagement announcement on Facebook? Oh, yes! Stunning ring. Poor Ben, he looked utterly terrified. I texted her, of course. It’s nice she found someone. She always said she wanted a big, fairytale proposal. Do you think they’ll go for a destination wedding? Probably. Amelia's always loved travelling. Remember when she went to Thailand after university?

…and honestly, the manual is written in what I suspect is ancient Sumerian. Honestly, for a coffee machine that cost nearly two hundred quid, you’d think they could manage a simple ‘press this button’. You and technology, Mam. It’s a classic. Let me have a look, I'm pretty good at deciphering IKEA instructions, which is basically the same skill set. Though, two hundred quid  is  steep for a coffee machine. Are you sure it’s better than the old percolator? The percolator made a perfectly good cup of coffee. Strong enough to stand a spoon in, that’s what I liked about it. This… this thing purrs like a kitten and produces something lukewarm and faintly beige. The beige is the problem, Arthur! It’s not  coffee  beige, it’s… regret beige. And it’s supposed to make lattes! Lattes, I tell you. I saw Brenda down the road with a beautiful froth on hers. Mine just looks like dishwater. Okay, okay, I’ll tackle the latte situation later. Right now, we need to talk about the removal quote. It’s… substantial. Seven hundred and fifty for two rooms and a shed. And that’s before storage. Seven hundred and fifty! Robbery, I tell you, pure robbery. They know we’re a captive audience. We have no choice but to move the stuff somewhere while the kitchen’s being done. It's daylight robbery. Remember when we moved all that stuff to the new house ourselves, years ago? Just a van and a lot of strong backs. Those were the days. Those were the days when you  had  a strong back, Dad. No offence, but… None taken, love. This back’s seen better decades. Still, seven hundred and fifty. I think we need to get another quote. Maybe someone local. I tried, love, but everyone’s booked solid for weeks. Apparently, everyone in Hunsonby is having a clear-out. It’s the Cumbrian spring-cleaning epidemic. The storage is another nightmare. Sixty pounds a week. Sixty! That’ll eat through savings in no time. We could maybe downsize a bit? Be honest with ourselves about what we  really  need to keep. That collection of porcelain thimbles, Mam… Don’t you  dare  touch the thimbles! They’re a family heirloom! My grandmother collected them. Each one tells a story! They mostly tell the story of a lifetime spent travelling to obscure gift shops, if I remember correctly.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of glitter involved in making those reindeer antlers was  shocking . It's  everywhere  still. I’m finding it in the dog's fur. Oh, you and those children. Sounds about right. Christmas with kids is less ‘Silent Night’ and more ‘Glitter Apocalypse’, isn’t it? Though, I do miss it, a little. Your brother's lot were always wonderful at the chaos. They are! Little terrors, the lot of them, but brilliant. Speaking of which, have you heard from Uncle David? He said he was feeling a bit under the weather last week. I did, yes. Just a bad cold, thankfully. He’s determined to be fighting fit for Christmas at our place, you know he is. He’s already asking about the board games. Though, realistically, he just wants an excuse to beat your father at Scrabble. Predictable! Dad will be furious if he loses again. He’s been ‘strategizing’ all year, apparently. Honestly, they’re like children themselves sometimes. Are you having a big Christmas this year then? We are. Everyone’s coming. Your Auntie Margaret is already planning the menu – a full Welsh feast, naturally. She’s practically built a spreadsheet. And your cousin, Rhys, is bringing his new girlfriend. Apparently, she’s a vegan. Oh dear. Auntie Margaret and veganism aren't exactly a match made in heaven. That could be interesting. I'm still trying to figure out our plans. I was thinking we might spend Boxing Day with my friend, Sarah, and her family. She’s been a bit down since her mum’s been ill. That’s lovely of you, love. Sarah’s a good egg. You always were a thoughtful one. But what about Christmas Day itself? Still at your flat? It's a bit cramped, isn't it, with all the presents? It is! That's the problem. I was hoping maybe we could come to yours? I know it's a lot to ask… it’s just… it would be nice to have a bit more space, and frankly, I'm slightly terrified of cooking Christmas dinner for eleven people in my tiny kitchen. Don't be silly! Of course, you can. We have plenty of room, and honestly, I’d rather have the chaos here than trying to supervise it remotely. Plus, I'm not getting any younger – a few extra hands with the washing up would be very welcome.

…and honestly, the racket coming from his room last night was unbelievable. I thought a badger had got stuck in the chimney or summat. You talkin' about Liam again? That lad  always  snores. Remember that camping trip to the Lake District? Proper disturbed everyone’s peace, he did. Sounded like a foghorn. Oh, don’t even  start  on Liam's snoring! It's worse than Grandad’s, and that's saying something. I genuinely thought the roof was coming off last time I stayed at his. Did you try poking him, Chloe? Aye, I did! Gently at first, then a bit more… forceful. Didn't even flinch, the stubborn bugger. Eventually I just shoved a pillow over me 'ead. Still heard it muffled, mind. It's a gift, honestly. Sounds awful! My flatmate, Sarah, is a mouth breather. Not quite a snore, but this little wheezing sound all night. Drives me mad. It's like sleeping next to a tiny asthmatic dragon. You lot are lucky you even  get  sleepovers. My mum would have a fit if I had anyone stay. She’s obsessed with cleanliness and quiet. And proper bed linen, none o’ this student duvet cover stuff. Yer mum’s a bit of a clean freak, innit, Ben? No offence. None taken. She’s… particular. Anyway, did anyone get a chance to pop into Waterfields today? I was craving one of their Eccles cakes. I did, actually! Got a loaf of their white bloomer. Smelt amazing as I walked past, couldn’t resist. They had Richmond sausages on offer too, three for a fiver. Nearly went for ‘em, but I’m trying to be good. Richmond sausages? Now  that’s  a temptation. They’re proper good, aren’t they? Mum always used to get ‘em for Sunday dinner. They are. Though I’m trying to cut down on processed meats. Trying to be all… virtuous. Failing miserably, naturally. Virtuous? You, Sarah? Pull the other one. I remember you polishing off a whole packet of Wagon Wheels on our Uni road trip. Hey! That was a stressful time! We were lost for hours. Wagon Wheels were a necessity. Emotional sustenance! Fair enough. Speaking of essentials… Grandad asked if I had a handkerchief on me the other day. A  handkerchief . Like I carry one of those around! He looked proper offended when I said I don’t. Handkerchiefs are ancient history!

…and honestly, the whole thing was just  chaos . Like, beautiful chaos, but chaos nonetheless. Old Man Hemmings decided mid-bake-off that his Victoria sponge needed lavender. Lavender! It tasted like soap. Lavender, you say? Sounds like Hemmings. Always one for a bit of… innovation. Though I suspect innovation isn’t always a good thing when it comes to baking. Was it at least a nice village fete then? Apart from the floral-infused sponge? It was lovely, actually. The weather held, which is a miracle for a British summer. Loads of people turned out. I was mostly running around trying to make sure the kids didn’t dismantle the bouncy castle, which, let me tell you, is a full-time job. How was  your  weekend? Anything more relaxing than wrangling small children and questionable baking? Relaxing is… a generous word. Spent the whole Saturday trying to get the new irrigation system sorted in the south field. Bloody thing refused to cooperate. Kept short-circuiting. Turns out, a badger had decided it was a good spot for a burrow. A badger? Seriously? So, the irrigation system versus wildlife? Sounds like a battle you were destined to lose. Precisely. Ended up having to call Old Man Fitzwilliam – he’s a wizard with anything mechanical. He reckons the badger’s disrupted the wiring. Said it happens more often than you’d think. Apparently, badgers have a penchant for plastic-coated cables. Well, that's…a very specific talent. I didn't know badgers were electricians in their spare time. Did Fitzwilliam manage to fix it? Eventually. Took him most of the day. And a considerable amount of tea and biscuits. He’s a stickler for a good biscuit with his brew. After that, Sunday was spent trying to repair the fence the badger also decided to investigate. Honestly, that animal has a vendetta against my farm. Perhaps you should invest in badger-proof fencing! Or just negotiate a peace treaty. Offer him a share of the crops. Tempting, but I suspect it’d just encourage him. No, best to keep a watchful eye and reinforce the weak points. It’s a constant battle, farming is. You wouldn’t believe the things you have to deal with. It's not all picturesque rolling hills, you know. I can imagine. It sounds… exhausting. Though considerably less stressful than trying to convince five-year-olds that they can't swing from the gazebo.

…and honestly, the kids were lovely, absolutely lovely. But marking 150 essays on the subjunctive  every  week? It just…drained me. I felt like all I was doing was correcting grammar, not actually  teaching  them anything useful. Ugh, the subjunctive. The bane of every French teacher’s existence, isn't it? I remember battling that one constantly at Northwood. You're brave for leaving, though. It felt so secure, that job. Secure, yes. Soul-crushing, also yes. That's a bit dramatic, I know, but it really felt that way. Plus, the commute was killing me. Two hours each way! This new role, tutoring online, is so much better. I can set my own hours, actually focus on what I enjoy – conversational French, helping people prepare for trips – and I’m not buried in paperwork. That sounds idyllic, actually. I'm still at Bishop Vasey, you know. Year 5. It's...fine. The kids are good, mostly. But the workload  is  ridiculous. They keep adding things onto our plates. We're now responsible for tracking wellbeing  and  doing all the usual teaching. It’s exhausting. Oh, that sounds awful. They did that at my school too, just before I left. Everything becomes about data and targets, doesn’t it? No room for actually enjoying the job. Are you thinking of a change? I don’t know. It’s scary. Especially… well, with everything going on. Pregnancy brain is a real thing, apparently. Ooh! That's brilliant! Congratulations! You didn't mention it last time we spoke. When are you due? December! It’s still pretty early days, just coming up to sixteen weeks. Hence the constant tiredness and inability to form coherent sentences. Hence, needing a vent session with you! Mark’s over the moon, obviously. He's already planning tiny football kits. Oh, that’s lovely! December babies are the best – Christmas presents built in! Honestly, though, a baby changes  everything . Suddenly your priorities shift so dramatically. I’m still trying to figure it out with Leo, he’s three now. Three! My goodness. It feels a lifetime ago when we were moaning about marking Year 11 mocks! So, you’re enjoying motherhood, despite the lost sleep? Absolutely. It’s terrifying and wonderful and exhausting and rewarding all at the same time. It’s just… different. I’ve had to relearn how to prioritise my time. Language learning, for example, has had to take a backseat.

…and honestly, Doreen, I’m telling you, that robin’s built its nest  right  on top of the security light. Can you believe it? Right where I was meaning to change the bulb. Little blighter’s got nerve, it ‘as. Aye, they do, don't they? Bold as brass, robins. Always ‘ave been. Remember old Mrs. Miggins down the lane? Had a robin build in ‘er watering can. Oh, bless her. She loved that robin. Used to talk to it like it was one of ‘er grandchildren. Speaking of little ones, Arthur, are you sure about leaving that puppet show stuff out? Little Timmy’s coming round later, and he’ll have a field day dismantling everything. It’s alright, Margaret. It's all packed mostly, just laid out for a bit of airing. Needed to check the felt on that dragon, it's gone a bit mothy. Besides, Timmy’s a careful lad, aren’t you, Roy? Careful enough. Gets into scrapes, that one. Like his father did, mind you. Always climbin’ things. This cake’s lovely, Margaret. What did you do, put a little lemon in it? Just a touch. I thought it might brighten things up a bit. Trying to use up the lemons before they go off. It's good to have a little treat, isn’t it? Though I’m watching my sugar, of course. Doctor keeps bangin’ on about the diabetes. They all bang on about the sugar, don't they? Used to be, a bit of cake never hurt nobody. Now it’s all ‘low fat’ and ‘sugar-free’ and tastes like cardboard. I’d rather have a proper slice, and enjoy it. You're right there, Arthur. Life's too short for cardboard cake. Though, to be fair, I’ve cut down a bit. Roy's been naggin' me. Says I need to watch the weight. Nagging is a wife’s prerogative, Roy. You know that. Though she's right, of course. We get a bit… settled, don't we, as we get older? Not much call for running around! Settled is one word for it! More like… anchored. It’s just… everything’s a bit harder now, isn’t it? Even walking around the garden leaves me breathless some days. Happens to the best of us, Margaret. We're not spring chickens any more. Remember when we used to walk to Cromer and back, just for the day?

…and honestly, the meze just  keeps  coming! I thought I’d ordered a small plate, but it’s a feast. Are you enjoying yours, Arthur? Enjoying it? Brenda, it’s magnificent. Best food I’ve had all summer, and that includes Mabel’s roast, which is saying something. Though, Mabel did make a rather questionable gravy last time… tasted faintly of cinnamon. Oh, Mabel. She’s a force of nature. Though, she still refuses to believe Colin’s arthritis is anything but a ‘fancy name for getting old’. Honestly, the man’s in agony. Bless him. It’s a modern world, Brenda, people need to understand these things. Speaking of aches and pains, I really must get these hearing aids adjusted. I missed half of what the waiter said about the fish. Something about being freshly caught? He said it was caught this morning, apparently. And he’s right, it smells wonderful. I think I’ll go for that, then. You’re having the lamb, aren’t you? Indeed. Lamb with lemon and herbs. Reminds me of my mother’s cooking, although she’d never have used lemon. Always rosemary, always. She was a proper traditionalist, your Auntie Elsie. Still, lost her too young, didn’t we? Lung cancer. Horrible business. It was. I still miss her terribly. She used to say I was destined for great things, though what those great things were, she never specified. She was a bit of a… believer, shall we say? Always talking about dowsing for water, and sensing energies. Oh, Elsie and her dowsing! Remember when she convinced old Mr. Hemmings, the butcher, that there was a spring under his shed? He dug up the entire garden looking for it! I’d almost forgotten that! He was furious. She just said he wasn’t ‘tuned in’ enough. She was fascinated by shamanism too, towards the end. Took a weekend workshop in Glastonbury. Glastonbury… that explains a lot! Elsie always had a… unique perspective. I always preferred a bit of solid logic myself. Although, I must admit, sometimes you wonder if there’s more to it all. Especially when you meet people. Like that chap over there, with the bright blue shirt. Oh, the one arguing on the phone? What about him? He’s been here every day since we arrived. Always on the phone, always animated. And always with a different woman. I'm placing bets on a three-way disaster brewing.

…and honestly, the spreadsheets are just multiplying. It’s like they breed when I’m not looking. Four different departments, all needing updates, all with slightly different systems. It's chaos, Mum, absolute chaos. Oh, love, you always did take on too much. You were always the one volunteering for everything at school. Remember the school play, you single-handedly did the costumes  and  the scenery? That was different! That was fun. This is…project co-ordination, yes, but feels more like damage control. Anyway, how’s work? Still battling teenagers and exam boards? Don’t even get me started. This year’s cohort is…spirited. And Ofsted are sniffing around again. Honestly, all I do is write risk assessments and pray nothing goes wrong. Mr. Henderson keeps hinting at early retirement, I swear he’s trying to lay the groundwork for me to inherit the headache. Henderson always was a clever one. Playing the long game, that lad. Still, you’re more than capable, Maureen. You run that school like a tight ship. That’s kind of you, Arthur, but a tight ship full of hormones and impending doom. Speaking of doom, did you manage to sort out that leaky gutter before the real storms hit? Aye, got young Ben down the road to have a look. Said it needed a new section, needed a bit of patching up. All done now, thankfully. Don't want the damp creeping back in. Thinking about a bigger job next year, though. Roof needs looking at, and I fancy getting the back patio redone. Oh, that sounds amazing! A new patio would be lovely. You’ve talked about that for ages, Dad. Is there a design you’ve got in mind? Just kicking ideas around. Maybe something with a bit of landscaping, a small fire pit… Somewhere we can sit out in the summer. But it all depends on the price, doesn't it? Everything's gone up. It has. Even Christmas is looking expensive this year. Have you started thinking about presents yet? I’m completely stuck for ideas for your brother. He says he doesn’t  want  anything. That’s always the hardest, isn’t it? Men who say they don't want anything. I’m thinking of getting Gran a new photo frame – she’s always complaining she can’t see the pictures of us properly. She’d love that, she really would.

… honestly, I still can’t believe Brenda fell for it. A  fishing boat captain  in Alaska? Come on! She’s usually so sharp. I know, right? Alaska! And she sent him money? How much money, even? I saw the screenshots, but I didn’t ask, didn't want to pry too much. She wouldn’t tell me the exact amount, just said it was “enough to cover his satellite phone bill and some gear.” Which, Brenda, is classic. Always the helpful one. She’s got a heart of gold, bless her, but… ripe for a catfish, she is. It’s just…it’s the modern version of those romance scams in the paper, innit? Used to be lonely old blokes, now it's anyone with an internet connection and a dodgy profile pic. Makes you wonder how many people are out there pretending to be someone they’re not. Loads. It’s terrifying. Remember that bloke on Jeremy Kyle a few years back? The one who turned out to be a 60-year-old man pretending to be a young woman called ‘Tiffany’? Oh god,  Tiffany . That was a legendary episode! The poor girl was heartbroken. And the reveal? Iconic. He was proper smug about it too, wasn’t he? “I just wanted a bit of fun!” Fun?! At someone else's expense. Aye, smug is an understatement. He was winding her up the whole time. Jeremy Kyle was brutal, but sometimes, like with that, it did expose these kinds of people. Though, I suppose it also  gave  them a platform. It’s a bit of a double-edged sword. Definitely a double-edged sword. And it’s getting worse, isn’t it? With all these filters and editing apps. You can’t even trust what you  see  in a photo anymore. Brenda thought she’d been chatting to someone who looked like Chris Hemsworth's long lost brother. Chris Hemsworth! That explains the Alaska story then, she needed a rugged outdoors type to match the face. She said he was a ‘man of the sea,’ didn't she? That’s a line straight out of a bad romance novel. She did! And she was going on about his ‘piercing blue eyes’ and his ‘strong hands’ – she’d never even  seen  him on a video call! Just photos. Actually, thinking about it, she said he always had ‘technical difficulties’ whenever she asked to video chat.

…and honestly, the Wi-Fi’s been a nightmare all morning. Trying to submit this essay on Virgil, and it just keeps timing out. It’s infuriating! Honestly, for a Classics degree, you’d think they’d appreciate a bit of… patience. It's not like we're demanding streaming 4K video, just a bloody Word document. Virgil, darling? Still wrestling with the Aeneid, are you? Honestly, you sound just like your grandfather. He’d get absolutely  incensed  when his typewriter jammed. Said it was a conspiracy against scholarship. It feels like a conspiracy! It’s stressing me out. I’m starting to think I should just go to the library, but… rain’s looking proper dodgy out there. Plus, this soup is amazing, Nan. Seriously. What did you put in it? Smells faintly Italian. Ah, a little secret, that. My mother’s recipe. She always said a pinch of fennel elevates everything. And yes, a little nod to our Italian roots. Though, Vienna felt more home to her, after a while. She never quite lost the longing for Italy though, always talking about the light. You know, she spoke five languages fluently. Five! Five? Wow. That’s… intimidating. I’m struggling with the basics of German for uni, and feeling like a right lemon. All those declensions. It’s completely different to Romance languages. It is a beast, German. Very precise. But useful! I travelled all over Europe in my youth, you know, painting. Germany, France… Paris, of course. Oh, Paris. That city steals your heart. Have you been, Leo? Only once, briefly, with a school trip. Didn't get to really  see  it. Mostly just remember queuing for croissants and trying not to get pickpocketed. I'd love to go back properly. Maybe next summer? If I can actually finish this degree. You  will  finish this degree. Don't talk like that. Though, Paris is best in the spring, I think. The light is… magical.
