I once spent a month sketching by the Seine. Met a fascinating group of artists, a Romanian sculptor, a Spanish poet… Sounds incredible. You always had such an adventurous life, Nan. We just seem to…stay put. Staying put isn't a bad thing, Leo. It allows you to cultivate roots. Though, I admit, I always felt the pull to move. Your mother was the same, thankfully. She found her peace in the countryside, with the bees.

… honestly, Dad, you nearly gave me a heart attack back there! That overtake was  insane . Seriously, what were you thinking? We’re on holiday, not the Grand Prix! Oh, don't be dramatic, love. Just a little bit of assertive driving. Needed to get past that lorry. Held everyone up, it did. Dorset’s lovely, but getting  to  Dorset… it’s a nightmare with all this traffic. He's right about the traffic, it’s been building since we left. Though, honestly George, you do have a habit of thinking you’re Lewis Hamilton. Remember that time in Brighton? Nearly took out a bus shelter. That was a perfectly legitimate manoeuvre! The bus shelter was… encroaching. And Brighton's a terrible place anyway. All students and overpriced chips. Never understood the appeal. Okay, okay, let's not rehash Brighton '08. Mum, are you alright back there? You've been awfully quiet. Just thinking about work, actually. Got a double shift on Monday. Old Mrs. Higgins is falling apart at the seams, poor love. Bit of a tumble yesterday. Hoping it's not a break. They’re desperately short-staffed though, so even if she needs a lot of care, I’ll be stuck with her all day. No days off in sight. That sounds rough. You really deserve a break. Honestly, care work must be absolutely draining. It's… it's physically and emotionally exhausting, isn't it? It is. But someone’s gotta do it. And it’s better than nothing. Although, the pay... well, you know. Makes me wonder if I should have stuck with the furniture upholstery course I started after sixth form. Upholstery? Good Lord, Margaret! That's a bit dusty for you, isn't it? No, you’re better suited to people. Though, speaking of furniture, I still can't believe the price they wanted for that sideboard at Mantiques last week. Highway robbery! Mantiques? You went to Mantiques again, Dad? I thought we agreed you wouldn't spend  all  your pension on old rubbish. It wasn’t rubbish! It was a vintage piece! And I didn't spend my  whole  pension. Just a significant portion. It needed a bit of work, that’s all. Which reminds me, have you got that solicitor's bill sorted? They've been chasing us for weeks about Aunt Mildred’s probate. Ugh, don't even mention it. It's dragging on forever.

…and honestly, Doreen, I still reckon they overcharge for a packet of biscuits these days. A  packet ! Used to be you could get a good, solid biscuit for pennies, now it’s… well, it’s daylight robbery, it is. Oh, Arthur, you say that every time you go to the shop. You’ve been saying it for thirty years! It’s inflation, dear. Everything goes up. Even biscuits. Though I agree, the quality’s gone downhill. They don’t  taste  like they used to. All fluff and no substance. Exactly! No substance. Just like… well, never mind. Doesn’t bear thinking about. I went to get some digestives, mind, thinking they’d be safe. Can’t go wrong with a digestive, can you? But even  they’ve  shrunk! Honestly, a right cheek, shrinking the biscuits and keeping the price the same. You’re a marvel, Arthur. A right marvel. Still getting worked up over biscuits. How’s your knee today? Any better after that heat pack I got you? A bit, a bit. Still a twinge when I try to get up from the chair, but not as bad as yesterday. That heat pack is a godsend, Doreen, I’ll give you that. Proper thoughtful of you. Though young Michael said I was looking like a baked potato, wrapped up like that. Oh, Michael! Always the comedian. He’s a good lad, though, isn’t he? Calls every Sunday, regular as clockwork. He is. Best thing that woman ever did, having him. Though I never did understand why she went off with that… that Geoffrey. Dreadful man. Never said a civil word to me. Now, Arthur, let's not start on Geoffrey again. It’s been twenty years. And it upset Michael enough as it was. He needed his father, and you were always there for him. That's what mattered. I was, wasn't I? Always was. Just… it’s still a bit raw, if I’m honest. Seeing him so happy with his own family now…sometimes I wonder… Wonder what, dear? Wonder if I could have done things different. Been...more. I wasn't much of a provider, was I? Always a bit of a dreamer. Never really held down a proper job. Your father, he always looked at me a bit sideways, didn't he? Oh, don’t be silly. My father was a grumpy old thing.

…and honestly, the brass band was  loud . Like, properly rattling-the-windows loud. Old Man Hemmings was conducting like he was leading a charge, all flailing arms and puffed-out cheeks. You wouldn’t believe it, considering it was a Tuesday afternoon in a village hall. Sounds about right for Hemmings. Still at it then? Last I heard he was threatening to retire and then immediately volunteered to organize the annual flower show. Still at it. Apparently, the flower show's on again this year, bigger and better than ever. He’s going full Monty Don on us, he is. Wants everyone to contribute a ‘statement bloom’. Honestly, it’s terrifying. A statement bloom? What does that even  mean ? Sounds like something out of a pretentious art exhibition, not a village fete. Precisely! That's what I said to Mum. She's roped herself into helping him, naturally. She's already got seedlings going, little rows of things I can’t even pronounce. She’s aiming for a David Austin rose, apparently. A ‘Peace’ rose. Very symbolic. Your mum and her roses. It’s a constant. How’s the allotment going, by the way? You mentioned you were battling slugs again. Don’t even  start  me on the slugs. They’re winning. Utterly winning. I tried copper tape, I tried beer traps… they just treat it like a five-star hotel. Little slimy ravers. Sounds grim. Maybe you need to get some ducks? A proper natural predator. Tempting, incredibly tempting. But then I’d have to build a duck pond, and our garden’s not exactly expansive. Besides, I doubt the neighbours would appreciate duck-related noise at 6 am. Fair point. So, a losing battle then? For now. I think I'm shifting focus. Maybe less delicate veg, more robust stuff. Perhaps some pumpkins. They're pretty slug-resistant, right? Although, they're hardly… subtle. Pumpkins are good. Very autumnal. Speaking of autumnal, did you catch Radio 6 Music’s ‘Autumn Sessions’ line-up? Oh, aye! Have a listen on the drive tomorrow. It's pretty good this year. Yard Act are playing, which is brilliant. They're proper Geordie lads, loads of energy. Makes me home sick sometimes, hearing their accent on the radio. Yard Act, yeah, I’ve heard a few tracks. Bit shouty, aren’t they? They are. But in a good way! It's proper observational stuff, social commentary set to a driving beat.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of applications for that Assistant Curator role was mental. Like, I genuinely thought my experience with the digital archive project at the university would put me in with a shout, but apparently everyone and their dog is suddenly an archiving expert. Sounds rough, love. Still, you’ve got a cracking CV. Something will come up. It’s just… the market’s brutal right now, isn't it? Especially for anything even remotely arts-related. Brutal is an understatement. I mean, I  get  it. Places are cutting budgets. But it's depressing. It makes you wonder what the point of all those student loans was, doesn't it? Twenty grand in debt for the privilege of competing with hundreds of others for a job that pays less than I earned stacking shelves at Tesco when I was sixteen. Don’t even get me started on student fees. I feel your pain. Although, thankfully, my funding’s holding for another year. But thinking about what everyone coming up behind me is facing… it’s just… unfair. My sister’s just started looking at unis, and the prices are terrifying. She wants to do history, and you know how passionate she is, but… how are people supposed to afford it? It’s scandalous. My mam and dad scrimped and saved to help me, and even then, I was working three part-time jobs. Honestly, I'd be lost without them. They still subtly remind me about it, though. "Remember who paid for that Masters, lass!" Mothers are mothers, eh? Mine does the same thing, always reminding me about the sacrifices they made. Although, hers usually revolves around the cost of my car. She still can’t believe I willingly chose a rear-wheel drive when there was perfectly good front-wheel drive available. Apparently, it's a financial black hole. Oh, bless her. Practical women, our mothers. So, how’s the PhD going, then? Still wrestling with… was it Bayesian statistics? Don't remind me. It's like trying to decipher ancient hieroglyphs with a hangover. I've made… some progress. I think. My supervisor keeps saying "promising," which is academic for "still a long way to go." But genuinely, it’s fascinating when it clicks. It's just getting to the 'click' that's the problem. It feels like an endless maze of data. I can imagine. It's a completely different academic world to what I’m used to.

Right, so the badger’s lost his spectacles  again ? Honestly, you’d think he’d tie ‘em to his head or something. He’s a bit of a scatterbrain, that badger. Just like… well, never mind. These photos are amazing, though. Look at this one of your Dad at Alton Towers. He looks terrified on the Nemesis! Terrified and probably regretting letting your Uncle Hamish talk him into it. Hamish was always a devil for a dare. Remember the time he convinced your grandfather to try water skiing on Loch Lomond? Oh,  please  tell me that story again! I love the one about Grandpa nearly losing his teeth. It’s a good one. Though it does highlight why your grandfather preferred a nice, quiet game of chess. It's just... looking at these pictures, it gets me thinking about family. About  our  family. It’s…complicated, isn't it? Complicated is a polite word for it, dear. A patchwork quilt, I’d say. Lots of different bits sewn together. And some bits…a bit wobbly, perhaps. What do you mean? Well, you know. Me and Mark being separated. You having…well, having Daniel, who's not…directly related to me. It’s not the ‘traditional’ family. Traditional is overrated. And children don't care much for tradition, only for love. Mark provides that for Daniel, and that’s what matters. Besides, I’ve seen plenty of ‘traditional’ families that were downright dysfunctional. Yeah, but sometimes it’s confusing. When I was drawing ideas for my kids’ book, I wanted to draw a family. But what family  do  I draw? Like, should it be just Mum and me? Or Mum and Daniel and me? Or…something else entirely? That’s actually a really good question. It's… it’s hard to represent everything. That’s why I thought about doing a book about different kinds of families. Maybe showing a family with two mums, a single dad, grandparents raising children… all sorts of things. That’s a brilliant idea, actually! You could show the similarities - the love, the support, the silly arguments – and the differences. It would teach children about acceptance. And illustrate that 'family' is about who loves you, not  how  they’re related to you. Ooh, and maybe one of the families could be like ours! With step-siblings and separated parents, but still getting along. But not in a cheesy, everything’s-perfect kind of way.

…and then Mr. Harrison, right,  Mr.  Harrison, started going on about ‘professionalism’ and needing to ‘maintain a certain image’ for the customers. Honestly, you’d think we were selling diamonds, not lukewarm coffee and slightly stale biscuits. Ugh, the image thing. I hate that. My uni supervisor keeps hinting I should tie my hair back more in the library. Says it’s “distracting.” Distracting to  who  exactly? The books? Exactly! Distracting to Brenda who’s spent the last hour meticulously colour-coding her highlighters. Honestly. It’s always something, innit? Makes you wonder what they really mean when they say that sort of thing. Probably just think you shouldn't look too…natural. Probably. It’s all about conforming, isn't it? You know, it got me thinking… I’ve been meaning to ask. You shaved your legs the other day, didn’t you? I noticed. Aye, I did. Had a date, see. Didn’t want to scare ‘im off with me looking like Chewbacca. Chewbacca! Oh, Sarah! Seriously though, is it…a bother? Doing it all the time? I’ve been meaning to start, but it seems like  so  much effort. It is a right faff, to be honest. Always has been. Mum used to make me do it when I was younger – said hairy legs weren’t ‘ladylike’ or some such nonsense. I rebelled for years, then just sort of…fell into doing it for myself, I suppose. That's so weird. My mum  never  mentioned it. She just didn’t really talk about…body stuff, much. It’s only since seeing other girls doing it, and, you know, feeling a bit self-conscious, that I’ve started considering it. See, there’s the pressure again. It's not like it  needs  doing, does it? It's all just…expected. I honestly think I’d happily grow a full-on beard if society didn't look at me like I’d lost me mind. A beard! You’d rock a beard. Though, might clash with the Yorkshire accent a bit…too much rugged masculinity? Oi! Don’t you start. I’m perfectly capable of being a sophisticated, bearded academic. Just watch me. But seriously, it’s ridiculous. Men can walk around looking like bears and it's 'masculine' and 'distinguished'. We pluck a few hairs and it’s ‘unhygienic’ or ‘unprofessional’. Double standards, obviously. It’s infuriating. I just… I don’t want it to become another chore.

… honestly, it’s just baffling. Like, why ‘H’ is pronounced ‘aitch’ and not just ‘h’? It makes absolutely no sense. We just  decided  that centuries ago, didn’t we? You’re still on about the alphabet, El? You've been dissecting it since we sat down. It’s a linguistic quirk, love. Don't try to apply logic to something that’s entirely historical. It's like asking why we drive on the left – it just  is . But it’s fundamentally illogical! Every other letter, you say the sound. A is ‘ay’, B is ‘bee’… H is just a weird outlier. It’s the Sunderland of the alphabet. Odd one out. Oh, you always bring it back to Sunderland, don’t you? Look, you spend your days analyzing data, searching for patterns. Maybe you’re just projecting that need for order onto something completely random. Fancy another gin and tonic? This one's actually pretty good. Proper botanical flavour. Alright, alright, you’ve made your point. Gin and tonic sounds good. Though, speaking of patterns… have you noticed how many footballers are getting caught up in stuff these days? Not just on the pitch, I mean. Proper dodgy behaviour. It’s always been there, El, hasn't it? Just more visible now with social media. Money, fame, that whole culture… it breeds trouble. And the pressure! Imagine being scrutinised for every single thing you do. It's the racism too, though. Still absolutely rife. That incident at the match last weekend was disgusting. People still shouting horrific things. It's 2024, for God's sake. It’s a massive problem, and football seems to be a focal point for it, unfortunately. It’s about more than just the sport though, isn’t it? It's a societal issue mirrored in a very public arena. I was reading an interesting piece about how the rise of far-right ideologies is feeding into it… Ugh, it’s depressing. Sometimes I just want to switch off. You know, my cousin Liam, he used to be  obsessed  with boxing. Proper obsessed. Said it was the purest form of competition. Liam? The one who got that black eye trying to impress a girl at a sixth form disco? Don't remind me. It wasn't a  black eye , it was mild bruising! But yeah, that's him. He was convinced boxing was this noble thing. I always thought it looked… well, brutal.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for the Heritage Lottery Fund these days is just… exhausting. It’s not about the historical merit anymore, is it? It feels more about ticking boxes and demonstrating ‘community engagement’ until you’re blue in the face. You’re absolutely right, Eleanor. It's become a performance, hasn’t it? I spent three months last year just crafting the ‘impact report’ for the little chapel in Aylesbury. Impact! As if restoring a 13th-century building  isn’t  impactful in itself. They want measurable outcomes, quantifiable benefits… it’s maddening when you’re dealing with intangible heritage. Exactly! And this Manor House project… it  is  a worthy cause. Old Man Hemmings left it to the village, wanting it restored as a community space. Lovely idea, desperately needed. But it’s a Grade I listed building, practically falling apart, and the village council has… well, let’s just say their fundraising efforts extend to a bake sale and a somewhat optimistic raffle. Bake sales are a good starting point, though. Don’t dismiss them entirely! But you’re right, a bake sale won't fix a crumbling roof. Have you considered Historic England? They’re usually more pragmatic than the Lottery Fund, though their grants are smaller. And they appreciate a solid, realistic plan. I have. I’ve sent them a preliminary inquiry. They want to see a comprehensive condition survey first, which, naturally, costs money the village doesn’t  have . It's a Catch-22. I was rather hoping your experience with the Winslow Tithe Barn might provide some insight. You navigated that funding maze so elegantly. Winslow was… challenging. That was a truly ambitious project. The key, I found, was presenting a multi-faceted business plan. Not just restoration, but a demonstrable financial sustainability post-restoration. They want to see it generate income, not become a drain on resources. We proposed a small museum, a tea room, and letting the upper floors as office space for local artisans. That’s clever. The Manor House has potential… it has a large garden, a stable block… could potentially be turned into workshops. The main house… well, the grand hall is beautiful, but impractical. Perhaps a space for weddings and events? Weddings are good! Always popular. But you need to factor in access, parking, catering facilities… all that. And don’t underestimate the cost of ongoing maintenance. Historic buildings are  forever  projects.

…and honestly, the phonetic variation even  within  Sunderland is wild. You’ve got folks in Ryhope sounding practically South Shields, and then you get up towards Houghton and it's a completely different kettle of fish. It’s a micro-cosm of the whole Northeast, isn’t it? Right, a linguistic patchwork quilt. You’re always bringing it back to Sunderland, aren’t you? Even when we’re talking about, like, general phonetic drift. Well, it’s where my ear’s trained! Plus, it’s a fascinating case study. I was explaining it to Dr. Anya Sharma at the conference last week – she’s doing work on urban dialect levelling in Manchester, and she was  fascinated  by the resilience of certain features in the Wearside dialect. Levelling, yeah. That’s what I’m worried about with some of the Brummie stuff. I’ve been recording my nan for my thesis – just natural speech, you know – and even  she’s  starting to soften some of the vowels. It's subtle, but it's there. Oh, that’s heartbreaking! Is it more influence from London, do you think? That’s what they suggested for the Yorkshire vowels, isn’t it? The “Estuary English” creep. Probably. Honestly, it's a bit of everything. Media, people moving around…Cambridge has a lot to answer for, attracting people from everywhere and homogenising things. It’s ironic, considering we  study  linguistic diversity. It is! It's like being a conservationist surrounded by developers. So, how’s the thesis going, actually? Still wrestling with the ‘oo’ sounds? You were pulling your hair out last time we spoke. Don't remind me. The 'oo' sounds are my nemesis. It’s not even a consistent change, it’s contextual. Depends on the following consonant, the speaker’s age… It’s a nightmare to model statistically. I think I’ve finally cracked a decent methodology, though. I'm using a variationist approach, looking at correlations with social factors. Good. Sounds properly rigorous. You'll be presenting at that phonetics conference in Edinburgh next month, right? Tentatively. I need to finish analysing the last batch of recordings. Speaking of which… …I really should get back to it. It’s just…nice to actually  talk  about something other than data for five minutes. I know, right? It's suffocating sometimes. Everything becomes a potential research subject. Though, I was thinking… maybe we should actually  use  our skills for something fun?

…and honestly, the amount of food they waste is just criminal. Honestly, criminal. Little plates piled high and then half of it ends up in the bin. But Miss Davies said we  have  to try everything! Even the broccoli trees. Broccoli trees, is that what they’re calling them now? Well, trying a little bit is good, darling. But you don't have to  eat  the whole forest, do you? I ate a whole forest! It made my tummy rumble. Oh, did it now? Well, that’s…enthusiastic. Listen, both of you. I’m just trying to figure out if we need to top up your dinner money. Are you actually eating enough at school, or is it mostly going to waste? Be honest. I eat the chips! And the smiley faces! And the chocolate pudding when they have it! It's got sprinkles! Okay, chips, smiley faces, sprinkles...that’s a good start. But what about the main course? The… broccoli trees? Sometimes. If it's with gravy. Gravy makes everything better. I trade mine to Leo for his sausage and mash. You  trade ? Oh, you little negotiator! That's resourceful. But is Leo getting a good deal? Are you sure you're getting enough to eat when you’re swapping meals? Leo says it's fair. He really likes broccoli trees. Right. Well, as long as it's a fair swap. Speaking of Leo, his mum mentioned the tennis tournament next month. Have you two been practicing? I can hit the ball really hard! Like  this ! . Whoa! Easy there, superstar! Maybe practice outside, eh? And gently. Don’t want to break anything. Lily, are you still a bit unsure about your serve? It's wobbly. Like jelly. We can practice this weekend. Maybe after we go to Granny’s. She promised to make her special apple crumble. Granny makes the BEST crumble! It's got extra sugar! That’s what I’m afraid of. She’s very generous with the sugar. Right, so, Granny’s on Saturday, tennis practice Sunday. Then it’s back to school and… more broccoli trees. I swear, I should write a letter to the school about their menu. Granny said when she was little, school dinners were awful! She said they had something called "spotted dick." Spotted Dick! Oh, my goodness. Yes, that was a classic. It's a suet pudding with… well, let’s not go into detail.

…and honestly, the special effects were just  exhausting . All flash, no substance. It felt like they’d spent the entire budget on explosions and forgotten to give the characters anything resembling a motivation. Remember ‘The Long Good Friday’ Dad?  That  was tension. This was just… loud. ‘The Long Good Friday’… now there was a film. Bob Hoskins at his best. Everything happened  because  of something. None of this ‘because the script said so’ nonsense you get nowadays. Though, I must admit, I struggle to keep up with all the explosions. My ears aren't what they used to be. It’s a wider problem, isn’t it? With everything. Substance over style. It’s why I find myself increasingly cynical about advertising, ironically. We  sell  the feeling, the aspiration, but often the product itself is… well, underwhelming. It’s the same principle. And that film felt entirely  designed  to be a TikTok moment. Exactly! It's all about the clip, the soundbite. It speaks to that debate in Cambridge last week, actually. The one about teaching history. They were arguing about whether to focus on ‘big events’ – impactful moments for social media – or on the nuances of social history, the everyday lives of people. I caught a snippet of that on the radio. Sounded like a right old dust-up. Seems to me, you can’t understand the big events without understanding what life was  like  for the people living through them. Just dates and battles… that’s not history, that’s chronology. It's what they did to us at grammar school, honestly. Rote learning. The problem is the National Curriculum, isn’t it? It’s so prescriptive. Teachers are forced to ‘teach to the test’ rather than fostering genuine curiosity. And the emphasis on memorization is bizarre in the age of Google. My niece is in Year 8, and she’s already completely switched off. It's dreadful. I try to encourage critical thinking, and source primary sources. But the pressure to hit those attainment targets… it’s suffocating. I remember my history teacher, Mr. Davies, at school in Dorchester. He'd make us debate, role-play. He’d get us  involved . It wasn't just about knowing when the Battle of Hastings happened. Dorchester! A lovely part of the world. I did my National Service down that way. Though my education was… somewhat different. More classics, less modern history.

…and I’m tellin’ ya, Doreen, this draught is somethin’ awful. Right through me bones it goes. Used to be, houses were built  to  keep the weather out, not let it blow straight through like a sieve. This modern stuff… plastic windows and all, fancy lookin’, but no substance. Oh, Arthur, you say that every time the wind blows a bit strong. It’s November, dear. Draughts are to be expected. Honestly, you'd think we were livin’ in a barn. Though I  do  agree about the buildin’ quality these days. My mother’s house, built in the thirties, stood like a rock. She’s got a point, Arthur. Though I suspect you’ve always been a bit sensitive to the cold. Remember that holiday in Cornwall when you refused to leave the pub all week? Said the sea air was “attackin’ your sinuses.” That was different, Geoffrey! That was a  salty  wind, a right nasty wind! And me sinuses  were  playin’ up. Besides, it weren’t just the cold. It reminded me too much of… well, things. Things? You mean the war, Dad? You rarely talk about it. Aye, the war. Always bringin’ back memories, the wind. Reminded me of the raids. Hearin’ the sirens, seein’ the searchlights… scary stuff for a young lad. Not like these youngsters today, playin’ at soldierin’ on computers. We were livin’ it. Your father, Arthur’s father, he was a brave man, you know. Worked at the airfield, kept those planes flyin’. Never said much about it himself, just got on with it. Like most of that generation. My own grandfather, lost at the Somme. Never knew him, of course. It's remarkable, isn't it? How much history is woven into our family. I’ve been doing a bit of genealogical research, you know. Tracing the family back. Apparently, my great-great-grandfather was a… well, a bit of a rogue. A poacher, apparently. Spent a week in the gaol for takin' a pheasant. A poacher? That's fantastic! So, a bit of rebellion in the blood, then? Explains a lot. Rebellion? Humph. More like common sense. A man's gotta eat, don't he? Land was owned by the posh folk, they didn’t need another pheasant. That sideboard, by the way, belonged to my grandmother. She swore it came over on a boat from France with some Huguenot ancestors. Whether that’s true, I wouldn’t know.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of stuff Mum’s accumulated is astonishing. I thought  I  had too much, but this is…a lifetime of ‘just in case’ purchases. Are you sure we've got everything? I feel like we've done about five loops of the garden already with boxes. Pretty sure, love. I triple-checked the shed. That was…a mission. Your mum’s got garden gnomes dating back to the Stone Age, I swear. And yes, everything  is  in the car. Though I’m starting to think we should’ve hired a van. My back’s going to be screaming tomorrow. This is the last trip, isn't it? The very last from Mum’s to Dad’s? Feels…odd. It does. Really odd. Like closing a chapter. Especially knowing Dad’s not…not going to be there to meet us. It just won't be the same, dropping things off at an empty house. No, it won't. He’d have been moaning about the parking, as usual. “Honestly, Daniel, can’t you find a spot closer? My knees aren't what they used to be!” Remember? And then he’d sneakily offer you a biscuit. Of course. Peculiarly, always a digestive. No matter what else was on offer. Speaking of, are you still feeling a bit off? You were looking a bit peaky at Mum's earlier. Just a bit of a cold, I think. Probably caught it from your nephew, the little germ factory. I’ve got a tickle in my throat. Nothing a good lie-down won’t fix. Though, to be honest, thinking about sorting out the mortgage on Dad’s place whilst feeling rubbish isn't ideal. It's a whole new level of paperwork, isn't it? It is. And utterly bewildering. I've been trying to wrap my head around all the probate stuff. It’s like learning a new language. Ironically, given what I  do  for a living… teaching English! You’d think I’d be good at deciphering complicated documents. You'd think! It’s different when it's actual  legalese , though, isn't it? Not analysing Shakespeare. How’s the new teaching job going, by the way? Still enjoying it? Yeah, it’s good. Challenging, but good. I've got a student from Brazil, Maria, who’s really struggling with the conditional tenses. It's fascinating, trying to explain something that feels instinctive to us, but is utterly alien to her.

…and honestly, the thought of trying to explain to Mum why Aunt Carol  has  to sit next to Uncle Bernard is going to be exhausting. They haven’t spoken a civil word since the garden gnome incident of ‘18. Oh, God, not the gnome! I’d almost forgotten. Still, she won’t remember it, will she? It’s… it’s getting harder to tell sometimes, isn’t it? The things she forgets. It is. It genuinely is. Which is why I’m trying to keep things as familiar as possible. Hence, her usual seat, Carol as far away as humanly possible, and a menu she’ll actually recognise. No deconstructed anything. Definitely no deconstructed anything. She’d think someone’s taken her dinner apart and needs help putting it back together. What are we thinking for the main course then? I was picturing roast chicken? Classic. Roast chicken is good. Safe. But she had that just last week with Fiona. I was leaning towards salmon. I could get a nice piece from Billingsgate tomorrow morning. They do a lovely wild salmon, though it’s a bit pricey. Salmon’s good! She always liked salmon. Fresh though, yeah? Not that pre-packed stuff. Remember that time Dad bought… oh dear, let’s not talk about Dad and fish. Yes, let’s not. Billingsgate it is, then. And I'll get some new potatoes and some green beans. Simple. Then there's dessert. I was thinking of a crumble? Apple or blackberry? Blackberry! Definitely blackberry. It's more… autumnal, and she loves a good blackberry crumble. Maybe with a dollop of clotted cream? Decadent. Right, blackberry crumble with clotted cream. Sorted. Okay, so we’ve got the food mostly planned. Now, the seating. I’ve sketched out a little plan. See? Mum here, obviously. You're opposite her, so you can talk to her easily. Then Fiona and George… and that’s where the Carol/Bernard standoff begins. Looks… strategically planned! Are you sure we can't just put someone  between  them? A buffer zone? Little Timmy, perhaps? He's usually pretty quiet. Timmy’s a danger to everything within a five-mile radius, especially candles. And this is Mum’s 80th, not a demolition derby. Plus, Timmy keeps trying to explain cryptocurrency to her. It’s… not going well. Good point. Okay, Carol and Bernard locked in combat. Fine. Have you thought about the candles?

…and honestly, the pain is just  ridiculous . Like, I knew it’d be bad, but this is a different level of bad. It feels like someone’s trying to dig out my brain with a spoon. Oh, no, you poor thing! Still with the wisdom teeth then? I thought you said they were supposed to settle down a bit by now. Did you take the painkillers? Took ‘em, yeah. They take the edge off, but it’s like…a dull ache layered over a stabbing pain. And the holes! Honestly, the holes they’ve left are massive. I’m scared to even floss near ‘em in case I dislodge something important. Dislodge something important? Dramatic, much? But seriously, that sounds awful. Mine weren't nearly that bad. Just a bit of swelling and a week of soft foods. Though, Mum did make me live on lukewarm soup for about ten days, which was its own kind of torture. Lukewarm soup sounds like heaven right now compared to trying to chew through a biscuit. Speaking of mums…mine’s been on at me about going back to uni. Says I’m “wasting my potential” pottering about after A-Levels. She always does that, doesn’t she? She’s ambitious for you. Mine’s practically breathing down my neck about finding an ‘experience’ for my CV. Like a gap year wasn’t enough experience! Exactly! It's exhausting. I  want  to go back, I do. But having everything sorted...finding somewhere to live…it's a right headache. Especially now Dad’s talking about moving house. Moving house? What,  now ? I thought they were settled in Doncaster. Apparently, Uncle Barry’s selling his place in Market Weighton, and Dad thinks it’s a “sound investment.” Honestly, I don’t know what’s going on in his head sometimes. It’s all talk of capital gains and potential rental income. Completely ignoring the fact we’ve just got settled. Oh, that’s… disruptive. Especially for your mum. She loves her garden. She’s fuming. Properly fuming. And it makes everything even more complicated with uni. If they move, I can’t just… pop home for weekends like I planned. It's a whole new commute. Right. That’s rough. You’ll have to factor that into where you apply. Though, thinking about it, I'm not much better off. I’m still trying to decide between York and Newcastle.

…and honestly, the buttercream was  almost  as good as the real thing. You honestly couldn’t tell it was lactose-free. Which, let’s be honest, is a miracle considering how I usually fail at baking. Did you put sprinkles on it, Mummy? The pink ones are my favourite. I did! Loads of pink sprinkles, just for you, Elsie. And some gold ones for Leo. They’re mostly gone now, aren’t they? Mmmhmm. Very gone. Can we make more tomorrow? Maybe with blue sprinkles? We can definitely think about blue sprinkles. Though we might need to go shopping first. Right, where were we? Oh, the acts of kindness! We were brainstorming things we could  do  for people, not just  buy  them. We could give Mrs. Peterson flowers! She lets me stroke her cat. That’s a lovely idea, Elsie. A really thoughtful one. But maybe we could do something a bit… bigger, you know? Something that really helps. Like… give her all our Chess pieces? So she can be rich! Leo! That’s very generous, but I think Mrs. Peterson would probably prefer a nice cup of tea and a chat. Though using the Chess pieces as money is a brilliant idea for a game. We could invent a whole new shop! And use the Draughts pieces for small money! Like pennies! Exactly! See? You two are full of ideas. Maybe after we finalise our act of kindness plan, we can set up "Elsie & Leo’s Emporium." What about visiting Old Man Hemlock? He doesn't get many visitors. He smells of wood. And biscuits. He does, doesn’t he? He used to be a carpenter. We could take him some of the lactose-free cookies, wouldn’t that be nice? And read him a story! I know a really good one about a princess. Perfect! Okay, so Old Man Hemlock is on the list. Now, thinking ahead… Chinese New Year is next week! I was thinking of trying to make dumplings. Have you two ever made dumplings? No! But can we use red food colouring in the dough?! Like dragons! We can  talk  about red food colouring. It might stain everything red. Maybe just decorate them with little bits of carrot to look like scales? Can we get lanterns? I want a sparkly red lantern! Absolutely! We'll get lanterns, and maybe some decorations for the house. It’s the Year of the Dragon, you know.

…and then Mr. Henderson just  completely  braked! Like, slammed on the brakes. It wasn’t even his fault, honestly. A seagull just flew right in front of his van. A massive one, apparently. Oh, goodness me. A seagull? Hastings seagulls are notorious, aren’t they? Little flying bandits. Are you alright, though? You sounded a bit shaken when you called. That happened this morning, right? Yeah, this morning. I'm fine now, just…a bit bruised. My arm mostly. It's nothing, honestly. Just a really nasty bump. It felt way worse at the time. Mr. Henderson was more upset about the van, I think. He kept saying something about his insurance. Well, that sounds dreadful for everyone involved. Glad you’re mostly okay. You know, it reminds me a little of that scene in Alice in Wonderland, the one where Alice keeps changing size. Everything feels huge, and then suddenly small, and a bit disorienting. Mum, seriously? A car crash and you're thinking about  Alice in Wonderland ? It’s a coping mechanism! Besides, Alice always bounces back, doesn't she? Like you will. Speaking of bouncing back... let me have a proper look at your arm. Still a bit purple, isn’t it? You’ll have a story to tell, darling, and probably a fantastic bruise to show for it. A little battle scar. It’s not a battle scar! It’s just…a bump. And I don't want to talk about it anymore. Can we please talk about something else? Like, did you get the tickets for  Wicked ? Oh! Yes! I did! Front row, stalls! They were terribly expensive, I’m not going to lie, but you deserve something lovely after all this. It's for next Saturday, are you still free? YES! Amazing! I’ve been listening to the soundtrack non-stop. Elphaba’s songs are just…powerful. I've been trying to learn 'Defying Gravity' on the piano. It's…challenging. That’s my girl! I knew you’d love it. And you  are  good at the piano, you’ll get there. Did you finish reading that book I lent you, the one by Neil Gaiman? Nearly. I got a bit distracted after…well, you know. But I'm really enjoying it. It’s really different from the stuff I usually read. A bit creepy but in a good way. I found some fan theories online, it's wild what people come up with!

…and honestly, Harold, I was up half the night thinking about it all. They were so grateful for the advice, that little group from Chedworth, bless them. But it felt like I was just handing them a slightly less terrifying version of what  we  went through with the turbines. Solar panels everywhere! It’ll ruin the landscape, just as surely. It’s the creeping industrialisation of the countryside, isn’t it, Margaret? They call it ‘green’ energy, but it feels distinctly  unnatural  when you’re looking at acres of reflective glass instead of fields. We fought tooth and nail for years over those turbines near Almondsbury, you remember. The council were completely in the pockets of the energy company. Pockets isn’t strong enough, David. They were practically living  in  the pockets. Remember old Councillor Grimshaw? Suddenly a massive advocate for wind power just as his son-in-law got a consultancy job with the firm building them. Outrageous. Exactly! And that’s what I tried to explain to the Chedworth lot. It's not just about presenting logical arguments against the proposals – which, naturally, we did, about bird migration and noise pollution and visual impact. It’s about understanding the  politics  of it all. Who benefits? Who’s pulling the strings? And it’s always the same. Local planners claiming they’re ‘duty bound’ to approve, citing government targets. The Development Control Committee, a rubber stamp exercise. Then you get a Planning Appeal if you dare object strongly enough, and suddenly you’re up against highly paid barristers. Barristers are the least of your worries. It’s the money, David. The sheer  volume  of money. Government’s throwing billions at these renewable energy subsidies, but peanuts at actual research. They’re happy to pay companies to  install  these things, but not to find a better way of  storing  the damn energy! You’re absolutely right, Arthur. That's what I was saying last night. We need breakthroughs in energy storage. That's where the real innovation lies, not just slapping solar panels on every south-facing field. I read an article about…oh, what was it now…some sort of compressed air energy storage system? Promising, but apparently requires geological formations we don’t have in abundance here. We need a new kind of battery, Margaret. Something that doesn’t rely on rare earth minerals harvested in… questionable conditions. And it needs to be affordable.

…and honestly, the roundabout at the end of Pershore Road nearly did for me. Three lanes, all going different ways! I swear, Birmingham roundabouts are designed to confuse visiting drivers. Though, you’d think after living here seventy-odd years I'd have got the hang of them. Dad, you say that every time. It’s not the roundabouts, it’s just…you haven’t driven in five years! Things change. Are you  sure  you want to start lessons again at this age? It’s not a walk in the park, you know. Nonsense! I was a perfectly competent driver in my day. Before they started putting computers in everything. Give me a good old Ford Cortina any day. Simpler times. Besides, I want to be able to visit Margaret in Cornwall without relying on trains. She keeps hinting I should drive down, says the scenery’s better. Cornwall, eh? Lovely. Though driving all that way on your own… Arthur, you’re a brave man. And a stubborn one, let's be honest. Stubborn? I prefer ‘determined’. And I won’t be entirely on my own. Elsie’s promised to navigate. She’s got a map-reading brain, that one. Though, she does occasionally read the map upside down. Mum, please don’t encourage him. Seriously, Dad, have you even looked at car insurance quotes? It’s going to be astronomical. Especially considering… well, your age and everything. I have had a quick look. It's… substantial. Elsie spoke to old Mr. Henderson down the road. Apparently, his nephew works for an insurance company. Might be able to get a discount. Henderson’s nephew? Oh dear. That boy’s a bit of a rogue, if you ask me. Still, it’s worth a shot. Speaking of shots, are we still on for lunch with David and Sarah on Wednesday? Yes, I confirmed it. They're bringing little Leo. He's at that stage where everything goes in the mouth. Prepare to have your biscuits stolen, Dad. Little Leo. Always grabbing. Reminds me of your cousin, Peter, when he was little. Sticky fingers, that boy. Always getting into jam. You’ve got a story for everything, haven’t you? Anyway, I've got a parent-teacher conference tomorrow evening. Little Maya is struggling with her French pronunciation. Honestly, the French 'r' is the bane of their existence. Oh, Maya. Such a sweet girl.

…and honestly, the parking in Brighton is  criminal . I spent twenty minutes circling yesterday just to drop off groceries. Twenty minutes! You wouldn't believe it, Dad. It's worse than trying to navigate Bluewater on a Saturday. Bluewater, eh? Used to be able to park right outside Woolworths back in the fifties. Not a thought given to parking permits or pay-by-phone apps. Everything was simpler then. Though, simpler didn’t always mean better, mind. Remember rationing? Now  that  was a pickle. You always bring it back to the fifties, don’t you? It's like a comfort zone. Still, a bit of rationing might do some people good. All this… convenience food. I tried to make a proper shepherd's pie last week, remember? Proper mash, everything. Liam just wanted chicken nuggets. Kids. Always been the same. My sister, bless her, wouldn’t touch a green vegetable until she was ten. Your mum had a battle on her hands! You're doin' good though, trying to cook from scratch. It’s expensive though, isn't it? Everything’s gone up. Even a loaf of bread’s a fortune. It is. I was looking at the price of butternut squash yesterday - ridiculous. I saw something on Facebook about people using food banks more and more, even those in work. It’s… depressing. Facebook…that blasted thing. Constantly pinging on my phone. I told you, I can barely work the thing, and when I do, it's just arguments and political nonsense. I turned off the notifications, mostly. Can’t stand it. All these politicians just talking, talking, talking. Never actually  doing  anything. I know, right? It's exhausting. Speaking of doing things, how are you managing with the benefits? Still a nightmare with the paperwork? Nightmare is an understatement. They keep sending me forms and asking the same questions over and over. They want proof of everything. It’s like they think I’m running a sophisticated fraud operation from me living room! Honestly, trying to explain my arthritis and how it affects my mobility to someone who’s never had a day’s pain in their life…it’s pointless. It's awful. I tried to help you with it online last week, remember? It's so badly designed. And then they want you to attend appointments miles away with no help with transport. It's deliberately difficult.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to mark down my essay for ‘lack of original thought’ when I literally quoted a relatively obscure sonnet! It felt personal, you know? Like he just…doesn’t  like  me. Henderson sounds delightful. A real bastion of academic freedom, that one. Though, honestly, half the lecturers at Cardiff are just waiting for an excuse to fail someone. It builds their reputations, apparently. Exactly! It's a power trip. It’s not about the quality of the work, it’s about asserting dominance through red pen. Shakespeare’s probably spinning in his grave. Speaking of which, did you read anything good for the module? I was slogging through  Troilus and Cressida …absolute misery. Oh god,  Troilus . It’s deliberately depressing, isn’t it? I stuck with  Measure for Measure . Found it surprisingly…sarcastic. Like Shakespeare was having a right laugh at everyone’s expense. Which, knowing the court he was writing for, probably wasn't far off. Sarcasm is a lost art. People just don’t  get  it anymore. They think you’re being genuinely rude. Remember old Mrs. Davies back in Exeter? She was a master. Could dismantle you with a single, sweetly spoken sentence. Oh, the Davies family! Now  there’s  a surname. It sounds like it should belong to a medieval knight. My grandma’s surname was Plumtree. Plumtree! Honestly. I always called her Nana Plum. She hated it, of course. Nana Plum! That's brilliant. My nan was a Bennett. Dreadfully common. We were all just ‘the Bennetts’ from down the road. I always wished we had a more…distinguished name. Something ending in ‘worth’ or ‘field’. Don’t we all. Although, a ‘worth’ or ‘field’ and you’d probably spend your life explaining if you were related to the one who owns half of Nottingham. Speaking of things I’m woefully bad at… I tried to learn golf over the summer. Utter disaster. Golf? Oh no. Don’t tell me you fell for that trap. It’s a conspiracy to relieve middle-aged men of their disposable income. And patience. It's infuriating! I spent three hours on a driving range and managed to hit…well, nothing consistently. The instructor kept saying, “It's about winning the small battles.” Winning the small battles?! It’s about hitting a tiny white ball into a slightly smaller hole, hundreds of yards away!

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of requests for gluten-free options at this conference next month is unbelievable. You’d think half of Yorkshire had suddenly developed coeliac disease! It’s not even a wellness retreat, it’s a plumbing and heating trade show! Plumbing and heating…gluten-free. Right. Sounds stressful, Liv. My job’s never that complicated. Mostly just shifting stuff around, making sure the lads ‘ave what they need on site. Doesn’t require a degree in dietary requirements, that's for sure. Honestly, it’s the same in production. People are getting so specific. “Low FODMAP, organic, ethically sourced, fair trade…” it’s a nightmare sourcing components sometimes, let alone catering for conference delegates! Though, I suppose it’s a good thing people are more conscious. Conscious, yeah. Or just trendy. Either way, it’s me doing extra spreadsheets at 10pm the night before. How’s work been, Ben? Still building skyscrapers, one brick at a time? Nah, not skyscrapers. Mostly extensions and renovations at the moment. A lot of folks trying to make more space now they’re working from home more, y’know? Keeps me busy, though. Pay’s alright. Still stuck livin’ with me mum, though. She's good as gold, but… freedom, innit? I can imagine! I'm trying to convince my landlord to let me get a dog. He's being really difficult. Says it'll "devalue the property". Seriously? It's a perfectly nice flat. I’d happily pay extra deposit. Honestly, landlords. They’re all the same. I finally moved out of me dad’s a couple of years ago, got a little flat share in Doncaster. It was alright, but I missed havin’ a proper kitchen. Couldn’t even make a decent Yorkshire pud! That’s a crime against humanity, really. Yorkshire puds  are  serious business. Though, I'm trying to cut back on all that stuff. Trying to eat a bit healthier. Mum makes a cracking roast, but…well, you know. It’s all gravy and roast potatoes, lovely as it is! Tell me about it. I started one of those meal prep services. It’s…okay. A bit bland, if I’m honest. But it means I don’t end up ordering takeaway five nights a week. Meal prep? Sounds…disciplined. I tried a diet once. One of those juice cleanses. Lasted about a day. Started craving a bacon butty

…and honestly, the picture quality on this blasted Skype is awful. You look like you’re shimmering, Arthur. Are you sure your internet's alright? Shimmering, am I? Well, you look a bit… pixelated yourself, Reg. It's probably just the light. Though, Millie did say something about the broadband being a bit slow this morning. Said young Tim’s been gaming all night again. Honestly, boys and their gadgets! It’s a wonder anything gets done. Oh, but look at the garden, Reg! You’ve been busy! Is that new bamboo? It’s… substantial. Aye, that’s new. Got a good deal on it down the garden centre, Millie insisted. Said it’d look lovely, give us a bit of privacy from Mrs. Higgins' constant gazing. Though it’s growing a bit fast, innit? Might need a proper trim. Speaking of Mrs Higgins, still grumbling about the fence, is she? Grumbling? Reg, she practically mounted an expedition to complain about a single panel being a centimetre over the line! I had to offer to move it just to get some peace. Honestly, the woman. Oh dear. Some people just  live  to complain, don’t they? It’s exhausting. Did you manage to get the owl box up, Reg? I remember you talking about wanting to encourage owls. I did, actually. Up in the old apple tree. Haven’t seen anything moving in yet, but it’s early days. I was reading about it - apparently they like a bit of wood shavings inside for nesting. And speaking of nature… did you two catch that eclipse yesterday? Remarkable. Did I! Stood right in the garden, with those silly eclipse glasses. Millie said I looked a right fool. But it  was  impressive, wasn’t it? Makes you think, doesn’t it? About the cosmos and all that. It does. I was watching a programme about black holes last night. Absolutely mind-boggling. Trying to understand the very beginnings of space… it’s almost too much to take in. Black holes… fascinating, but a bit frightening, if you ask me. All that gravity, sucking everything in. Reminds me of the TV licence people, actually. Sucking the money out of you! We really need to sort that out, Millie’s been on at me for weeks. Oh, don't get me started on the TV licence. Daylight robbery, it is. And everything’s got to be ‘politically correct’ these days, hasn't it?

…and honestly, the traffic on the A19 was mental. Absolutely mental. I swear, every single person from Durham decided to come to Newcastle at the same time. Sounds delightful. You’re lucky I insisted on driving then, aren’t you? Though, I’m starting to regret offering if we’re going to be stuck in another jam before we even  get  to Alnwick. Are we even sure this Italian place is worth the trek? Oh, it is. Fabrizio’s. My auntie Maureen raves about it. Says it's the best pasta she’s had outside of Italy, and she went interrailing around Europe for six months, so she’s a fairly good judge. Plus, you know how I am about needing proper Italian. None of this spaghetti bolognese with loads of minced beef nonsense. Fair enough. Maureen’s a good barometer then. Though, six months interrailing… that’s a lifetime ago. Everything tastes better when you’re 18 and subsisting on bread and questionable cheese, doesn't it? Still, Alnwick… it's a lovely little town. Have you been before? Briefly, when I was a kid. We went to the castle, obviously. All dramatic and spooky. I remember being terrified of the dungeons. But I don’t remember the town itself, not really. It’s a long way from Sunderland, isn’t it? Seems like a different world. All those big houses… It is a bit. Very different from the terraces around the Stadium of Light. Alnwick's got a proper medieval feel, apparently. Plenty of beautiful old architecture. They've got a cathedral too, have you heard? Not as grand as Durham, obviously, but still… worth a look if we have time. Durham Cathedral’s hard to beat, to be fair. It’s right  there , dominating everything. You can see it from practically anywhere in the city. Makes Sunderland look a bit…flat. No offense. None taken. Sunderland’s got…character. A raw, gritty character. And the sea air is good for you. Speaking of which, did you manage to get the bus times checked for your mum next week? She’s still worried about getting to that appointment in Newcastle. Aye, I did. It’s a nightmare, though. They’ve changed the route again. She’ll have to get two buses now, and the connection at Washington Galleries is only five minutes. Five minutes! She'll be legging it.

…and honestly, it weren’t a robin at all, were it? I was convinced. Proper bright red breast, flitting about. But Elsie – bless her, sharper than a tack for ninety-two – Elsie said, “Nay, Margaret, that's a bullfinch. Look at the black cap.” And she were right, o' course. Always is. Oh, Elsie’s brilliant with birds. She's got that little bird table outside her kitchen window, doesn’t she? Covered in activity all day long. I try, I really do, but I can never tell ‘em apart. They all just look…feathery. Aye, she does. Feeds ‘em all sorts. Sunflower seeds, nyjer seed, the posh stuff. I just bung out a bit of stale bread, feelin’ a bit guilty about it, if I’m honest. Though they seem to enjoy it enough. I was thinking of getting a proper feeder, mind. Something squirrel-proof. Those little blighters are relentless. Squirrel-proof is a myth, Margaret, a complete myth. They  will  find a way. Trust me. I've spent a small fortune on supposedly squirrel-proof feeders. It’s an entertainment for  them , mostly. Speaking of entertainment…did you see old Mr. Henderson practically leaping out of his skin when his alarm clock went off yesterday morning? No! Old Harry? What time did he set it for? He’s usually still asleep when I’m takin’ Dobbin for his morning walk. Seven o’clock. Said he’d decided to “seize the day.” Didn't seize it very gracefully, I can tell you. Woke half the street. He's still complaining about it, says it scared the life out of him. Reminds me, I need to change mine. It's got a particularly grating sound. Always wakes me up feeling…aggrieved. Aggrieved is a good word for it. I just have mine on quiet. Feel the vibrations more than hear it, you see. Though sometimes…sometimes I wake up with a nosebleed. Dreadful things. Always happen at the most inconvenient time. Oh, bother those! Horrible. Dry air, probably. I find a little dab of vaseline up the nostril helps. Sounds a bit gruesome, I know. It does, but I'll try anything! Anything’s better than that awful metallic taste. Anyway, back to the birds… I was reading about how important it is to clean feeders regularly. Apparently, they can get riddled with diseases. Absolutely. Brenda told me all about that.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of perfectly curated lives on Instagram is exhausting. Little Timmy's organic, home-schooled existence, perfectly posed family portraits… it's just not  real , is it? Makes you feel inadequate just scrolling through. Oh, absolutely. I know exactly what you mean. It's a highlight reel, always. And it’s cleverly engineered. I was talking to a client yesterday, a teenager really struggling with body image, and it’s entirely fuelled by social media. It's brutal. She’s comparing herself to filtered photos and thinking she’s failing. It’s heartbreaking. It is. I try to limit my time on it, I really do. But then I fall down the rabbit hole, comparing myself to…well, everyone. Especially seeing Sarah’s photos of her kids. You know, the ones we went to school with? Picture perfect. Makes my little chaos feel… insufficient. Sarah  always  was a bit of a perfectionist. Remember how she colour-coded her notes in sixth form? Anyway, don’t let it get to you. Your life is perfectly lovely, even with the chaos. And you’re doing an amazing job raising Leo on your own. It’s not easy. Thanks, Helen. It’s… it’s good to hear you say that. It’s different, isn’t it? Sometimes I feel like I'm constantly justifying choices, explaining why I didn’t follow the ‘script’. You know, marriage, two point four children… The script! Exactly! And honestly, who even wrote that script? You wanted to be a mum, and you  are  a mum. The route might have been different – the IVF, the solo parenting – but Leo is lucky to have you. How’s the yoga been helping with the stress of it all, by the way? You started those classes ages ago. It’s been a lifesaver, actually. I initially went because my back was killing me from chasing Leo around, but it's become so much more than that. An hour to just focus on breathing, stretching… it’s my little pocket of calm. Although, even  that  I feel guilty about sometimes. "Self-care," they call it. Feels selfish when there’s a mountain of marking to do. Don’t be silly! You need that time. We all do. It’s not selfish, it’s sustainable. Speaking of things you need time for… how’s the book coming along? Last I heard you had a first draft finished.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking is just relentless. Fifteen year olds, you know? It's like they think punctuation is optional! It's a lost art. Though, I suppose when everything's communicated in emojis these days… Emojis, eh? Progress, they call it. Though, I always said, a good sentence, properly constructed, says more than any little yellow face ever could. Reminds me of Old Man Hemmings from the English department. He’d deduct marks for dangling participles with a  glee  that was truly unsettling. Oh, that sounds terrifying! I try to be encouraging, but there’s a certain standard. It's GCSE year for them all, so the pressure's on, for them  and  me. What did you teach, if you don't mind me asking? You mentioned retirement… History, love. Ancient history mostly. Romans, Greeks, that lot. Used to love it. Getting them excited about Caesar and Cleopatra... though, these days, they’re more interested in TikTok than togas. Didn’t manage to get my passion across to everyone, mind you. Had one lad convinced the Romans invented reality television. Oh dear! Well, you can’t blame them for trying to relate it to their own world, I suppose. It’s a teacher’s job to bridge that gap. I teach French, which has its own challenges. Trying to get them to roll their ‘r’s… it's a losing battle. French, right. Always sounded clever to me. I took it at school, couldn’t get past “Bonjour.” My wife, bless her, was fluent. Used to go to France every summer, she did. Lovely woman, Margaret. Sadly, she’s gone now. Been five years this August. Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that. That must be incredibly difficult. I lost my mum a few years back, so I understand. It doesn't really  get  easier, does it? Just… different. Different, that’s a good way to put it. It's the little things you miss, you know? She used to make the best shepherd’s pie. Absolutely the best. My son, David, tries, but it’s just not the same. He lives up in Manchester now, works for a tech company. Doesn’t have much time for shepherd’s pie, I suspect. Manchester's booming, isn’t it? My sister lives near Stockport. She says it's changed beyond recognition. I worry about the crime rate up there, though.

…Aye, so then ‘e just looks at me, dead serious, and says “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight, it’s the size of the fight in the dog.” I nearly choked on me crisps, I did. Old Man Hemmings, always comin’ out wi’ gems like that down t'pub. Oh, bless him! Your Grandad sounds… colourful. Though, I think that’s a fairly common saying, isn't it? My Nana used to say it. Though hers was usually directed at my brother when he was getting picked on. It is, yeah. Pretty widespread. A bit cliché now, really. Though I’ll admit, hearing it delivered by a Yorkshire Grandad immediately makes it ten times better. Speaking of better… has anyone tried that new Thai place on Mill Road? I heard it's amazing. Oh, ‘Spice Paradise’? I went last week. It  is  good. Properly spicy, which is a relief. Some places tone it down for the… less adventurous palate. I had the green curry, and it definitely had a kick. Aye, I need a good curry. Been ages. Cambridge is alright for food, but it’s missin’ a proper chippy, that’s what it’s missin’. None of this fancy “hand-cut chips with truffle oil” rubbish. Give me a good battered haddock and mushy peas any day. You're a lost cause, Liam. Truly. But seriously, we should all go to Spice Paradise. Maybe next week? I'm free most evenings after work. We could do a film afterwards? There’s that new Wes Anderson one,  Asteroid City , everyone’s talking about. Thai and Wes Anderson sounds perfect. I’m in. Though, I’m slightly worried about the hype around  Asteroid City . Anderson can be a bit style over substance sometimes, don’t you think? I wouldn’t say ‘style over substance’, but it  is  undeniably… stylized. It’s definitely one you need to be in the right mood for. I'm game, though. I've always enjoyed his visual flair. Actually, have you guys heard that new album by Yard Act? Yard Act? Nah. What kind of music are they? Sounds a bit...Yorkshire. That’s the point! They  are  Yorkshire. Post-punk, kinda. Really clever lyrics, really dry wit. They're from Leeds, actually. You'd probably like them, Liam. They're a bit like a modern Pulp. Pulp? Now you're talkin’. Jarv is a legend.

… honestly, the free weights section was like a demolition derby. Some bloke nearly dropped a barbell on my foot! I’m starting to think PureGym isn’t worth the £20 a month, even if it  is  convenient. Oh, you’re still going to PureGym? I switched to The Gym Group, the one near the Grafton. It’s…less intense. Fewer grunting weightlifters, more people actually using the cardio machines. Though, to be fair, it smells distinctly of Lynx Africa. Lynx Africa is the perfume of a generation, isn't it? Speaking of smells, Cambridge is  baking  today. It’s hitting nearly thirty degrees. Makes the thought of a gym even less appealing. I’d rather be… anywhere with a breeze, really. Maybe somewhere in Cornwall? Remember that trip we took after uni, Liam? Cornwall was brilliant. Except for that torrential downpour we got stuck in, trying to get to St. Ives. I was soaked to the bone, and my phone died. Good times. This heat is decent though, isn't it? Better than the constant drizzle we had last summer. Definitely. I'm itching to get away somewhere. Been looking at flights to Greece, maybe Crete. Need a break before this new game launch. The crunch is real. Still, getting code to work is less stressful than dodging falling weights, I reckon. Greece sounds amazing. Though, thinking about holidays makes me realise how little notice we've had with organising Leo’s summer camp. Have you guys sorted anything yet? I’ve been looking at Adventure Tots – it’s a bit pricey, but they do outdoor activities. Adventure Tots? Sounds… energetic. I haven’t even  started  looking. My mum offered to have my little cousin for a week, but he's a whirlwind. A lovely whirlwind, but a whirlwind nonetheless. He'd probably dismantle the house. I looked at a few camps, but they either had massive waiting lists or were ridiculously expensive. I ended up finding this one in Grantchester – it’s a smaller arts and crafts-focused thing. Might not be total chaos like Adventure Tots, but it's at least keeping Elsie occupied for a few days. It's run by a theatre group, apparently. Elsie doing drama? That’s fantastic! She's always been a little performer. Leo would just build a fortress out of blankets and refuse to come out. He’s a practical sort. Actually, talking of Leo, have you guys heard that new Arctic Monkeys album?

Honestly, this is painful to watch. Newcastle are playing like they’ve never seen a football before. And it's only half-time! Now, now, don't write them off just yet, love. It's a derby, anything can happen. Momentum shifts, someone gets a dodgy penalty... the usual. Besides, you always get a bit  too  invested when it's the Magpies. Reminds me of you during the exams – intense doesn't even cover it. That’s completely different! Exams are about my future, Newcastle are about... well, pride, mostly. And avoiding relegation, let’s be honest. It's just… they're gifting chances to Brighton. Gifting them! My dad would be apoplectic. Your dad's apoplectic if the kettle takes too long to boil. Remember last Easter when he swore the shop had deliberately hidden the Creme Eggs just to spite him? Oh, god, don't remind me. The Great Creme Egg Hunt of 2023. He interrogated the shop assistant! Speaking of Easter… are we doing anything special this year? Your mum mentioned something about a roast lamb? She did. And yes, the grand plan is lamb, horrible chocolate eggs – because tradition, apparently – and a very competitive game of Scrabble. She's been practicing. She’s terrifying when she gets competitive over Scrabble. Oh, no. I'm terrible at Scrabble. You always win. You and your ridiculously large vocabulary from all that PhD-ing. It’s not fair. It’s called being well-read, darling. And I'll happily let you win… maybe. Depends how much lamb I’ve had. Did you ever finish watching that film I recommended, 'Everything Everywhere All at Once'? Nearly. I got distracted by… well, a lot of work. Being a Research Manager is basically living on caffeine and spreadsheets. But I saw enough to know it's brilliant. Absolutely bonkers, but brilliant. Michelle Yeoh is phenomenal. It's the kind of film you need to dedicate actual  time  to, though, you know? Can't just have it on in the background while you're doom-scrolling. Exactly! It's a commitment. It's like trying to understand my research sometimes – requires full mental capacity. Speaking of commitments, I’m presenting some preliminary findings next week. I'm completely bricking it. You’ll be fine! You  always  are. You're brilliant at what you do. And you've practiced it a million times, haven’t you?

Ah, now look at young Leo there. Must’ve been… eight, maybe nine? At that funfair down in Midleton. He was obsessed with those whirly-gig rides, weren’t he? Nearly threw up every time, God love him, but he'd queue right back up for another go. Wow, he looks tiny! And Ms. MacIntyre is right behind him, looking terrified  for  him. She always did fuss. That’s Margaret to a T. She’d worry herself sick over anything. She practically had a heart attack when Daniel climbed that little climbing frame at the park. Ach, mothers, eh? Always seeing danger lurkin’ where there’s none. Though, funfairs  are  a bit dodgy, mind you. All those poorly maintained rides. Still, good memories. Good memories indeed. Reminds me… I nearly didn’t make it to Daniel’s eighth birthday. Remember I was running the London Marathon that year? Oh, yes! The one where you said your legs felt like jelly for a week afterwards? You were so determined, though. Determined and foolish, maybe! But I got a medal, and I got back in time for the party. Saw Leo’s face light up… worth every ache and pain. Did you get any pictures of that, Margaret? I did, actually. Let me see… Ah, here we are. A rather blurry one, admittedly. Daniel blowin’ out the candles, Leo smearing cake all over his face, and your wife, God rest her, laughing ‘til she cried. That's a good one! He looks like a monster! He was a messy eater, that one. Still is, to be fair. . They all are at that age. Leo’s thinking about planning a trip though, you know. He’s been going on about Iceland. Iceland? Really? That’s a bit ambitious. Aye. Says he wants to see the Northern Lights. Wants to go hiking on glaciers. The boy's got his head full of adventures. Iceland’s cool. I saw a documentary about it. All volcanoes and ice caves. Sounds cold! I’m quite content with a warm cup of tea and a good book, thank you very much. Have you lads been to the cinema lately? They’re showing that new superhero film, isn’t it? Not for ages. With wee Thomas here, it's a bit… challenging. He doesn't sit still for two seconds. I went with Ben last week! It was amazing! Loads of explosions.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for even a small client these days is ridiculous. It’s not  sales  anymore, it's document management! Honestly, sometimes I feel like I should’ve trained as a paralegal. Tell me about it! Though I suppose that’s my job, in a way, isn’t it? Making sure everyone’s dotted ‘i’s are dotted and crossed ‘t’s are crossed. Though mostly it’s chasing people  for  the dotted ‘i’s. You wouldn’t believe the expense reports I’ve seen. Expense reports. Fancy. When your grandfather worked for the railway, it was a notebook and a receipt stuck in an envelope. And trust was all that mattered. Everything's so complicated now. It is! You know, Mum, you mentioned Granddad working on the railway… I was reading a book the other day, an eBook actually – much easier than lugging a hardback around – about the history of the railways in Lincolnshire. And there was a whole section on Boston station! Apparently, it was a vital link for transporting… beetroot. Beetroot? Seriously? Seriously! Huge quantities. Apparently, the smell was something else. I tried to picture Granddad amidst all that… beetroot. Oh, he’d have loved that. He wasn't bothered by smells, your grandfather. Nothing bothered him much, really. Except perhaps people messing with his trains. He had a whole layout in the shed, you know. A proper enthusiast. You two used to spend hours watching him, didn't you? Hours! And trying to “help”. I distinctly remember nearly derailing the entire thing with a rogue plastic dinosaur. He wasn’t best pleased. Though he recovered quickly. He always did. I was better behaved. I was obsessed with the little figurines, the people. I used to make up whole stories about their lives. It’s probably why I ended up in sales, actually. Creating narratives, persuading people… it all started with those tiny railway passengers. You're stretching, aren't you? Maybe! But it's a nice thought. Speaking of little things… I was clearing out the attic last weekend and found my old Sindy dollhouse. It was... battered. But still there. Do you remember how obsessed I was with Sindy? Oh yes, Sindy was the one. Far better than Barbie, if you ask me. More… realistic. You spent weeks knitting clothes for her. Knitting? You? I thought you couldn't tell a cast-on from a dropped stitch.

…and then young Timmy, bless ‘is cotton socks, decided the best place for a jam sandwich wasn’t on his plate, but  in  ‘is ‘air. Covered the poor lad head to toe. Sticky little fingers everywhere! Reminds me a bit o’ you, Elsie, always gettin’ into a bit o’ a muddle. Oh, don't you start, Arthur. A muddle? I was  resourceful . And Timmy’s just a whirlwind, isn’t he? Though honestly, jam in the hair… sounds like a right nightmare to get out. This sandwich is lovely, by the way. Cucumber and cress, just how I like it. You remembered! Well, I  try  to remember, don't I? After all these years, you’d think it’d be ingrained in me memory. Though, truth be told, me memory ain't what it used to be. Sometimes I forget what I went upstairs for, and I was only just there a minute ago! Still, better than forgetting  you , eh? Oh, Arthur. You’re a sweet talker. Though I do worry about you and these little… lapses. Should we maybe mention it to Dr. Peterson at your next check-up? Peterson? Oh, no, no. Doctors just want to poke and prod and tell you to eat less biscuits. I’m alright. It's just… age, Elsie. Plain and simple. It catches up with you in the end. Used to be able to recall every single fishing trip to the Yare, every perch, every chub… now… well, it’s all a bit hazy. The Yare... you haven't been down there in ages. Remember old Mr. Higgins? Used to sell the best tackle, right by the bridge? Always had a story to tell. Higgins! Now  there  was a character. He could tell you the best bait for every fish, and spin a tale that’d keep you riveted for hours. Said he learned it all from his grandfather, who fished for the Royal Family, he claimed! Doubt it was true, but a good story nonetheless. Things were simpler then, weren't they? Back in Costessey. They were. Harrow was alright, of course, but it never had that… Norfolk charm. All concrete and busy roads. You grew up with fields and rivers, Arthur. That makes a difference to a person, I think. Being close to the land. It does. My father, ‘e was a farmhand. Honest work, hard work. Never made much money, but we never went without.

…and honestly, little Timmy actually  ate  a crayon yesterday. A purple one. He was convinced it was a sweet. Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the state of him! Covered head-to-toe. Oh my god, no! Poor Timmy! And poor  you ! Sixth graders are bad enough, but reception? They're just little chaos agents. I had a girl try to trade me a pebble for a sticker this morning. A pebble! They’re brilliant, aren’t they? Though, slightly exhausting. You get used to the weirdness. Did you manage to get that marked before home time, then? The Year 2 literacy ones? Just about. Nearly missed the deadline. Honestly, the workload is insane. How are  you  coping, Chloe? Still loving primary school? You always seemed more suited to the little ‘uns than I am. It's…challenging, definitely. But rewarding. Seeing their faces when something clicks, that makes it worthwhile. Plus, I’m finally getting the hang of behaviour management. Although, purple-crayon-eating aside, this week has been  interesting . Speaking of interesting, how’s the copywriting going, Maisie? Still churning out catchy slogans? Surprisingly busy! A new client, vegan dog food. Apparently, ethical pet ownership is HUGE right now. I’ve written so many lines about ‘wholesome, plant-based goodness for your furry friend’ I could scream. It’s… niche, shall we say? Vegan dog food! Oh, that’s wonderful. My Aunt Carol would  love  that. She's trying to put Buster on a kale-only diet. He's a French Bulldog, he looks profoundly offended at all times. Kale?! That sounds… cruel. Buster deserves a proper sausage, surely? Anyway, enough about pampered pooches. Has anyone got any plans for Christmas yet? I’m still stuck on what to get my brother. He says he doesn’t want anything. You know how men are. The classic ‘I don’t want anything’ line. It usually translates to ‘I secretly want that ridiculously expensive gaming chair.’ I’m thinking of getting my dad a ridiculously impractical, but very loud, Hawaiian shirt. He’ll hate it, but it'll be funny. Oh, good one! I’m still failing at presents for my mum. She has everything. I was thinking a weekend away, maybe? Somewhere quiet? She’s recently been going on about wanting to see the Cotswolds. Ooh, the Cotswolds are lovely. Very posh, though. You’ll need to pack your best wellies. I’m going home to Bristol for Christmas.

…and honestly, the bins haven’t been emptied on Acacia Avenue for a fortnight. A fortnight, I tell you! It’s attracting all sorts. Not just foxes, mind - bigger, bolder things. You wouldn’t believe the state of it. Tell me about it, Klaus. It’s the same on our street. They said it was staff shortages, but it’s always something, isn’t it? Though, worse than bins, it’s the kids racing about on those electric scooters. Near misses  every  day. Little Leo nearly went flying into Mrs. Davies’ garden last week. It's not just the scooters, is it? It's like everyone's got a quad bike now. The noise is awful, especially when you're trying to take calls at reception. Mr. Henderson complained again just yesterday. Says he can't concentrate. They're alright. Better than being inside all day. Alright for  you , maybe, lad. You’ve got the energy of a… well, a ten-year-old. Though, what are you reading there, anyway? Still on the Potter books? Yeah.  Order of the Phoenix . It’s really good. Umbridge is… awful. Oh, she is. Always thought she was a right nasty piece of work. Remember when I used to read those to your sister, Liam? She was obsessed. She even tried to learn a few of the spells, bless her. She did, didn't she? Nearly set fire to the kitchen trying to ‘Wingardium Leviosa’ the biscuit tin. Good times. How  is  Sarah, by the way, Brenda? Haven’t seen her about. She’s alright. Bit stressed, though. Working extra hours at the school, they're short-staffed there too. And little Mikey's got a cough that won't shift. Keeps me up all night. Doctor says it’s just a virus, but you worry, don't you? It's always something with kids. My little brother’s got chickenpox. Mum’s run ragged. It is, isn't it? This city… it feels like everyone's perpetually juggling. Remember when things felt a bit…slower? Before everything was 'urgent' and 'crisis'? Speaking of crises, did you see that piece on the news about… well, you know… the situation with ISIS again? It's terrifying. Don’t even mention it. I try to shield the kids from it as much as possible, but they hear things at school. It’s just awful. Makes you appreciate what we have, even with the overflowing bins and noisy scooters.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for even  one  child with a gluten intolerance now is unbelievable. It used to be a quiet word with Mrs. Higgins in the canteen, now it’s forms in triplicate, doctor’s notes, allergen charts… Honestly, you’d think they were launching a space mission, not providing a school lunch! Oh, you’re telling  me ! I’m dealing with it at both ends now. The new free school meals system is meant to be simpler, but it’s just shifted the burden onto us teachers to verify everything. And the lunchboxes… Honestly, some of the things children are bringing in! Mountains of processed snacks. It’s a far cry from what we had. Speaking of what we had… My mother always told me about the food during the war. Not glamorous, to say the least. She used to talk about powdered eggs and everything being rationed. Though, she always said her biggest treat was when your father, Margaret, would share a bit of black market sausage with her! Oh, don't remind me! Your mother had a nose for a good sausage, Beatrice.
