You’d think with postgrad degrees, people could manage a bit more… maturity. You’d think! But no. It’s all passive-aggressive emails and ‘accidental’ exclusions from meetings.

…and honestly, the chicken Kievs weren’t the same. Not a patch on what you’d get back home, you know? All sauce and no… substance. It just  exploded . Nearly took out young Leo. Haha! Serves him right for trying to steal a chip off my plate. He’s always doing that. Leo’s a little rascal, alright. Though, honestly, I’m more concerned about the state of the kitchen after that Kiev explosion. It looked like a Jackson Pollock painting. Colin, you promised you'd clean up! I  will , love, I will. After the rugby. Important match tonight, you know. Ireland versus France. Can’t miss a minute. Though I’m bracing myself for the usual yelling from young Master O’Connell here. He's a fair weather supporter, always jumping on the bandwagon when we’re winning. I am  not ! I supported them when they lost to New Zealand last year. It was just… frustrating. And they were rubbish. Oh, here we go. The backchat begins. Honestly, you’re your father all over again. Always questioning everything. Now, now, Mary. Let the boy have his opinion. It’s good for him. Though I admit, sometimes it’s like talking to a brick wall. Speaking of walls, have you remembered to remind your mother about our visit next weekend? Granny's been dropping not-so-subtle hints about wanting to see Leo. I did, this morning. She was talking about knitting him a “Wallies” jumper. Honestly, ‘Wallies’? Where does she come up with these ideas? I told her he’s at the age where he’d rather have a football shirt. She means well. She’s just… Granny. Remember when she tried to send him a cassette tape? A what?! What’s a cassette tape? Sounds ancient. Oh, my god, you’re right. He wouldn’t have a clue. It’s a pre-digital music storage device, darling. Practically a museum piece. Anyway, I also mentioned we might bring some photos. I’ve been trying to get them properly organised. It's a nightmare. Between Dropbox and Flickr, everything's scattered all over the place. Flickr! That brings back memories. I used to have a whole collection of photos of… well, never mind. It's been years. Listen, speaking of photos, I saw a hedgehog in the garden this afternoon. Massive one. A hedgehog? Cool! Have you got a picture? No, I was too busy trying not to trip over the garden gnome.

…and honestly, the floral pattern on that Shelley is just  divine . I had to win it. It was a bidding war, you wouldn’t believe, but I got it for, well, let's just say less than I feared. Another one for the collection. Another one? Eleanor, you know the dresser is groaning. Where are you going to  put  it? We’re bordering on a museum here. Are you planning on opening a tea room? Don't be ridiculous, David. It’s a hobby! And they’re beautiful. This one’s from the 1930s, apparently. You appreciate a bit of history, don't you? Besides, I shifted a couple of the lesser pieces on eBay to make room. It’s a self-funding obsession, really. A self-funding obsession. Right. Well, as long as it doesn't involve raiding the grocery budget. Speaking of which, this buckwheat bread is…interesting. A bit dense, isn't it? It is. Old Man Hemmings at the market swore it was the best. Said it’s proper artisan stuff. I should have stuck with the sourdough. But I thought we’d be adventurous. It’ll be fine with the soup. Fine. Adventurous. Those are… diplomatic words. Look, I’m glad you're enjoying the market, though. It's good to see you getting out and about. After… everything at work. It is good. It's nice talking to people who aren't discussing spreadsheets and performance reviews. Honestly, I feel like I've shed five years. And Hemmings is a character. Reminds me a bit of your Uncle Alistair, all gruff charm. Don't even. Alistair's charm involved a healthy dose of complaining and a misplaced sense of superiority. Although, I wouldn’t put it past him to try and corner the buckwheat bread market if he knew anything about it. So, are you all set for the leaving do on Friday? Have you decided what you’re wearing? Nearly. I'm thinking the navy dress, the one with the little floral print? It's comfortable and doesn't scream 'I'm trying too hard'. Although, after my eBay purchases, maybe I  should  be screaming elegance… Don't start. The navy dress is perfect. They're all just relieved you're not taking your transcription skills  with  you, honestly. Apparently, Brenda nearly had a breakdown when she realised she'd have to actually take minutes herself.

…and honestly, Dad, I still don’t understand  why  you’re getting so worked up about Auntie Brenda’s ‘business’. It just sounds like she’s really good at what she does. Moving money around for people. Good at what she does, Elsie? That's… a very polite way of putting it. It’s borderline money laundering, love. Borderline is generous, actually. She’s basically a conduit for untraceable cash. Remember old Mr. Hemmings? Suddenly had enough money to revamp his entire house after selling off his allotment? Brenda handled that. Hemmings always was a bit shifty, though. Shifty doesn’t cover it, Liam. He was running a whole operation out of his shed, selling knock-off DVDs. But that’s beside the point. Brenda facilitated it. And now, because one of  her  clients got caught with a lorry full of dodgy electronics, she's attracting attention. But you said yourself she's got accountants, Dad. Proper ones. They’d flag anything truly illegal, wouldn't they? Accountants can be…persuaded, Elsie. And they can be very good at structuring things to  look  legal. It’s all about layers. And Brenda is exceptionally good at layers. That's why she can afford a flat in Paris, for goodness sake. Exactly. She’s been clever for years, skimming a little off the top of every transaction. It adds up. A  lot . And now HMRC are sniffing around. She’s already gotten a hefty fine, apparently. Something about ‘failure to report suspicious activity’. A convenient excuse, that. A fine? How much is ‘hefty’ in this case? Sounds like peanuts to her. More than peanuts, Liam. Enough to make even her twitch. Apparently, it’s a warning shot. They’re signaling they know  something . And they want her to cooperate. Or things will get significantly worse. Prison is a distinct possibility. Prison! Auntie Brenda? She wouldn’t cope. Remember when she lost her car keys and nearly had a meltdown? She's a survivor, Elsie. She'll bluster and threaten and try to intimidate. But this is different. This isn’t a lost set of keys. This is serious criminal activity. It's why I've been trying to convince her to wind things down for years. It’s the risk to the family I worry about, too. If they dig deep enough, they'll start asking questions about where  her  money comes from, and suddenly we’re all under scrutiny.

…and honestly, the rain just  came down . Biblical, it was. Drove all the way back from Birmingham thinking I was going to aquaplane on the M6. Did anyone else get soaked? Just a bit damp, love. I popped out to post a few letters for the hospice, nothing too dramatic. Though, the garden could definitely do with a good drink, that’s for sure. Been a dry spell, hasn’t it? I walked to school, and managed to avoid the worst of it. Though little Leo insisted on splashing in every puddle he could find! He absolutely  loved  it. I’m going to have to wrestle a change of clothes out of him tonight, I suspect. Sounds about right. I was lucky, bus stop’s covered. Though work was… chaotic. Had a delivery go completely wrong, ended up with three times the stock of oat milk and zero almond. You wouldn’t believe the complaints! Oh, horrors! Oat milk versus almond milk – a battle for the ages. Honestly, people. Anyway, how’s the fundraising going, David? Anything exciting planned? Slowly but surely. We’re aiming for a big push next month, a sponsored walk around Cannock Chase. Trying to get local businesses involved, offering sponsorship per kilometre. It’s hard work, drumming up support, but it’s for a good cause. Honestly, seeing the difference the hospice makes… it’s worth every phone call. It really is. You’re doing amazing work, David. Have you told everyone about the sign language class I’m starting? I thought a few of you might be interested. Ooh, tell us more! I’ve always wanted to learn. It seems so useful, and just… a lovely skill to have. It's at the community centre, Tuesdays evening. It's a beginner's course, so perfect for absolute newbies. I thought it would be good, especially with the baby coming. Trying to be prepared, you know? Even basic signing could be so helpful. That’s a brilliant idea, Sarah! I might join you actually. It's something I’ve always meant to do. It’s important for little ones to be able to communicate before they can properly speak, isn't it? Plus, it's good for the brain! It sounds fascinating. I’d be terrible, I’m sure, all thumbs. But I’d happily sponsor you both! Though, honestly, you two are always learning something new.

…and honestly, the phonetic transcription was  awful . Like, genuinely, did they even  listen  to the speaker? The glottal stops were just… missing. Entirely. It’s Aylesbury, you know? We practically breathe glottal stops. You’re sounding very Aylesbury about Aylesbury right now, El. It’s Cambridge, though. They probably think we all speak like the Queen. Which, let’s be honest, a lot of people  do  around here. It’s funny, isn’t it? People’s perceptions of ‘received pronunciation’. I grew up in KL, but my mum insisted on elocution lessons when we moved back to the UK, terrified I’d pick up…well, anything remotely regional. She still corrects my ‘h’ dropping sometimes, even though I’ve got a Masters in English Literature! My grandma did the same thing, but in reverse. She’s Chilean-Swedish, grew up bouncing between Stockholm and Santiago, and she was horrified when I came back from uni sounding… well, Northern. She'd say, “Darling, you sound like you’re from  up there !” as if it were a disease. Oh, I know that tone! My nan did that about anything south of the M25. "Sounds a bit common, doesn't it?" she’d say. Being a Language Research Co-ordinator and spending all day analysing accents, it’s just… ironic, isn’t it? The whole point is there  is  no inherently ‘better’ accent. It’s a power thing, I think. ‘Proper’ English used to equal social standing. It’s shifting, thankfully. Although, even just in publishing, you do notice certain voices get amplified more than others. Definitely. It’s subtle, but it’s there. We had a manuscript recently – brilliant, genuinely ground-breaking stuff – but the author wrote in a very distinct Bristolian dialect. The editor was… hesitant. Said it might be “difficult for some readers to connect with.” Which, honestly, is code for “sounds too working class.” That’s awful! Did you push back? I did. I pointed out that authenticity was key to the piece, that erasing the dialect would fundamentally alter the story and its impact. Thankfully, the editor agreed, but it was a battle. It feels like we're constantly navigating these unseen expectations. It’s exhausting. And it’s ridiculous. I was interviewing someone last week for a project – a lovely older woman from Norfolk – and I had to actively  fight  the urge to correct her ‘dropped Hs’. It’s ingrained, isn’t it?

…and honestly, the visa application is a right pain in the backside. They want, like, three months of bank statements? Three! Like they think we’re suddenly laundering money through this Mongolia rally. Tell me about it. I've been wrestling with it all morning. And the photo requirements are  insane . Passport photo, but apparently it has to be a specific shade of white backdrop, no smiling, no squinting… It’s like trying to get a mugshot that’s actually acceptable. Did you get yours done yet? Nah, not yet. I was thinking of just popping down to that booth in the market. They’re usually alright, bit dodgy-looking but they get the job done. You? I tried a proper studio. Cost me a tenner for two, but even then, the bloke said my expression looked "too enthusiastic". Too enthusiastic for a visa application?! What does that even  mean ? I look like I'm excited to be going to Mongolia, is that a crime? Classic. Sounds about right. Look, the visa’s a nightmare, but we'll get through it. The bigger thing stressing me is donations. We’re miles off the target. I put a post on Facebook, but it’s mostly just family liking it. I’ve been pestering everyone at Uni, but everyone’s skint. It’s end of term, everyone’s blown their student loans on… well, everything. I did have an idea, though. What about Gumtree? We could put an ad up, offering to do, like, odd jobs for donations – gardening, washing cars, that sort of thing? Gumtree? That’s… surprisingly good actually. A bit desperate, but good. “Two lads, one battered car, driving to Mongolia for charity. Will wash your car, mow your lawn, even attempt to assemble flatpack furniture for a worthy cause!” Exactly! We could get some decent photos of us looking suitably determined, maybe even covered in mud. Appeal to people's sympathetic side. I’ll knock up an ad tonight. Brilliant. While you're doing that, I'll have another go at the donation page. Maybe I need to change the wording. It's for "Hope and Homes for Children" right? Yeah, that’s the one. And if we hit a certain target, we promised to get someone to wax your chest, didn’t we? Don't remind me. That was a moment of weakness. A desperate attempt to incentivise donations.

…and honestly, the fluorescent lights in that A&E were  criminal . They made everything look gray. Even the biscuits they gave me tasted… muted. Muted biscuits? Sounds about right for a night in hospital. You were looking pretty grey yourself when I finally got you back, mind. Honestly, Elsie, what  did  you do to your arm? I still can’t believe you managed to dislocate it just… dancing. It wasn’t just ‘dancing’, Liv. She was attempting a particularly ambitious interpretive movement to ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’ and somehow launched herself into a potted fern. Hey! It was a very poignant fern. And Freddie deserved my full dramatic expression! Besides, it wasn’t  just  the fern, the floor was slippy! Honestly, I'm still aching all over, not just the arm. This entire university experience is exhausting. Tell me about it. Lectures, societies, trying to remember people’s names… I’m running on fumes and caffeine. Speaking of, want a cuppa? I'm making some builder's brew, proper strong stuff. Please. The strongest you’ve got. I feel like I haven't properly slept in days. And honestly, the doctor was all, “Rest it, take paracetamol," like that’s some groundbreaking medical advice. Well, rest  is  important, Elsie. You need to take it easy. No more impromptu fern-related performances for a while, yeah? I’m worried about you pushing yourself. You’ve been trying to do everything, join every society, go to every party… I just want to make the most of it! Back home in Falmouth, things were… quieter. This is new, you know? Everyone seems to have their thing, their group. I don’t want to miss out. You’re not missing out, you’re burning out. Look, we’re your ‘thing’. We're your group. You don't need to be president of the pottery club  and  a regular at life drawing  and  mastering the ukulele to have a good time. Easy for you to say, you seem to effortlessly glide through uni life, Liv. You’re thriving with your history course. Thriving is a strong word. It’s a lot of reading, mostly. Plus, Ben keeps texting me about some lecture on the Magna Carta. Honestly, boys. They think all we care about are ancient documents. Oh, Ben? Still going strong then? Yeah, he’s alright. A bit… intense about medieval history. And he  always  wants to debate.

…and honestly, lad, your Auntie Brenda nearly took young Timmy’s head off with her handbag when he went for the buffet before everyone else. Honestly, the drama! It were like watching a particularly feisty episode of Coronation Street. No way! Timmy? He’s usually so quiet. I didn't even  know  Auntie Brenda  had  a handbag that could be weaponised. Oh, she does. It’s a black leather beast. She says it holds everything a woman needs to survive a family gathering. Apparently, that includes emergency Werther’s Originals and… well, potential projectiles. Did you manage to get a word in edgeways with Grandad at all? He was holding court by the fireplace, as usual. Briefly. He asked me about my A-Level choices again. Said I should definitely consider accountancy. “Solid as a rock, lad,” he said. “Always a good job, accountancy.” I told him I was leaning towards Physics. He just blinked at me. He’s hopeless with anything that isn't involving spreadsheets and a good bargain. Bless him. He means well, though. Did you tell him about the offer from Leeds? Yeah, eventually. He grunted. Then asked if Leeds was a good place for “business opportunities.” Honestly, it’s like he thinks every university course is just a stepping stone to becoming a used car salesman. He did spend a fair bit of time running that car lot, didn’t he? It’s ingrained in ‘im, I reckon. Still, thirty years! That's a proper milestone for Mum and Dad. I thought they handled the speeches really well. Your Mum was a bit tearful, weren't she? A little. But Dad was brilliant. He actually made a joke about the time he accidentally set fire to the kitchen trying to make her breakfast in bed. She wasn’t impressed  then  either, apparently. Oh, I remember that! The smell of burnt toast lingered for weeks. Your father's a menace in the kitchen, that one. He thinks a spatula is some sort of power tool. But it was a lovely touch, bringing it up. It showed everyone how much they still wind each other up – in a good way, mind. It did. And the photos! Old Uncle Arthur dug out some right embarrassing ones from when they were teenagers. Mum with that awful perm… Don't even mention it. She’ll never forgive him. And your Dad in those flares!

…and honestly, Dad, I don’t even  need  this many water bottles. Three? Seriously? It’s like we’re prepping for a desert crossing, not a trip to Cornwall. Remember last year when you insisted on bringing five and we barely touched one? Now, now, lass. Better to have and not need than need and not have, eh? You get thirsty, especially in the heat. And this one’s got the filter built in, remember? For when we’re properly out and about, climbing about on those cliffs. Besides, I’ve got a new pen in this bottle bag – a really good one, proper gel ink. Thought you might want to borrow it for notes or sketching. A pen? That's your justification for three water bottles? It's a bit much, isn't it? Anyway, how much further you reckon? My legs are already starting to ache. Oh, we've only just left Manchester, sweetheart. It’s a long haul. Six, seven hours, depending on traffic. I packed sandwiches, yeah? And those cheese and onion crisps you like. We can stop for a proper dinner down near Exeter. Fancy a pub meal? Pub meal sounds good. Are we going to that Holland & Barrett you mentioned? You said you needed something… Aye. Need some stuff for me stomach, honestly. This IBS is playing up again. Doctor says stress, and well, moving house and all that…it’s a right palaver. Honestly, I’m glad we finally got it sorted though. That old place was doing me head in. It  was  a bit cramped. And the garden was always damp. Are you going to try and get all your cooking things organised straight away at the new house, or leave it for a bit? Probably a bit of both. Gotta get the kettle set up first, naturally. Can’t function without a brew. And I’ll get the basics sorted – plates, cutlery, that sort of thing. But unpacking all the spices and stuff… that can wait. I’ve got a craving for chocolate, actually. Got any in your bag? Naturally. Dark chocolate, because you’re trying to be ‘healthy.’ Though last time I checked, no amount of dark chocolate can offset a full English every Sunday. Point taken. You know, speaking of houses, I was reading about those old manor houses in Cornwall. Proper history, some of ‘em. Apparently, smuggling was rife down there.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of it is just… overwhelming. Three hours of Mrs. Higgins talking about her prize-winning begonias. Three! Hours! I swear, she described the  veining  on each petal. Sounds… thorough. Is it all like that, then? Just extended monologues on niche hobbies? Oh, don’t be unkind, David. Old Mrs. Higgins is a lovely woman. And those begonias  are  rather spectacular, if you ever see them. Though, admittedly, listening to a detailed account of their fertilization schedule isn’t everyone’s cup of tea. Fertilization schedule? Right. Sounds about par for the course for this project, eh, Eleanor? You’re the one sifting through this, aren’t you? Must be like archaeological digging – uncovering layer upon layer of mundane detail. Exactly! Archaeological is a  perfect  word, Gareth. And it's not just Mrs. Higgins. Old Mr. Davies recounting his wartime experiences, painstakingly detailing every ration book coupon... lovely stories, potentially, but they’re… long. I'm supposed to be extracting key details for the historical society, not creating verbatim transcripts of life stories. So what  is  the actual directive? Because it sounded to me like they just wanted everything recorded. Purely for posterity, I assumed. They originally wanted full transcripts, yes. But the committee realised the sheer impossibility – and cost – of that fairly quickly. Now they want summaries, focusing on anything relating to the village's history, significant local events, or changes in life over the past century. Eleanor's job is to find the nuggets of gold in all that…begonia-related dust. Nuggets of gold. Good analogy, Agnes. Though, I’m betting the nuggets are pretty small. You got a proper setup for this, Eleanor? Good headphones? Because listening to this stuff for hours must be draining. I do, thankfully. Noise cancelling ones. It’s still… mentally taxing. It feels incredibly intrusive, listening to people’s most private memories, even if they  did  volunteer for the project. And the accents! Good Lord, the accents. Trying to decipher some of the older speakers is a linguistic puzzle in itself. Well, you’re good at that sort of thing, aren’t you? You have an ear for detail. That’s what makes you such a good transcriber. It’s one thing to transcribe a formal interview, David, quite another to try and make sense of a rambling monologue delivered in broad Scots dialect with a mouthful of Werther’s Originals.

…and honestly, the glitter is  still  turning up. I found some in the toaster this morning! Honestly, Leo, you were like a glitter bomb exploded in here yesterday. But it was for Nana's card! It had to be sparkly! Yeah! Nana likes sparkly things. More than Dad likes football. That’s…a pretty high bar, actually. Right, so, Mother’s Day. Card is nearly done, judging by the glitter situation. What else have we got planned? Remember we talked about breakfast in bed? I can make toast! I’m really good at toast now. But not without help. And I can get the juice! Orange squash, definitely orange. Nana likes orange. Excellent. Teamwork. I’ll handle the actual cooking, maybe some pancakes? And we need to think about what we're going to  do  with Nana. She said she didn’t want presents this year, remember? She said she wants ‘quality time’. What’s ‘quality time’? Sounds boring. It’s not boring! It just means spending time together, doing things you both enjoy. Like… maybe a trip to Forest School? It’s a lovely day, and she always enjoys watching you two get muddy. Ooh, yes! Can we build a fairy house? I want to make a really good one this time, with tiny furniture. And a moat! Every fairy house needs a moat. To keep the goblins out. A very important detail. Right, Forest School it is. I’ll book a slot. Now, speaking of goblins... Did you hear the one Old Man Hemmings told me over the fence yesterday? What one? Is it a scary one? No, it's silly. He said, “A watched pot never boils, but a watched kettle definitely does!” But… kettles always boil. That doesn't make any sense. Exactly! That's the joke! It's… it’s an idiom, a silly saying. It means if you wait for something to happen by just staring at it, it’ll take forever. An id-ee-um? Like a secret code? A bit like a secret code, yes. English is full of them. Like, “break a leg” – when you tell someone good luck, you tell them to break a leg. It’s completely bonkers, isn’t it? That  is  bonkers. Why would you want someone to break their leg? You don’t! It’s just…a way of wishing them well. It’s an old theatre tradition.

…and honestly, the guilt is awful, isn’t it? Just knowing she’s pushing herself to ‘be strong’ for everyone, when really she just needs to  feel  things. Mum always was one for stiff upper lip. Oh, God, yes. It's the classic Mum thing, isn't it? Mines the same. “Mustn’t be a burden,” she says. As if  she's  the burden! It's ridiculous. Are you talking about your sister, Sarah? How's the chemo going? Last I heard, it was…rough. It is rough. Really rough. She lost her hair completely last week. It hit her harder than I expected, actually. Not the vanity side of it, though that played a part, more…it felt  final , you know? Like a visible sign of what's happening. They’ve adjusted the dosage slightly, trying to mitigate the sickness. She’s managing to keep some food down, which is good. But the fatigue…she’s just wiped out. Poor love. It’s horrifying seeing someone you care about going through that. Remember Auntie Brenda? Her reaction to losing her hair felt similar, that hollowness. It’s more than just the hair, isn’t it? It’s losing control. It’s…a physical manifestation of the cancer taking over. Exactly. And John, her husband, is…well, he's trying. He’s always been brilliant, a real rock. But you can see he’s cracking. He’s taking time off work, which is good, but he’s not  good  at just…being. He needs to  do  things. He keeps offering to re-organise the shed. Sarah just wants him to sit with her and hold her hand. Men. Bless ‘em. They try, but sometimes it’s like they’re solving a problem, rather than providing comfort. My David was the same when my Grandad was ill. Constantly offering to ‘fix’ things. Like you can fix death with a new set of shelves. It's infuriating and heartbreaking all at once. How are the kids coping? Little Emily must be so confused. Emily’s…surprisingly resilient, actually. She’s asking a lot of questions, which is good. John and Sarah are trying to be honest, but age-appropriately, of course. They’ve explained Mum is ‘very poorly’ and needs medicine to get better. Tom, though, his teenage angst has gone into overdrive. He's just withdrawn completely, spends all his time in his room.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking is ridiculous. Twenty essays on the historical development of the definite article! It’s fascinating stuff, don’t get me wrong, but grading them all feels like climbing Everest in slippers. Everest in slippers. That’s a perfect analogy. You’d think a postgraduate degree would prepare you for…  this . I swear, my dissertation feels like a light snack compared to the workload you’re describing. How much longer have you got on this module? Two weeks. Two weeks of ‘the’ and ‘a’ dominating my life. Then it’s onto syntax, which is… less dry, thankfully. How’s the linguistics reading going for  you ? Still tackling Chomsky? Slowly but surely. It’s dense, isn't it? I finally grasped the concept of deep structure versus surface structure, but then got completely lost in the transformational rules. I might need to bribe you with a proper dinner for an explanation. Which, by the way, is nearly ready. Vegetarian chilli, if that sounds alright. Vegetarian chilli sounds  amazing . You know my weakness for a good spicy bean concoction. And absolutely, bribe away. Syntax is my happy place. Though explaining it coherently… that’s the challenge. It's a bit like trying to explain Korean gendered language to someone who’s never encountered that concept. Remember when we were in Seoul, and I kept accidentally being too polite to those guys at the convenience store? Oh god, yes! You were practically bowing and using honorifics like you were addressing the President! They looked so confused. And you then explained to me the whole ingrained societal hierarchy influencing their speech…it was a linguistics lesson in real-time. It really highlighted how much language is tied to culture. Precisely! It's brilliant, isn’t it? More interesting than declensions, any day. Speaking of culture, have you been thinking about that trip to China we were talking about? I saw some cheap flights… I have! But the university is putting the pressure on about dissertation data collection. Professor Davies wants my fieldwork completed by the end of November. It’s just… finding the time, and the money. Tuition fees have bled me dry, honestly. Tell me about it. I'm seriously considering selling my old PlayStation. The retro gaming market is surprisingly buoyant. I’ve seen people pay good money for a perfectly preserved PS2. Sacrifices have to be made, right?

…and then, honestly, the airport security guard  stared  at me. Like, full-on scrutiny. Apparently, my sports bra set off the scanner? It was mortifying! Ooh, aye, that’s grim. Happens to the best of us, though. Remember when Sarah nearly got flagged for her… well, never mind. Not one for the table. Oh, go on! Spill! No way! She’d kill me. It involved a very questionable souvenir from Magaluf and a rather strategically placed pocket. Anyway, back to you, Liv. What did you  say  to the guard? I just mumbled something about needing support, and he just… waved me through. It was so awkward. Speaking of awkward, has anyone finished their physics work? Professor Davies is  serious  about the deadline. Nope. Still battling with quantum entanglement. It's making my brain hurt. Honestly, give me a module assessment on  Twilight  any day. At least I understand sparkly vampires. Don’t even  start  with Twilight. It’s objectively awful. Honestly, Bella Swan is the most annoying protagonist ever. I’m more of a  City of Bones  girl, myself. Jace Wayland, anyone? You and your fictional boyfriends, Chloe! I’m firmly in the  Vampire Diaries  camp. Damon Salvatore is… a mood. But seriously, physics. It's like trying to understand hieroglyphics. You’re telling me! I spent all afternoon trying to wrap my head around it. It’s a good job we have that quiz night at Sugarhouse on Wednesday. Need to forget about superposition and remember useless facts about Jack Whitehall. Oh god, the Big Fat Quiz. Always a source of immense stress. Last year I genuinely thought the capital of Australia was Sydney. I’m still recovering from the shame. You’re not alone. I thought Henry VIII had six wives and just… forgot the last one's name. It was a disaster. Remember that terrible Secret Santa last year? I got a knitted tea cosy. A  knitted tea cosy ! Oh, the tea cosy! Bless you. I got a packet of stale biscuits. From Nan. My nan always gives questionable presents. One year it was a pair of bright orange boxers. For a grown woman. That’s… something. Speaking of questionable, anyone remember that camping trip last summer? The flooding in Lancaster was insane. We were practically waterlogged. Don't remind me. I think I still haven’t fully dried my sleeping bag. It felt like we were recreating Noah’s Ark.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of data is mental. Like, mountains of text, all needing tagging for grammatical features. You wouldn't believe how many people misuse semicolons. It’s a national crisis, I tell ya! Semicolons, huh? Sounds… thrilling. Is it at least interesting stuff you're tagging, or is it all, like, academic papers on the mating habits of the Bolivian tree lizard? Mostly it’s news articles, political speeches, some fiction. There’s a surprising amount of online forum posts too. Which, let me tell you, is a deep dive into the human psyche. Some of the things people write… You’d think people would be nicer behind a keyboard, wouldn't you? You’d think. The internet seems to bring out the worst in everyone. Still, a job's a job. At least it's using your degree, right? Better than, I don't know, serving lattes. No offense to baristas, of course. None taken! My cousin Kev does alright serving coffee, he's building up a little side hustle doing graphic design. But yeah, it  is  good to be using the linguistics degree. Though sometimes I feel like a digital librarian, endlessly categorizing. It’s a bit… removed from actual speaking, you know? I get that. My job's similar, in a way. I’m designing drainage systems - vital, obviously, keeps towns from flooding – but it’s all models and calculations. I haven’t actually  seen  a flood I’ve prevented, if that makes sense. It's all theoretical. That's exactly it! It’s all… abstract. Speaking of abstract, remember old Mrs. Higgins from next door? The one who collected gnomes? Oh god, Mrs. Higgins! How could I forget? Her garden was terrifying. A full-scale gnome invasion. She called them her ‘little people’. And she genuinely believed they moved around at night. My mam used to tell me stories about her chasing shadows with a watering can, convinced they were gnome thieves. I remember being utterly convinced, aged about seven, that she  was  onto something. We'd sneak around her garden, trying to catch them in the act. Obviously, we never saw anything. We were idiots, weren’t we? But it felt so real at the time. She used to give us biscuits, though. Little shortbreads. Best biscuits ever. They probably  were  the best biscuits. She had that knack, didn't she? Always smelled of lavender and slightly damp earth.

…and I tell you, this knee’s playing up something awful. Worse than yesterday, it is. Feels like someone’s taken a hammer to the bone, it does. Never known owt like it. Oh, Arthur, you say that  every  time the weather changes. Honestly, you’re a walking barometer, you are. Did you take your paracetamol this morning? Course I did, Ethel. Don’t treat me like a daft old man! Two of ‘em. Didn’t touch it, though. Not a jot. Just a dull ache now, mostly, but when I try to… well, when I try to get up from this chair, it’s like a bolt of lightning. Gran, maybe you should actually  see  a doctor about it? You keep saying it’s just the weather, but it’s been “just the weather” for months now. Doctors! Humph. They just poke and prod and tell you to lose weight. What good would that do? It’s age, love, plain and simple age. This body’s seen seventy-eight winters, you know. It’s bound to creak a bit. With respect, Arthur, a proper diagnosis could help. They might be able to offer something to manage the pain, even if it’s just physiotherapy. Your Grandad’s right in a way, though. They don't seem to listen anymore. Remember when Dr. Peterson used to come out to the house? Now you’re lucky if you get five minutes face-to-face. Things have changed, I know. But there are good doctors out there, and Dad, ignoring it won’t make it go away. Speaking of changes, has anyone noticed how mild this winter is? It’s practically spring already. Don’t talk to me about mild! Mild’s bad for the joints, you know. Gives ‘em that damp feeling. I prefer a good, hard frost. Clears the air, it does. Though my roses won’t be too pleased. You're still fussing over those roses, then? Despite the knee? Of course! A man's gotta have his hobbies. Even a creaky old man. Ethel keeps telling me to get someone in to do them, but what’s the point of that? They wouldn’t understand ‘em like I do. It's just, dear, you shouldn't be straining yourself. You nearly fell last week when you were pruning. I nearly had a heart attack! Nonsense! A slight wobble, that’s all.

…and honestly, the seating plan is giving me actual nightmares. Aunt Carol  insists  on being next to Uncle Barry, despite the fact they haven’t spoken a civil word to each other since… well, since forever. Oh,  god , family weddings are the worst for that. Remember Sarah’s? The drama with her cousins over who got to be closest to the cake? It was appalling. But hey, at least  your  wedding isn’t going to involve a cake-related feud, right? Let’s hope not! Though knowing your family, anything’s possible, Liv. Seriously though, have you asked your mum to mediate? She’s usually pretty good at diffusing situations. I have, but she just says, “Oh, they’ll be fine, dear. They always make up.” They. Do. Not. Always. Make up. They glare at each other competitively during Christmas cracker pulls, for goodness sake! Sounds…festive. Listen, just put them as far apart as physically possible. And strategically place some loud, chatty people between them. Problem solved. Good shout, Chloe. Distraction is key. So, how are  you  finding wedding planning, Jess? You’re further along than Liv, aren’t you? Last I heard you were finalising catering. Yeah, pretty much done with that. Honestly, the food tasting was the best part. I ate for England! We've gone with a hog roast, which I'm really excited about. It feels…rustic. And very  us . Ooh, a hog roast! That  is  good. Though I’m picturing you covered in gravy and stuffing by the end of the night. Worth it. The dress is still the biggest stress, though. I found one I love, but it needs alterations, and the seamstress is booked solid for months. Alterations are the bane of every bride’s existence. It always takes longer than you think. Speaking of things taking longer than you think… Ben keeps dropping hints about wanting kids almost immediately after the wedding.  Immediately ? Has he met himself? He's still borderline incapable of doing laundry! That’s what I said! I mean, I want kids eventually, obviously, but I need at least a year to recover from planning a wedding and, you know,  be  married. Plus, I'm still enjoying having a bit of freedom. It's your life, Liv. You don’t need to rush into anything because he’s got baby fever. Just be firm. Exactly. Tell him you need to establish yourselves financially, travel…learn to do his own laundry.

…and honestly, Doreen, I still can’t get me ‘ead around this telly. It’s not like the old days, is it? Used to just ‘ave three channels and you knew where you were. Now it’s all streaming and on demand… feels like a right fiddle to me. Oh, Arthur, you say that every time! It’s not  that  bad. My granddaughter, Lily, she showed me how to watch things on this ‘iPlayer’ thing. It's quite clever, actually. Though I do miss just flicking through the Radio Times. Remember those days? Radio Times were a national institution. I remember planning my week around what was on. Though, now with kids, the planning revolves more around school events and who needs a lift where. It's a different kind of busy, isn't it? Busy indeed. Though I can’t say I miss school runs. Never ‘ad any of me own, you see. Always preferred the company of a good ‘orse. Simpler creatures, ‘orses. Don’t ask you to explain what ‘buffering’ means. Oh, don't get me started on buffering! Little Timmy was trying to show me a funny cat video the other day and it just kept stopping and starting. He got so frustrated! Said I was ruining it. Kids and their technology… It's the way things are going, though. I’m trying to integrate more tech into the classroom. Interactive whiteboards, online learning platforms… it’s a constant learning curve, for all of us. It's stressful, sometimes, especially with funding cuts making it difficult to get the resources we need. Funding cuts… that's the truth of it, isn't it? Everything’s getting squeezed. Used to be you could rely on a decent pension, now… well, let’s just say I’m glad I didn’t spend me life saving. Wouldn’t ‘ave been worth the paper it was written on. You’re not wrong there, Arthur. I managed alright with the childminding, but it wasn’t a fortune. And the self-employed tax… a nightmare. Still, it meant I was able to be there for me grandchildren, which was the important thing. Lily's always been a clever one, though. She's thinking of going to university to study computer science. Good for her! We need more young people going into STEM fields. It’s where the jobs are, unfortunately. Though, finding the money for university is a whole other issue.

…and honestly, the sheer variety of accents  within  Birmingham is fascinating. I had a student yesterday, born and raised here, but with a really noticeable Brummie twang - proper ‘bah missus’ style. It’s lovely, really. Makes my job interesting, trying to decipher what they  mean  sometimes, not just what they  say . Ah, Brum. A language all its own, isn’t it? Different from Essex, naturally. We used to have a bit of a… shall we say,  pronounced  accent down our way. More estuary, really. Though it’s softened a bit now, I reckon, with everyone moving around. Less distinct. Exactly! It's the movement of people, isn’t it? And the media, probably. Though I actively  encourage  my students to hold onto their local speech. It’s part of their identity. I teach English to speakers of other languages too, and they’re always so impressed by the nuances here. They think everyone in England speaks like the Queen! The Queen! Now  there’s  a carefully cultivated accent. Reminds me of my old boss, Reginald. Always trying to sound terribly refined. Never quite managed it, sounded more like a constipated penguin, if I’m honest. Oh, dear! That’s a vivid image. So, how have you been keeping yourself busy since you retired, Arthur? Still tinkering in the garden? Gardening keeps me sane, mostly. Though the weeds are winning at the moment. Need to get out there later, give 'em a good seeing-to. And I've taken up woodturning. Bit of a late-in-life hobby, I know. Bought myself a lathe and everything. Makes a terrible mess, but very satisfying. Woodturning! That sounds lovely. My grandfather used to do a bit of carpentry. I remember him making little wooden animals for me when I was small. It’s a wonderful skill. Do you make anything specific? Bowls, mostly. Small ones, for fruit. Tried a candlestick once, nearly set the shed on fire. Learnt my lesson. Your mum mentioned you were thinking of a trip abroad? Yes, potentially. I'm looking at Portugal. I’ve always wanted to go. It seems lovely and warm, and the language is… well, it’s familiar enough for me to have a go. I think a bit of immersion is the best way to learn. Plus, the seafood is supposed to be incredible. Portugal! Good choice. Went there with Margaret – that's my late wife – a few years back.

… honestly, the whole day was just  weird . Like, everyone was making such a big deal about it. It’s just another Friday, innit? Though, admittedly, the canteen was smelling particularly romantic with that dodgy lasagne. Dodgy lasagne  is  romantic, in a student budget kind of way. You didn't, like,  have  plans, did you? That's why you're so wound up? I thought you were going to that vintage shop with your cousin? I  was  going to, yeah. But then she cancelled last minute ‘cause her boyfriend suddenly decided Valentine’s Day shopping was crucial. Crucial! Like, seriously? It’s just clothes, babe! And then Mum kept texting, asking if I’d “had a lovely evening” and if I was “seeing anyone special.” It was relentless. Oh, bless. Mums, eh? Mine was doing the same. She kept going on about how my Auntie Linda met Uncle George on Valentine’s Day, like it’s some sort of guarantee of everlasting happiness. Honestly, it’s putting pressure on me already, and I’m nowhere near thinking about all that. Want a bite of my chips? They’re surprisingly decent. Ta. Yeah, please. And you? Had a whirlwind romance ignited by a rose and a box of chocolates? Nah, nothing like that. I ended up watching a terrible rom-com with Aisha. We ordered pizza, and basically spent the whole time ripping it to shreds. It was actually a really good night, but Mum would be disappointed to know it didn't involve flowers or a fancy dinner. She’d probably say, “Filipina girls are  so  romantic!” - with that tone. Oof, the tone. I know that tone. My Nan does the same when she’s trying to push me towards someone she approves of. “He’s a  lovely  boy, darling, very stable.” As if stability is the only thing that matters! Exactly! It's like, what about shared interests? A sense of humour? The ability to tolerate my terrible music taste? Anyway, speaking of terrible things…have you seen what's on at the Odeon this weekend? They’re showing that new superhero thing. I saw! I was thinking of going on Saturday. But then I remembered I promised to help my little brother with his maths. He’s struggling with… well, everything maths-related to be honest. It's tragic. Aww, you’re a good sister. But seriously, superhero movies are  essential  weekend viewing.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the new planning bill just feels like a green light for developers to build whatever they want, regardless of community needs. It’s terrifying. Especially in London, you know? It’s already so unaffordable. Seriously! I was reading about that. It’s basically handing them permission to ignore local councils, isn't it? And they’re framing it as “solving the housing crisis” which is such a joke. It’s solving  their  profit crisis, more like. This Dan Dan noodles are amazing though, aren’t they? Bit spicy. Amazing. I’m regretting going for the extra chilli already, but I’m committed now. And you’re absolutely right. It's the classic capitalist move – create a problem, then profit from the 'solution' that makes it worse for everyone else. It feels so… deliberate. Deliberate is the word. It's not even like they  try  to hide it anymore. I was interviewing a housing activist the other day, a really sharp woman. She was saying it’s a continuation of decades of policy designed to financialize housing, turning homes into investments instead of… well, homes. God, financialized housing. It sounds so clinical and awful. It  is  awful. Remember when we were looking at flats around Clapham a couple of years ago? Every single viewing was an ‘investment opportunity’ pitch. No one cared if we actually wanted to  live  there. Oh, don’t even remind me. That estate agent, Reginald, was practically salivating at the thought of flipping a tiny, damp box to an overseas investor. He barely even looked at us! It's just… exhausting. And it’s not just London, is it? My cousin in Manchester is facing the same thing, rent hikes everywhere. It's everywhere. It’s national. And it's intertwined with everything else, isn't it? Like, the rhetoric around immigration, the constant dog-whistling. It's always about ‘protecting our communities’ and subtly implying… well, you know. Yeah. The not-so-subtle implication that certain people don’t  belong  here, and therefore shouldn't have access to decent housing. It's disgusting. I've been trying to pitch a piece on the link between housing inequality and the rise of far-right groups, but editors are hesitant. They say it's "too political." “Too political?” They mean it challenges the status quo. It’s infuriating! You’d think, as a journalist, you’d be encouraged to explore those connections.

…and honestly, the form itself was a  nightmare . Seven pages! Seven! And half of it was about allergies. Honestly, Leo hasn’t even  met  an allergen yet, how are we supposed to know? Sounds about right. Bureaucracy for babies. They make everything so complicated, don't they? Is it definitely the right nursery, though? You seemed a little unsure last week. I  am  still a bit unsure. It’s just…it’s the only one with spaces that fit with the days I need to be back at work. And Mrs. Davies seemed lovely. Very ‘child-centred’, apparently. Though, child-centred also seems to mean ‘covered in glitter and paint’ judging by the photos. Glitter and paint is good! It means they’re having fun. Better than staring at beige walls, right? And it's only two days a week to start with? Two days, thankfully. But still…leaving him. It just feels…monumental. And then trying to juggle everything with going back to work. My boss has been really understanding, but still. The deadlines are piling up already, even  before  I’m back full time. You’ll be fine, Mum. Honestly. You're Superwoman. You always are. And you're good at your job, they'd be daft to let you struggle. Have you thought about maybe asking for flexible hours even after you've settled back in? I have, but I’m worried it’ll look like I’m not committed. Apparently, there’s a real ‘face time’ culture now. Being seen to be working hard, even if you  are  actually working hard efficiently from home. It’s ridiculous. Ugh, sounds awful. Millennials are trying to dismantle that, slowly but surely. Speaking of dismantling things, how’s the weaning going? Any success with actual food, or is it still just pureed everything? Slowly. He grimaces at everything. Everything! Yesterday I tried sweet potato, and he looked at it like I’d offered him gravel. Honestly. It’s a mess. And then he gets cross when it’s not milk. It’s exhausting. Babies are drama queens. Trust me. Remember when I refused to eat anything green for a whole year? Vaguely. Mostly I remember your Dad attempting to hide broccoli in your mashed potato. He wasn’t very subtle. Anyway, Leo will get there. It just takes time. Have you thought about… a holiday? A proper holiday? We haven't had one since… well, since before Leo!

…and honestly, the sheer audacity of it! They’re claiming I used data roaming when I  specifically  checked with EE before I went to Cornwall that my allowance covered everything. It's just infuriating. EE are notorious for that, love. Daylight robbery, they are. I had a nightmare with them a few years back, a similar thing. Kept adding charges, saying I’d gone over… I had to threaten to go to Ofcom to get it sorted. Ugh, phone companies. Don’t even get me started. We had a till malfunction at the shop today, and the support line was… well, let’s just say I aged ten years in twenty minutes. You’d think they’d employ people who actually  understand  the systems they’re supposed to be helping with. Sounds stressful, both of you. Did you manage to sort it, Sarah? The EE thing, I mean. Not yet. I spent an hour on hold, then got someone who just read back the terms and conditions. Completely unhelpful. I'm going to have to write a formal complaint, I think. It's not just the money, it's the principle! Definitely write a complaint. Keep copies of everything. And mention Ofcom. That usually gets their attention. Speaking of things needing attention, I had a call from Detective Inspector Davies today. About the… well, you know. The incident. Oh, right. How did it go, Dad? Were they pushy? Not pushy, exactly. Just… thorough. They wanted a detailed statement, re-confirming everything I told the officers at the scene. It took a good hour. They were particularly interested in who else was around before it happened. Did you mention the neighbour’s dog barking constantly? I remember that being quite loud. Yes, I did. And Old Man Hemmings puttering about in his garden. They’re building a timeline, apparently. Trying to piece everything together. It's unsettling, to be honest. It makes it feel… real, you know? It  is  real, Geoff. And it's good you're cooperating. It’s the right thing to do. Though I still can’t believe someone would… do that. It's awful. Are you okay, Dad? You haven’t touched your Yorkshire pudding. I’m alright, love. Just… processing. It’s just shaken me up a bit. Being questioned like that. It brings it all back. Look, Dad, if you want to talk about it more, just say.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Lucius Barius was just  bad  writing. Completely contrived. Like, he had to die dramatically right before… well, you know. It just felt cheap. You’re still on about  Spartacus ? Blimey, Jamie, you’ve been obsessed since, what, uni? Thought marriage might’ve, I dunno, broadened your horizons? Marriage hasn’t changed my appreciation for historical dramas, thank you very much. It's just…the historical inaccuracies bug me. And the blatant foreshadowing. It’s like they’re shouting, “THIS PERSON IS GOING TO DIE!” Right. Well, I’ve been shouting at weeds all week so dramatic irony isn’t really high on my agenda. How's Sarah settling in? Still teaching those kids to properly use a present perfect tense? She is. Says she has a class who think ‘been’ and ‘gone’ are interchangeable. A constant battle. She’s good though, proper patient. She’s made a lovely lemon drizzle cake, by the way. Have you tried some yet? It’s on the counter. Oh, good shout! Always up for a bit of cake. Makes a change from the lukewarm builder’s tea and a biscuit I usually get. Speaking of, you still using that ridiculous mortar and pestle for your tea? It’s not ridiculous! It’s… artisanal. And it makes a difference! You get a proper grind on the leaves. You wouldn’t understand, living amongst the roses and petunias. Roses and petunias pay the bills, mate. And I can tell you, grinding anything to a fine powder is back-breaking work, even with machinery. I saw old man Hemmings doing it with hazelnuts for his baklava last week - he was  struggling . Hazelnuts for baklava? Interesting. I’d always assumed pistachios were the go-to. How’s your mum doing, by the way? I remember she always had a massive herb garden. She’s good. Still obsessed with her herbs. Trying to convince me I need to start making my own spice blends. She sent me home with a carrier bag full of dried oregano and chili flakes. Says it's “good for the soul”. And she's been trying to get me to eat more chickpeas. Apparently, they’re “brain food”. Your mum is a force of nature. Mine just sends passive-aggressive texts about needing to visit more often. Did you bring anything back from Cyprus last time you went? Any little souvenirs?

…and honestly, Miss Davies just  loves  to hear herself talk, doesn’t she? Like, the whole lesson was just her going on about symbolism in poetry. We didn't even  do  any actual writing! Tell me about it! I zoned out halfway through. Honestly, I think she forgets we’re all just trying to pass the English test next week. I’m proper stressing about that, actually. Did you revise the poetry section? A little. I made flashcards, but there’s  so  much. All those Victorian poets…Tennyson, Browning…it all just blends into one long, gloomy mess. You’re good at poetry though, aren’t you? Always have been. I’m alright. I get the gist of things, but analysing it all? Ugh. It's the 'what did the poet  mean  by the colour blue?' questions that get me. It's blue, Miss Davies! It's a colour! What else could it mean?! Exactly! It’s like, sometimes a rose is just a rose, yeah? Anyway, at least Art is good. Mr. Henderson is brilliant. We're doing lino printing next week, which should be fun. I'm thinking of doing a cityscape of Cambridge. Ooh, that’s a good idea! I was going to do something floral, but a cityscape sounds way more interesting. Are you still in wind band? I haven’t seen you rush home with your clarinet lately. Yeah, still in it! Practice is Thursdays after school. It's a bit hectic trying to get everything done, honestly. And Old Man Hemmings, the conductor, is being a right pain. He’s insisting on this ridiculously difficult piece for the winter concert. It’s all fast runs and complicated chords. My fingers are aching just thinking about it. Oh dear. Hemmings  is  a bit… intense. Remember when he made Tom Wilkins cry because he was slightly flat during scales? Oh god, don't remind me! Poor Tom! He swore he was never picking up a trombone again. Though he went back, didn’t he? Hemmings has that effect on people. Speaking of intense, French is killing me. Madame Dubois is lovely, but the grammar! It's just... chaotic. I agree. All the genders for everything! It’s just unnecessary. And the verb conjugations… I keep getting them muddled up. Did you hear Leo Thompson completely blanked on how to say ‘the cat’ in French during the role-play yesterday?

…and honestly, the price of a scone these days! Three pound fifty? In Darlington! It's daylight robbery, I tell you. When I were a lass, you got a scone, jam and cream for… well, not much, but definitely not  that  much. Three fifty? Seriously? Is it, like, a gold-plated scone or somethin’? I only wanted a packet of crisps, Mam. They were two fifty. Oh, don’t start, Brenda. You’ll be having a right rant about inflation next. Everything’s gone up, love. Though I do agree, three fifty  is  a bit steep for a scone. Remember old Mrs. Higgins' café, Brenda? She did a cracking scone for a quid. Oh, don't even  mention  Mrs. Higgins! The best scones ever made. And she always had a little wireless on, playing Vera Lynn. Proper Northern comfort, that was. You wouldn’t get that now, would you, Liam? You’re all about your… what is it you listen to? Grime? It’s not  all  grime, Mam! I listen to loads of stuff. But yeah, sometimes grime. It’s good. And it’s proper music, not… well, not Vera Lynn, no offence. No offence taken, lad. Times change. Though I do think there’s a lot to be said for a good melody. Still, I'm trying to understand what all the fuss is about with these TikToks you’re always on. Honestly, it’s just people dancing, isn't it? It's more than that, Auntie Carol! It's like... everything's on there. Funny videos, news, music, people showing off their skills… I’m learning a new football trick from one at the moment. Football, always football. Your dad was the same. Took you to every match going, didn’t he? Still can’t believe he insisted on getting that Newcastle United flag. Living in Darlington! It's practically treason. Now, Brenda, don't be like that. He was a proud Geordie, your husband. You knew that when you married him. And it's a good flag! Properly designed, too. Better than some of the bland, corporate branding you see these days. Look at that coffee chain’s logo. Utterly forgettable. Dad said it was about loyalty. He always said you should support your team, no matter where you are. Speaking of loyalty, is Uncle George alright? I haven't seen him in ages. Heard he wasn't feeling too well.

…and honestly, the traffic getting up here was  brutal . Absolutely brutal. I swear, every single slip road was backed up. Did you two have a good journey? Good? It was alright. Took a bit longer than I thought, more lorries than usual, I reckon. Though, mind you, relaxin’ to listen to the radio. Got a good classic rock station on. You wouldn’t catch  her  listenin’ to that, would ya? Oh, don’t start, Arthur. I have perfectly good taste in music. I enjoy a bit of Vera Lynn, thank you very much. It reminds me of happier times. And frankly, all that…  guitar  noise gives me a headache. A classic divide, then. Mum, Vera Lynn is timeless. Dad, rock is… well, also timeless, in a different way. Though, I did spend the last hour of the drive trying to explain to my students the concept of ‘slow food’ versus our current obsession with speed. It’s linked to obesity, you know. Everything is about convenience now. It is, isn’t it? And it’s not just food. Everything. People want instant gratification. Speaking of which, are you both helping yourselves to seconds? I made a huge lasagne. Don’t mind if I do. Lookin’ good, that. Though, I gotta say, I’m watchin’ me weight. Doctor’s been on at me. Said somethin’ about my cholesterol. Oh, Arthur, you know you’re a bit… solid. It runs in the family, though, doesn’t it? Your grandfather was a big man. Mine was quite slight. I think it’s all to do with genes, really. And a fondness for a biscuit with your tea. There is a genetic component, absolutely. But lifestyle plays a huge role. It’s fascinating stuff, actually. I was reading a paper on epigenetic inheritance… basically, how your habits can affect your  grandchildren . Right, the idea that trauma or lifestyle choices can alter gene expression. It's quite a revolutionary area of research. It makes you think about responsibility to future generations, doesn’t it? Responsibility? Sounds a bit grand, that! I’m just tryin’ to enjoy me retirement. Though, speaking of responsibility, I had Old Man Hemmings in today. Keeps complainin’ his car makes a funny noise. Turns out, it's just his allergies acting up. Says the pollen sets off his sinuses and he thinks it's the engine. Honestly! Oh, that man! He always thinks the worst.

…and honestly, the student feedback was brutal. Not  brutal  brutal, but… pointed. A lot of “Moodle is confusing,” “Instructions unclear,” the usual. Oh, the joys of Moodle. What specifically are they struggling with this time? Is it the assignment submission, the forums, the quizzes? It's always something. A bit of everything, actually. But predominantly the assignment submission. They’re getting tripped up on the different file types, and the fact that sometimes it doesn’t  immediately  show up in their list. They panic, think it hasn’t gone through, and then resubmit, creating a glorious mess for me to sort through. Right. The double submissions. The bane of our digital existence. Have you considered doing a screencast walk-through? A quick five-minute video showing exactly how to upload, confirm submission, and where to find it afterwards? I did, actually. I started one, but I kept getting distracted fiddling with the screen recording software. It’s all a bit… clunky, isn't it? I used OBS, thinking it was the professional choice, but it felt overly complicated for a simple demo. OBS is overkill for that, definitely. You’re a lecturer, you should be comfortable with Panopto! It’s integrated with everything, the recording quality is good enough, and it links directly into Moodle. You can even embed the video right into the assignment instructions. You’re right, of course. It’s just… I always associate Panopto with lectures. Long, prepared presentations. Doing something quick and informal feels…wrong somehow. Stupid, I know. Not stupid. Habit, probably. We get stuck in our ways. But think about it from their perspective. They're not looking for a polished performance, they just need a clear demonstration. Besides, a less-than-perfect screencast is better than a load of confused emails. What about the forums? Are they engaging with those at all? Not really. I post discussion questions, linking them to the reading, but it’s mostly tumbleweeds. A couple of students will answer, but it doesn’t spark much debate. I feel like I’m talking to a void sometimes. Classic. They think of forums as optional, don't they? Like a bonus round. Have you tried making participation mandatory? Even just a ‘post one question and respond to one other student' sort of thing? I haven't. I was hesitant, worried it would feel forced and they'd just write rubbish to get the points.

…and honestly, the jetlag is  real . I keep waking up thinking it’s seven AM and then remembering it’s… well, nearly lunchtime. It's utterly ridiculous. Though, slightly preferable to waking up at 3 AM convinced little Leo needs feeding when he’s fast asleep. Tell me about it. You looked like a zombie this morning. I was bracing myself for a full-on meltdown when you tried to make toast. Leo’s been pretty good, thankfully. Slept through most of the night, which is a miracle considering the time difference  we  were dealing with, let alone you flying back from Australia! Miracles are definitely required. Although, I think he senses when I’m exhausted and takes pity. Or maybe he’s just plotting. They’re surprisingly strategic, these tiny humans. Anyway, enough about my pathetic attempts at functioning. Did you confirm the tickets for ‘The Tempest’ on Friday? I did. Got us good seats, row D, just back from the stalls. Apparently, Old Man Hemmings is playing Prospero. You know, the one who used to teach Shakespeare at my undergrad? Absolute legend. Bit of a ham, but brilliant. Oh, brilliant! I’ve heard hushed whispers about his Prospero. He apparently cries  every  time. True method acting, apparently. Friday works perfectly. I was starting to worry we'd get stuck with the balcony seats again. My neck still hasn't forgiven us for ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’ last year. You did complain rather a lot about that. Fine, I admit, the balcony wasn’t ideal. This is much better. We can actually  see  the expressions. Are you free to meet beforehand? Maybe around six? We could grab a bite at that little Italian place near the theatre? ‘Luigi’s’? Six sounds good. Luigi’s is perfect. I’ve been craving pasta all week. It’s either that or chocolate biscuits… and I’m trying to be vaguely healthy. Though, considering the jetlag and baby-induced sleep deprivation, my willpower is practically non-existent. Healthy can wait. Pasta is  essential . Especially before dissecting Shakespeare. We can debate the symbolism of Ariel’s freedom over a plate of carbonara. You know me so well. Speaking of dissecting things, have you thought any more about the departmental meeting next week? Professor Davies is really pushing for us to overhaul the first-year syllabus. I have. And I'm not thrilled. It feels like such a huge undertaking, especially mid-term.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Omar’s cousin, Farid, trying to get a visa to come visit, it’s a complete shambles. He’s got all the paperwork, the invitation from Omar, proof of funds… everything. But the embassy keeps asking for more, and more, and more. It’s ridiculous, isn’t it? You, of all people, dealing with NRPSI, must know how Kafkaesque it can be. Kafkaesque is putting it mildly, Andreas. It  is  ridiculous. It’s not about the paperwork being deficient, it’s often about… well, let’s just say certain nationalities are subjected to a higher level of scrutiny. It’s infuriating, especially when they are genuinely wanting to visit, contribute to the economy, see friends… Farid’s from Kurdistan, right? That’s right. Omar is fiercely proud of his Kurdish heritage. He keeps saying it’s down to the political situation, the ongoing tensions, and… well, the oil. Everything comes back to the oil, doesn't it? It’s just… exhausting. It reminds me of trying to explain the nuances of post-colonial literature to first years – you get bogged down in layers and layers of complexity. You're spot on about the oil. It’s always about the oil. And the geopolitics. Kurdistan's position is… complicated. There’s also a shadow cast by the wider regional instability. And, unfortunately, the association, rightly or wrongly, with certain extreme ideologies. There’s a lot of fear-mongering. Fear-mongering is a good word. It's connected to what I was reading about the rise of Wahabi influence in parts of Libya, actually. The instability there creates a vacuum, doesn’t it? And these extremist groups exploit it. It’s frightening. I was talking to Dieter, my brother - he's still in Germany – and he’s saying they’re worried about ramifications there too. Libya is a mess. A complete, avoidable mess. And yes, the Wahabi influence… it's deeply concerning. It’s not representative of the vast majority of Muslims, of course, but it’s the vocal minority that gets all the attention. It’s the same story everywhere, isn't it? Extremes dominate the narrative. Do you think Farid understands the hoops he's having to jump through are down to all this? I think Omar’s tried to explain it, but it's hard to articulate the inherent bias. He’s getting increasingly frustrated though, and frankly, so am I.

…and honestly, the gravy was the saving grace. Lamb itself was a little dry, wasn't it, David? Though I suspect that's my fault, I probably left it in a bit too long checking emails. Old habits die hard, even on a Sunday. No, no, it was fine, honestly, Margaret. Perfectly edible. Though, a bit more mint sauce wouldn’t have gone amiss. You always make a lovely roast, don't undersell yourself. Are you having another slice, Agnes? Oh, I’m quite full, thank you, David. A truly substantial portion. Reminds me of the dinners we used to have at the school. Hearty fare to keep the staff going. Though, we didn't have the telly on  in  the dining room back then, goodness no! Well, progress, isn’t it? Though I do confess I was only half-watching that documentary about penguins. They're surprisingly judgemental birds, you know. Judgemental penguins? Now  that’s  a headline. I was trying to follow the rugby, but honestly, with the chatter… Chatter is what makes life worth living, David! All this quiet modern living! Back in my day, a dinner party was a  performance . Conversation, wit, a little bit of scandal… Scandal? Oh, Agnes, do tell! Though maybe not with the lamb still settling. Speaking of settling, have you decided about that cruise yet? I know you were looking at the Mediterranean ones. I have. It's tempting, very tempting. Italy, Greece, Croatia… all that history. Though I’m a wee bit worried about being cooped up on a ship with hundreds of people. I need my space, you know? And a good walk. I can understand that. It's not really  my  cup of tea either, to be honest. I prefer somewhere I can poke about a bit, get lost in a town. Though, a bit of sunshine would be nice. This weather is dreadful. Tell me about it! I tried to get my usual park run in this morning, and it was like running through treacle. Honestly, I felt like I’d aged ten years just getting to the five kilometre mark. You still doing those workouts, David? Trying to. Though I missed a couple of sessions last week. Too much overtime. That new system at work is a nightmare to implement. And Mr. Henderson, the landlord, is dragging his heels about fixing the leaky roof. Honestly, the man is infuriating.

…and honestly, me mam’s shepherd’s pie is just… a different league, innit? Like, this is decent, Sarah, really, it is. But it's missin’ somethin’. A bit o’ Worcestershire sauce, maybe? And more proper gravy. Proper, like, made with the meat juices. Oh, here we go. You and your mam’s cooking. You’d think she was a Michelin star chef the way you carry on, Liam. It’s a perfectly good shepherd’s pie. I’m a student, I haven't got time to be reducing meat juices! It  is  good, Liam. Don't be so picky. I'm starving, honestly. Uni life means living on pot noodles half the time, this is luxury. Aye, well, I’m just sayin’. It’s the little things. It's the flavour profiles, you know? It's not bein’ picky, it's…appreciatin’ quality. Plus, I’ve had nowt to do all day, so I  can  appreciate flavour profiles. Stop tormenting Sarah, Liam. She’s put in effort, let her have her moment. Here, drinks all round. Anyone want anything specific? I grabbed some Irn Bru, knowing your penchant, Liam. Now  you're  talkin', Ben! Appreciate it, mate. Irn Bru's the proper stuff. Cheers. So, Ben, how was work today? More little horrors running around screaming? You have no idea. Year twos are prepping for their GCSE options. Absolute chaos. Everyone wants to be an influencer. It’s exhausting trying to explain the merits of a solid career path. Honestly, it’s wild. Everyone's obsessed with TikTok now. Even my little brother’s convinced he’s gonna be famous. He's 12! It's the dream, isn't it? Instant fame. Easier than, like, actually workin' for somethin'. I’m dreading choosing my A-Levels… it all feels so…final. Final? It’s not final, Jess. You can change your mind. You're not locked into anything. Easy for  you  to say, Liam. You’ve been ‘finding yourself’ since graduating. No offence. None taken. It's… complicated. Just haven’t found somethin' that clicks, y'know? Feels a bit like driftin’, though, I won’t lie. Mam keeps askin’ if I’ve applied for anythin’ at the council. Says Old Man Hemmings is lookin’ for apprentices. You should, actually. It's steady work, and it's not the worst. Better than… well, better than doing nowt, let's be honest.

…and honestly, the buttercream was a disaster. Way too soft. It just  slid  off the biscuits. You’d have thought I’d never made a simple Victoria sponge before! Did it look like a slide, Mummy? A really, really slippery slide? It kind of did, actually, Lily. A very sticky, sugary slide. That’s why I’m attempting round two  with  you both as official taste-testers. And Leo, you’re on sprinkles detail. No eating the sprinkles beforehand. But sprinkles are the best part! They are like tiny, colourful magic! They  are  pretty magical. But magic has to wait until they’re  on  the biscuits. We need these to be presentable for my Year 3s. I'm doing a lesson on instructions – following a recipe, that sort of thing. Are you going to tell them about the slippery slide? Maybe! It’s a good example of what happens when you  don't  follow the instructions properly. Like, when the recipe says ‘beat the butter and sugar until light and fluffy’, it doesn't mean ‘beat it for five seconds and hope for the best!’ Do they get to eat the biscuits too? They do! That’s the best bit, isn't it? Although, knowing Year 3, half of them will just squish them. Year 3 is amazing! Miss Davies read us a really scary story last week. About a ghost! Oh, lovely! Miss Davies is brilliant. I’m glad you’re enjoying your lessons. I built a really cool house in Tomodachi Life today. It had a swimming pool and everything. And my Mii character fell in love! Oh, wow! That  is  impressive, Leo. Maybe you should write down the instructions for building that house. You could be a game designer! Speaking of instructions and things… I was in Morrisons yesterday, trying to find a book on basic gardening for old Mrs. Higgins. She's started a little allotment. Did you find it? Eventually! It was tucked away behind the celebrity biographies! Honestly, the logic of book placement in Morrisons… Anyway, while I was there, I saw this gorgeous children’s book, ‘The Little Gardener.’ It’s all about a tiny snail who helps flowers grow. I thought of you both. Can we get it? We can absolutely look at getting it. It's on my list. It reminded me, it’s nearly Lily’s half-birthday! Didn’t realise how quickly the year was going.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Brenda posting that picture of her new car. It's not even a nice car, is it? It's just…beige. Utterly beige. Beige is a perfectly respectable colour, darling. Though, admittedly, not a colour that screams ‘look at me, I’ve just spent a fortune!’ Respectable? It screams ‘I have no imagination!’ And the caption! “So thrilled with my new wheels!” Thrilled with beige? Really? You'd think she’d at least have gone for a metallic beige, something with a  little  pizzazz. You're letting Facebook get to you again, aren’t you? It's a highlight reel, you know that. Nobody posts pictures of their struggles with parallel parking or the dent they got reversing into a bin. I know, I know. Logically, I  know . But it’s just…seeing everyone apparently living these perfect lives, with perfect cars, perfect holidays… it’s exhausting. And Brenda’s always been one for showing off. Remember when she spent a week documenting every single stage of re-tiling her bathroom? How could I forget? The grout colour debate alone was legendary. But honestly, if that’s the worst thing she does, we’re all doing alright. Speaking of cars, though, I’ve been looking at electric ones. Saw a really nice Volvo the other day. Oh? Seriously? I thought you were quite attached to your…well, your slightly-held-together-by-hope Alfa Romeo. It  is  starting to feel like hope and duct tape are the main components holding it together, to be fair. And the emissions are getting ridiculous. Plus, with petrol prices the way they are… It's a big commitment, obviously, but I’ve been reading about the charging infrastructure in Norfolk. It's improving. It is, yes. They’ve put a bank of chargers down at the supermarket in Aylsham, haven't they? Though, I read an article the other day about how the National Grid is going to struggle to cope with everyone switching over. Said entire villages could experience power cuts if too many people start charging their cars at peak times. That’s concerning. I hadn’t thought of that. Everything’s connected, isn’t it? You solve one problem, create another. It’s like trying to fix the internet. Always something going wrong. Tell me about it. I had a student email me today complaining they couldn't submit their essay because their broadband was down.

…and honestly, Mrs. Higgins actually asked me if the ‘buy one get one free’ offer applied to individual crisps. Individual! Like, one crisp. I just… stared at her. It was the highlight of my shift, actually. A genuinely baffling moment. Oh my god, look! It’s getting worse! I still don't understand why the mayor didn't just… I don’t know,  move  the town? It’s a flying food storm, surely relocation is the logical option? Logical option. Right. You’re applying adult reasoning to a film about sentient spaghetti. You’ll ruin it for yourself. Besides, it's a metaphor, isn't it? Like, about embracing change or something equally profound. Profound? It's meatballs! Although… maybe about not being afraid of new things? Sam at school was terrified of trying sushi, and now she loves it. That’s kinda like Flint Lockwood inventing food from the sky. See? You're already digging deeper. So, how was uni today? Anything exciting happen beyond the existential dread of essays? Pretty much just essays. Though we had a debate in my feminism module which got… heated. Someone argued that all male characters in films are inherently problematic. Honestly, it felt a bit extreme. Even Flint Lockwood’s just trying to help people with his inventions, even if they do go horribly wrong. Okay, that  is  a bit of a stretch. It's like looking for things to be offended by. Remember when we used to just… enjoy stuff? I know, right? Everything’s got to be dissected now. And everything's a 'problem.' It's exhausting. Pass the remote, though? I think I can change the volume. This meatball barrage is giving me a headache. Here you go. Honestly, operating this thing is a nightmare. Mum still hasn’t figured out how to record things. She just ends up watching the news on repeat for three hours. Got it. Still baffled why remotes have so many buttons. Half of them do nothing. Anyway, back to the meatballs. Do you think they represent… societal excess? Like, we have so much food, we're literally throwing it at each other? You've been spending too much time with your professors. I was thinking it was more about a kid wanting his dad's attention. Isn’t that the core of the story? Maybe. It’s just… It feels weird watching this after a day thinking about inequality and global hunger.

…and honestly, the sheer arrogance of it all! Claiming this new infrastructure plan is for the ‘people’ when it’s clearly benefiting developers and… well, let’s just say people with already overflowing coffers. It reminds me too much of the early days of New Labour, all spin and very little substance. You’re gettin’ all political on me now, are ya, ANON? Thought we were ‘avin’ a chat about the footie. Though, I suppose they’re both games played with a lot of… let’s say ‘creative accounting.’ Difficult to separate the two, isn’t it? Especially when you’re watching the modern game. The money in football, the influence… it’s a microcosm of everything that’s wrong with the political landscape. It all feels… rigged. And look at the state of Everton! Absolutely rigged, that. Don’t even  start  me on Everton. Years of promising, years of ‘almost,’ and then… nothing. Sean Dyche is doin’ his best, mind, but he needs investment. Proper investment.
