Remember Uncle George used to mimic him constantly? He thought he  was  Churchill. Honestly, it was quite entertaining, until he started demanding his own ‘war cabinet’. Sounds about right.

… honestly, the level of basic grammar some of my online students have is appalling. I mean,  appalling . You’d think after twelve years of schooling… Tell me about it! Though mine are mostly adult learners, trying to unpick years of ingrained bad habits is… a challenge. I had one yesterday, convinced ‘have been’ was interchangeable with ‘had been.’ It took half an hour to gently explain the difference. Are you still doing mostly beginners? Mostly. A couple edging towards intermediate, but it's mostly present perfect versus past simple disasters. It’s alright money, though. Keeps the biscuits in the cupboard, as they say. Though 'alright' is being generous, let's be honest. Not exactly living the high life on TEFL wages, especially not when you factor in the exchange rate. How's the actual  teaching  going, with a classroom and everything? More rewarding than staring at a screen? Massively. The energy, the interaction... it’s brilliant. Though the marking. Oh, the marking! And the parents. You get all sorts. It’s a proper job, though, you know? Proper pension contributions and everything. Speaking of which… how  are  things with all that? Still the same circus? Don’t even. It’s a joke. I checked my projected pension the other day, and it’s… well, let’s just say I’ll be relying heavily on your generosity when I hit seventy. The system is absolutely broken, you know? All these promises, and then… nothing. Feels like having worked and paid in for nothing. It's terrifying, isn't it? That’s partly why I went for a proper teaching post, despite the workload. At least I’m building something up. Though even  that  comes with its issues. Student loans are a beast. I’ll be paying those off until I’m ancient. Oh, student loans. Don't get me started. They were practically giving them away when you were at Uni, weren't they? My generation… well, we weren’t burdened like you lot are. It's just… unfair. Everything feels so skewed towards the young being perpetually indebted. It is. Although, on the bright side, at least I'm not worrying about getting the car through its MOT. You remember how stressful that was last year? Oh, God, don't remind me! Old Betsy barely made it. I swear that mechanic was trying to bleed me dry. I’m seriously considering just getting rid of it.

…and honestly, the lecturer just kept going on about Bayesian statistics. Like, alright, it's important, but after an hour and a half, you just glaze over, you know? It felt like he was deliberately trying to make it boring. Seriously? Maths lectures can be brutal. Ours aren’t  that  bad, but Professor Davies definitely has a knack for sounding like he’s reading a phone book. Still, better than thinking about essays. How’s the Human Sciences application coming along? You actually submitting it? Yeah, nearly done. Personal statement’s a nightmare though. How do you summarise seventeen years of being a person into five hundred words? It feels… reductive. Plus, everyone else applying seems to have volunteered in the Amazon rainforest or cured a disease or something. I just, you know, played rugby and did alright in my A-Levels. Don't sweat it, man. Universities aren't just looking for superheroes. They want to see  you . And your rugby is a massive thing! Shows commitment, teamwork, discipline… All that stuff. My personal statement is basically a long brag about getting 9s in everything. Feels a bit pathetic, actually. A bit? You absolute swot! So, still dead set on Maths then? Even though you already practically have the offer? Pretty much. Though Dad keeps trying to convince me to look at Engineering. "More employable, better prospects," the usual spiel. Honestly, I just want to  do  Maths. It’s the only thing that makes sense sometimes. Speaking of things that make sense… fancy another drink? I’m thinking a lemonade this time. Maybe. Still feeling the effects of that mocktail earlier. It was deceptively strong. Deceptively strong is Westfield’s speciality. They charge £9 for a watered-down orange juice and call it ‘artisan’. I’m good for now, thanks. Got a rugby training session tomorrow morning, need to keep a clear head. Captain’s run, apparently. Big match against Bishopshalt next week. Bishopshalt? Ouch. They’re good. You’ll need all the clear heads you can get. Are you guys still short on a prop? Remember Ben mentioned something… Actually, yeah! Ben bailed, said he’s focusing on his music. Pain in the neck. You didn't happen to, uh, fancy a run-out, did you? Just kidding… mostly. Don't push it. My rugby days ended with a dislocated shoulder in Year 9. No thanks! I'd be more of a liability than an asset.

…and that’s why National Insurance contributions are separate, you see. It’s not  just  for your pension, though everyone bangs on about that. It’s also for things like the NHS, unemployment benefit… the whole social safety net. Complicated, innit? It is. Honestly, Dad, trying to explain all this to my students is a nightmare. They all think taxes just vanish into a black hole. I try to explain where the money goes, but when the government keeps changing things… it feels like moving targets. Changing things is what governments  do , love. Always have, always will. It's rarely about making things better, more about staying in power, if I'm honest. Though, I suppose some genuinely try. Remember Thatcher? Changed everything, she did. Not always for the best, mind you. You always say that. I was barely a kid then. Mum used to talk about it a lot, the miners’ strikes, everything. It felt… divisive. But you always defended some of her policies, didn’t you? About personal responsibility and controlling spending? Well, someone had to try and get a grip on the economy. Before her, it was all going to pot. Too much handing out, not enough encouraging people to earn. But yes, she was… blunt. And didn't always consider the human cost. This latest lot… different kettle of fish. Spending like there’s no tomorrow, borrowing left, right, and centre. It feels like that, doesn’t it? But they say it’s necessary, post-pandemic, with the cost of living crisis… I mean, energy bills are still insane, and food prices… Excuses, excuses. Every generation says that. “Times are hard.” My father used to say it during the war, after the war. There’s always something. It's how they  manage  the money that matters. And this current lot… well, I wouldn’t trust them to run a bath, let alone an economy. Look at this tax cut for the wealthy. Absolutely bonkers. It does seem… counterintuitive. When so many people are struggling. I read something about trickle-down economics, the idea that if the rich have more money, they'll invest and create jobs. Trickle-down! Hah! That’s an old one. It never trickles down, does it? It just stays at the top. It’s a myth peddled by people who  benefit  from the myth. What's needed is investment in public services. Proper investment.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails is just  insane . I feel like all I do is triage requests. It's not even proper project coordination, it's just firefighting all the time. Oh, darling, that sounds dreadful. Still at BrightSpark, then? I thought you were starting to feel a bit…stifled there? Still here, unfortunately. Stifled is putting it mildly. The money's alright, I suppose, which is why I'm still there, but the actual  work …it’s draining. Remember how excited I was about getting to actually  plan  projects, not just react to everyone else's chaos? I do. You were practically vibrating with enthusiasm when you first started. And all that studying, getting your degree…it's frustrating when it doesn't translate into what you hoped for, isn't it? Is there any chance of moving departments? Anything a little more…structured? I’ve asked. Repeatedly. There’s talk of a restructuring, apparently, but it’s been ‘talk’ for six months now. Everyone's just waiting to see who gets what, so no one wants to make any decisions. It’s utterly paralysing. How are things at school? Still battling with teenagers and exam boards? You have no idea. Year 11s are currently in full-blown panic mode. Mock results came out last week and the wailing has been…extensive. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I’m a teacher, a therapist, or a glorified admin assistant for teenage existential crises. Sounds familiar! Except my existential crises are usually 30-something professionals who can’t work their PowerPoint. Oh, bless them. At least yours are a bit more articulate. Did you hear from Auntie Margaret? She said she was trying to call you about the garden party. Oh, right! No, I haven't spoken to her yet. I saw a missed call, but I was in the middle of emailing Geoff about… honestly, I can't even remember what now. It’s all a blur. I should probably ring her back. It’s Mum’s birthday next month, isn’t it? She’ll want to discuss that. It is. The 18th. And yes, Auntie Margaret will have a  very  firm opinion on the cake. She’s already started subtly questioning whether Mum's still capable of choosing a sensible flavour. Last year it was passionfruit, remember? The absolute horror! Oh god, yes. Mum loved it, of course, but Auntie Margaret practically had a stroke.

…and honestly, the amount of plastic the delivery companies use now is scandalous. They used to take the cardboard back, you know? Now it's just… landfill fodder. Even the fruit comes in these little plastic clamshells! Daft, isn’t it? I try to recycle everything I can, but it feels like a drop in the ocean. Especially with how much  you  order online, Dad. Well, somebody’s gotta keep the Royal Mail busy, lass. And I can’t exactly nip down to the shops now, can I? My knees aren't what they were. Though I did see Old Man Hemmings hobbling about the other day…looked like he’d been run over by a bus. Speaking of keeping busy, how’s the job hunt going, Geoff? Any luck with those applications you were working on last week? Oh, don't even start, Tom. It's soul-destroying. All these online forms, demanding the same information repeated five times. And then…silence. Radio silence. They say experience is valued, but they want someone who can use all this new-fangled software I've never even  looked  at. Back in my day, a good microscope and a sharp mind were all you needed. I said it before, Dad, maybe a bit of retraining? There are courses… Retraining! At my age? I’d sooner teach a cat to play the trombone. No, I'm thinking of just accepting my fate as a professional biscuit dunker. You and your biscuits. Seriously, though, there must be something. Your knowledge of biomedical science is valuable. Have you considered volunteering somewhere? Just to keep your skills sharp, and get you out of the house? I did think about the hospital, but… too many memories, you see? Used to spend half my life in that place. Better to just… reminisce with a glass of wine, I reckon. Did you bring that Shiraz, Tom? The one from Sainsburys? Aye, it’s in the kitchen. I also grabbed a bottle of that Italian white you like, Sarah. Thought we could have a proper evening in. Ooh, nice! We should definitely dig out that Scrabble board. I haven't played in ages. Dad, you always cheat, though. Cheat? I do  not  cheat! I'm just… strategically resourceful. And I know all the obscure words. Like ‘qi’ – six letters for a surprisingly low score. You and ‘qi’. Remember that time you tried to argue it was a valid word in a pub quiz?

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of worksheets was just…criminal. Like, did no one think to just, I don’t know,  talk  to the students? It was all gap fills and matching exercises. Oh, don’t even get me started on worksheets. Old habits die hard, don’t they? Especially with the older guard. Was this at the conference, then? The one in Bristol? Yep. Bristol. Supposedly ‘innovative approaches to TEFL’. It felt remarkably…un-innovative. Lots of people sharing stuff they were doing ten years ago. Did  you  go to that one, or were you at the Cambridge one? Cambridge. Much better, actually. Though the hotel was… aggressively beige. Seriously, every surface. Beige. But the sessions were genuinely useful. I went to one on incorporating neuro-linguistic programming into lesson planning. NLP? Right. Sounds… intense. Is it actually  useful , or is it one of those things that sounds good on paper but falls apart when faced with a class of teenagers who just want to know if there's homework? Honestly, a bit of both. It’s about understanding different learning styles and how to build rapport. It’s not about mind control, you know? I’ve already tried a few things with my Year 10s and it seems to be making a difference. They’re actually… engaging. Shocking, I know. Engage? With English? The dream! My students in Italy just want to know how quickly they can learn enough to order a pizza. Which, fair enough, I suppose. But it's hardly Dickens. I did go to a session on using authentic materials, which was alright. They showed some examples of using YouTube clips and song lyrics, but nothing I hadn’t already been doing for years. See? Un-innovative! It's frustrating, isn’t it? You pay a small fortune for these conferences, travel miles, and end up feeling like you could have learned the same things from a good online forum. Exactly! And the networking… don't even. Mostly just people trying to sell you their overpriced course materials. One guy cornered me for twenty minutes trying to convince me to buy a set of flashcards. Flashcards! In 2024! Oh, the flashcard evangelists. They’re everywhere. I did meet one really interesting woman at Cambridge, though. She's working with refugees, teaching English for integration. Now  that's  impactful work. That sounds amazing. Much more rewarding than trying to explain the difference between ‘present perfect’ and ‘past simple’ to a room full of disinterested tourists.

… honestly, I just don’t understand the obsession with these fitness influencers. They all look exactly the same! Sculpted abs, perfect teeth… it’s exhausting just  looking  at them. It’s not real life, is it? You sound exactly like my mum. She calls them “plastic people.” But I think for some, it's aspirational. A goal. Though, yeah, a lot of it is heavily filtered and… unattainable for most of us. Still, it’s got people thinking about their health, hasn’t it? Which can't be a bad thing. Thinking about health and needing to contort yourself into a pretzel to fit into tiny sportswear are two different things, darling. I remember a time when people just  walked  for exercise. We used to walk everywhere in Cambridge. Remember the Backs? Beautiful. Shame about the tourists now, though. I do! You’ve told me stories. Bury wasn’t exactly brimming with picturesque back gardens, though. More like… back alleys lined with bins. We did a lot of running around playing street games. Probably counts as cardio, right? I suppose it does. Although, street games involved a lot of strategically dodging older boys with footballs, which sounds more like obstacle training. Speaking of dodging, are you sure we’re going the right way? This road is getting awfully narrow. Google Maps says so. We’re heading towards Sandomierz first, then cutting across to Rzeszow. It’s supposed to be a really pretty town, Sandomierz. Medieval, apparently. I've been trying to read more about Polish history on the journey, rather than scrolling through Instagram. Good for you! I’ve got my Agatha Christie, naturally. Always reliable. Though, honestly, this campervan isn't the ideal reading environment. Every bump sends me flying forward. You’d think after all these years of travelling, I'd be used to it. You  are  a bit of a fair-weather traveller, aren't you? Glamping is more your speed. Remember that campsite in Devon last year? You insisted on bringing the fairy lights. They added ambience! And I’m perfectly happy with a bit of comfort. It’s not as if I’ve had a physically demanding career. Which brings me to… what  are  you doing with your TEFL teaching? Still in Vietnam? No, I finished up there last month. I'm volunteering with a refugee centre in Manchester when I’m back home. Helping them with English classes.

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it, you know? The Great Pyramid. People talk about aliens, but the tectonic plates themselves were shifting  during  its construction. Imagine the calculations needed, even without modern tools, accounting for that instability! It's mind-boggling. It is, isn’t it? Though, I always think about the human cost, too. The sheer amount of labour… and for what? A tomb? It feels… excessive. We’re obsessed with immortality, aren't we? Or at least, delaying the inevitable. All this talk about telomeres and anti-aging therapies. Aye, it’s the grand human obsession. The Egyptians tried it with mummification, we’re trying it with science. Though, I’m skeptical of a lot of it. Seems a lot of snake oil being peddled. It's all energy, isn't it? Maintaining that cellular energy. Makes you wonder about the Vikings, actually. Those seafaring lads. Their lifespan wasn’t long, mind you, but the  energy  they had! Raiding, exploring… They were definitely lacking in gerontology expertise, though! Poor dental hygiene probably didn’t help. Little Leo is starting speech therapy next week, actually. They said a slight delay, nothing major, but it’s always a worry, isn’t it? You compare him to other kids his age… Now, hold on. Don't do that, love. Every child develops at their own pace. Especially now, there’s so much discussion around the spectrum, and a lot of it just normal variation. My cousin’s boy was a late talker, now he's a brilliant history student – obsessed with the same stuff as me, actually. Icons, you know? Figures who capture the imagination. He's fascinated by Boudicca. That’s true. It's just… it feels like everyone's racing ahead. And I’m stuck here, in a bubble, worrying about purees and nap times while the world is… well, melting. Have you seen the latest reports on the Greenland ice sheet? It’s terrifying. I have. Bloody terrifying. And the political will… it’s just not there to do what needs to be done. We’re fiddling around with carbon capture while massive corporations are still pumping out pollution. It's like watching a comet head straight for the Earth and arguing about which colour the impact crater should be painted. A bit dramatic, don't you think? Maybe. But it  feels  that way. Look, we need a break.

…and honestly, the chips were  stone cold . Stone. Cold. I sent them back, but by the time they brought new ones, everyone else had finished. It completely ruined the whole thing. Honestly, ‘The Codfather’? More like ‘The Cod Disaster’. Oh, darling, that sounds awful. Blackpool restaurants, eh? Always a gamble. We should have just stayed in and I’d have made that pasta bake you love. It’s much more reliable. Aye, Blackpool's gone downhill a bit. Used to be decent fish and chips, back in the day. Still, better than that fancy Italian place you wanted to try in Lytham, love. Remember how much that set us back? Nearly fifty quid for two pizzas and a garlic bread! That was a special occasion, Arthur! And the wine was lovely. Speaking of expenses, did you remember to put the new baby chair on the list for the garden centre? It's supposed to be really good for support. Aye, got it down. Along with them petunias you wanted. And I've been lookin' at fruit trees, actually. Thought maybe a little apple tree for the back garden. We’ve got the space, haven’t we? Ooh, that’d be nice! A proper orchard vibe. Though, remember what happened with Gran’s plum tree? The birds ate everything before we could. We’ll need netting. And maybe…we should really talk about finances again, Arthur. We’re juggling a lot now with the extra costs coming with the little one. Did you ever use those vouchers I gave you for B&Q last month? Um… about that… I used one. For some screws. Needed 'em for... well, something. Don’t you worry about it, love. I’m a master of budgeting, remember? Screws?! Seriously? You had a whole voucher and you spent it on  screws ? You could have got a new filter for the coffee maker! That thing’s making noises like a dying walrus. She’s right, Arthur. That coffee maker… it’s on its last legs. We could get a proper bean-to-cup one. But they're expensive. Although… I did see a good deal online. Hold on, hold on! Changing the subject, are we? You were starting on the money again. Listen, I'm thinkin' about finally gettin' some sunglasses. Lost mine down the beach last week. Proper pricey ones they were. You always lose your sunglasses! Honestly, it's like a tradition.

…and honestly, Mrs. Higgins actually  waved  at me this morning. Waved! Usually it's just a sort of pursed-lip acknowledgement, you know? Like I've offended her prize-winning roses just by  existing . No way! Mrs. Higgins waving? That  is  a Christmas miracle. Maybe the tree finally convinced her we’re not complete heathens. It's a particularly good one this year, isn’t it? Dad really outdid himself. It is lovely. Though, I’m still finding needles everywhere. Barnaby’s decided it’s his personal scratching post, the fluffy menace. He nearly took a whole branch off yesterday. Oh, Barnaby! He's a nightmare, but a cute nightmare. Speaking of cute, did you see what Chloe did with her nails for the Christmas party? Full glitter, shaped like little snowflakes. Oh, don’t even  start  with nails. Mine are a disaster. I chipped one just rinsing up this morning. Work’s been… hectic, to say the least. Old Man Hemmings decided to have a little tumble again, and then young Timmy’s mum came in practically in tears about the flu going around nursery. It's all sniffles and worried faces. Ugh, sounds exhausting. You’re a saint, Mum, honestly. I’m lucky I just have to worry about deadlines and persuasive ad copy. Although, ironically,  persuading  people to buy things is sometimes harder than dealing with a poorly patient. Don’t underestimate the power of a good sales pitch, love. Remember when you were trying to convince me to let you get that rather…loud pink jacket? Oh, please don’t bring that up! It was a  statement piece ! And you did eventually come around. Anyway, what about your birthday? Have you given any thought to what you’d like to do? Liam's been asking. He has, bless him. I honestly haven’t. I’m just…tired. Maybe a quiet weekend somewhere? We were talking about Canterbury. It’s not far, and I’ve always wanted to properly explore the Cathedral. Canterbury’s lovely! You could go to that German Christmas market they have sometimes. Liam knows you have that fascination with German history, right? All the Prussian kings and whatnot. It’s not a fascination, it’s an… interest. They had such a complicated history, didn’t they? All that fracturing and unification. It's fascinating how different regions developed their own cultures. Completely different from down here in Kent, which is a bit…well,  Kentish .

…and honestly, the removal guys were brilliant. Got everything up three flights of stairs without complaining  once . Though I think they were secretly thrilled to be finished. Did you want a cuppa? I’ve managed to unearth the kettle, amongst the chaos. God, yes please! That sounds incredible. Three flights? You're a masochist, moving all your worldly possessions up three flights. My back aches just  thinking  about it. Though, honestly, this flat  is  amazing. The light is incredible. And the view! Right? Worth the leg day, I reckon. It’s a bit…bare, admittedly. It’s going to take ages to feel properly settled. I was thinking, we should hit that little furniture shop in Brighton tomorrow? We need a rug, definitely. And a proper sofa, this beanbag isn't going to cut it long-term. Definitely a sofa. And maybe a little side table? Somewhere to put a mug that  isn’t  balanced precariously on a stack of books. Speaking of which… have you found the WiFi password yet? I need to let my mum know I survived the move intact. She was convinced I’d break something. Ah, the eternal struggle. The letting agent said it’s on the router, but I haven’t located the rogue device yet. It’s probably hiding behind a mountain of boxes. Operation: Find the Router is now in effect. We can tackle it after tea. What are we thinking? I grabbed some pasta and pesto, that's the extent of my forward planning. Pasta and pesto is perfect. Easy and quick, which is exactly what we need right now. And maybe we can swing by that farm shop near Lewes on Saturday? I saw they’ve got Kentish strawberries in, and it’s officially strawberry season. Ooh, yes! Good shout. We’re proper spoiled for choice down here, aren't we? Sussex and Kent both brimming with amazing produce. Though, quick change of subject… have you seen where they collect the rubbish? I haven’t spotted any bins. I think the agent mentioned something about communal bins around the back? Said it’s recycling and general waste, separate ones. We should probably figure out the schedule too, don’t want to get a fine on our first week. Good point. Bureaucracy even follows you to beautiful Sussex. Right, I’ll add ‘Rubbish Collection Schedule’ to the ever-growing list. Oh! And banking.

…and honestly, the carbonara was  huge . I thought I’d be delicately picking at it, but I genuinely had to admit defeat about halfway through. Did you manage to finish your burger? It looked substantial. Substantial is an understatement! It was delicious, though. Proper juicy. I managed, but I’m definitely feeling food-comatose now. It's so good to actually  sit  and eat properly, isn’t it? University food was… an experience. Mostly a negative one. Oh god, don’t remind me. Remember those microwave meals? The ones that were suspiciously grey, even when they were supposed to be chicken? Ugh, yes! And the communal kitchen situation. Always someone leaving dirty dishes. It's a miracle we didn't all succumb to some kind of student plague. Speaking of surviving… how's the job going? Project Co-ordinator, right? Sounds very…grown up. It is, actually. It's a bit of a whirlwind, honestly. Lots of spreadsheets, lots of meetings, lots of trying to keep everything on track. It’s good experience, though. Very different to essays and deadlines, that’s for sure. I’m working on a systems implementation at the moment, which is…fun? In a stressful, “if-this-goes-wrong-people-will-be-very-upset” kind of way. Wow, that  does  sound stressful! I’m on placement with a marketing firm, mostly doing social media analytics. It’s… less world-ending if it all goes south, I think. It's good to get some real-world experience, though. University feels like a lifetime ago already. It does, doesn't it? It’s weird. It feels like yesterday we were cramming for exams, and now we're both trying to navigate ‘adulting’. Are your parents happy with how things are going? Mine are constantly asking about a ‘five-year plan’. It's suffocating. Oh, the five-year plan! Mine are the same! Mum’s already subtly suggesting I start looking at graduate schemes for next year, even though I’ve barely started this placement. My dad's more laid back, thankfully. He just wants me to be happy. They’re good, though. Dad's been trying to learn how to use Instagram so he can ‘keep up’ with my life, it's hilarious. That’s sweet! My dad refuses to touch anything more complicated than a landline. He’s very firmly stuck in the 1980s. He keeps asking when I'm going to "settle down."

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of beige in that conference room was criminal. Like, everyone was trying to blend into the walls. Did they get a bulk discount on taupe paint or something? Sounds… stimulating. Conference life, eh? Still, better than slogging through data all day, I suppose. How’s the research going, anyway? Still wrestling with the coastal erosion project? Wrestling is putting it mildly. It’s more like being repeatedly slapped in the face by data that refuses to cooperate. Honestly, I’m starting to think the North Sea just  wants  to reclaim Sunderland. It’s got a personal vendetta. Sunderland, huh? You always bring it back to Sunderland. Is it really  that  different from everywhere else? I’ve only been up there the once, remember? For that gig – what was it, The Futureheads? Oh aye, The Futureheads! Proper good night. And yes, it is different. It’s…grittier, you know? More real. People are just…blunter. We don’t do small talk. If we don’t like your shoes, we’ll  tell  you we don’t like your shoes. And we’re fiercely proud. Fiercely proud of… bluntness and questionable footwear choices? No! Fiercely proud of our shipbuilding history, our industrial heritage, our… well, our general Northern-ness! And even the questionable footwear. It’s a statement! Honestly, coming down here to Cambridge is a culture shock. Everyone’s so…beige. In all senses of the word. You’ve mentioned beige a lot. Is this a new fixation? It genuinely is! It’s a visual representation of everything I’m finding slightly suffocating about being down south for work. Back home, even the council estates have a bit of personality. Here, everything feels… curated. And the fashion… oh, the fashion. Everyone’s rocking the preppy look. Cardigans and chinos. It’s like stepping back into a 1950s boarding school film. Fair enough. I’m mostly in jeans and band t-shirts, so I probably blend in less than you think. Speaking of bands, have you heard the new Idles album? Oh my god, yes! It’s incredible, isn’t it? Properly angry, proper lyrical, proper  everything . It feels like someone finally put the anxieties of the last few years into music form. They remind me a bit of Gang of Four, that raw energy. Exactly! Been listening to it on repeat while I’m trying to decipher these climate models.

…and then Mr. Harrison, right, he starts going on about how all young people these days are just glued to their phones and don’t care about anything. Honestly, Grandma, it’s like, he’s stuck in the 1950s! He was going on about ‘proper jobs’ and ‘respect for authority’ and all that. Oh, Mr. Harrison. Always a wind-up merchant, that one. Been saying the same thing since I knew him, fifty years ago. Though back then, it wasn’t phones, it was rock and roll corrupting the youth, as he put it. Seriously? Rock and roll? That’s… ancient history! But it’s the same argument, innit? Just a different thing to blame everything on. He was saying all politicians are liars now, too. Like, duh! Has there  ever  been a time when politicians weren’t a bit dodgy? There’s a bit of truth in that, lad. Though I remember a time when they at least  pretended  to have principles. Attlee, now  he  was a man who believed in things. Built the National Health Service, didn’t he? Something proper for the working man. Nowadays, they just line their pockets, the lot of ‘em. See! Even  you  think they’re all bent! I was trying to explain to him about the different parties, you know, Labour and Conservative and the Lib Dems… and he just waved his hand and said they're all the same. Said they all send us to war for oil. He's not entirely wrong about the wars, mind. That Blair… sent our young men to Iraq on a false premise, he did. Terrible shame. Though, I don’t think  all  of them are motivated by oil, pet. Just… power. And money usually follows power, doesn’t it? But what  can  you do? Every time there's an election, it feels like choosing the least awful option. And then they just do whatever they want anyway. I’ve started following this YouTuber, 'Left Wing Logic', who explains stuff really well, but Mum says he's biased. "Left Wing Logic"? Sounds a bit… strident. Your mother’s right to be cautious. You have to hear both sides, you know. Though, to be fair, the news these days… it’s all spin. Used to be you could trust the BBC, more or less. Not so much anymore, is it? Nah, it’s all about ratings now.

…and honestly, Leo, elbows off the table, for the love of God. It's not a resting place, it's a dining surface. You're seventeen, not seven! But it's comfy… and you always say I slouch when I  don’t  have my elbows up. Oh, teenagers. Always finding a reason to disagree. He’s right, sweetheart, elbows off. It’s just polite, isn’t it? Your manners reflect on all of us. Och, let the lad be, Fiona. A bit of slouchin' never hurt anyone. When I was teachin', I had bairns hangin' off chandeliers, and  that  was a greater concern than elbows. Granny, with all due respect, chandeliers weren’t a common feature in our classrooms, even back then. And it  does  hurt my back when he leans like that. It feels like I’m bracing for an impact. Dramatic, Dad. Seriously dramatic. Leo! Don't be rude. Your father's just trying to have a peaceful dinner. Speaking of peaceful, did either of you manage to catch the blood moon last night? It was absolutely stunning. Aye, I did. Got up just to see it, didn’t I. Quite a sight, that was. Reminded me of the stories my grandmother used to tell about bad omens and such. Though I never put much stock in that nonsense. I saw a photo online. Looked pretty spectacular. I was too busy firefighting a server issue to stay up. Typical. It’s always something with work, isn’t it. Server issues? Sounds… exciting? Exceedingly. Trust me. It involved a rogue update and a very angry CEO. But enough about my woes, how was Fitzgerald’s Park today, Fiona? You took little Maisie, didn’t you? It was lovely, actually. She absolutely adored the swans. Kept shouting “Ducky!” at them, though. And she tried to feed them her biscuit… it was a sticky situation. Oh, they’re a messy lot, those swans. Always lookin’ for a free lunch. It's good Maisie’s having a good time, though. Honestly, I don’t know what we’d do without you offering to babysit. It gives us both a chance to breathe. It’s no bother at all, really. I enjoy spending time with her. Keeps me young, you know? Although chasing a toddler around a park is definitely good cardio. Cardio? You make it sound like a military operation. Now listen here, young man.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the Scottish referendum all those years ago, it still rankles. All that energy, all that debate… and for what? Seems like a lot of fuss for something that’s just… simmering again now. Though, to be fair, things  are  rather different now, aren’t they? More complicated. You’re telling  me  about complicated. Trying to run a small business these days is complicated enough without another independence vote looming. Honestly, Arthur, it’s constant uncertainty. I’m not taking on any new staff until I know which way the wind is blowing. Sensible. Very sensible. I remember when I was Head of History at the school, trying to explain the nuances to the kids. It was a nightmare. Half of them hadn’t even  been  to Scotland! Though, talking of work… did you ever hear anything back about young Thomas’s interview? He was quite anxious, you know. Ah, Thomas. Good lad, Thomas. Yes, I did. Old Man Hemmings called me, actually. Said Thomas did… adequately. Didn’t exactly set the world alight, but he wasn’t dreadful. Hemmings is a hard man to impress, you know that. Thinks anyone under fifty is practically a toddler. Hemmings hasn’t changed a bit, then. Still the same grumpy old badger. Poor Thomas. He was hoping for a really solid start after leaving university. He’ll get there. It just might take a bit longer than he’d hoped. He needs to network more, I told him. It's not what you know, it's who you know, that old chestnut. Speaking of which, how’s Beatrice getting on with that new colleague of yours? The one who keeps borrowing your stapler? Don’t even  mention  her. Penelope. She’s… enthusiastic. Overly enthusiastic. She’s taken to leaving me little notes with ‘helpful suggestions’ on my desk. Mostly about changing the way I mark essays. As if thirty years of teaching hasn’t taught me a thing or two! Oh, lord. A 'helpful' colleague. The worst kind. I had a similar one once, always reorganizing my paperwork. Drove me up the wall. You need to put your foot down, Arthur. Gently, of course. You don’t want to create an HR incident. Easier said than done! She’s very… determined. Though, it's good to have something to complain about, I suppose. Keeps the mind active. How is your daughter, Eleanor?

…and honestly, the removals van was mental. They tried to charge us extra for 'difficult access' because of, like,  one  slightly narrow gate. One! I had to argue with ‘em for a good ten minutes. Oh, removals firms. Always trying it on, aren’t they? Your dad had the same with the last house. Remember, dear? They said the garden was too long to carry furniture down. Too long! Don’t even  start  me on removals firms, Ann. Highway robbery, that's what it is. They see a bit of stress and sniff it out like a bloodhound. Still, glad you got everything shifted, Aaron. Looks a bit bare still, doesn't it? It does, yeah. Feels a bit…echoey. But that’s the fun part, innit? Making it our own. I’m already planning the gallery wall in the living room. Got some prints I’ve been meaning to frame for ages. Speaking of making things your own, how’s the online tutoring going? Still doing alright with the Japanese students? Yeah, it’s good. Honestly, it's a lifesaver with the rent being what it is. Sometimes the time difference is a killer though – 6 am lessons aren’t exactly ideal. Though it beats working another shift at that chip shop, that's for sure. Oh, the chip shop! That was a smelly business. You always came home reeking of vinegar. And grease. Don’t forget the grease. But it kept you busy, didn’t it? Better than nothing. Though this tutoring, it’s a proper skill, that. Proper proper. Any talk of needing a loan for more education, Aaron? Those tuition fees are… well, they’re something else these days. I'm hoping to avoid loans if I can. Maybe pick up some freelance graphic design work on the side. I’ve been looking at some online courses, but they're pricey. It’s a balancing act, you know? I can imagine. Everything's expensive. I'm trying to save for a new laptop. This one's on its last legs. Keeps freezing mid-lesson, which is pretty mortifying when you’re trying to explain the nuances of keigo to a very polite businessman. Keigo? What's that? It’s the polite form of Japanese, Dad. Very important for showing respect. You’ve got different levels depending on who you’re talking to. It’s…complicated. Sounds exhausting. Reminds me of trying to understand my mother-in-law.

…and honestly, the satnav took us the scenic route, didn’t it? I swear it thinks every B-road is a shortcut. We’ve seen more sheep than people in the last hour. Sheep? Aye, plenty o’ sheep ‘round here. Used to be even more, back in my day. Proper farming country this is, or  was . Not like when I was a lad, everything’s getting…tidied up. Less roughage, you know? Tidied up? You mean less fields? More housing estates? It’s happening everywhere, isn’t it? Progress, I guess…though I’m not sure it's always progress. It’s just… surreal coming from Sunderland. We’ve got a few parks with sheep in, for the kids, but that’s about it. It’s all houses and roads and…well, more houses. And this smell! It’s not  bad , exactly, just…farmy. Farmy is a good word for it, lass. That’ll be the muck spreading, most likely. Good for the land, though. Keeps it fertile. We used to help Old Man Hemmings with that, me and my brother. Dreadful job, stinking to high heaven. But he’d give us a bottle of lemonade afterwards. Lemonade sounds good. Though, are we sure that’s just muck spreading? I think I saw a pig farm back there. A  big  one. That's a whole different level of… aroma. Oh,  lovely . A pig farm. Just what I needed to complete the rural experience. Seriously though, Grandad, you were a telephone engineer, right? Did you ever have to deal with cable faults  out here ? In the middle of nowhere, surrounded by livestock? BT man, through and through. Forty-two years. And aye, I had my share of rural repairs. Sheep were always a nuisance, chewing on the cables. Especially the lambs. Little blighters. Pigs weren’t so bad, mostly just dug holes. It was the cows you had to watch out for. They'd just… lie down  on  the junction box. Couldn’t move ‘em. That’s… a mental image. Imagine trying to explain that to your supervisor. "Sorry the line's down, sir, there's a cow parked on it." Exactly! Bet that went down well. And did you ever get chased by geese? I’ve heard they’re terrifying. Geese! Don’t even  mention  geese. Had one take a chunk out of my backside once. Near Timperley, it was. Thought it was going for my lunch.

…and honestly, the shepherd’s pie was a bit bland, wasn’t it, love? Not enough Worcester sauce, I reckon. Your mother always used a generous splash. It was alright, Mum. A bit…beige, perhaps. I did offer to add some, but Dad insisted it was “perfectly traditional.” You know Dad. Now, now, don't go criticising my shepherd's pie. It’s a classic for a reason! Besides, I was aiming for subtlety. Less is more, you know. Though, admittedly, I did forget the rosemary. That’s probably where it lacked a bit of  oomph . Subtlety? Arthur, darling, you put enough potatoes on top to feed the entire Hunsonby choir! It wasn't subtle, it was substantial. Speaking of the choir, practice is Tuesday, isn’t it? I need to remember my scarf this time. That village hall gets draughty. Tuesday. Got it. Are you still worried about hitting the high notes in ‘Pie Jesu’? You sounded lovely at the last practice, honestly. Lovely is kind. I’m terrified of cracking. My voice isn’t what it used to be. Though Mrs. Henderson says I have a good tone. She’s a bit of a choir tyrant, mind you, but she knows her stuff. She used to teach music at the grammar school, you know. Dreadful woman, apparently, when it came to discipline. Grammar school teachers were all like that back in my day. Strict as anything. I remember old Mr. Davies, the physics teacher, throwing chalk at anyone who dared whisper. Good grief. I used to be terrified of logarithms. Logarithms... ugh, flashbacks to A-levels. I switched to English Literature as soon as I could. Much less terrifying. So, have you two started thinking about Christmas yet? I was looking at train tickets back to Birkenhead and they're already extortionate. Christmas… well, your Auntie Maureen phoned yesterday and wants to know if we're all coming down to Brighton. Says young Leo is practicing his recorder, apparently. A recorder at Christmas… the thought! Oh dear. That  is  a brave choice. Brighton's a bit of a trek though, isn't it? We could suggest they come up here. More room for presents. Honestly, either is fine. It's just… coordinating everyone is always a nightmare. Especially trying to get Mum to leave the house before lunchtime. Now, that’s unfair! I’m perfectly punctual. Just…enjoy a leisurely start to the day.

…and honestly, Mr. Davies just kept circling back to the fractions. Apparently, Leo is  really  struggling with equivalent fractions. It’s not a lack of effort, he says, just…doesn’t quite  click . Fractions are yucky. They’re all broken. Like when I broke Mummy’s favourite mug? Was that a fraction? Not quite, darling. That was a whole, completely broken mug. And we talked about being careful, remember? Leo, though, it’s not about breaking things, it’s about understanding how pieces make up a whole. Like building Lego? Exactly! But with numbers. We might need to do some extra work at home. Maybe some online games? Do you think that would help, Leo? Can we play Lego  after  dinner? I built a spaceship! It needs laser beams. We can definitely look at Lego after, yes. But finish your spaghetti first. It’s getting cold. So, Mr. Davies also said you were a lovely, well-mannered boy, and participate really well in class discussion. Which is good! It’s just the maths… Mrs. Peterson said my reading is really good! I read a whole chapter of ‘The Worst Witch’ myself! That’s fantastic, Maisie! I'm so proud of you. See, Leo? Everyone has things they’re good at. Maisie shines at reading, you're brilliant at everything science and building. It's okay to find some things tricky. What about World Book Day? Are we dressing up? I want to be…a dinosaur! A really scary one! We can absolutely talk about costumes. We haven’t properly discussed it yet, have we? Maybe something from one of your favourite books? I'm going to be Hermione Granger! I already have the Gryffindor scarf! Dinosaurs ARE in books! About fossils! They are indeed. Okay, so dinosaur it could be. Right… let me just finish this email to Mr. Davies about arranging a time to chat specifically about strategies for fractions. It's always a bit much to cover in a five-minute parent's evening. Mummy, when are we going to the circus? Oh! That’s next Saturday, isn’t it? Auntie Sarah and Uncle David are taking us. I'm really excited – I haven't been to a circus in ages. Will there be elephants? And lions? I think so! They usually have lots of different animals and acrobats. It should be fun. Now, about after school tomorrow... I’ve got a staff meeting, so I won't be able to collect you both.

…and honestly, the lad at the curtain shop, young Eamon, he was telling me about his summer job. Working his way through college, he was. Seems everyone’s doing a bit of everything these days. Not like when  we  were students, scraping by on chips and… well, scraping by generally. You make it sound positively Dickensian, Seamus. Though you’re right, it's good they’re all being proactive. It’s just… scary how quickly they grow up, isn’t it? One minute you’re chasing a toddler around the garden, the next they’re discussing…curtains and college funds. Curtains are  boring . Want juice! Aye, boring for a wee man with important things to do! Like, what  is  more important than juice, eh? Now, about young Oisin here… he’s got a vocabulary all his own, hasn’t he? I was listening to him earlier, telling you about ‘the sparkly digger’ and I swear half the words were completely made up. He is a character, our Oisin. “Sparkly digger” is a classic. He’s developing, alright. He picks things up from everywhere. He was repeating something about ‘being the treasurer of the garages’ yesterday. No idea where  that  came from. Probably overheard you on the phone talking about the garages, Seamus. You and finances… a dangerous combination! Seriously, are you still treasurer for the garage owners’ association? It sounds… stressful. It pays for the rugby tickets, doesn’t it? Speaking of which, Sarah, are you free next Saturday? Big match, Munster versus Leinster. I’ve managed to snag a couple of tickets. Oh, that sounds lovely! But… I’m not sure. We need to finalize Oisin’s party arrangements. It’s only a couple of weeks away now. Have we booked the bouncy castle? Bouncy castle? Oh, the joy on their faces! I used to watch the children bouncing at school… pure bliss. Are you having a theme, dear? We thought dinosaurs. He’s absolutely obsessed. Though getting a realistic dinosaur cake might be a challenge. I’ve been looking at options online. It’s surprisingly expensive. And then there’s the guest list… His cousin, Lily, wants to bring her friend. And then there's your brother's new family… It gets complicated, doesn’t it? Dealing with step-relations. Tell me about it. My brother, bless him, thinks Liam needs a full dinosaur costume. One of those inflatable ones.

…No, no, that’s absolutely wrong! You’re thinking of ‘scrimshank’, not ‘skelper’. A skelper is a woman who goes around washing clothes, usually by a stream. A scrimshank is someone who shirks their work. Completely different! Honestly, you Southerners… Alright, alright, calm down, Lucy. It’s just a game. And for the record, I  knew  you were going to say something about me being a Southerner. It's predictable. And honestly, “skelper”? That sounds…aggressive. It does, doesn’t it? Like a medieval weapon. Though, I suppose washing clothes relentlessly  could  feel weaponized. I side with Lucy on this one, though. ‘Scrimshank’ is definitely the slacker term. I remember my grandma using that a lot when talking about my uncle. See! Liam gets it. It’s all about context, isn’t it? It's a North East thing, a proper Mackem word, you wouldn’t pick it up down in…Hertfordshire. Hey! We have regional words too, you know. We just don’t all shout them from the rooftops. What’s a ‘narking’, then? Bet you haven’t heard  that  one. Ooh, narking. Tricky. Is that…being annoyed? Being a bit bothered? It’s more than just annoyed, Lucy. It's actively getting under your skin. Like, deeply irritating. Someone is deliberately ‘narking’ you. It's rather elegant, actually. Elegant irritation? Right. Well, that’s a bit posh, isn’t it? Sounds like something you’d say at a garden party whilst sipping Earl Grey. Right, my turn. Okay, what’s a ‘bairn’? Easy. Child. A baby. Scottish, though, isn’t it? Aye, but it's used up North too. Northumbria, originally. You've been doing some dialect research, have you, Alex? I may have… fallen down a Wikipedia rabbit hole after last week’s conversation. You lot and your unusual vocabulary are fascinating. It’s so different from the standard English I use all day at work. Conceptual stress analysis doesn't really lend itself to slang. Conceptual stress analysis? Sounds thrilling. Though, to be fair, trying to explain finite element modelling to my supervisor  is  sometimes as difficult as explaining ‘skelper’ to Alex. See? Everything’s relative. Right, a harder one. What’s a ‘clarty’? Clarty…hmm. That’s…sticky? Muddy? Something unpleasant and clinging? It’s definitely sticky. Like, thick with mud. Usually used to describe something…messy, after it’s rained. A clarty path. A clarty boot.

…and honestly, the lecture just  drifted . Professor Davies was talking about post-structuralism, and I swear, my eyelids started weighing about a tonne each. I nearly full-on face-planted onto my notes. No way! Davies? Seriously? He's usually so engaging. You alright, though? No concussion from the near-miss? I’m grand, just… exhausted. I think I need to start scheduling mandatory power naps into my week. Like, a non-negotiable 20 minutes after lunch. You think that’s sad? Sad? It’s sensible! I’ve been doing that since uni started. Helps immensely. Especially after a bad night. Speaking of which… how was Saturday? Did you manage to actually enjoy yourself, or was Liam monopolising your ears again with his obscure Icelandic techno? Liam. Don’t even get me started. It wasn't  just  Icelandic techno. It was “the raw, unfiltered emotion of the Nordic soundscape.” Honestly, he’s a menace. I love him, but sometimes I want to duct tape his mouth shut. Oh god, the soundscapes. Remember when he tried to explain the "emotional core" of dubstep to your Nan? She nearly choked on her sherry. Oh, brilliant! I’d almost forgotten that. She just kept saying it sounded like “a washing machine having a breakdown.” She has a point, actually. Did you see the photos I put up from Saturday? Yeah, quickly scrolled through. You and Chloe looked proper buzzing. Is she still raving about that new band, ‘Static Bloom’? Obsessed. Absolutely obsessed. She’s convinced they’re going to be huge. I think they’re alright, a bit… much. All guitars and shouting. But she's brilliant fun, proper energy. It was good to catch up with her, hadn’t seen her since… well, ages. How’s Mark doing? Haven't bumped into him in weeks. He usually crashes our pub quizzes. He’s… complicated. Apparently, he and Sarah had a massive barney last week. Something about him accidentally liking a picture of his ex on Instagram. Classic Mark. He’s a disaster, but a lovable disaster. I tried calling him, but he didn't pick up. Probably wallowing. Ah, typical. He’s always been a drama magnet. Remember that time he pretended to be a Norwegian diplomat to get into that gig? Oh my god! The accent! It was appalling! He lasted about five minutes before the bouncer clocked him. “My name is Bjorn, from Oslo!”

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to suggest our extension would ‘detract from the character of the street’! As if his pebble-dashed monstrosity is some kind of architectural masterpiece. You’re still fuming about that, then? It was a pretty standard “save our view” objection, wasn’t it? They always come up with something. Standard? It’s patronising! We’ve put so much thought into this, made sure it’s sympathetic to the existing houses, and he just dismisses it like that. It felt…personal. And the woman from the Residents’ Association just nodded along! Look, the council planning committee are a notoriously tricky bunch. Remember old Mrs. Davies and her obsession with garden gnomes? Anything can sway them. We anticipated some pushback. The key thing is, we have a solid application. Ben from the architect’s firm did a brilliant job with the drawings. I know, I know you’re right. It just…it's  our  home. And we’re trying to create a little more space for, well, for everything. For the future. Selling it feels…a bit premature now, doesn’t it? Especially after all this planning hassle. I said the same thing this morning, actually. But rationally, it still makes sense. The market's good, we can get a really decent price, and it frees us up to… well, to chase that little cottage in Cornwall we’ve been talking about for years. Remember? Sea views, proper garden, maybe even a smallholding? I remember. It sounds idyllic. But leaving here…it's where we brought Leo home from the hospital, all those Christmas mornings, the garden parties… And the leaky roof, the wonky floorboards, and the constant need for painting? Look, it's a lovely house, it really is. But it's not  quite  right anymore. It feels cramped, doesn't it? And the commute for both of us is becoming a nightmare. We’ve talked about this for six months, love. I know we have. It's just… facing the action of it all. Actually putting it on the market. It feels more real now. I was hoping that getting planning permission would feel like a win, a solid step forward. But it just feels like another hurdle. It  is  a win! Getting that permission was huge. It proves the extension was viable, it adds value. And regarding the 'hurdle' – Ben said we can highlight that in the sales brochure.

…and honestly, the queue at Sainsbury’s was  insane . I swear, everyone decided to do their big shop at exactly 6pm on a Tuesday. It took me nearly an hour just to get the pasta and pesto! Oh, no way! Tuesday isn’t even peak Sainsbury’s, is it? I usually go then to avoid the weekend rush. You’re not still going there after… well,  the incident  are you? Don't remind me. Brenda and her rogue trolley. It’s just…convenient, you know? And frankly, I was already halfway through making a mental list of everything I needed. It’s not worth the hassle of going elsewhere. But seriously, she just  launched  it towards the biscuit aisle! Brenda. Honestly. She's a menace. Did you hear she’s started complaining about Mr. Henderson’s bird feeder again? Apparently, the seeds are "attracting pigeons and causing a public health hazard." The drama! No! Honestly, she finds  something  to complain about every single week. I think she genuinely thrives on it. Speaking of thriving, how was your shift today? Anything exciting happen at the hospital? Surprisingly quiet, actually. Which is nice for a change. Had a new patient, though, a young lad, really struggling. Reminded me a bit of Leo, actually. Oh, really? Leo from school? Wow, it feels like ages since we’ve talked about him. He ended up in Bristol, didn't he? Doing…architecture, I think? Yeah, Bristol. I saw him tagged in a photo on Facebook, looking all arty and sophisticated. He's doing really well apparently. It just struck me how easily things could go different ways, you know? Leo always seemed so…grounded. Definitely. Remember when he convinced Mr. Davies to let us build that ridiculous cardboard castle in the school hall? He had plans, sketches, everything. Mr. Davies was not amused. Oh my god, yes! And then it collapsed during assembly! Good times. Although, looking back, it was probably quite disruptive. Anyway, enough reminiscing about our misspent youth. What are you up to this weekend? Fancy a day trip somewhere? I need a break from…everything. That sounds amazing! I was thinking we could go to Rye. It’s been ages. We could wander around the shops, get some lunch… maybe even brave the castle again, but this time  without  building anything. Rye is a brilliant idea! I've been meaning to go back for ages.

…No, seriously, look at that advert. Another one for meal replacement shakes. “Lose two stone by Tuesday!” Honestly, who falls for that rubbish? It's all airbrushing and desperation, isn't it? Mmm, probably people who are really unhappy with how they look, I suppose. It’s clever marketing, tapping into insecurities. Though, two stone by Tuesday? That’s just…dangerous. Remember Auntie Brenda and that cabbage soup diet? She was miserable for a month. Aye, miserable and smelling of cabbage! Honestly. I’d rather just, well, not eat quite as many biscuits, like. Speaking of which, did you finish the Hobnobs? I was looking forward to one with me tea. Guilty as charged. Needed a little sugar rush after that case study this morning. Little Liam, the seven-year-old? Definitely showing dyslexic markers. It's just… heartbreaking seeing how frustrated he gets when he can’t decode the simplest words. Right, that's rough. You’ve got a knack for spotting that stuff, haven’t you? All that NLP training paying off then? Still sounds like magic to me, reading people’s eyes and whatnot. It’s not magic, it’s observation. And understanding how the brain processes information. It's really fascinating. Though ironically, sometimes I feel like  I'm  struggling to process information… like, the sheer volume of junk mail I get online. Did you know they’re advertising those meal replacement shakes  to me  now? Ha! The algorithm knows. It’s relentless. I keep deleting them, but they just keep coming. I swear, half our week is spent just unsubscribing from things. Speaking of relentless, you still thinking about going to that car boot sale on Sunday? Yep. I’ve got a list. Looking for some old frames for some prints I want to make. And maybe a vintage teapot. You coming or are you gonna be glued to FIFA all day? I might actually join you. I need to get out the house, to be honest. And I’m skint. Might find a bargain. Though, I saw on the news this morning about a spate of thefts from car boot sales. Proper brazen, apparently. Oh, great. Just what I needed to hear. Don't worry, I'll be all eyes. Plus, I'm deceptively good at giving people the stink eye. Years of dealing with challenging behaviour in placement comes in handy. You are fierce.

…and honestly, the estate agent was  awful . Didn’t even bother to point out the damp patch in the bedroom – I spotted it myself! It’s all well and good saying “cosmetic issues” but damp is a bit more than cosmetic, isn't it? Right? They’re supposed to be on  your  side, aren't they? Trying to offload a problem property, more like. Birmingham’s house prices are just… ridiculous at the moment. We’re saving, but it feels like we’re running to stand still. Tell me about it. I’ve been looking vaguely, just to get a feel for things. Even something relatively small in Moseley is pushing £350k. It’s mental. And the view of the ring road doesn’t exactly add value, does it? Oof, Moseley is pricey. I was looking over towards Kings Heath. A little more affordable, maybe, but still… competitive. I’m starting to think we might just be renting forever. Although, honestly, after the saga you're having, Sarah, I’m starting to feel a bit better about that! Don’t tempt fate, Alice! Seriously though, I’m starting to think a full structural survey is worth every penny. Even if it unearths more horrors. Better to know now, right? Absolutely. It's a massive commitment buying, you can't skimp on due diligence. Speaking of commitment... anyone tried that new Duolingo music app? It tries to teach you languages  through  songs. It’s surprisingly sticky, I'm trying to brush up on my Italian before the Rome trip. Duolingo? Is that still a thing? I thought everyone moved onto Babbel years ago. I’m more obsessed with Forest at the moment. It's a productivity app. You plant a virtual tree, and if you leave the app before a set time, the tree dies. Ridiculously motivating. Forest sounds… intense. I can barely keep a real houseplant alive. I’m still using Spotify, obviously. Have you guys heard the new IDLES album? It’s proper raw, brilliant stuff. Full of angry energy. IDLES are fantastic. I saw them live at the Hare & Hounds a couple of years ago – absolutely electric. Actually, talking of Hare & Hounds, I’m doing a piece on independent music venues for the paper. It’s getting harder and harder for them to survive, you know? The rising costs… It's awful. They're vital for the cultural landscape.

…and honestly, the whole estate was just fields then, Geoff! Fields! You wouldn't recognise it now. We moved here in ‘68, just after David was born, and it felt so  rural . Coming from Almondsbury, even  that  felt… developed, relatively speaking. But this? Cows in the fields opposite, proper country life. I remember. I came down here for an interview at the grammar school in ‘67. Drove all the way from Ramsgate, expecting… well, expecting something a bit more  substantial . It was all very new build, even then, but very… sparse. I nearly turned around and went back! Sparse is an understatement, my friend. I interviewed at the hospital in ‘66. Had to practically navigate a muddy track to get to the place. And the accommodation! They tried to put me up in a boarding house run by a woman who clearly hadn’t updated her decor since the war. Wallpaper peeling, floral everything… Sounds delightful, Bernard! Though, compared to the digs I had in Manchester while doing my postgrad, that sounds like the Ritz. Honestly, it was a bedsit above a chip shop. The smell of vinegar permeated  everything . Oh, student accommodation. Don’t even get me started. We were lucky, we managed to find a little terraced house to rent fairly quickly. Though ‘renting’ in those days meant having a landlord who’d pop round unannounced expecting a pint and a gossip. Exactly! We ended up buying almost immediately. Couldn’t believe the prices. It was still possible to get a semi for under five thousand pounds. And the mortgage rates! I used to joke that the bank was  paying  me to borrow money. Five thousand? You were lucky! I remember stretching to get a mortgage for eight. And the renovations… oh, the renovations! This house was a bit of a fixer-upper, to say the least. Damp, dodgy wiring, the whole nine yards. Spent half my savings just getting it habitable. I was a bit more sensible. Rented for a couple of years while I figured things out. Didn't want to tie myself down. Plus, the university had a decent staff housing scheme. Met Margaret through a colleague there, by the way. She was a librarian. Quiet, bookish… the perfect foil for a chaotic lecturer like myself. How lovely! I met John – my husband - at a conference. He was teaching history at the boys’ school. Actually, it was a rather underwhelming conference on Victorian poetry.

…and honestly, the chipped glaze on that particular teapot just  screamed  Regency. Old Mrs. Higgins didn’t have a clue, bless her. She thought it was ‘a bit wonky’. Wonky! It was character, I told her. Character! But she wanted perfect. People don’t  want  perfect anymore, do they, Penelope? They want a story, a bit of history. No, I suppose they don’t. Though I encountered a fair bit of perfectionism in my work, actually. Trying to get a child to pronounce a ‘th’ sound correctly… that's a battle against natural development, and sometimes parents want instant results. A perfect ‘th’ by age four. It’s… unrealistic. A therapist, was it? Speech therapy? Always admired that, you know. Taking something so fundamental – communication – and helping people with it. It’s far more… useful than selling chipped teapots, even if the teapots  are  beautiful. What brought you to that, then? Sydney to Taunton is quite a leap. A long story! My husband, David, was a botanist. He got a research position at the University here, specializing in rare orchids. I followed, naturally. And honestly, after a while, I missed the work. It was rewarding, you know? Helping a child finally  say  their name, or connect with others. It’s a good feeling. I did some locum work for a few years, but… well, it wasn’t the same without a full caseload. It felt a bit… fragmented. I understand. It's hard to suddenly switch off a passion. Though my ‘passion’, if you can call it that, was more about the hunt, I think. The thrill of finding something overlooked, something with a story buried inside. My father always said I had a magpie’s eye. Everything shiny, everything interesting… I’d collect it. He was a farmer, you see. Practical man. Didn’t understand the appeal of ‘dust collectors’, as he called them. A farmer. That’s… rather different from antiques. Was it a big farm in Somerset? Oh, substantial. Well, substantial for Somerset. Dairy mostly. We were near Wells, actually. Spent my childhood clambering about in haystacks and dodging cows. I wasn’t a very good farm girl, if I’m honest. Always had my nose in a book, or sketching in a notebook. My mother encouraged it, though. She’d been a teacher before she married. She saw something in me, that… creative streak. Mothers often do.

…and honestly, the guy barely flinched. Like, I was expecting a yelp,  something . He just kept chatting about football. Proper weird. Sounds like a proper Londoner then, doesn't it? We’re built different. Probably secretly loved the attention. So, you’re definitely going ahead with the sleeve then? That phoenix design? Yeah, booked in for the outline next week. Bit nervous, init? It’s a commitment, yeah? More than just a little flash on the arm. This is… substantial. It'll look wicked. You've been talking about it for ages. Anyway, less about permanently marking your body, more about temporarily satisfying it. This chilli’s smelling amazing. You grabbing the rice, yeah? On it. This is good, though. Proper comfort food after that hellish lecture on post-structuralism. Honestly, sometimes I think my professor just makes stuff up as he goes along. Sounds about right. Uni’s good for that. Oh! Speaking of making stuff up… remember old Mrs. Higgins asking if I could do her a gingerbread house this Christmas? Like a proper, Hansel and Gretel situation? Vaguely. The one who always buys a ridiculous amount of fudge from the bakery? The very same. Said it’s for her grandkids. But she wants edible glitter  and  working lights. Working lights, Liam! In a gingerbread house! Blimey. That's… ambitious. You gonna charge her extra for the electrical engineering degree you didn’t get? I’m thinking a hefty “festive complexity” surcharge. It’s not just candy and icing, you know? It’s structural integrity!    Hellooooo! Sorry I’m late, the supermarket was absolute chaos. You two cooking up a storm? Smells incredible! Hi, Chloe! Just a chilli. And contemplating the logistical nightmares of edible architecture. Edible…? Oh god, not Mrs. Higgins and her gingerbread demands again! She tried to get me to create a fondant replica of Buckingham Palace last year. A  full  replica. Honestly? Sounds like she’s aiming for world domination via confectionery. Right?! Anyway, I got most of the Christmas bits. Got the tree – a proper Nordmann fir, naturally – and loads of decorations. I even snagged some of those really cute little ceramic robins everyone’s after. Oh, nice one! I was hoping to get some of those. Are you doing a proper Christmas feast at the café this year? Absolutely. Bookings are already looking insane. I’m doing a whole set menu, everything from turkey and all the trimmings to a vegan Wellington.

… honestly, Mum, the whole thing’s just a bit overwhelming, innit? Three years feels like forever ago now, and suddenly I'm supposed to have a  plan . Like, a real one. Not just 'pass the thesis' which, let's be real, has been my only plan for the last year. Oh, darling, everyone feels like that. It’s the great post-university void. Though, you always were a bit of a last-minute Larry, weren’t you? Remember that history project in year ten? Finished it the night before. Hey, it got an A! And this is different. This is…life. And potential jobs. And deciding whether to become a proper Londoner or… I don't know, disappear to the countryside and raise alpacas. Alpacas? Seriously? Just throwing it out there! It’s a reaction to all this pressure. Everyone at uni is either applying for these fancy graduate schemes at banks or heading off to do a Master’s, and I'm just… thinking about fluffy animals. Well, a sensible plan involving less spitting and more income might be advisable. Have you had any luck with the applications you mentioned? The publishing houses? A couple of interviews, yeah. They were okay. Stood out a bit too much for being a History grad wanting to edit, though. They liked my enthusiasm, but kept asking about experience. It’s the classic catch-22. It is. Look, you’ve got a good eye, a clever head, and you  love  books. Those things count for a lot more than a specific degree. And truthfully, the publishing world is changing. They need people who can think outside the box, who aren't just regurgitating academic jargon. Thanks, Mum. That’s… helpful. But what about housing? If I  do  get something in London, where am I going to live? Rent's insane. I was looking at places in Tooting, but even sharing a flat is… frighteningly expensive. We’ve talked about this. You can always stay with me and Dad for a bit, while you get on your feet. It’s not ideal, I know, you’d be back in your childhood bedroom… but it’s an option. I know, and I appreciate it. But I don’t want to, you know? Be that 24-year-old living with his parents. It feels… regressive. It’s practical, not regressive. And it gives you time to save. Besides, it's not a permanent situation.

…and honestly, the train was  packed . I swear, everyone with a Cambridge connection decided to descend on the city this weekend. It took me nearly three hours from Aylesbury just to get to King’s Cross, then another squeeze onto a commuter train. Worth it though, isn't it? Seeing the faculty again, even if it’s just for a day. Oh, tell me about it! I drove down from Lincoln, thinking I'd beat the traffic. Massive mistake. The A1 was basically a car park for a good stretch. Still, it’s lovely to be back. I hadn’t realised how much I missed wandering these courts. Are you involved with the faculty directly now? I am, yes. I’m the Language Research Co-ordinator. Bit of a mouthful, I know. Mostly I help organise the linguistic fieldwork, data analysis… all the nitty-gritty stuff. And you? I'm an Administrator, focusing on research support. Similar sort of thing, really. Less fieldwork, more grant applications, unfortunately. Excuse me, ladies. Didn't mean to eavesdrop, but I couldn't help overhearing you mention Cambridge connections. Lovely to see so many familiar faces – and new ones too, of course. Name’s Arthur Penhaligon. Used to lecture here, in the History Faculty. Oh, hello! I'm Eleanor, and this is Sarah. It’s a pleasure to meet you, Professor Penhaligon. I think I actually attended one of your lectures, years ago, on the Arab Golden Age. Fascinating stuff. Eleanor, is it? Good, good. I remember a rather bright young woman asking perceptive questions about the translation movement. Could have been you! Though, truth be told, they all start to blur after a while. I've lost count of the alumni days. Always a good turn-out. What brings you both back to Cambridge today? We both work with the faculty now, actually. Sarah’s an administrator and I coordinate the language research. It's nice to be back on the other side of things. Excellent! Keeping the academic flame burning, are you? That’s splendid. My last big project before I retired was actually a collaboration with archaeologists excavating a Roman village in Shropshire, near where I grew up. Oh, really? That sounds incredible! Did the linguistic side involve deciphering inscriptions? A little. Mostly it was trying to reconstruct the local Vulgar Latin dialect. Fascinating, but incredibly difficult. So much lost. It really highlights the importance of preserving languages, doesn't it?

… honestly, the deadline's just looming, yeah? Dissertation’s a beast. And Professor Davies keeps changing his mind about what he  wants  it to be about. It's driving me round the bend. Ugh, sounds awful, Liam. At least kneading dough doesn't require constant philosophical shifting. Though, getting a sourdough starter to  actually  start… that’s a battle of wills in itself. How’s it going with the actual writing, though? You’ve got a good head for research, haven’t you? Yeah, the research is fine. It's the  argument . He wants something ‘groundbreaking’ but also ‘rooted in established theory’. Like, which is it, mate? Pick a lane! Sounds like academics, alright. I had enough of that nonsense after sixth form. Never looked back. Running the café’s stressful, sure, but at least I know if something’s working – people either buy the cake or they don’t. No essay feedback needed. True, quantifiable results. I envy that sometimes. Though, trying to get funding for a short film feels like begging for scraps while simultaneously being told to be ‘visionary’. It's a similar brand of… frustration. Actually, speaking of frustration and vision, have you guys seen that video going viral of the bloke trying to assemble IKEA furniture? Oh my god,  yes ! The one where it just… collapses into a heap? It's brilliant. So relatable. I swear, IKEA is designed to test the limits of human patience. It's a perfect metaphor for being a student. All this effort, all these parts… and at the end, you've got something wobbly and vaguely resembling what you intended. It's a generational thing, isn’t it? Everyone's sharing it. My younger cousins are obsessed. It’s funny, though – my dad was saying it shows how useless young people are these days, can’t even put a shelf together. Right. Classic. That whole “kids these days” narrative. It’s amazing how quickly people forget what it was like to be young and figuring things out. It's more than that, though, isn’t it? My cousin, Ethan, he's brilliant with computers, can code anything… but give him a screwdriver and he’s lost. It's like we’re specializing so early, getting funnelled into these specific skills, that practical stuff gets left behind. And the pressure! Everyone’s on this track – go to uni, get a ‘good’ degree, get a ‘good’ job.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of him to suggest I wasn’t pulling my weight with the marking! Like I haven’t been up until midnight every night this week? He just breezes in with his perfectly curated research and assumes everyone else is just… coasting. Professor Harding, eh? Still at it, I see. He always did have a knack for making people feel inadequate. It’s a power thing with him, I reckon. Keeps his position secure by subtly undermining everyone else. It's exhausting, Ben. It really is. And then he had the nerve to quiz me about my research grant application! As if he doesn’t know I've been battling the university bureaucracy for weeks just to get the paperwork sorted. It’s not like I’m just applying for fun, you know? We  need  that money for the lab equipment. You’re brilliant at what you do, El. Don't let him get to you. You always deliver. Remember that conference in Berlin? He was practically eating his words after your presentation. Though, speaking of needing money… did you look at the energy bills this month? They're positively criminal. Don't even get me started on the energy bills! It’s ridiculous. I swear, they go up every single time I turn on the kettle. And the government just… shrugs. All this talk about leveling up, and yet ordinary people are being squeezed dry. It feels like they're deliberately making life harder. It's frustrating, isn’t it? Sunak keeps saying things are improving, but I'm not seeing it. It's all smoke and mirrors, designed to distract from the fact that the country’s essentially… wobbling. I saw a piece on Newsnight last night about the potential for winter blackouts. Blackouts! It’s the 21st century! Seriously? I missed that. Sounds grim. Maybe we should invest in a generator? It feels ludicrous even suggesting it, but… what if? And then there's the NHS. Mum was telling me about her appointment last week – she waited  three  hours to see a doctor for a simple blood test. Three hours! It’s a disaster. And it’s not the doctors' fault. They're working themselves ragged. It's the underfunding, the mismanagement, the endless reorganisations… it just never ends. Honestly, sometimes I switch off the news, it's just too depressing. I know. I’ve been trying to escape into some mindless telly.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of choice at that farm shop was overwhelming. I mean, twenty different types of apple chutney! Twenty! In my day, you got apple chutney, and you were grateful. Times change, Gran. It's good to have options, though, isn't it? I saw a really interesting article about heritage apple varieties – apparently, we’ve lost so much biodiversity with focusing on just a handful of commercially viable ones. Biodiversity, eh? Sounds like something you’d read in one of your science magazines, Elsie. Still, twenty chutneys… that  is  a bit much. Reminds me of when we took the kids to that American supermarket on our holiday to Florida. The size of the place! They had aisles dedicated to cereal. A  dedicated aisle ! Florida! Oh, that was a trip. Little Amy insisted on wearing that bright pink sunhat the entire time, even indoors. Said it brought her luck. She was convinced she’d see a real-life Disney princess. I remember photos of that hat! Bright pink against everything. You both looked completely exhausted by the end of it, though. All the theme park queues? Exhausted is an understatement! But the kids loved it. And honestly, seeing them so happy... that’s what mattered. Though, I still think the Everglades tour was the best part. Alligators, Elsie,  alligators ! Proper wildlife. Not like these overfed squirrels in the garden. Those squirrels are getting bolder, aren't they? One tried to come in through the kitchen window the other day. I gave it a stern talking-to, naturally. I used my ‘teacher voice’. Your teacher voice still works on squirrels? Amazing. Did it work? Well, it startled it, at least. It scampered off. Though I suspect it'll be back. Speaking of startling, have you seen that new David Attenborough documentary? The one about deep-sea creatures? Absolutely breathtaking. And terrifying! I haven’t. Attenborough’s a national treasure, that man. Always has been. I liked the one he did on the migration of the Arctic terns. That little bird travelling all that way… unbelievable. It's incredible, isn't it? The things nature does. I was reading about some new research on octopus intelligence, actually. Apparently, they can solve complex puzzles and even recognise individual humans. Octopuses! Clever things. Makes you think, doesn’t it? All that going on under the sea while we're worrying about apple chutney and squirrels.
